knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Barrier Methodology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic-barrier stationarity represented as perturbed primal-dual KKT conditions for smooth nonlinear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the nonlinear program \[\min_{x\in U} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad h(x)=0,\qquad g(x)\ge 0.\] For \(\mu>0\), its logarithmic-barrier subproblem is \[\min_{h(x)=0,\,g(x)>0}\; f(x)-\mu\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log g_i(x).\] If \(x_\mu\) is stationary for this subproblem with equality multiplier \(y_\mu\), define \((z_\mu)_i=\mu/g_i(x_\mu)\). Then \[\nabla f(x_\mu)-J_h(x_\mu)^\top y_\mu-J_g(x_\mu)^\top z_\mu=0,\quad h(x_\mu)=0,\quad G(x_\mu)z_\mu=\mu\mathbf 1,\quad g(x_\mu)>0,\quad z_\mu>0.\] Conversely, these equations imply barrier stationarity. If such tuples converge to \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\) and \(\bar x\in U\), then \[\nabla f(\bar x)-J_h(\bar x)^\top\bar y-J_g(\bar x)^\top\bar z=0,\quad h(\bar x)=0,\quad g(\bar x)\ge0,\quad \bar z\ge0,\quad G(\bar x)\bar z=0,\] so the limit satisfies the original KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationary log-barrier points are exactly strictly positive solutions of the perturbed KKT equations whose complementarity products equal the barrier parameter. Any convergent family whose primal limit remains in the problem domain satisfies the original KKT conditions at that limit.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open, and \(f:U\to\mathbb R\), \(h:U\to\mathbb R^p\), and \(g:U\to\mathbb R^m\) are continuously differentiable.
Each stationary barrier point considered admits an equality-constraint multiplier.
For the limit assertion, \((x_\mu,y_\mu,z_\mu)\to(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\) with \(\bar x\in U\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Barrier stationarity is equivalent to the displayed perturbed KKT system; if \((x_\mu,y_\mu,z_\mu)\to(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\) with \(\bar x\in U\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\), then the limit satisfies the displayed KKT conditions.

notation.meaning: Jacobians of the equality and inequality constraint mappings.
Equality and positive inequality multipliers at barrier parameter \(\mu\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier function and its Hessian-induced local geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(Q\subset E\) be closed and convex with \(\operatorname{int}Q\neq\varnothing\), and let \(F:\operatorname{int}Q\to\mathbb R\) be convex and three times continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth convex barriers with positive-definite Hessian; self-concordance is not required by this foundational definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((Q,F)\) defines a barrier geometry when \(F(x_k)\to+\infty\) for every sequence \(x_k\in\operatorname{int}Q\) converging to \(\partial Q\), and \(H_x:=\nabla^2F(x)\succ0\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{int}Q\). At each such \(x\), define the primal and dual local norms by \[\|h\|_x=\langle H_xh,h\rangle^{1/2},\qquad \|s\|_x^*=\langle H_x^{-1}s,s\rangle^{1/2}.\] The associated open Dikin unit ellipsoid is \(W(x)=\{x+h:\|h\|_x<1\}\), and the Newton decrement of \(F\) is \(\lambda_F(x)=\|\nabla F(x)\|_x^*\). Thus the barrier supplies both boundary exclusion through divergence and a point-dependent metric through its Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A barrier geometry consists of a closed convex set \(Q\) with nonempty interior and a smooth convex function \(F\) on that interior. The function must diverge to positive infinity along every interior sequence approaching the boundary, and its Hessian \(H_x\) must be positive definite. The Hessian defines the local norm \(\|h\|_x\), its inverse defines the dual norm \(\|s\|_x^*\), the local unit ellipsoid is \(W(x)\), and the local size of the gradient is the Newton decrement \(\lambda_F(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subset E\) is closed and convex, with \(\operatorname{int}Q\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((Q,F)\) is a barrier geometry precisely when \(F(x_k)\to+\infty\) for every \(x_k\to\partial Q\) from the interior, with local metric tensor \(H_x=\nabla^2F(x)\) and norms \(\|h\|_x\), \(\|s\|_x^*\) as defined above.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Positive definiteness gives the local Cauchy inequality \(|\langle s,h\rangle|\leq\|s\|_x^*\|h\|_x\).
The boundary condition is equivalent to boundedness away from \(\partial Q\) of every sublevel set \(\{x\in\operatorname{int}Q:F(x)\leq\alpha\}\), whenever that sublevel set is nonempty.
special_cases_latex: For \(Q=\mathbb R_{++}^n\) and \(F(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\), \(H_x=\operatorname{diag}(x_i^{-2})\) and \(\|h\|_x^2=\sum_i(h_i/x_i)^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The Newton direction is \(-H_x^{-1}\nabla F(x)\), whose local norm equals \(\lambda_F(x)\).
The metric changes with \(x\), so distances and neighborhoods are intrinsic to the barrier rather than fixed Euclidean quantities.
boundary_notes: A merely lower-semicontinuous extended-valued indicator is not a smooth barrier geometry under this definition.
If \(H_x\) is singular, it defines only a seminorm; quotient-space or relative-interior formulations require separate treatment.
The inclusion \(W(x)\subset\operatorname{int}Q\) requires additional structure such as standard self-concordance.

notation.meaning: Hessian \(\nabla^2F(x)\), viewed as the local metric tensor.
Barrier-induced primal and dual local norms.
Open unit ellipsoid in the local norm at \(x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical interior barrier model for inequality constraints
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_j(x)\leq0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed and \(f,g_j\) are continuous. Define \(S=\{x\in X:g_j(x)<0\ \forall j\}\) and assume \(S\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional primal barrier models; the definition permits nonconvex data, although convexity is needed for global convex barrier subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A classical barrier function for the represented feasible set is a continuous map \(B:S\to\mathbb R\) such that, whenever \(x_k\in S\) and \(g_j(x_k)\uparrow0\) for at least one index \(j\), one has \(B(x_k)\to+\infty\). For each barrier parameter \(\mu>0\), the associated interior barrier model is \[\Phi_\mu(x)=f(x)+\mu B(x),\qquad x\in S.\] A classical barrier family is the collection \(\{\Phi_\mu\}_{\mu>0}\), interpreted with \(\mu\downarrow0\). The logarithmic and inverse barriers are \(B_{\log}(x)=-\sum_j\log(-g_j(x))\) and \(B_{\mathrm{inv}}(x)=-\sum_j1/g_j(x)\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A classical barrier model is formed on the strict interior \(S\). Its barrier \(B\) is continuous there and tends to positive infinity whenever any constraint approaches activity from the feasible side. For a positive parameter \(\mu\), the constrained problem is represented by the interior objective \(\Phi_\mu=f+\mu B\). The family obtained as \(\mu\) decreases toward zero progressively weakens the interior penalty while retaining an infinite boundary wall for every fixed positive parameter.
assumptions_latex: Every feasible boundary point under consideration is approachable by points of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is a classical barrier exactly when it diverges as any \(g_j(x)\) approaches \(0\) from below, and \(\Phi_\mu=f+\mu B\) is the corresponding parameterized interior model.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(b_j:(-\infty,0)\to\mathbb R\) with \(b_j(t)\to+\infty\) as \(t\uparrow0\), a separable barrier has the form \(B(x)=\sum_j b_j(g_j(x))\).
Extending \(B\) by \(+\infty\) outside \(S\) converts each barrier subproblem into unconstrained extended-valued minimization over \(X\).
special_cases_latex: \(b_j(t)=-\log(-t)\) gives the logarithmic model.
\(b_j(t)=-1/t\) gives the reciprocal-growth model.
immediate_consequences_latex: For fixed \(x\in S\), \(\mu B(x)\to0\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
Every finite-valued iterate of an exact-domain barrier subproblem lies in \(S\).
If \(f\) and all \(g_j\) are convex and the scalar barrier profiles are convex and nondecreasing, then \(\Phi_\mu\) is convex on \(S\).
boundary_notes: Equality constraints are retained explicitly or eliminated; they are not represented by a one-sided classical barrier.
The definition excludes barriers that remain finite at an active inequality.
Existence or uniqueness of a minimizer of \(\Phi_\mu\) is not part of the barrier definition.

notation.meaning: Positive barrier parameter tending to zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical inverse and logarithmic barrier functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior penalty functions for inequality-only problems under the convention c_i(x)≥0.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(m_e=0\) and consider the strict interior \(\mathcal I=\{x:c_i(x)>0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). An interior penalty, or barrier, is defined on \(\mathcal I\) and tends to \(+\infty\) as an interior point approaches the feasible boundary. For \(\sigma>0\), classical examples are \(P_{\mathrm{inv}}(x)=f(x)+\sigma^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m c_i(x)^{-1}\) and \(P_{\log}(x)=f(x)-\sigma^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\log c_i(x)\). Barrier-method iterates are kept in the strict interior where these models are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For inequality-only problems, a barrier is used on the strict interior and diverges as the boundary is approached. The inverse and logarithmic barriers are the classical examples, and barrier methods keep their iterates within their interior domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{inv}}(x)=f(x)+\frac1\sigma\sum_{i=1}^m\frac1{c_i(x)},\qquad P_{\log}(x)=f(x)-\frac1\sigma\sum_{i=1}^m\log c_i(x),\qquad P(x)\to+\infty\text{ as }x\to\partial\mathcal I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robust feasible sets and barrier functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions for classical interior barrier models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is called robust if \(\operatorname{int}S\neq\varnothing\) and \(S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{int}S}\). For such a set, a barrier function is a continuous function \(B:\operatorname{int}S\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(B(x)\geq0\) and \(B(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\in\operatorname{int}S\) approaches \(\partial S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust feasible set has nonempty interior and every feasible point can be approached from that interior. A barrier function is continuous and nonnegative on the interior and diverges to infinity as the boundary is approached from within.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{int}S\neq\varnothing,\quad S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{int}S},\quad B\in C(\operatorname{int}S),\quad B\geq0,\quad \lim_{\operatorname{int}S\ni x\to z}B(x)=+\infty\ \text{for every }z\in\partial S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior-Point Penalty Reformulation Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the reformulation role, strict-feasibility behavior, and terminology of classical barrier methods; it is not a convergence claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interior-point penalty function, also called a barrier function, transforms a constrained problem into an unconstrained problem or a sequence of unconstrained problems. Its barrier term is infinite at the constraint boundary, and the associated method maintains its generated sequence in the strict interior of the feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior-point penalty, or barrier, function replaces a constrained problem by one or more unconstrained problems. Its boundary-singular term is used to keep the generated points strictly feasible.
assumptions_latex: \text{The barrier term is infinite on the constraint boundary.}
\text{The barrier method operates in the strict-feasibility domain.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The barrier reformulation yields unconstrained subproblems while preserving strict feasibility of the generated sequence.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General Separable Interior-Point Penalty Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the mandatory boundary singularity and monotonicity, the source's parameter convention, and the optional positivity property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\sigma>0\), a separable interior-point penalty function has the form \[P_\sigma(x)=f(x)+\frac{1}{\sigma}\sum_{i=1}^m h(c_i(x)),\] where \(h:(0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \[\lim_{t\to0^+}h(t)=+\infty,\qquad 0<t_1<t_2\Longrightarrow h(t_1)\ge h(t_2).\] Some choices additionally satisfy \(h(t)>0\) for all \(t>0\). If \(\sigma_k\to+\infty\), the coefficient \(1/\sigma_k\) tends to zero, so the barrier contribution becomes negligible at each fixed strictly feasible point while retaining singular growth near the boundary. Reciprocal and logarithmic barriers are special cases; the reciprocal barrier satisfies the positivity property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable barrier adds (1/σ) times a sum of scalar barrier terms to the objective. Each scalar term is defined for positive constraint values, is nonincreasing, and diverges as its argument approaches zero from above. Positivity is optional. Reciprocal and logarithmic barriers are special cases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_\sigma(x)=f(x)+\sigma^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m h(c_i(x)),\quad\text{with optional }h(t)>0\text{ and reciprocal and logarithmic special cases.}

children.top_down_role: Logarithmic barriers for scalar inequalities, bounds, and cone interiors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Blow-Up Does Not Imply Coercivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of logarithmic growth when other slacks become unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The logarithmic barrier need not be bounded below or coercive on an unbounded strict interior. On \(D=(0,\infty)\), \(B(x)=-\log x\to-\infty\) as \(x\to\infty\). Moreover, if \(g_1(x_k)=k^{-1}\), \(g_2(x_k)=k^2\), and \(w_1=w_2=1\), then \[g_1(x_k)\downarrow0,\qquad -\log g_1(x_k)-\log g_2(x_k)=-\log k\to-\infty.\] Thus a vanishing slack forces blow-up of a summed logarithmic barrier only when the remaining negative-log terms are controlled, for example by upper bounds on the other slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A log barrier need not be coercive, and growth from one vanishing slack can be offset by another slack becoming unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither strict interiority nor one vanishing slack alone guarantees \(B(x_k)\to+\infty\) for a summed logarithmic barrier.

notation.meaning: positive scalar slacks along the example sequence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential Geometry and Convexity of Scalar Log Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient, Hessian, and convexity conditions for logarithms of smooth positive slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log barriers have explicit inverse-slack derivatives. Concave slacks yield convexity; for affine slacks, strict convexity is equivalent to the normals spanning the ambient space.
assumptions_latex: For convexity, \(D\) is convex and every \(g_i\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed derivative formulas hold; concavity of the slacks implies convexity, with the stated affine strict-convexity criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Differential Geometry and Convexity of Scalar Log Barriers
Logarithmic Barrier Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard logarithmic barriers for positive slacks, box interiors, and the positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)>0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(m\) is finite. The logarithmic barrier of the scalar inequalities is \[B_{\log}(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\log g_i(x),\qquad w_i>0,\quad x\in D,\] and is assigned value \(+\infty\) outside \(D\). If an interior sequence \((x_k)\) satisfies \(g_j(x_k)\downarrow0\) for some \(j\) and every other slack \(g_i(x_k)\) is bounded above, then \(B_{\log}(x_k)\to+\infty\). A bound \(\ell_j<x_j<u_j\) contributes \(-\log(x_j-\ell_j)-\log(u_j-x_j)\). For a symmetric positive-definite matrix variable \(X\), the standard cone-interior logarithmic barrier is \(-\log\det X\); it tends to \(+\infty\) when \(X_k\) converges from the positive-definite cone to a singular positive-semidefinite matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logarithmic barrier sums negative logarithms of positive constraint slacks. It diverges when a slack approaches zero while the other slacks remain bounded above; box barriers and the log-determinant barrier on the positive-definite cone are important special cases.
assumptions_latex: For the scalar divergence claim, \(g_j(x_k)\downarrow0\) for some \(j\) and each \(g_i(x_k)\) is bounded above.
For the matrix divergence claim, \(X_k\succ0\) and \(X_k\to\bar X\succeq0\) with \(\det\bar X=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\log}(x_k)\to+\infty\) under the stated scalar boundary-approach conditions, and \(-\log\det X_k\to+\infty\) under the stated cone-boundary conditions.

notation.meaning: positive slack of the ith inequality

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-dimensional logarithmic-barrier definition with explicit boundary-approach conditions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic Barrier for the Nonnegative Orthant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The logarithmic formula is finite on the strict interior of the nonnegative orthant; points with a zero coordinate lie outside its finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $Q=\mathbb{R}_+^n$ and $x\in\operatorname{int}Q=\mathbb{R}_{++}^n$, define
\[
F(x):=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln x^{(i)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithmic barrier for the nonnegative orthant is the negative sum of the coordinate logarithms and is finite only when every coordinate is strictly positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-orthant logarithmic barrier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the logarithmic barrier for componentwise nonnegative variables and records its boundary singularity without asserting the later convergence claims whose assumptions are unspecified here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C=\mathbb R_+^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x\geq0\}\), where the inequality is componentwise. For \(\mu>0\) and \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal C)=\mathbb R_{++}^n\), define \(b^{\log}(x,\mu)=-\mu\langle e,\log x\rangle=-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\) and \(\phi^{\log}(x,\mu)=f(x)+b^{\log}(x,\mu)\). The barrier is finite in \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\), tends to \(+\infty\) as the boundary is approached from the interior, and is undefined outside \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For componentwise nonnegative variables, the logarithmic barrier subtracts mu times the sum of the component logarithms from the objective. It is finite in the strictly positive orthant, diverges when the boundary is approached, and is undefined outside the feasible orthant.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\text{ for the finite-valued formula}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b^{\log}(x,\mu)=-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i,\qquad \phi^{\log}(x,\mu)=f(x)+b^{\log}(x,\mu),\qquad b^{\log}(x,\mu)\to+\infty\text{ as }x\to\partial\mathcal C\text{ from within }\operatorname{int}(\mathcal C).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic barrier for a QCQP epigraph domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The scalar-inequality logarithmic barrier specialized to the strict epigraph domain of a QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \mathcal F=\{(x,\tau)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\tau-q_0(x)>0,\ \beta_i-q_i(x)>0\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m\}, define F:\mathcal F\to\mathbb{R} by F(x,\tau)=-\ln(\tau-q_0(x))-\sum_{i=1}^m\ln(\beta_i-q_i(x)).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the strict epigraph-feasible region of a QCQP, the logarithmic barrier is the negative logarithm of the objective-epigraph slack plus the negative logarithms of the constraint slacks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic barrier for generalized inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the barrier on the strictly feasible domain and states its convexity under cone-ordered convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K_i\subseteq\mathbf R^{q_i} be proper cones, let f_i be K_i-convex, and let \psi_i be generalized logarithms for K_i with degrees \theta_i, for i=1,\ldots,m. Define \phi(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\psi_i(-f_i(x)) with \operatorname{dom}\phi=\{x\mid f_i(x)\prec_{K_i}0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}. Since each \psi_i is K_i-increasing, \phi is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For cone-ordered inequalities, the logarithmic barrier is the negative sum of generalized logarithms evaluated at the strict slacks. Its domain is the strictly feasible set. Cone-convexity of the constraint mappings and cone-monotonicity of the generalized logarithms imply that the barrier is convex.
assumptions_latex: K_i\subseteq\mathbf R^{q_i}\text{ is a proper cone for }i=1,\ldots,m

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic Barrier for Scalar Inequality Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the logarithmic barrier and its strict-feasibility domain, and records its boundary-divergence behavior without asserting divergence along sequences where other terms could offset it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For inequality functions \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), the logarithmic barrier is
\[
\phi(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(-f_i(x)),
\qquad
\operatorname{dom}\phi=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f_i(x)<0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{dom}\phi\) is precisely the strictly feasible set for the inequalities. If a strictly feasible sequence approaches a finite boundary point at which some \(f_i(x)\to0^-\), then the corresponding term \(-\log(-f_i(x))\to+\infty\); consequently \(\phi(x)\to+\infty\) provided the remaining barrier terms are bounded below, as they are under the usual finite boundary approach with continuous inequality functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithmic barrier is the negative sum of the logarithms of the inequality slacks, and its domain is exactly the strictly feasible set. A barrier term diverges to positive infinity when its inequality approaches zero from below; the full sum diverges at an ordinary finite boundary approach when the other terms cannot offset that divergence.
assumptions_latex: f_i(x_k)\to0^-\text{ for some }i\text{ and }\inf_k\sum_{j\ne i}-\log(-f_j(x_k))> -\infty\quad\text{for the full-sum divergence conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(-f_i(x)),\quad \operatorname{dom}\phi=\{x\mid f_i(x)<0\ \forall i\},\quad f_i(x_k)\to0^-\Longrightarrow-\log(-f_i(x_k))\to+\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic barrier function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-interior transformation for inequality-constrained nonlinear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the inequality constraints are written as \(c_i(x)\ge 0\) and the feasible region has a nonempty strict interior. For \(r>0\), the logarithmic barrier function on \(c_i(x)>0\) is \[B(x,r)=F(x)-r\sum_{i=1}^m\ln c_i(x).\] As any \(c_i(x)\downarrow0\), the corresponding barrier term tends to \(+\infty\), so any unconstrained minimizer within the barrier domain is strictly feasible. The transformation does not directly apply to equality constraints. Decreasing \(r\) toward zero is intended to produce a strictly feasible approach to the constrained minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For inequalities with a nonempty strict interior, the logarithmic barrier subtracts a positive parameter times the sum of the logarithms of the constraint functions from the objective. It diverges at the boundary and therefore keeps any barrier minimizer strictly feasible. It does not directly transform equality constraints; decreasing the parameter toward zero is intended to approach the constrained solution from the interior.
assumptions_latex: \(c_i(x)>0\) for every barrier constraint at points in the barrier domain
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B(x,r)=F(x)-r\sum_{i=1}^m\ln c_i(x),\qquad B(x,r)\to+\infty\text{ if some }c_i(x)\downarrow0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse or reciprocal-growth inequality barrier
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(g_j:D\to\mathbb R\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), define the strict interior \(S=\{x\in D:g_j(x)<0\ \forall j\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional inequality constraints under the sign convention \(g_j(x)\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The reciprocal-growth barrier is \[B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m rac{1}{-g_j(x)}=-\sum_{j=1}^m rac{1}{g_j(x)},\qquad x\in S.\] Its parameterized family is \(\Phi_\mu(x)=f(x)+\mu B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x)\) for \(\mu>0\). If the constraints are twice differentiable, then \[
abla B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x)=\sum_j rac{
abla g_j(x)}{g_j(x)^2},\qquad 
abla^2B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x)=\sum_j\left( rac{
abla^2g_j(x)}{g_j(x)^2}- rac{2
abla g_j(x)
abla g_j(x)^	op}{g_j(x)^3}ight).\] The defining reciprocal boundary growth is \(B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x_k)	o+\infty\) whenever some \(g_j(x_k)\uparrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For constraints written as \(g_j(x)\leq0\), the reciprocal barrier adds the reciprocal of each positive slack \(-g_j(x)\). It is finite only on the strict interior and diverges at rate \(1/(-g_j(x))\) as the corresponding slack vanishes. Multiplication by a positive parameter \(\mu\) produces the associated barrier family.
assumptions_latex: \(g_j(x)<0\) for every \(j\) at each point in the domain \(S\).
For the derivative formulas, every \(g_j\) is twice continuously differentiable on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{rec}}=-\sum_j1/g_j\) is the canonical reciprocal-growth barrier and \(f+\mu B_{\mathrm{rec}}\) is its interior penalty family.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With slack variables \(s_j=-g_j(x)>0\), \(B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x)=\sum_j s_j^{-1}\).
Under the opposite convention \(c_j(x)\geq0\), the same barrier is \(\sum_j1/c_j(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For affine inequalities \(g_j(x)=a_j^\top x-b_j\), \(\nabla^2B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x)=\sum_j2a_ja_j^\top/(b_j-a_j^\top x)^3\succeq0\).
A weighted form \(\sum_jw_j/(-g_j(x))\) with \(w_j>0\) has the same boundary-growth order.
immediate_consequences_latex: The reciprocal barrier grows faster near an active constraint than the logarithmic barrier.
If every \(g_j\) is convex, then \(-1/g_j(x)\) is convex on \(\{g_j<0\}\), hence so is \(B_{\mathrm{rec}}\).
boundary_notes: The barrier is undefined when any \(g_j(x)\geq0\); it does not admit infeasible iterates.
Its curvature can become more severely ill-conditioned than logarithmic-barrier curvature near the boundary.
Reciprocal barriers are not automatically self-concordant.

knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Boundary Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order reciprocal barrier for scalar positive slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the strict interior \(D=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)>0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) and weights \(w_i>0\), the reciprocal boundary barrier is \[B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{w_i}{g_i(x)},\qquad x\in D,\] with extended value \(+\infty\) for \(x\notin D\). If an interior sequence \((x_k)\) satisfies \(g_j(x_k)\downarrow0\) for at least one index \(j\), then \(B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x_k)\to+\infty\). Thus finite sublevel sets of \(B_{\mathrm{rec}}\) exclude points whose weighted slacks approach zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal barrier sums positive weights divided by constraint slacks, becoming infinite when any slack approaches zero from inside.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_j(x_k)\downarrow0\Rightarrow B_{\mathrm{rec}}(x_k)\to+\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reciprocal-barrier definition is mathematically precise, agrees with the leaf container, and its positive summands ensure the stated boundary divergence. No inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal barrier for nonnegative variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an inverse-power barrier on the strict interior of the nonnegative orthant and states its boundary-growth comparison with the logarithmic barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For variables constrained by \(x_i\ge 0\), let \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) and \(\alpha\ge 1\). The reciprocal barrier term is
\[
b^{\mathrm R(\alpha)}(x,\mu)=\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\alpha x_i^{\alpha}}.
\]
Its boundary singularity and resulting repulsive effect are stronger than those of the logarithmic barrier, and the strength of the singularity increases with \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative variable constraints, the reciprocal barrier term on the strictly positive orthant is μ times the sum of 1/(α x_i^α), with α at least 1. It has a stronger boundary singularity and repulsive effect than the logarithmic barrier, and the singularity strengthens as α increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b^{\mathrm R(\alpha)}(x,\mu)=\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\alpha x_i^{\alpha}},\qquad\text{with a stronger boundary singularity than the logarithmic barrier and strength increasing with }\alpha.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential Geometry of Inverse-Power Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient, Hessian, and convexity of inverse-power barriers for smooth slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-power barriers have explicit inverse-slack derivatives. Concave slacks yield convexity, and affine slacks yield strict convexity exactly when their normals span the space.
assumptions_latex: For convexity, \(D\) is convex and every \(g_i\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed derivative formulas hold; concavity of the slacks implies convexity, with the stated affine strict-convexity criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Differential Geometry of Inverse-Power Barriers
Inverse-Power Barrier Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-power generalization of the reciprocal barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p>0\), let \(w_i>0\), and let \(D=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)>0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). The inverse-power barrier of order \(p\) is \[B_p(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i g_i(x)^{-p},\qquad x\in D,\] with \(B_p(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin D\). The choice \(p=1\) gives the reciprocal barrier. For every \(p>0\), if some slack tends to zero from above along an interior sequence, then \(B_p\) diverges to \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-power barriers raise each positive slack to a negative power; every positive exponent gives boundary divergence, and exponent one recovers the reciprocal barrier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_j(x_k)\downarrow0\Rightarrow B_p(x_k)\to+\infty\), and \(B_1=B_{\mathrm{rec}}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct positive-power generalization of the reciprocal barrier

children.title: Boundary-Growth Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Structural contrasts among reciprocal and inverse-power growth profiles.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative-Growth Hierarchy at the Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of slope and curvature singularities for logarithmic and inverse-power profiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), define \(\ell(t)=-\log t\) and \(b_p(t)=t^{-p}\), \(p>0\). Then \[|\ell'(t)|=t^{-1},\quad \ell''(t)=t^{-2},\quad |b_p'(t)|=p t^{-p-1},\quad b_p''(t)=p(p+1)t^{-p-2}.\] Hence, as \(t\downarrow0\), \[|\ell'(t)|=o(|b_p'(t)|),\qquad \ell''(t)=o(b_p''(t)).\] If \(0<p<q\), then \(|b_p'|=o(|b_q'|)\) and \(b_p''=o(b_q'')\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value-growth hierarchy also holds for boundary slopes and curvatures: inverse powers dominate logarithms, and larger powers dominate smaller ones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inverse-power slopes and curvatures asymptotically dominate their logarithmic counterparts, with dominance increasing with the exponent.
knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Growth Hierarchy at the Boundary
Boundary-Growth Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic comparison of logarithmic and inverse-power growth near zero slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scalar slack \(t\in(0,1)\) approaching zero and exponents \(0<p<q\), \[\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{-\log t}{t^{-p}}=0,\qquad \lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{t^{-p}}{t^{-q}}=0.\] Hence every inverse-power barrier grows asymptotically faster than the logarithmic barrier, and a larger positive power grows faster than a smaller one. Componentwise, if one constraint slack is the unique vanishing scale while all other barrier terms remain bounded, these ratios also determine the relative growth of the corresponding summed barrier models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a zero slack, every inverse power dominates logarithmic growth, and higher inverse powers dominate lower ones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\log t=o(t^{-p})\) and \(t^{-p}=o(t^{-q})\) as \(t\downarrow0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The little-o comparisons are correct and the property kind fits the comparison leaf. The qualification on extending the scalar ratios to summed models is appropriate, but no source with a locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modified logarithmic barrier with a relaxed interior domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let inequalities be written \(g_j(x)\leq0\). Fix multipliers \(\lambda_j>0\) and scaling parameters \(c_j>0\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyak-type modified logarithmic barriers that enlarge the finite domain beyond strict feasibility by a controlled amount.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\psi(t)=-\log(1-t)\) on \(( -\infty,1)\). The interior-relaxed modified barrier model is \[M_{\lambda,c}(x)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{\lambda_j}{c_j}\psi(c_jg_j(x))=f(x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{\lambda_j}{c_j}\log(1-c_jg_j(x)),\] with domain \(D_c=\{x:c_jg_j(x)<1\ \forall j\}\). Because \(\{g_j\leq0\ \forall j\}\subset D_c\), the model is finite at feasible boundary points and also at controlled violations satisfying \(0<g_j(x)<1/c_j\). It diverges when \(c_jg_j(x)\uparrow1\). The associated multiplier update is \(\lambda_j^+=\lambda_j/(1-c_jg_j(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The modified logarithmic barrier replaces the strict-interior expression \(-\log(-g_j)\) by \(-\log(1-c_jg_j)\), scaled by \(\lambda_j/c_j\). Its domain requires only \(g_j<1/c_j\), so it includes the original feasible set, its boundary, and a layer of mildly infeasible points. The new barrier wall occurs at the shifted boundary \(g_j=1/c_j\).
assumptions_latex: The model is evaluated only where \(c_jg_j(x)<1\) for all \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{\lambda,c}\) is an interior-relaxed barrier family with relaxed domain \(D_c\), shifted singular boundary \(g_j=1/c_j\), and multiplier update \(\lambda_j^+=\lambda_j/(1-c_jg_j(x))\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using \(\psi(t)=-\log(1-t)\), each term is \((\lambda_j/c_j)\psi(c_jg_j(x))\).
At \(g_j(x)=0\), the term equals zero and its gradient contribution is \(\lambda_j\nabla g_j(x)\), matching the corresponding Lagrangian first-order term.
special_cases_latex: A common scalar scaling uses \(c_j=c\) for all \(j\).
As \(c_j\to\infty\), the permitted violation width \(1/c_j\) contracts to zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict feasibility is not required merely to evaluate the modified barrier.
The denominator in the multiplier update stays positive throughout \(D_c\).
Conditioning deteriorates as an iterate approaches the shifted singular surface.
boundary_notes: This is not the classical logarithmic barrier and does not retain a singularity at \(g_j=0\).
The enlarged domain does not make arbitrary infeasible points admissible.
Convergence requires an outer update policy for \(c_j\), multipliers, and subproblem accuracy; those policies are not part of this definition.

Positive shift or scaling parameter controlling admissible violation.

knowledge_statements.title: Modified Barrier Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized finite extensions or smooth modifications of a classical barrier near its singular boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) be a scalar barrier with \(b(t)\to+\infty\) as \(t\downarrow0\). A modified barrier family is a collection \(\{b_\delta:\mathcal D_\delta\to\mathbb{R}\}_{\delta>0}\) such that \((0,\infty)\subseteq\mathcal D_\delta\), each \(b_\delta\) is finite and continuously differentiable on \(\mathcal D_\delta\), and \[b_\delta(t)\longrightarrow b(t)\quad\text{for every fixed }t>0\text{ as }\delta\downarrow0.\] For positive slacks \(g_i(x)\), the associated model is \(B_\delta(x)=\sum_i w_i b_\delta(g_i(x))\). If \(\mathcal D_\delta\) contains nonpositive values, the modification relaxes strict interiority.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A modified barrier replaces a singular scalar barrier by smooth parameterized functions that converge to it on positive slacks and may remain finite beyond the original interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_\delta(x)\to\sum_i w_i b(g_i(x))\) at every point whose slacks are fixed and positive.

Shifted Boundary Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic barrier whose singular boundary is displaced outward by a positive shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For inequalities written as \(g_i(x)\geq0\), weights \(w_i>0\), and shift \(\delta>0\), define the shifted logarithmic barrier by \[B_\delta^{\mathrm{sh}}(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\log\bigl(g_i(x)+\delta\bigr)\] on \(D_\delta=\{x:g_i(x)>-\delta,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), and assign value \(+\infty\) outside \(D_\delta\). Its singular boundary is \(g_i(x)=-\delta\), so points with violations smaller than \(\delta\) may lie in its domain. For every point with strictly positive slacks, \(B_\delta^{\mathrm{sh}}(x)\to B_{\log}(x)\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a positive shift inside each logarithm moves the singular boundary outward, admits limited constraint violation, and recovers the ordinary logarithmic barrier as the shift vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\subset D_\delta\) and \(B_\delta^{\mathrm{sh}}(x)\to B_{\log}(x)\) for every \(x\in D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shifted-logarithm construction, relaxed domain, and pointwise recovery of the ordinary logarithmic barrier are correct and fit the definition container. No authoritative citation with a locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Zero-Shift Recovery Away from the Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform function and derivative recovery on compact strict-interior sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be compact and suppose \(g_i(x)\geq\eta>0\) on \(K\) for every \(i\). Then \[\sup_{x\in K}|B_\delta^{\rm sh}(x)-B_{\log}(x)|\to0.\] If every \(g_i\in C^2\) on a neighborhood of \(K\), the gradients and Hessians also converge uniformly on \(K\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Away from the original boundary, shifted logarithmic barriers and their first two derivatives converge uniformly to the ordinary log barrier.
assumptions_latex: g_i\in C^2\text{ near }K\text{ for derivative convergence}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B_\delta^{\rm sh}\to B_{\log}\text{ uniformly on }K,\text{ and in }C^2(K)\text{ under the stated smoothness}.

notation.meaning: uniform separation from the original boundary

children.title: Interior-Domain Relaxation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where barrier domains are relaxed or displaced relative to strict feasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed Relaxation Does Not Recover Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating uniformly relaxed and asymptotically tightened domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For g(x)=x\geq0 and fixed \delta>0, the sequence x_k=-\delta/2 belongs to D_\delta=(-\delta,\infty) for every k but converges to the infeasible point -\delta/2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistently positive domain shift can admit a convergent sequence whose limit remains infeasible for the original constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k\in D_\delta\ \forall k,\qquad \lim_kx_k=-\delta/2\notin\{x:x\geq0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Relaxation Does Not Recover Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility of Finite Accumulation Points under Vanishing Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit consequence of progressively tightened relaxed-domain membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be continuous, let \delta_k\to0 with \delta_k\geq0, and suppose g_i(x_k)>-\delta_k for every i,k. If x_{k_j}\to\bar x, then g_i(\bar x)\geq0 for every i.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous constraints and vanishing domain relaxation force every finite accumulation point to be feasible for the original inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_i(\bar x)\geq0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility of Finite Accumulation Points under Vanishing Relaxation
Interior-Domain Relaxation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by whether and how a relaxed barrier domain converges to the strict interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{x:g_i(x)>0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(D_\delta=\{x:g_i(x)>-\delta,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). A barrier iteration \((x_k,\delta_k)\) is strictly interior when \(\delta_k=0\) and \(x_k\in D\) for every \(k\); uniformly relaxed when \(\inf_k\delta_k>0\) and \(x_k\in D_{\delta_k}\); and asymptotically interior-relaxed when \[\delta_k>0,\qquad \delta_k\downarrow0,\qquad x_k\in D_{\delta_k}.\] In the last regime, every iterate satisfies the explicit violation bound \(g_i(x_k)>-\delta_k\), so its maximum possible constraint violation vanishes with \(\delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation regimes are distinguished by zero, persistently positive, or vanishing domain shifts; a vanishing shift forces allowable constraint violation toward zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_k\downarrow0\Rightarrow \max_i[-g_i(x_k)]_+<\delta_k\to0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classification induced by shifted barrier domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three regimes are internally consistent, and membership in the shifted domain yields the displayed vanishing violation bound. The classification terminology is introduced without an inspectable source, so its status as established knowledge is uncertain.

children.title: Mixed Barrier–Penalty Models
children.top_down_role: Hybrid interior–exterior penalty families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parameter Schedules Alone Do Not Ensure Constrained Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of conclusions obtainable solely from barrier and penalty parameter schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The limits \(\mu_k\downarrow0\) and \(\rho_k\uparrow\infty\) alone do not imply feasibility, stationarity, or optimality of arbitrary iterates \(x_k\) for mixed barrier–penalty models. For example, minimize \(f(x)=0\) subject to the penalty-treated inequality \(g(x)=x\ge0\). With \(\rho_k\to\infty\), the fixed sequence \(x_k=-1\) remains infeasible although every model value is finite. Limit conclusions require additional conditions such as controlled subproblem minimization or stationarity, boundedness or existence of accumulation points, and suitable regularity at a limit point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sending the barrier weight to zero and the exterior-penalty weight to infinity gives no convergence guarantee for uncontrolled iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameter limits by themselves imply no feasibility or KKT property of \((x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Schedules Alone Do Not Ensure Constrained Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness Boundary of the Quadratic-Violation Hybrid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability and curvature behavior of the squared-hinge penalty component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(t)=[-t]_+^2\). Then \(\phi\in C^1(\mathbb R)\), with \(\phi'(t)=2t\) for \(t<0\) and \(\phi'(t)=0\) for \(t\ge0\), but \(\phi\notin C^2\) at \(t=0\). Consequently, for \(C^1\) data, \[M_{\mu,\rho}(x)=f(x)-\mu\sum_{i\in I_B}w_i\log g_i(x)+\frac\rho2\sum_{i\in I_P}v_i[-g_i(x)]_+^2\] is \(C^1\) on \(\{x:g_i(x)>0\ (i\in I_B)\}\). Even for \(C^2\) data it is generally only piecewise \(C^2\) across \(g_i(x)=0\), \(i\in I_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared-violation hybrid is continuously differentiable but generally not twice differentiable where a penalty-treated constraint switches activity.
assumptions_latex: The protected slacks are strictly positive.
The problem data possess the stated derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{\mu,\rho}\in C^1\) on its protected interior but is generally not \(C^2\) across a penalty-treated switching surface.
knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness Boundary of the Quadratic-Violation Hybrid
Mixed Barrier–Penalty Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid objective using interior barriers for protected constraints and exterior penalties for relaxable constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition inequality indices into disjoint sets \(I_B\) and \(I_P\), with constraints written as \(g_i(x)\geq0\). For \(\mu>0\) and \(\rho>0\), a mixed logarithmic-barrier and quadratic-penalty model is \[M_{\mu,\rho}(x)=f(x)-\mu\sum_{i\in I_B}w_i\log g_i(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\sum_{i\in I_P}v_i[-g_i(x)]_+^2.\] Its domain requires \(g_i(x)>0\) for \(i\in I_B\), while constraints in \(I_P\) may be violated at a finite cost. The parameters \(\mu\downarrow0\) and \(\rho\uparrow\infty\) respectively weaken the barrier and strengthen the exterior penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed model barriers constraints that must remain strictly feasible and penalizes violations of other constraints, with separate barrier and penalty parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{\mu,\rho}\) is finite on the protected interior even when constraints indexed by \(I_P\) are violated.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of conclusions obtainable solely from barrier and penalty parameter schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The limits \(\mu_k\downarrow0\) and \(\rho_k\uparrow\infty\) alone do not imply feasibility, stationarity, or optimality of arbitrary iterates \(x_k\) for mixed barrier–penalty models. For example, minimize \(f(x)=0\) subject to the penalty-treated inequality \(g(x)=x\ge0\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed Interior–Exterior Unconstrained Minimization Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of the objective used by the mixed interior–exterior penalty construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
V(x,r_k,t_k)=f(x)+s(r_k)I(x)+p(t_k)O(x).
\]
The pair \((s,I)\) has for \(V\) the properties it has in the associated interior construction, and \((p,O)\) has for \(V\) the properties it has in the associated exterior construction. The function \(I\) is defined for \(x\) strictly satisfying constraint system \((4.10)\), whereas \(O\) is defined relative to constraint system \((4.11)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mixed unconstrained objective is the original objective plus weighted interior and exterior penalty terms. The interior function is defined on points strictly satisfying the designated interior constraints, while the exterior function is defined relative to the designated exterior constraints.

(p,O)\text{ has the stated exterior-function properties for }V.
I(x)\text{ is defined for }x\text{ strictly satisfying }(4.10).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(x,r_k,t_k)=f(x)+s(r_k)I(x)+p(t_k)O(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Outer continuation through barrier subproblems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonempty strict feasible region, let \(B:S\to\mathbb R\) be a barrier, and define \(\Phi_\mu=f+\mu B\) for \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal outer–inner continuation for exact-domain barriers; both exact and inexact inner solves are admitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequential barrier continuation is a sequence \(\{(\mu_k,x^k)\}_{k\geq0}\) satisfying \[0<\mu_{k+1}<\mu_k,\qquad \mu_k\to0,\qquad x^k\in S,\] where each \(x^k\) is an exact or prescribed-accuracy solution of the subproblem \(\min_{x\in S}\Phi_{\mu_k}(x)\). In the smooth unconstrained-interior form, an inexact solve may be specified by \(\|\nabla\Phi_{\mu_k}(x^k)\|_{x^k,*}\leq\eta_k\), where the dual norm is induced by a chosen positive-definite subproblem Hessian metric. The continuation is warm-started when the inner solve for \(\mu_{k+1}\) begins from \(x^k\) or from a forecast based on earlier subproblem solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential barrier continuation is the outer process that decreases a positive barrier parameter to zero and, at each parameter value, solves or approximately solves the corresponding interior barrier subproblem. Every accepted point remains in the barrier domain. The preceding point is normally used to initialize the next inner solve because neighboring barrier problems have related solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is finite on \(S\) and diverges at the represented boundary.
Each accepted \(x^k\) meets the declared exact or inexact subproblem criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled sequence \(\{(\mu_k,x^k)\}\) is a sequential barrier continuation through the family \(\Phi_{\mu}=f+\mu B\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using \(t_k=1/\mu_k\), continuation is equivalently described by \(t_k\uparrow+\infty\) and subproblems \(\min_x t_kf(x)+B(x)\).
Exact continuation has \(x^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}\Phi_{\mu_k}(x)\); inexact continuation replaces this membership by a quantitative residual condition.
special_cases_latex: Geometric reduction uses \(\mu_{k+1}=\theta\mu_k\) with fixed \(0<\theta<1\).
Short-step continuation uses parameter ratios close to one; long-step continuation uses more aggressive reductions and typically more inner corrections.
immediate_consequences_latex: For each fixed interior point \(x\), the term \(\mu_kB(x)\) vanishes as \(k\to\infty\).
Warm starts turn the collection of independent subproblems into a path-tracking process.
boundary_notes: The definition alone does not assert convergence to a global solution.
A reduction that is too aggressive can place the warm start outside the fast-convergence neighborhood of the new subproblem.
Barriers with relaxed domains require their own domain condition in place of \(x^k\in S\).

notation.meaning: Outer barrier parameter at continuation stage \(k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity-Only Inner Solves Can Follow a Nonoptimal Branch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of primal barrier continuation when inner stopping certifies only stationarity in a nonconvex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(D=(-2,2)\), let \(f(x)=(x^2-1)^2\) and \(B(x)=-\log(4-x^2)\). For every \(\mu>0\), \[\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(f(x)+\mu B(x)\bigr)\big|_{x=0}=0.\] Thus \(x_k=0\) satisfies an exact gradient stopping test for every \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), but \(f(0)=1\), whereas the minimum of \(f\) on \([-2,2]\) is zero at \(x=\pm1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nonconvex barrier subproblem, exact first-order stationarity can track a branch whose limit is not globally optimal for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla(f+\mu_kB)(x_k)=0\ \forall k,\qquad 0\notin\operatorname*{argmin}_{[-2,2]}f.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity-Only Inner Solves Can Follow a Nonoptimal Branch

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality of Exact Primal-Barrier Accumulation Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global limit theorem for exact minimizers of vanishing primal barrier subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact and convex with nonempty interior \(D\), let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let \(B:D\to\mathbb R\) be a finite-valued barrier bounded below on \(D\). For \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), let \[x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}\{f(x)+\mu_kB(x)\}.\] Then every accumulation point \(\bar x\) of \((x_k)\) belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact minimizers of successively weakened primal barrier problems have only original-problem minimizers as accumulation points under compactness and a lower-bounded barrier.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is compact and convex with }\operatorname{int}C\ne\varnothing.
B\text{ is finite valued and bounded below on }D=\operatorname{int}C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\text{for every accumulation point }\bar x.

notation.meaning: exact minimizer of the kth primal barrier subproblem

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality of Exact Primal-Barrier Accumulation Points

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonic Tradeoff Along Exact Primal Barrier Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter monotonicity for exact global minimizers of a common primal barrier family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\mu_2<\mu_1\), and choose \(x_j\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}\{f(x)+\mu_jB(x)\}\). Then \[B(x_1)\leq B(x_2),\qquad f(x_2)\leq f(x_1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reducing the barrier parameter cannot worsen the original objective selected by exact global minimization, while the selected barrier value cannot decrease.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B(x_1)\leq B(x_2),\qquad f(x_2)\leq f(x_1).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonic Tradeoff Along Exact Primal Barrier Minima
Primal Barrier Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer continuation through approximate minimizers of successively weakened primal barrier subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\mu_0>0\), contraction \(\theta\in(0,1)\), tolerances \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), a barrier \(B\) on the strict interior \(D\), and \(x_0\in D\), repeat for \(k=0,1,\ldots\): approximately solve \[\min_{x\in D}\ \Phi_{\mu_k}(x):=f(x)+\mu_k B(x)\] from the previous iterate until \(\|\nabla\Phi_{\mu_k}(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon_k\); then set \(\mu_{k+1}=\theta\mu_k\). Stop when prescribed feasibility, stationarity, and parameter tolerances hold, and return the latest \(x_k\). The sequence \((x_k)\) is the primal barrier sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximately minimize successive primal barrier objectives, reduce the barrier parameter geometrically, warm-start from the previous solution, and stop at requested optimality and feasibility tolerances.
assumptions_latex: \(x_0\in D\) and \(B(x)\to+\infty\) at the boundary of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_k=\theta^k\mu_0\downarrow0\), with each reported iterate satisfying \(\|\nabla\Phi_{\mu_k}(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon_k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact primal barrier minimizer sequence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\) be the strict interior of an inequality-constrained problem, let \(B:S\to\mathbb R\) be a barrier, and suppose each \(f+\mu B\) has at least one minimizer on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal minimizers of successively weakened barriers; no dual variables are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given any sequence \(\mu_k>0\) with \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), a primal barrier sequence is a selection \[x^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}\{f(x)+\mu_kB(x)\},\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.\] If \(f\) and \(B\) are differentiable and the subproblem has no retained equality constraints, every selected interior minimizer satisfies \(\nabla f(x^k)+\mu_k\nabla B(x^k)=0\). If each subproblem is strictly convex, the minimizer is unique and the sequence is the sampling \(x^k=x(\mu_k)\) of the primal barrier path \(x(\mu)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}(f(x)+\mu B(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal barrier sequence is the sequence of exact primal solutions obtained by minimizing \(f+\mu_kB\) for positive parameters decreasing to zero. It is a sequence of points, not an inner algorithm. Under differentiability its members satisfy the barrier stationarity equation, and under strict convexity they are uniquely determined samples of a parameterized primal path.
assumptions_latex: For the stationarity formulation, \(f\) and \(B\) are differentiable on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x^k\}\) is a primal barrier sequence exactly when each \(x^k\) minimizes the primal barrier objective at parameter \(\mu_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(t_k=1/\mu_k\), the same points minimize \(t_kf(x)+B(x)\).
When the minimizer is unique, \(x^k=x(\mu_k)\) for the single-valued primal barrier path \(x(\cdot)\).
special_cases_latex: For the logarithmic barrier, \(x^k\) minimizes \(f(x)-\mu_k\sum_j\log(-g_j(x))\).
For linear programming with positive slacks, this sequence is the primal central path sampled at \(\mu_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(x^k\) is strictly feasible for an exact-domain barrier.
The barrier force \(\mu_k\nabla B(x^k)\) balances the objective gradient at an unconstrained interior minimizer.
Nonuniqueness permits several primal barrier sequences for the same parameter schedule.
boundary_notes: Approximate inner iterates are not exact primal barrier sequences unless they are explicitly treated as an inexact variant.
A primal barrier sequence need not converge when level sets are unbounded or minimizers escape to infinity.
Equality constraints add a multiplier term to the stationarity equation.

notation.meaning: Unique primal barrier minimizer when it exists.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariance Under Additive Barrier Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal barrier minimizers do not depend on an additive constant in the barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constant \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), let \(\widetilde B=B+\beta\). For every \(\mu>0\), \[f(x)+\mu\widetilde B(x)=f(x)+\mu B(x)+\mu\beta,\] and therefore \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}\{f(x)+\mu\widetilde B(x)\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}\{f(x)+\mu B(x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a constant to the barrier leaves every exact primal barrier minimizer unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_D(f+\mu(B+\beta))=\operatorname*{argmin}_D(f+\mu B).
knowledge_statements.title: Invariance Under Additive Barrier Normalization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of Primal Barrier Values and Cluster Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of exact primal barrier minimizers as the barrier parameter tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^\circ=\{x\in X:g(x)<0\}\), \(S=\{x\in X:g(x)\leq0\}\), and \(\theta(\mu)=\min_{x\in S^\circ}[f(x)+\mu B(x)]\), with minimizer \(x_\mu\). Assume the barrier-subproblem hypotheses and suppose the primal problem has an optimizer \(\bar x\in\overline{S^\circ}\). Then, writing \(p^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x)\), \(\lim_{\mu\downarrow0}\theta(\mu)=\inf_{\mu>0}\theta(\mu)=p^*\). Every limit of a convergent subsequence \(x_{\mu_k}\), where \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), is primal optimal, and \(\mu B(x_\mu)\to0\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a primal optimizer can be approached by strictly feasible points, exact barrier values converge to the primal optimum as the parameter tends to zero. Every cluster point of corresponding barrier minimizers is primal optimal, and the weighted barrier term vanishes.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ and }g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ are continuous}
X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and closed}
B\text{ has the stipulated barrier form and is continuous on }\{x:g(x)<0\}
\forall\mu>0,\quad x_k\in S^\circ,\ f(x_k)+\mu B(x_k)\to\theta(\mu)\implies \{x_k\}\text{ has a convergent subsequence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\mu\downarrow0}\theta(\mu)=\inf_{\mu>0}\theta(\mu)=p^*;\quad \mu_k\downarrow0,\ x_{\mu_{k_j}}\to x^*\implies x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x);\quad \mu B(x_\mu)\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Primal Barrier Continuation Scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer continuation using exact barrier-subproblem solutions, geometric parameter reduction, and a weighted-barrier stopping test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\varepsilon>0\), \(x_1\in X\) with \(g(x_1)<0\), \(\mu_1>0\), and \(\beta\in(0,1)\). For \(k=1,2,\ldots\), compute \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{f(x)+\mu_kB(x):x\in X,\ g(x)<0\}\). If \(\mu_kB(x_{k+1})<\varepsilon\), stop; otherwise set \(\mu_{k+1}=\beta\mu_k\) and continue. The strict inequality may be suppressed in an inner unconstrained implementation only when that implementation guarantees an interior result; otherwise strict feasibility must be checked explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin from a strictly feasible point and solve each barrier subproblem exactly. Stop when the weighted barrier value is below tolerance; otherwise reduce the barrier parameter geometrically. If the inner solver does not guarantee an interior result, it must explicitly check strict feasibility.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ satisfies the stipulated barrier conditions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X,\,g(x)<0}[f(x)+\mu_kB(x)];\quad \mu_kB(x_{k+1})<\varepsilon\Rightarrow\text{stop};\quad \mu_kB(x_{k+1})\geq\varepsilon\Rightarrow\mu_{k+1}=\beta\mu_k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Parameter Monotonicity of Primal Barrier Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment, value bounds, and parameter monotonicity for exact primal barrier subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^\circ=\{x\in X:g(x)<0\}\), \(S=\{x\in X:g(x)\leq0\}\), and \(\theta(\mu)=\inf_{x\in S^\circ}[f(x)+\mu B(x)]\). Under the stated continuity, barrier, and sequential-compactness assumptions, for every \(\mu>0\) there is \(x_\mu\in S^\circ\) attaining \(\theta(\mu)\). Moreover, \(\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\leq\inf_{\mu>0}\theta(\mu)\). For any choices of minimizers \(x_\mu\), both \(f(x_\mu)\) and \(\theta(\mu)\) are nondecreasing in \(\mu\), while \(B(x_\mu)\) is nonincreasing in \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive barrier parameter has a strictly feasible exact minimizer under the stated compactness condition. The original constrained infimum is no greater than the infimum of the barrier values. As the parameter increases, the minimizer's objective value and the barrier value do not decrease, while its barrier value does not increase.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and closed}
B\text{ has the stipulated barrier form and is continuous on }\{x:g(x)<0\}
\forall\mu>0,\quad x_k\in S^\circ,\ f(x_k)+\mu B(x_k)\to\theta(\mu)\implies \{x_k\}\text{ has a convergent subsequence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\mu>0\ \exists x_\mu\in S^\circ:\ \theta(\mu)=f(x_\mu)+\mu B(x_\mu);\quad \inf_{x\in S}f(x)\leq\inf_{\mu>0}\theta(\mu);\quad f(x_\mu),\theta(\mu)\text{ are nondecreasing and }B(x_\mu)\text{ is nonincreasing in }\mu.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order tangent forecast of a barrier path
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x(t)\) be the unique minimizer of \(\Psi_t(x)=t f(x)+\phi(x)\) for \(t>0\), with \(f,\phi\in C^2\), and assume \(H(t)=t\nabla^2f(x(t))+\nabla^2\phi(x(t))\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained or equality-eliminated primal barrier paths with a nonsingular centrality Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The first-order continuation forecast from \(t_k\) to \(t_{k+1}\) is \[\widehat x^{k+1}=x(t_k)+(t_{k+1}-t_k)x'(t_k).\] Differentiating the centrality equation \(t
abla f(x(t))+
abla\phi(x(t))=0\) defines the tangent by \[x'(t)=- igl[t
abla^2f(x(t))+
abla^2\phi(x(t)) igr]^{-1}
abla f(x(t)).\] A continuation predictor–corrector uses \(\widehat x^{k+1}\) as the starting point for Newton correction of the \(t_{k+1}\) barrier subproblem. The forecast is therefore a neighboring-path approximation, not an accepted solution by itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuation path forecasting predicts the next barrier solution by moving from the current exact path point along the tangent of the parameterized minimizer curve. The tangent is obtained from the differentiated stationarity equation. The predicted point is then corrected by solving the new barrier subproblem, usually with Newton steps.
assumptions_latex: For every relevant \(t\), \(x(t)\) exists and is locally unique.
\(f\) and \(\phi\) are twice continuously differentiable near the path.
\(H(t)\succ0\), so the path tangent is well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x^{k+1}=x(t_k)+(t_{k+1}-t_k)x'(t_k)\), with \(x'(t_k)=-H(t_k)^{-1}\nabla f(x(t_k))\), is the canonical first-order continuation forecast.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using \(\mu=1/t\), the forecast is \(\widehat x(\mu_{k+1})=x(\mu_k)+(\mu_{k+1}-\mu_k)\,dx/d\mu(\mu_k)\).
The tangent is the solution of the linear system \(H(t)x'(t)=-\nabla f(x(t))\), so no explicit matrix inverse is required.
special_cases_latex: If \(f(x)=c^\top x\), then \(x'(t)=-\nabla^2\phi(x(t))^{-1}c\).
For equality-constrained paths, the tangent is obtained from the differentiated bordered KKT system.
immediate_consequences_latex: For a differentiable path, the local forecast error is \(o(|t_{k+1}-t_k|)\).
The same factorization used for a Newton system can often be reused to compute the tangent direction.
boundary_notes: The predicted point may leave the barrier domain when the parameter change is too large.
At a singular path point or a nonunique minimizer, the stated tangent need not exist.
Higher-order extrapolation and primal-dual affine predictors are distinct variants.

children.title: Tangent Path Prediction
children.top_down_role: Local path forecasts based on central-trajectory tangent information.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Path Prediction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order continuation predictor obtained by differentiating the barrier stationarity equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a differentiable stationary path \(x(\mu)\) satisfy \(F(x(\mu),\mu)=\nabla_x\Phi_\mu(x(\mu))=0\), and suppose \(H=\nabla_{xx}^2\Phi_\mu(x(\mu))\) is nonsingular. Compute the tangent \(d(\mu)\) from \[H d(\mu)=-\partial_\mu F(x(\mu),\mu).\] For a new parameter \(\widehat\mu\), form the predictor \(x^{\mathrm{pred}}=x(\mu)+(\widehat\mu-\mu)d(\mu)\). If the predicted point lies in the barrier domain, use it to initialize the corrector solve at \(\widehat\mu\); otherwise shorten the parameter step until interiority is restored.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiate the stationary barrier equations, solve one Hessian system for the path tangent, and extrapolate to initialize the next barrier subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathrm{pred}}=x(\mu)+(\widehat\mu-\mu)x'(\mu)\), where \(x'(\mu)=-H^{-1}\partial_\mu F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implicit-function tangent equation and first-order predictor are correctly stated under nonsingularity, and algorithm is the appropriate kind. No continuation-method source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Secant Path Extrapolation
children.top_down_role: Continuation estimates derived from neighboring barrier solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Secant Path Extrapolation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-free linear predictor from two previously corrected continuation points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given corrected continuation points \((\mu_{k-1},x_{k-1})\) and \((\mu_k,x_k)\) with \(\mu_{k-1}\neq\mu_k\), and a proposed parameter \(\mu_{k+1}\), form the secant predictor \[x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pred}}=x_k+\frac{\mu_{k+1}-\mu_k}{\mu_k-\mu_{k-1}}(x_k-x_{k-1}).\] Accept it as the initial point for the corrector at \(\mu_{k+1}\) only if it belongs to the barrier domain and passes the chosen residual safeguard. Otherwise reduce \(|\mu_{k+1}-\mu_k|\) or revert to \(x_k\). This predictor requires no path derivative or additional linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extrapolate from two corrected parameter–solution pairs along their secant, accepting the prediction only when domain and residual safeguards hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}^{\mathrm{pred}}=x_k+\frac{\mu_{k+1}-\mu_k}{\mu_k-\mu_{k-1}}(x_k-x_{k-1})\).

notation.meaning: corrected point at parameter mu k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-point secant extrapolation formula is correct, internally consistent, and appropriately classified as an algorithm. The safeguard policy and its use in barrier continuation lack an inspectable citation.

children.title: Predictor Reliability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Curvature, degeneracy, or parameter changes that limit predictive accuracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Secant Predictor Curvature Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature-controlled accuracy boundary for two-point path interpolation or extrapolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x(\mu)\) be twice continuously differentiable and satisfy \(\|x''(s)\|\leq M\) on the convex hull of \(\mu_{k-1},\mu_k,\widehat\mu\). If \(p(\widehat\mu)\) is the affine predictor through \((\mu_{k-1},x(\mu_{k-1}))\) and \((\mu_k,x(\mu_k))\), then \[\|x(\widehat\mu)-p(\widehat\mu)\|\leq\frac{M}{2}|(\widehat\mu-\mu_{k-1})(\widehat\mu-\mu_k)|.\] The bound deteriorates with path curvature and extrapolation distance; the secant predictor is undefined when \(\mu_{k-1}=\mu_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The secant predictor has a curvature-controlled error that grows with both distances from the sampled parameters and is undefined for coincident samples.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is twice continuously differentiable on the relevant parameter interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|x(\widehat\mu)-p(\widehat\mu)\|\leq\frac M2|(\widehat\mu-\mu_{k-1})(\widehat\mu-\mu_k)|.
knowledge_statements.title: Secant Predictor Curvature Error
Predictor Reliability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy and feasibility limits for tangent or secant continuation predictors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the exact continuation path is twice differentiable on the parameter interval from \(\mu\) to \(\widehat\mu\) and \(\|x''(s)\|\leq M\) there. The tangent predictor satisfies \[\|x(\widehat\mu)-x^{\mathrm{pred}}\|\leq\frac{M}{2}|\widehat\mu-\mu|^2.\] If each slack \(g_i\) is locally Lipschitz with constant \(L_i\), the computable condition \(g_i(x(\mu))>L_i\|x^{\mathrm{pred}}-x(\mu)\|\) guarantees predicted strict feasibility. This reliability guarantee ends when the relevant stationarity Jacobian becomes singular, the path loses twice differentiability, or the parameter step violates a feasibility or residual safeguard; then shortening the step or using a corrector is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangent prediction has quadratic local error on a smooth path, but guarantees fail near singular Jacobians, nonsmooth path changes, or steps large enough to threaten interiority.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is twice differentiable and \(\|x''(s)\|\leq M\) on the prediction interval.
The current point is strictly feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x(\widehat\mu)-x^{\mathrm{pred}}\|\leq\frac{M}{2}|\widehat\mu-\mu|^2\), while the displayed slack margin certifies predicted interiority.

notation.meaning: local Lipschitz constant of the ith slack

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Taylor remainder and Lipschitz feasibility safeguard

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tangent-predictor error bound and Lipschitz slack-margin certificate are correct under the stated assumptions, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. The record supplies no authoritative source for the combined reliability and breakdown statement.

children.title: Inner–Outer Accuracy Schedules
children.top_down_role: Accuracy regimes coupling barrier reduction with subproblem solution quality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonvanishing Inner Gaps Need Not Recover an Optimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of continuation when objective-gap tolerances remain bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[0,3]\), \(D=(0,3)\), \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\), and \(B(x)=-\log x-\log(3-x)\). For \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), take \(x_k=2\). Then \[\phi_{\mu_k}(2)-\inf_{x\in D}\phi_{\mu_k}(x)\to1.\] Thus the fixed tolerance \(\delta_k\equiv2\) accepts every sufficiently large \(k\), although \(x_k\to2\notin\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed positive inner objective tolerance can accept a sequence converging to a nonoptimal point as the barrier parameter vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k\to2\notin\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in[0,3]}(x-1)^2.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonvanishing Inner Gaps Need Not Recover an Optimizer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Convexity Conversion from Stationarity to Objective Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation between gradient stopping tolerances and objective-gap schedules for barrier subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi_{\mu_k}\) be differentiable and \(m_k\)-strongly convex on its convex domain, with minimizer \(x_k^*\). If \(\|\nabla\phi_{\mu_k}(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon_k\), then \[0\leq\phi_{\mu_k}(x_k)-\phi_{\mu_k}(x_k^*)\leq\frac{\varepsilon_k^2}{2m_k}.\] Hence \(\varepsilon_k^2/m_k=O(\mu_k)\) gives proportional objective accuracy, while \(\varepsilon_k^2/m_k=o(\mu_k)\) gives objective accuracy asymptotically exact relative to the barrier scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity converts an inner gradient tolerance into an objective-gap tolerance and makes its required coupling to the barrier parameter explicit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi_{\mu_k}(x_k)-\min\phi_{\mu_k}\leq\frac{\varepsilon_k^2}{2m_k}.

notation.meaning: strong-convexity modulus of the kth barrier subproblem

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Convexity Conversion from Stationarity to Objective Accuracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality of Vanishing-Gap Barrier Accumulation Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit guarantee for approximately minimized barrier subproblems under a vanishing objective-gap schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact and convex with nonempty interior \(D\), let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let \(B:D\to\mathbb R\) be finite valued and bounded below. Suppose \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), \(\delta_k\to0\) with \(\delta_k\geq0\), and \(x_k\in D\) satisfies \[f(x_k)+\mu_kB(x_k)\leq\inf_{x\in D}\{f(x)+\mu_kB(x)\}+\delta_k.\] Then every accumulation point \(\bar x\) of \((x_k)\) belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When both the barrier parameter and inner objective gap vanish, every accumulation point of approximate barrier minimizers solves the original compact problem.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is finite valued and bounded below on \(D=\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\text{for every accumulation point }\bar x.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality of Vanishing-Gap Barrier Accumulation Points
Inner–Outer Accuracy Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Couples approximate barrier-subproblem solves to a vanishing outer barrier parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) have nonempty interior, let \(F\) be a barrier on \(C\), and define \(\phi_\mu(x)=f(x)+\mu F(x)\) for \(\mu>0\). An inner–outer accuracy schedule consists of \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), tolerances \(\delta_k\geq0\), and \(x_k\in\operatorname{int}C\) satisfying \(\phi_{\mu_k}(x_k)-\inf_{x\in\operatorname{int}C}\phi_{\mu_k}(x)\leq\delta_k\). It is proportionally accurate when \(\delta_k\leq c\mu_k\) for some finite \(c\), and asymptotically exact relative to the barrier scale when \(\delta_k/\mu_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each barrier subproblem is solved to an error tied to its barrier parameter; proportional and asymptotically exact schedules use error of order μ and little-o of μ, respectively.
assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and bounded below on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_k=O(\mu_k)\) defines proportional accuracy, while \(\delta_k=o(\mu_k)\) defines relative asymptotic exactness.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional proportional and forcing-term schedules for sequential barrier minimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and local scope fit the accuracy-schedule container, and the proportional and little-o regimes are internally coherent. No inspectable source is cited, however, so the choice of objective-suboptimality error and its interpretation relative to the barrier scale require authoritative support.
