knowledge_statements.statement_title: Volumetric Barrier and Volumetric Center of a Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^Tx<b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) be a bounded full-dimensional polyhedron, with \(s_i(x)=b_i-a_i^Tx\) and \(H(x)=\sum_i a_ia_i^T/s_i(x)^2\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral volumetric geometry based on the Hessian of the standard logarithmic barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[V(x):=\frac12\log\det H(x),\qquad x\in P.\] A volumetric center is any point \[x_{\mathrm{vol}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}V(x).\] Equivalently, it maximizes the Euclidean volume of the unit Dikin ellipsoid \(E_D(x,1)\), since that volume is proportional to \((\det H(x))^{-1/2}\). The local volumetric metric is the Hessian metric generated by \(V\) wherever \(\nabla^2V(x)\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The volumetric barrier is one half of the logarithm of the determinant of the logarithmic-barrier Hessian. A volumetric center minimizes this function, equivalently maximizing the volume of the local unit Dikin ellipsoid associated with the given inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_{\mathrm{vol}}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\operatorname{vol}E_D(x,1)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}\frac12\log\det H(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: At an interior differentiable minimizer, \(\nabla V(x_{\mathrm{vol}})=0\).
special_cases_latex: Under an invertible affine coordinate change, \(V\) changes by an additive constant, so the center transforms affinely.
immediate_consequences_latex: Multiplying all defining inequalities by positive constants leaves \(H(x)\) unchanged.
Adding redundant inequalities can change the volumetric center because the defining Hessian changes.
boundary_notes: Existence is not asserted for arbitrary unbounded polyhedra.
The volumetric center differs in general from the analytic center, which minimizes \(-\sum_i\log s_i(x)\).
No supplied source was found that directly supported this complete definition.
review_flags: A precise source for the volumetric-barrier definition and center equivalence is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Volumetric Barrier and Volumetric Center of a Polyhedron

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Volumetric Center Depends on the Inequality Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of representation invariance under duplication of an inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The interval \(P=(-1,1)\), represented by \(x<1\) and \(-x<1\), has \(H(x)=(1-x)^{-2}+(1+x)^{-2}\), whose unique minimizer is \(0\). Duplicating \(x<1\) gives \(\widetilde H(x)=2(1-x)^{-2}+(1+x)^{-2}\), whose unique minimizer is \[\widetilde x=\frac{1-2^{1/3}}{1+2^{1/3}}\ne0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating an inequality can move the volumetric center without changing the represented open polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{P}V=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{P}\widetilde V=\left\{\frac{1-2^{1/3}}{1+2^{1/3}}\right\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Volumetric Center Depends on the Inequality Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Convexity and Uniqueness of the Represented Volumetric Center
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness criterion for a full-dimensional represented polyhedron whenever the volumetric minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax<b\}\) have nonempty interior and row normals spanning \(\mathbb R^n\). With \(s_i(x)=b_i-a_i^Tx\), \(H(x)=\sum_i a_ia_i^T/s_i(x)^2\), and \(V(x)=\tfrac12\log\det H(x)\), the function \(V\) is strictly convex on \(P\). Consequently, if \(V\) attains its minimum on \(P\), that minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spanning constraint normals make the represented volumetric objective strictly convex, so any attained volumetric center is unique.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is convex with nonempty interior}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V\text{ is strictly convex on }P,\qquad |\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}V(x)|\leq1.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Convexity and Uniqueness of the Represented Volumetric Center

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Implicit Calculus of a Central Trajectory
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb R^q\times(0,\bar\mu)\to\mathbb R^q\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(z(\mu)\) denote an interior solution of the parameterized centrality system \(R(z,\mu)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional central paths represented by a square residual system with nonsingular state Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\mathcal C:=\{z(\mu):0<\mu<\bar\mu,\ R(z(\mu),\mu)=0\}.\] Central-path calculus consists of the local trajectory and its sensitivity determined, whenever \(R_z(z(\mu),\mu)\) is nonsingular, by \[z'(\mu)=-R_z(z(\mu),\mu)^{-1}R_\mu(z(\mu),\mu).\] A centrality neighborhood generated by a scaled residual map \(M(z,\mu)\) is \(\mathcal N(\theta)=\{z:\|M(z,\mu(z))\|\le\theta\}\), with the norm and parameter estimator specified by the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A central path is the parameterized zero set of a centrality residual. Its calculus uses the Jacobian of that residual to define local sensitivity, tangents, predictor directions, and residual-based neighborhoods. The definition applies only where the state Jacobian is nonsingular.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a barrier minimizer \(x(t)\) satisfying \(t\nabla f_0(x)+\nabla F(x)+A^Ty=0\) and \(Ax=b\), the tangent is defined by differentiating this KKT residual with respect to \(t\).
special_cases_latex: For linear programming, \(R\) can be the primal-dual residual \((Ax-b,A^Ty+s-c,XSe-\mu e)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The tangent supplies a first-order predictor when the central parameter changes.
Loss of invertibility marks a boundary of the regular calculus and may signal branching or degeneracy.
boundary_notes: The displayed derivative is local and does not itself guarantee global existence or convergence to an endpoint.
Nonsmooth or set-valued central trajectories require a different sensitivity framework.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Barrier and Perturbed-KKT Representations of the LP Central Path
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), and suppose the strictly feasible primal-dual set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-form linear programming with logarithmic barriers and positive central parameter \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\mu>0\), a central triple \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) has the coupled representation \[Ax=b,\qquad A^Ty+s=c,\qquad XSe=\mu e,\qquad x>0,\ s>0.\] Its primal component is equivalently \[x(\mu)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=b,\ x>0}\left(c^Tx-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\right),\] and its dual components arise from the corresponding dual logarithmic-barrier problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly feasible linear program, the same central trajectory can be represented as minimizers of primal barrier subproblems, maximizers of dual barrier subproblems, or solutions of a coupled perturbed KKT system with equal componentwise complementarity products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C=\{(x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu)):\mu>0\}=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^Ty+s=c,\ XS e=\mu e,\ x,s>0\text{ for some }\mu>0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x_i(\mu)s_i(\mu)=\mu\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\]
\[\mu=\frac{x(\mu)^Ts(\mu)}{n}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has full row rank, the multiplier component \(y(\mu)\) is unique; otherwise \(x(\mu)\) and \(s(\mu)\) can remain unique while \(y(\mu)\) is not.
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal-dual gap on the path is \(c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts=n\mu\).
The primal and dual projections of the coupled trajectory are the corresponding one-sided central paths.
boundary_notes: This definition concerns strictly feasible LPs and does not cover infeasible-start residual trajectories.
The sign of the multiplier changes under alternative Lagrangian conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Central Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained primal path generated by barrier-penalized objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in\operatorname{int}K\},
\]
where \(F\) is a strictly convex barrier for \(K\). For each \(\mu>0\), the primal central point is
\[
x(\mu)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=b,\,x\in\operatorname{int}K}\{\langle c,x\rangle+\mu F(x)\}.
\]
Equivalently, there exists a multiplier \(y(\mu)\) such that
\[
Ax(\mu)=b,
\qquad
c-A^\top y(\mu)+\mu\nabla F(x(\mu))=0.
\]
The curve \(\{x(\mu):\mu>0\}\) is the primal central path whenever these minimizers exist uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal central path consists of unique minimizers of the linear objective plus a positive barrier weight, subject to the primal equalities.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed and convex with nonempty interior.
For every \(\mu>0\), the barrier subproblem is feasible and has a unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(\mu)\) is characterized by primal feasibility and barrier-perturbed stationarity.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Barrier-subproblem minimizers and their stationarity equations define the standard primal central path.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The barrier-subproblem representation and perturbed stationarity equations match the primal-central-path leaf. The multiplier sign convention is internally possible, but an authoritative central-path locator must establish the exact formulation and assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Logarithmic-Barrier Central Path
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and suppose \(\{x:Ax=b,\ x>0\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly feasible standard-form linear programming; uniqueness is understood for each barrier subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), the primal central point is \[x(\mu):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=b,\ x>0}\left\{c^Tx-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\right\}.\] The primal central path is \(\mathcal C_P:=\{x(\mu):\mu>0\}\). Equivalently, \(x(\mu)>0\) belongs to \(\mathcal C_P\) if there exist \(y(\mu)\) and \(s(\mu)>0\) such that \(Ax=b\), \(A^Ty+s=c\), and \(x_i s_i=\mu\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal central path is the curve of minimizers of the primal logarithmic-barrier objective as its positive coefficient varies. Each point is strictly feasible and is also the primal projection of a perturbed primal-dual KKT solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_P=\left\{\operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=b,\ x>0}\left(c^Tx-\mu\sum_i\log x_i\right):\mu>0\right\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using \(t=1/\mu\), the same points minimize \(tc^Tx-\sum_i\log x_i\).
special_cases_latex: At \(c=0\), whenever the minimizer exists, the path is constant at the analytic center of \(\{x:Ax=b,\ x>0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every path point satisfies primal feasibility and strict positivity.
Its barrier first-order condition generates a dual slack \(s=\mu X^{-1}e\).
boundary_notes: A nonempty primal interior alone need not provide a well-behaved full primal-dual path without the corresponding dual conditions or boundedness.
The endpoint \(\mu=0\) is not part of the path.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Central Path for a Nonlinear Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-space central path defined by logarithmic-barrier subproblems that retain equality constraints explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le 0\), and assume \(\mathring{\mathcal F}=\{x:h(x)=0,\ g(x)<0\}\ne\varnothing\). For \(\mu>0\), let \(x_\mu\) be a solution of \[\min_x\left\{f(x)-\mu\sum_{i=1}^p\log(-g_i(x)):h(x)=0\right\}.\] The solution family parameterized by \(\mu\to0\) is called the primal central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the nonlinear program has a strictly feasible point relative to its equality constraints, the solutions of its logarithmic-barrier subproblems as the positive barrier parameter approaches zero form the primal central path.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family \(\{x_\mu\}\) parameterized by \(\mu\to0\) is the primal central path.

children.top_down_role: Central trajectories represented through dual barrier models.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Central Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual path generated by a conjugate barrier on conic slack variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the conic dual problem
\[
\max\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^\top y+s=c,\ s\in\operatorname{int}K^*\},
\]
let \(F_*\) be a strictly convex barrier for \(K^*\). For each \(\mu>0\), define
\[
(y(\mu),s(\mu))\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{A^\top y+s=c,\,s\in\operatorname{int}K^*}
\{\langle b,y\rangle-\mu F_*(s)\}.
\]
Equivalently, for some \(x(\mu)\),
\[
A^\top y(\mu)+s(\mu)=c,
\qquad
Ax(\mu)=b,
\qquad
x(\mu)=-\mu\nabla F_*(s(\mu)).
\]
These dual solutions form the dual central path when they exist uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual central path maximizes the dual objective minus a barrier on the dual slack and satisfies dual feasibility with barrier-perturbed stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a proper cone and \(F_*\) is a strictly convex barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K^*\).
For every \(\mu>0\), the dual barrier problem has a unique solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((y(\mu),s(\mu))\) is characterized by dual feasibility and \(x(\mu)=-\mu\nabla F_*(s(\mu))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Applying a barrier to the conic dual slack gives the dual central-path representation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual barrier optimization model and its stationarity relation fit a dual-central-path representation. The signs in the multiplier and conjugate-barrier conventions require verification against a specific authoritative source, which is absent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Logarithmic-Barrier Central Path
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For the standard-form primal LP, let the dual feasible variables satisfy \(A^Ty+s=c\) and suppose \(\{(y,s):A^Ty+s=c,\ s>0\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly feasible linear-programming dual with a logarithmic barrier on the slack vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), a dual central point is \[(y(\mu),s(\mu))\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{A^Ty+s=c,\ s>0}\left\{b^Ty+\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log s_i\right\}.\] The dual central path is \(\mathcal C_D:=\{(y(\mu),s(\mu)):\mu>0\}\). Equivalently, its points admit \(x(\mu)>0\) with \(Ax=b\) and \(x_i(\mu)s_i(\mu)=\mu\) for all \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual central path is the curve of maximizers of the dual objective plus a positive logarithmic barrier on dual slacks. It is the dual projection of the coupled perturbed KKT trajectory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_D=\left\{\operatorname*{argmax}_{A^Ty+s=c,\ s>0}\left(b^Ty+\mu\sum_i\log s_i\right):\mu>0\right\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The same points minimize \(-b^Ty-\mu\sum_i\log s_i\) subject to \(A^Ty+s=c\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) lacks full row rank, \(y(\mu)\) may be nonunique even when the slack \(s(\mu)\) is unique.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every path point is dual feasible with \(s(\mu)>0\).
The associated primal variable is \(x=\mu S^{-1}e\), when it also satisfies \(Ax=b\).
boundary_notes: The sign in the dual barrier objective follows the maximization convention.
The path excludes \(\mu=0\) and does not itself define an infeasible-start trajectory.

children.title: Primal–Dual Central Paths
children.top_down_role: Coupled central trajectories for primal and dual systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Central Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled conic central path under logarithmically homogeneous conjugate barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a proper cone, let \(F\) be a \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous Legendre barrier on \(K\), and define the conjugate dual barrier by \(F_*(s)=F^*(-s)\). For every \(\mu>0\), a primal–dual central point satisfies
\[
Ax=b,
\qquad
A^\top y+s=c,
\qquad
s=-\mu\nabla F(x),
\]
with \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) and \(s\in\operatorname{int}K^*\). Equivalently,
\[
x=-\mu\nabla F_*(s).
\]
Logarithmic homogeneity also gives the complementarity identity
\[
\langle x,s\rangle=\mu\nu.
\]
The resulting triples \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) form the primal–dual central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual central points are coupled by feasibility and conjugate barrier gradients; their complementarity equals the barrier weight times the homogeneity parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a proper cone and \(F\) is a \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous Legendre barrier.
The primal and dual equality systems admit strictly feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled gradient equations are equivalent and imply \(\langle x(\mu),s(\mu)\rangle=\mu\nu\).

notation.meaning: conjugate barrier on the dual cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Conic central-path coupling follows from logarithmically homogeneous barrier conjugacy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coupled feasibility, conjugate-gradient, and logarithmic-homogeneity relations fit the primal–dual central-path duality container. A precise source is required to verify the definition \(F_*(s)=F^*(-s)\), the scaling by \(\mu\), and the complementarity identity under the stated conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coupled Primal–Dual Central Path for Linear Programming
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), with a nonempty strictly feasible primal-dual set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-form linear programming with componentwise logarithmic complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\mu>0\), the primal-dual central point is a triple \(z(\mu)=(x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) satisfying \[Ax=b,\qquad A^Ty+s=c,\qquad XSe=\mu e,\qquad x>0,\ s>0.\] The primal-dual central path is \[\mathcal C_{PD}:=\{z(\mu):\mu>0\}.\] Thus feasibility is exact and every componentwise complementarity product has the common target \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal–dual central path is the curve of strictly feasible primal-dual triples whose componentwise products \(x_i s_i\) all equal the same positive parameter. It couples the primal and dual central trajectories in one perturbed KKT system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_{PD}=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^Ty+s=c,\ x,s>0,\ x_is_i=\mu\ \forall i\text{ for some }\mu>0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[XSe=\mu e\iff s=\mu X^{-1}e\iff x=\mu S^{-1}e.\]
\[\mu=\frac{x^Ts}{n}.\]
special_cases_latex: The primal projection of \(\mathcal C_{PD}\) is \(\mathcal C_P\), and the \((y,s)\)-projection is \(\mathcal C_D\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The duality gap is \(x^Ts=n\mu\).
As \(\mu\downarrow0\), the perturbed complementarity equation approaches ordinary complementary slackness.
boundary_notes: Strict feasibility is essential for this exact feasible-path definition.
Central neighborhoods permit unequal products near \(\mu\); those points are not themselves on this path.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standard-form LP primal–dual central path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP specialization of the coupled primal–dual central-path representation. The extract's unconditional convergence wording is narrowed because path existence, boundedness, and multiplier regularity assumptions are not stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(D=\max\{b^T\lambda:A^T\lambda+\mu=c,\ \mu\geq0\}\), a primal\text{-}dual central-path point at parameter \(\tau>0\) is a triple \((x(\tau),\lambda(\tau),\mu(\tau))\) satisfying \(Ax(\tau)=b\), \(x(\tau)>0\), \(A^T\lambda(\tau)+\mu(\tau)=c\), \(\mu(\tau)>0\), and \(X(\tau)\mu(\tau)=\tau e\), where \(X(\tau)=\operatorname{diag}(x(\tau))\). Every such point is strictly primal and dual feasible. If a sequence of these points with \(\tau_k\downarrow0\) has a finite accumulation point \((\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\), then that accumulation point satisfies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness and hence is a primal\text{-}dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LP primal–dual central path consists of strictly feasible primal and dual points whose componentwise complementarity products equal a positive parameter. Any finite accumulation point as the parameter tends to zero is a primal–dual solution; unconditional convergence requires assumptions absent from the extract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ax=b,\ x>0,\ A^T\lambda+\mu=c,\ \mu>0,\ X\mu=\tau e;\quad \tau_k\downarrow0,\ (x_k,\lambda_k,\mu_k)\to(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\Rightarrow(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\text{ is primal\text{-}dual optimal}.

children.title: Weighted Central Paths
children.top_down_role: Generalized trajectories with nonuniform complementarity targets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Weight Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of strict interior complementarity if a purported weight vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(w_i=0\) and \(\mu>0\), then \(s_i z_i=\mu w_i=0\), which is incompatible with \(s_i>0\) and \(z_i>0\). A strictly interior weighted path therefore requires \(w_i>0\) for every component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero weight is incompatible with simultaneous positivity of its slack and multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w_i=0\Longrightarrow\neg(s_i>0\wedge z_i>0).
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Weight Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common Weight Scaling Reparameterizes the Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundancy between the common scale of the weights and the central-path parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\alpha>0\), \(Sz=\mu(\alpha w)\) is identical to \(Sz=(\alpha\mu)w\). Thus, when the remaining equations depend on \(\mu\) and \(w\) only through this target, common weight scaling leaves the geometric solution set unchanged and reparameterizes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only relative complementarity weights affect the geometric path.
assumptions_latex: The remaining path equations do not depend separately on \(\mu\) or \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C_{\alpha w}(\mu)=\mathcal C_w(\alpha\mu)\).

notation.meaning: solution set of the weighted central equations

knowledge_statements.title: Common Weight Scaling Reparameterizes the Path

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Complementarity Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate complementarity identity along the weighted central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Sz=\mu w\), then \[s^{\mathsf T}z=\sum_i s_i z_i=\mu\sum_iw_i.\] Hence complementarity normalized by total weight equals \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total complementarity equals the path parameter times the sum of the weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s^{\mathsf T}z=\mu e^{\mathsf T}w\).
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Complementarity Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Log-Barrier Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal weighted-barrier formulation whose first-order conditions generate componentwise weighted complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(s=-g(x)>0\) and \(w\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\), stationary points of \[\min_{h(x)=0,\ g(x)<0} f(x)-\mu\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\log(-g_i(x))\] satisfy \(\nabla_xL(x,y,z)=0\), \(h(x)=0\), \(g(x)+s=0\), and \(Sz=\mu w\) after setting \(z_i=\mu w_i/s_i\). Conversely, every solution of these equations is stationary for the displayed barrier subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementarity weights are precisely the coefficients of the logarithmic barrier terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z_i=\mu w_i/s_i\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Sz=\mu w.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Log-Barrier Equivalence
Weighted Central Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inequality-constrained weighted primal–dual path with positive complementarity weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\), and \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, and define \(L(x,y,z)=f(x)+y^{\mathsf T}h(x)+z^{\mathsf T}g(x)\). For a fixed weight vector \(w\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^m\), the weighted primal–dual central path is the set of tuples \((x(\mu),y(\mu),z(\mu),s(\mu))\), indexed by \(\mu>0\), satisfying \[\nabla_xL(x,y,z)=0,\qquad h(x)=0,\qquad g(x)+s=0,\qquad S z=\mu w,\qquad s,z\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^m.\] Here \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\); equivalently, \(s_i z_i=\mu w_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted central path satisfies primal feasibility, stationarity, positivity, and componentwise complementarity targets proportional to fixed positive weights.
assumptions_latex: A solution of the displayed system exists for each parameter value under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_i(\mu)z_i(\mu)=\mu w_i\) for every \(i\) and \(\mu>0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-dimensional primal-dual weighted-complementarity formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the weighted-central-path leaf, and the variables and sign convention are internally consistent. However, no inspectable source is cited for this particular weighted nonlinear primal–dual formulation, so the convention and scope remain unsupported.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Primal–Dual Central Path
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider a strictly feasible standard-form primal-dual linear program and fix a weight vector \(w\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear programming with fixed positive, nonuniform componentwise complementarity weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), a weighted central point \((x_w(\mu),y_w(\mu),s_w(\mu))\) satisfies \[Ax=b,\qquad A^Ty+s=c,\qquad XSe=\mu w,\qquad x>0,\ s>0.\] The weighted central path is \[\mathcal C_w:=\{(x_w(\mu),y_w(\mu),s_w(\mu)):\mu>0\}.\] Its primal component equivalently minimizes the weighted logarithmic barrier \[c^Tx-\mu\sum_{i=1}^nw_i\log x_i\quad\text{subject to }Ax=b,\ x>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted central path replaces the uniform complementarity target by positive targets proportional to fixed weights. It is equivalently generated by a logarithmic barrier in which constraint or coordinate logarithms receive unequal positive coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_i(\mu)s_i(\mu)=\mu w_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The scalar parameter can be normalized as \(\mu=x^Ts/(e^Tw)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(w=e\), \(\mathcal C_w\) is the ordinary primal-dual central path.
Multiplying \(w\) by a positive scalar only reparameterizes the same geometric curve.
immediate_consequences_latex: The duality gap on the weighted path is \(x^Ts=\mu e^Tw\).
Relative products satisfy \(x_is_i/(x_js_j)=w_i/w_j\).
boundary_notes: Weights must be strictly positive to preserve strict complementarity along the path.
Iteration-dependent weights define a moving target and are not the fixed weighted path defined here.
The inspected sources supported the uniform path but not this weighted generalization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lifecycle Data of a Parameterized Central Path
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R(z,\mu)=0\) be a centrality system on an interior state domain \(\mathcal Z^\circ\), with parameter \(\mu\in I\subseteq(0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional barrier or primal-dual paths; endpoint behavior is recorded separately from interior existence and regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lifecycle of a central path is the tuple \[\mathfrak L(\mathcal C):=(I,\ z:I\to\mathcal Z^\circ,\ \mathcal R,\ \Omega_0),\] where \(R(z(\mu),\mu)=0\) for every \(\mu\in I\), \(\mathcal R:=\{\mu\in I:R_z(z(\mu),\mu)\text{ is nonsingular}\}\), and \[\Omega_0:=\{\bar z:\exists\mu_k\downarrow0,\ z(\mu_k)\to\bar z\}\] is the endpoint cluster set. Existence, uniqueness, smoothness, sensitivity, and endpoint selection are distinct lifecycle properties of this tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Central-path lifecycle data record the parameter interval on which the path exists, the selected solution branch, the subset where its centrality Jacobian is regular, and the set of accumulation points as the barrier parameter tends to zero. These components distinguish interior path existence from endpoint convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal R=I\implies z\text{ is locally continuously differentiable throughout }I,\quad \Omega_0\text{ records all finite zero-parameter limits}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\Omega_0=\{z^*\}\) and the path is bounded near zero, the lifecycle has a uniquely selected endpoint \(z^*\).
special_cases_latex: For a strictly feasible LP, the central path exists for every \(\mu>0\), and its primal and slack components are unique.
For a locally regular nonlinear program, the lifecycle may be defined only on \((0,\bar\mu)\) near a particular KKT solution.
immediate_consequences_latex: A singular value of \(R_z\) lies outside the regular portion \(\mathcal R\).
Non-singleton \(\Omega_0\) represents endpoint nonuniqueness or failure of full convergence.
boundary_notes: This definition does not assert that \(I=(0,\infty)\) or that \(\Omega_0\) is nonempty.
Divergent trajectories have no finite endpoint in \(\Omega_0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Primal–Dual Feasibility Regime for Central-Path Existence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a standard-form LP, define the strictly feasible primal-dual set \(\mathcal F^\circ:=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^Ty+s=c,\ x>0,\ s>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear programming; the nonlinear-programming analogue replaces strict LP feasibility by local regularity assumptions around a KKT solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The global interior-feasibility existence regime is \[\mathfrak E_{PD}:=\{(A,b,c):\mathcal F^\circ\ne\varnothing\}.\] A problem lies in this regime precisely when it possesses simultaneously a strictly feasible primal point and a strictly feasible dual slack. For data in \(\mathfrak E_{PD}\), the centrality equations \[Ax=b,\quad A^Ty+s=c,\quad XSe=\mu e,\quad x,s>0\] are the defining system for every \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict primal–dual feasibility regime consists of linear programs having both a positive primal feasible point and a positive dual slack. This is the natural global existence regime for the ordinary feasible central path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal F^\circ\ne\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists x>0:Ax=b\ \text{ and }\ \exists(y,s),\ s>0:A^Ty+s=c.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\mathfrak E_{PD}=\mathfrak E_P\cap\mathfrak E_D,\] where \(\mathfrak E_P\) and \(\mathfrak E_D\) denote strict primal and strict dual feasibility regimes.
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has full row rank, the central multiplier is unique once the dual slack is fixed.
For nonlinear programs, LICQ, strict complementarity, and second-order sufficiency yield a local rather than global existence regime near a selected solution.
immediate_consequences_latex: Within this regime, the LP central path has a central point for every positive parameter.
Outside this regime, homogeneous self-dual embeddings or infeasible-start paths are separate constructions.
boundary_notes: Ordinary feasibility with zero components is not strict feasibility.
The definition does not claim that the optimal set is bounded.

children.title: Primal Strict-Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Central-path existence questions governed by nonempty primal interiors.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Strict-Feasibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict feasibility for equality and inequality constraints in slack form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the feasible set defined by \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le 0\), the primal strict-feasibility condition is \[\exists\,x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\quad h(x)=0,\qquad g_i(x)<0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Equivalently, there exist \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(s\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^m\) such that \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)+s=0\). This condition makes the logarithmic barrier \(-\sum_{i=1}^m\log s_i\) finite at at least one equality-feasible point. It does not, without convexity, coercivity, and regularity assumptions, guarantee existence or uniqueness of a central-path point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal strict feasibility means that all equalities hold while every inequality has strictly positive slack.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:h(x)=0,\ g(x)<0\}\ne\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Slater-type primal interior condition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly expresses primal strict feasibility and appropriately warns that it alone does not ensure central-path existence. The condition kind fits the terminal container, but the record supplies no source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator.

children.title: Dual Strict-Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Central-path existence questions governed by nonempty dual interiors.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Strict-Feasibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict positivity of inequality multipliers within the dual-stationary system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L(x,y,z)=f(x)+y^{\mathsf T}h(x)+z^{\mathsf T}g(x)\), a dual strictly feasible stationary tuple is a triple \((x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}_{++}^m\) satisfying \[\nabla_xL(x,y,z)=0.\] Thus the dual strict-feasibility regime is characterized by nonemptiness of \(\{(x,y,z):\nabla_xL(x,y,z)=0,\ z>0\}\). In a conic or linear specialization, this is the usual requirement that the dual affine constraints admit a point in the interior of the dual cone. This condition alone neither imposes primal feasibility on \(x\) nor ensures a central-path solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual strict feasibility requires a stationary dual tuple whose inequality multipliers are all strictly positive.
assumptions_latex: Inequality multipliers use the convention \(z\ge0\) for constraints \(g(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,y,z):\nabla_xL(x,y,z)=0,\ z\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^m\}\ne\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but calling existence of a positive stationary tuple “dual strict feasibility” for a general nonlinear program is convention-dependent and is not equivalent to ordinary dual feasibility without a specified dual construction. A precise nonlinear-programming or specialized central-path source is required.

children.title: Simultaneous Interior Regimes
children.top_down_role: Path behavior when compatible primal and dual interior points are available.

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Interior Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint primal and dual interior availability, allowing distinct witnessing points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonlinear program is in a simultaneous interior regime when there exist \(x^{\mathrm p}\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(s^{\mathrm p}\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^m\), and a possibly distinct triple \((x^{\mathrm d},y^{\mathrm d},z^{\mathrm d})\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}_{++}^m\) such that \[h(x^{\mathrm p})=0,\qquad g(x^{\mathrm p})+s^{\mathrm p}=0,\qquad \nabla_xL(x^{\mathrm d},y^{\mathrm d},z^{\mathrm d})=0.\] For convex linear or conic problems, analogous primal and dual Slater conditions are the standard interior hypotheses for central-path existence. For a general nonlinear program, the displayed condition remains only an interior-availability condition and requires additional solvability and regularity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simultaneous interior regime has both a strictly feasible primal witness and a strictly positive dual-stationary witness.

children.title: Path-Existence Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Existence Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary interior conditions and a concrete empty-barrier-domain obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Any primal–dual central-path point satisfying \(g(x)+s=0\), \(s>0\), and \(S z=\mu w\) with \(\mu>0\) and \(w>0\) necessarily has \(g(x)<0\) and \(z>0\). Consequently, emptiness of either the primal strict-feasibility set or the positive dual-stationary set rules out such a point. The obstruction is sharp on the primal side: the problem \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}} x^2\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad x^2\le0\] has the feasible optimum \(x=0\), but no point satisfies \(x^2<0\). Its logarithmic-barrier domain is empty, so no positive-parameter primal barrier path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A central path cannot exist when required interiors are empty; even a solvable problem may have an empty logarithmic-barrier domain.
assumptions_latex: Central-path slacks and multipliers are required to be positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\{x:h(x)=0,\ g(x)<0\}=\varnothing\), then no positive-parameter primal–dual central-path point exists.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct consequence of positive slack and complementarity equations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Central-Path Branch and Its Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb R^q\times(0,\bar\mu)\to\mathbb R^q\) be \(C^k\), \(k\ge1\), and let \(z:(0,\bar\mu)\to\mathbb R^q\) satisfy \(R(z(\mu),\mu)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth regularity of a selected finite-dimensional central-path branch; endpoint regularity at \(\mu=0\) is not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The branch \(z(\mu)\) is regular on an interval \(J\subseteq(0,\bar\mu)\) when \[\det R_z(z(\mu),\mu)\ne0\qquad\forall\mu\in J.\] Its first-order parameter sensitivity is then the uniquely defined vector \[\dot z(\mu):=-R_z(z(\mu),\mu)^{-1}R_\mu(z(\mu),\mu).\] If \(R\) is \(C^k\), regularity designates the corresponding locally \(C^k\) solution branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A central path is regular on an interval when the Jacobian of its defining residual with respect to all state variables is nonsingular at every point of that interval. The inverse Jacobian then defines a unique path tangent and local parameter sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R_z(z(\mu),\mu)\dot z(\mu)=-R_\mu(z(\mu),\mu),\qquad \mu\in J.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Regularity is equivalent to local single-valued solvability of the centrality system as a smooth function of \(\mu\).
special_cases_latex: For nonlinear programming, LICQ, strict complementarity, and second-order sufficient conditions provide a standard local regime in which the perturbed KKT branch is locally unique for sufficiently small \(\mu>0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The condition number of \(R_z\) quantifies first-order sensitivity to residual and parameter perturbations.
A singular Jacobian excludes the point from the regular branch, even if a continuous path still passes through it.
boundary_notes: Regularity on \(J\) does not guarantee boundedness or a limit as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
At degenerate endpoints, differentiability may fail even when the interior branch is smooth.

notation.meaning: State Jacobian of the centrality system.
Derivative of the regular branch with respect to \(\mu\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Analytic Central-Path Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Analytic implicit-function regularity for a regular central-path branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\times I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be real analytic, where \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) are open. If \(F(u_0,\mu_0)=0\) and \(D_uF(u_0,\mu_0)\) is nonsingular, then there are neighborhoods of \(u_0\) and \(\mu_0\) on which the solutions of \(F(u,\mu)=0\) form a unique real-analytic branch \(u=u(\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An analytic central-path residual produces a locally unique analytic path wherever its path Jacobian is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u(\mu)\) is locally unique and real analytic.
knowledge_statements.title: Analytic Central-Path Regime
Central-Path Differentiability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local implicit-function regularity for a primal–dual central-path branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u=(x,y,z,s)\) and define \[F(u,\mu)=\bigl(\nabla_xL(x,y,z),\ h(x),\ g(x)+s,\ S z-\mu w\bigr).\] Suppose \(f,h,g\) are twice continuously differentiable, \(F(u_0,\mu_0)=0\), \(s_0,z_0>0\), and the Jacobian \(D_uF(u_0,\mu_0)\) is nonsingular. Then there are neighborhoods of \(\mu_0\) and \(u_0\) containing a unique continuously differentiable function \(u(\mu)\) such that \(u(\mu_0)=u_0\) and \(F(u(\mu),\mu)=0\). If the problem data are \(C^k\), the local path is \(C^{k-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular primal–dual Jacobian makes the central path locally unique and differentiable in the barrier parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a unique local \(C^1\) branch \(u(\mu)\) satisfying \(F(u(\mu),\mu)=0\).

children.title: Barrier-Parameter Sensitivity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Barrier-Sensitivity Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise conditioning of the central path with respect to the barrier parameter at a regular point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(u(\mu),\mu)=0\), let \(J(\mu)=D_uF(u(\mu),\mu)\) be nonsingular, and suppose the complementarity block is \(Sz-\mu w\), with fixed \(w\). For every subordinate operator norm, \[\|u'(\mu)\|=\|J(\mu)^{-1}(0,0,0,w)\|\le \|J(\mu)^{-1}\|\,\|w\|.\] Consequently, if \(u\) is continuously differentiable on an interval \(I\) and \(\sup_{\mu\in I}\|J(\mu)^{-1}\|<\infty\), then \(u\) is Lipschitz on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse central-path Jacobian bounds barrier-parameter sensitivity; a uniformly bounded inverse gives a Lipschitz path on the parameter interval.
assumptions_latex: The complementarity residual is \(Sz-\mu w\), with fixed \(w\).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Barrier-Sensitivity Bound
Barrier-Parameter Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative equation for a regular weighted primal–dual path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(u,\mu)=0\) denote the weighted central-path system with complementarity residual \(S z-\mu w\), and suppose \(u(\mu)\) is differentiable and \(J(\mu)=D_uF(u(\mu),\mu)\) is nonsingular. Differentiating the residual identity gives \[J(\mu)u'(\mu)+\partial_\mu F(u(\mu),\mu)=0,\qquad \partial_\mu F=(0,0,0,-w).\] Hence the barrier-parameter sensitivity is uniquely represented by \[u'(\mu)=J(\mu)^{-1}(0,0,0,w).\] Equivalently, it is the solution of the linearized KKT system whose only nonzero right-hand-side block is the complementarity-weight vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular path point, the derivative with respect to the barrier parameter solves one linearized KKT system.
assumptions_latex: The complementarity equation is \(S z=\mu w\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint Data-Sensitivity Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjoint evaluation of derivatives of scalar outputs of a regular central-path point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(u,\mu,a)=0\), with \(J=D_uF\) nonsingular, and let \(\psi(u,a)\) be a differentiable scalar output at fixed \(\mu\). Define the adjoint \(\lambda\) by \[J^{\mathsf T}\lambda=\nabla_u\psi.\] Then \[D_a[\psi(u(\mu,a),a)]=D_a\psi-\lambda^{\mathsf T}D_aF.\] Thus one transposed KKT solve evaluates the gradient of a scalar output without forming the full state-sensitivity matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transposed linearized KKT solve converts state sensitivity into an adjoint derivative formula for scalar outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_a[\psi(u(\mu,a),a)]=D_a\psi-\lambda^{\mathsf T}D_aF\), where \(D_uF^{\mathsf T}\lambda=\nabla_u\psi\).

notation.meaning: scalar output of the central-path state

knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Data-Sensitivity Formula
Problem-Data Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local derivative of a regular central path under smooth data perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\in\mathbb{R}^q\) parameterize the objective or constraints, and let \(F(u,\mu,a)=0\) be the associated central-path residual. Fix \((\mu_0,a_0)\), and suppose \(F\) is continuously differentiable and \(J=D_uF(u_0,\mu_0,a_0)\) is nonsingular. Then the locally unique path solution \(u(\mu,a)\) is differentiable with respect to \(a\), and for every perturbation direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^q\), \[D_a u(\mu_0,a_0)d=-J^{-1}D_aF(u_0,\mu_0,a_0)d.\] Thus first-order path sensitivity is obtained by solving the same linearized KKT operator with a right-hand side induced by the data perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth data perturbations change a regular central-path point according to an implicit linearized KKT sensitivity equation.

children.title: Path-Regularity Loss

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular Jacobian Without Path Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp example showing that Jacobian singularity removes a guarantee but does not force an irregular solution branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(u,\mu)=(u-\mu)^3\), the equation \(F(u,\mu)=0\) has the unique solution branch \(u(\mu)=\mu\), which is analytic. Nevertheless, \[D_uF(u(\mu),\mu)=3(u(\mu)-\mu)^2=0\] at every point of the branch. Thus singularity of the implicit Jacobian is not sufficient for branching, nonuniqueness, or loss of differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path can remain unique and analytic even though its implicit Jacobian is singular everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_uF=0\) along the unique analytic branch \(u(\mu)=\mu\).
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Jacobian Without Path Loss
Path-Regularity Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular implicit Jacobians mark the boundary of guaranteed smooth path continuation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a central-path residual \(F(u,\mu)=0\), nonsingularity of \(D_uF\) is sufficient for a locally unique differentiable parameterization. Therefore the implicit-function guarantee can fail only upon leaving the smooth domain or reaching a point where \[\det D_uF(u,\mu)=0.\] At such a point the sensitivity equation may have no solution or multiple solutions, and its inverse-based condition number is unbounded. Singularity alone does not prove that every continuous parameterization fails, but it permits folds, branching, loss of uniqueness, or unbounded derivatives. The scalar residual \(F(u,\mu)=u^3-\mu\) illustrates endpoint loss: \(u(\mu)=\mu^{1/3}\) is not differentiable at \(\mu=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth continuation loses its guarantee when the central-path Jacobian becomes singular; branching, nonuniqueness, or unbounded sensitivity may then occur.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near the point considered.
Path regularity is assessed through the implicit residual equation \(F(u,\mu)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det D_uF=0\) is the boundary at which local uniqueness and differentiability are no longer guaranteed by the implicit function theorem.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: boundary of the implicit-function regularity condition

A source is still required for the asserted central-path interpretation, permitted failure modes, and conditioning statement; the scalar example alone does not establish those specialized claims.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal-Face Selection Depends on Constraint Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation dependence of logarithmic-barrier endpoint selection on a fixed non-singleton optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every point of \(F^*=[0,1]\) be optimal. The barrier for \(x\ge0\) and \(1-x\ge0\) maximizes \(\log x+\log(1-x)\) and selects \(x=1/2\). Duplicating \(x\ge0\) gives \(2\log x+\log(1-x)\) and selects \(x=2/3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating an inequality can change the analytic-center point selected from an unchanged optimal face.
assumptions_latex: Each listed inequality contributes one logarithmic-barrier term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{\mathrm{center}}=\tfrac12\text{ before duplication and }x_{\mathrm{center}}=\tfrac23\text{ afterward}.

Optimal-Face Limit Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted analytic-center selection for a bounded linear-program optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), assume strict feasibility, and let its nonempty optimal face \(F^*\) be bounded. Let \(I_0\) contain the inequalities active at every point of \(F^*\), and suppose the weighted analytic center \[x_w^*=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\operatorname{relint}F^*}\sum_{i\notin I_0}w_i\log(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)\] exists uniquely for \(w>0\). Then the weighted logarithmic-barrier minimizers \(x(\mu)\), when uniquely defined, satisfy \(x(\mu)\to x_w^*\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). Thus the weights select a distinguished point within a non-singleton optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded linear-program optimal face, the weighted barrier path selects its weighted analytic center.
assumptions_latex: The linear program is strictly feasible and has a nonempty bounded optimal face.
The weighted barrier minimizer exists uniquely for every sufficiently small \(\mu>0\).
The relative weighted analytic center of the optimal face exists uniquely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle\lim_{\mu\downarrow0}x(\mu)=x_w^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Central-Path Selection of a Point in an Optimal Face
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron, let \(F^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^Tx\) be its nonempty optimal face, and let \(x(\mu)\) be a primal central path for \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral convex optimization with a bounded central trajectory and possibly nonunique primal optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x^\dagger\in F^*\) is selected by the central path when \[\lim_{\mu\downarrow0}x(\mu)=x^\dagger.\] More generally, the selected optimal-face limit set is \[\operatorname{Sel}(\mathcal C_P,F^*):=\left\{x^\dagger\in F^*: \exists\mu_k\downarrow0\text{ with }x(\mu_k)\to x^\dagger\right\}.\] Selection is unique exactly when this set is a singleton and the full path converges to its member.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimal-face limit selection records which point or points of a non-singleton optimal face arise as zero-parameter limits of the interior central trajectory. A unique selected limit is a point approached by the whole path, not merely by one subsequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Sel}(\mathcal C_P,F^*)\subseteq F^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\operatorname{Sel}(\mathcal C_P,F^*)=\{x^\dagger\}\) and the path is relatively compact near zero, then \(x(\mu)\to x^\dagger\).
special_cases_latex: For logarithmic LP central paths, the selected point is typically an interior point of the optimal face rather than an extreme-point solution.
If \(F^*\) is a singleton \(\{x^*\}\), every finite selected limit must equal \(x^*\).

Different barriers or weights can induce different selection rules on the same optimal face.

children.title: Degenerate Central-Path Endpoints
children.top_down_role: Irregular or ill-conditioned endpoint regimes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square-Root Approach to a Degenerate Endpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional barrier path with a complementarity-degenerate endpoint and unbounded parameter derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_{x\ge0}\ \frac12x^2.\] Writing the bound as \(-x\le0\), the primal-dual central equations are \(x-z=0\), \(s=x\), and \(sz=\mu\). Their positive solution is \[x(\mu)=s(\mu)=z(\mu)=\sqrt{\mu}.\] The endpoint has \(s^*=z^*=0\), and \(x'(\mu)=1/(2\sqrt{\mu})\to\infty\). Thus a finite, unique central path can approach a degenerate endpoint with only Hölder, rather than Lipschitz, dependence on \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound-constrained quadratic has a unique central path that approaches its degenerate endpoint at square-root rate with an unbounded derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(\mu)=s(\mu)=z(\mu)=\sqrt{\mu}\) and \(x'(\mu)\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Square-Root Approach to a Degenerate Endpoint

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Endpoint Complementarity Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise rates implied by perturbed complementarity near a finite endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(s_i(\mu)z_i(\mu)=\mu w_i\), where \(w_i>0\), and \((s_i(\mu),z_i(\mu))\to(s_i^*,z_i^*)\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). If \(z_i^*>0\), then \[s_i(\mu)=\frac{\mu w_i}{z_i(\mu)}=\Theta(\mu).\] If \(s_i^*>0\), then \[z_i(\mu)=\frac{\mu w_i}{s_i(\mu)}=\Theta(\mu).\] If \(s_i^*=z_i^*=0\), complementarity alone determines neither factor's rate; balanced decay \(s_i,z_i=\Theta(\sqrt{\mu})\) is possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly complementary endpoint pairs force linear decay of the vanishing factor, whereas degenerate pairs may exhibit slower balanced decay.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_i^*>0\Rightarrow s_i(\mu)=\Theta(\mu)\), and \(s_i^*>0\Rightarrow z_i(\mu)=\Theta(\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint Complementarity Scaling
Degenerate Central-Path Endpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint degeneracy through failure of strict complementarity or nonsingular KKT linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^*,y^*,z^*,s^*)\) be an accumulation point of a primal–dual central path as \(\mu\downarrow0\), so that \(s^*,z^*\ge0\) and \(s_i^*z_i^*=0\). The endpoint is complementarity-degenerate if \[\exists i:\qquad s_i^*=0\quad\text{and}\quad z_i^*=0,\] equivalently, strict complementarity \(s_i^*+z_i^*>0\) fails. More generally, it is KKT-degenerate when the limiting linearized KKT system is singular, as can occur through dependent active-constraint gradients or failure of a second-order sufficient condition. Such degeneracy removes the standard nonsingularity basis for bounded sensitivity and smooth continuation to the endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A central-path endpoint is degenerate when strict complementarity fails or the limiting KKT linearization is singular.
assumptions_latex: The central path has an accumulation point as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
The endpoint satisfies nonnegative slack and multiplier complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complementarity degeneracy occurs exactly when \(s_i^*=z_i^*=0\) for at least one inequality index \(i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate central-path endpoint in linear optimization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the primal–dual linear programs \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\), with nonempty strictly feasible set. Let \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\), \(\mu>0\), satisfy \(Ax(\mu)=b\), \(A^Ty(\mu)+s(\mu)=c\), and \(X(\mu)S(\mu)e=\mu e\). Denote the primal and dual optimal sets by \(\mathcal P^*\) and \(\mathcal D^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear optimization with a well-defined, bounded central-path limit; degeneracy is used in the multiple-optimum sense adopted by the cited source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The endpoint \(z^*=(x^*,y^*,s^*)=\lim_{\mu\downarrow0}(x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) is called a degenerate central-path endpoint when \(\dim\mathcal P^*>0\) or \(\dim\mathcal D^*>0\), equivalently when the primal or dual problem has more than one optimal solution. In this case \(x^*\) and \((y^*,s^*)\) are the analytic centers of their respective optimal sets: on each set they maximize the product of all coordinates that can be positive on that set. Thus the endpoint is uniquely selected by the central path even though the underlying optimal solution set is not a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate central-path endpoint is the unique limit selected by the linear-programming central path when at least one of the primal or dual optimal sets contains multiple points. Equivalently, at least one optimal set has positive affine dimension. The selected limiting primal and dual solutions are the analytic centers of their respective optimal sets, formed using the coordinates that can be positive somewhere on those sets.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and the primal–dual pair has a nonempty strictly feasible set.
The central path exists for every \(\mu>0\) and its optimal set is bounded, so its limit and the relevant analytic centers are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*\text{ is degenerate}\iff \dim\mathcal P^*>0\ \text{or}\ \dim\mathcal D^*>0\), while \(z^*\) remains the uniquely determined analytic-center endpoint.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The endpoint is degenerate exactly when the primal or dual problem has multiple optimal solutions.
Using the optimal partition \((B,N)\), primal nonuniqueness is equivalent to \(|B|-\operatorname{rank}(A_B)>0\), and dual nonuniqueness is equivalent to \(m-\operatorname{rank}(A_B)>0\).
special_cases_latex: If both \(\mathcal P^*\) and \(\mathcal D^*\) are singletons, the endpoint is nondegenerate in this multiple-optimum sense.
If only \(\mathcal P^*\) has positive dimension, the primal endpoint is its analytic center while the dual optimum is unique.
immediate_consequences_latex: Degeneracy does not destroy endpoint uniqueness: the central path selects one distinguished point from each optimal face.
The limiting pair is strictly complementary under the stated linear-optimization hypotheses even when an optimal face has positive dimension.
boundary_notes: This definition is not simplex-basis degeneracy, which concerns zero basic variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–dual centrality neighborhood
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a standard-form linear program, let \(\mathcal F^o=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^Ty+s=c,\ x>0,\ s>0\}\). For \(z=(x,y,s)\in\mathcal F^o\), set \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), \(e=(1,\ldots,1)^T\), and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal–dual linear-programming neighborhoods measured by the balance of componentwise complementarity products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A centrality neighborhood is a parameterized subset of \(\mathcal F^o\) that bounds the deviation of \(XSe=(x_is_i)_{i=1}^n\) from its central-path value \(\mu e\). Canonical instances are \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\{z\in\mathcal F^o:\|XSe-\mu e\|_2\leq\theta\mu\}\), where \(0\leq\theta<1\), and \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{z\in\mathcal F^o:x_is_i\geq\gamma\mu\ \text{for every }i\}\), where \(0<\gamma\leq1\). Membership therefore requires strict primal–dual feasibility and a quantitative balance condition on all complementarity products.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal–dual centrality neighborhood consists of strictly feasible points whose componentwise complementarity products remain quantitatively balanced around their average. The standard narrow neighborhood bounds the Euclidean deviation of the product vector from the constant vector with value equal to the duality measure. The standard wide neighborhood instead requires every product to be at least a fixed fraction of that average.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has full row rank and \(\mathcal F^o\neq\varnothing\).
The neighborhood parameters satisfy \(0\leq\theta<1\) for \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)\) and \(0<\gamma\leq1\) for \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\) is central to the prescribed tolerance precisely when it belongs to the corresponding sublevel set \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)\) or one-sided balance set \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(z\in\mathcal N_2(\theta)\iff \|(XSe)/(\mu)-e\|_2\leq\theta\).
\(z\in\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\iff \min_i x_is_i/\mu\geq\gamma\).
special_cases_latex: \(\mathcal N_2(0)\) is exactly the central path because \(XSe=\mu e\).
\(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(1)\) is exactly the central path, since the products have average \(\mu\) and every product is at least \(\mu\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(z\in\mathcal N_2(\theta)\), each product satisfies \((1-\theta)\mu\leq x_is_i\leq(1+\theta)\mu\).
For \(z\in\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\), no complementary pair can approach zero independently while \(\mu\) stays positive.
boundary_notes: These definitions impose exact primal and dual equality feasibility; infeasible-start neighborhoods add residual bounds.
Other norms and barrier geometries produce related neighborhoods but are not identified with these two canonical LP sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nesting and Zero-Radius Core of Narrow Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic set ordering and endpoint of feasible Euclidean centrality neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\theta\ge0\), let \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)\) be the primal-dual feasible positive points satisfying \(\|Xs-\mu e\|_2\le\theta\mu\), where \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\). If \(0\le\theta_1\le\theta_2\), then \(\mathcal N_2(\theta_1)\subseteq\mathcal N_2(\theta_2)\). Moreover, \(\mathcal N_2(0)\) is exactly the feasible positive central-path slice \(Xs=\mu e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Narrow Euclidean neighborhoods expand with their radius, and radius zero is the feasible central-path slice.
assumptions_latex: Primal-dual feasibility and strict positivity hold
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_2(\theta_1)\subseteq\mathcal N_2(\theta_2)\) and \(\mathcal N_2(0)=\{(x,y,s):Xs=\mu e\}\) within the feasible positive domain.

notation.meaning: feasible Euclidean centrality neighborhood of radius theta

knowledge_statements.title: Nesting and Zero-Radius Core of Narrow Neighborhoods
Narrow Centrality Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean narrow neighborhood for feasible primal–dual linear-program iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal–dual feasible linear-program point with \(x,s\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), define \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\) and \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\). For \(0<\theta<1\), the narrow Euclidean centrality neighborhood is \[\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\left\{(x,y,s):\ Ax=b,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ x>0,\ s>0,\ \lVert Xs-\mu\mathbf 1\rVert_2\le\theta\mu\right\}.\] Every point in this neighborhood satisfies \((1-\theta)\mu\le x_i s_i\le(1+\theta)\mu\) for all \(i\). Small fixed \(\theta\) enforces uniformly tight componentwise proximity to the primal–dual central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A narrow neighborhood consists of feasible positive iterates whose complementarity products remain tightly clustered around their mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert Xs-\mu\mathbf 1\rVert_2\le\theta\mu\), implying \((1-\theta)\mu\le x_i s_i\le(1+\theta)\mu\) for every \(i\).

children.title: Wide Centrality Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Broader centrality regimes permitting more aggressive progress.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parameter Nesting and Unit-Parameter Core
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic ordering and limiting endpoint of the one-sided wide-neighborhood family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Extend the one-sided family to \(0<\gamma\le1\) by \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(x,s)>0:x_is_i\ge\gamma\mu\ \forall i\}\), where \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\). If \(0<\gamma_1\le\gamma_2\le1\), then \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_2)\subseteq\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_1)\). At \(\gamma=1\), the mean identity forces \(x_is_i=\mu\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing the lower-fraction parameter shrinks the wide neighborhood, and the unit endpoint is exactly the central-product set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_2)\subseteq\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_1)\) and \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(1)=\{(x,s)>0:x_is_i=\mu\ \forall i\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Nesting and Unit-Parameter Core

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Component Spread in a Wide Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp upper component bound implied by the one-sided neighborhood condition and the mean identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_i=x_is_i\), \(\mu=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nq_i>0\), and suppose \(q_i\ge\gamma\mu\) for every \(i\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(0<\gamma<1\). Then \[\gamma\mu\le q_i\le\bigl(n-(n-1)\gamma\bigr)\mu\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] The upper factor is sharp: equality is attained when \((q_1/\mu,q_2/\mu,\ldots,q_n/\mu)=(n-(n-1)\gamma,\gamma,\ldots,\gamma)\). Hence the one-sided condition alone permits upper deviation growing linearly with dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The wide condition has a sharp dimension-dependent upper bound and can permit one product to be much larger than the mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_iq_i/\mu\le n-(n-1)\gamma\), sharply.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Component Spread in a Wide Neighborhood
Wide Centrality Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual linear-programming neighborhood defined by a one-sided componentwise complementarity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For strictly positive primal–dual variables \(x,s\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), define \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(e=(1,\ldots,1)^\top\), and \(\mu=x^\top s/n\). For a fixed parameter \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), the wide centrality neighborhood is
\[
\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(x,s):x>0,\ s>0,\ x_i s_i\geq \gamma\mu\text{ for every }i=1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
Primal and dual feasibility conditions may be appended when the neighborhood is used by a feasible path-following method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive primal–dual pair is widely central when no componentwise complementarity product falls below a fixed fraction of their average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,s)\in\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\iff \min_i x_i s_i\geq\gamma x^\top s/n\).

notation.meaning: average complementarity, equal to x-transpose-s divided by n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Upper Spread Bound in a Wide Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The strongest upper component bound implied solely by the one-sided wide-neighborhood condition and the mean identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_i=x_i s_i\), \(\mu=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n q_i>0\), and suppose \(q_i\ge\gamma\mu\) for every \(i\), where \(0<\gamma<1\). Then \[\gamma\mu\le q_i\le\bigl(n-(n-1)\gamma\bigr)\mu\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] The upper factor is sharp: equality is attained by normalized products \((q_1/\mu,4,q_n/\mu)=(n-(n-1)\gamma,4,\gamma)\). Consequently, this wide condition permits a componentwise deviation of order \(n\) and supplies no dimension-independent symmetric centrality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-sided wide condition has a sharp dimension-dependent upper bound, so it can permit one complementarity product to be much larger than the mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i q_i/\mu\le n-(n-1)\gamma\), sharply.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two scalar representations of primal–dual centrality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(z=(x,y,s)\in\mathcal F^o\), \(w=XSe\), and \(\mu=x^Ts/n>0\). The normalized complementarity vector is \(q=w/\mu\), whose entries are positive and satisfy \(e^Tq=n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The Euclidean-deviation and one-sided minimum-ratio representations of centrality for feasible primal–dual linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The canonical centrality representation pair is \(\delta_2(z)=\|XSe-\mu e\|_2/\mu=\|q-e\|_2\) and \(\delta_{-}(z)=1-\min_{1\leq i\leq n}x_is_i/\mu=1-\min_iq_i\). The first records symmetric Euclidean dispersion around equal complementarity; the second records only the worst downward deviation. Their parameterized level sets recover the standard neighborhoods: \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\{z\in\mathcal F^o:\delta_2(z)\leq\theta\}\) and \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{z\in\mathcal F^o:\delta_-(z)\leq1-\gamma\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The representation pair assigns two scalar centrality scores to a strictly feasible primal–dual point. The first is the Euclidean norm of the normalized complementarity vector minus the all-ones vector. The second is one minus the smallest normalized complementarity product. Thresholding the first score gives the standard narrow neighborhood, while thresholding the second gives the standard wide one-sided neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The normalization uses the arithmetic mean \(\mu=n^{-1}\sum_i x_is_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\delta_2,\delta_-)\) gives two distinct scalar organizations of path proximity whose sublevel sets are exactly \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)\) and \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\delta_-(z)=\max_i(1-x_is_i/\mu)\).
special_cases_latex: \(\delta_2(z)=0\iff\delta_-(z)=0\iff XSe=\mu e\), so both scores vanish exactly on the central path.
A point can have small \(\delta_-\) while having comparatively large upward complementarity deviations; the one-sided representation does not symmetrically penalize them.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\delta_-(z)\leq\delta_2(z)\), because each coordinate deviation is bounded by its Euclidean norm.
Every \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)\) point belongs to \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(1-\theta)\).
boundary_notes: The pair represents centrality, not primal or dual equality infeasibility.
The notation \(-\infty\) traditionally denotes a one-sided infinity-type neighborhood; it is not an extended-real value of the score.

children.title: Componentwise Centrality Criteria
children.top_down_role: Path-proximity measures resolved across individual complementarity components.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Positivity Boundary for Relative Componentwise Centrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp tolerance boundary at which the componentwise criterion ceases to exclude zero complementarity products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in\mathbb R_+^n\), \(n\ge2\), \(\mu=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nq_i>0\), and \(|q_i-\mu|\le\theta\mu\) for every \(i\). If \(0\le\theta<1\), then \(q_i\ge(1-\theta)\mu>0\) for every \(i\). This threshold is sharp: for \(\theta=1\), \(q=(0,n\mu/(n-1),\ldots,n\mu/(n-1))\) has mean \(\mu\), satisfies the criterion, and has a zero component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative componentwise tolerance below one guarantees positive products; at tolerance one a zero product can satisfy the criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta<1\Rightarrow\min_iq_i\ge(1-\theta)\mu>0\), and the implication fails at \(\theta=1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Positivity Boundary for Relative Componentwise Centrality
Componentwise Centrality Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative componentwise proximity of complementarity products to their common average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x,s\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) and \(\mu=x^\top s/n\). For \(\theta\in[0,1)\), the componentwise centrality criterion is
\[
|x_i s_i-\mu|\leq\theta\mu\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n).
\]
Equivalently, every scaled complementarity product satisfies \(1-\theta\leq x_i s_i/\mu\leq1+\theta\). Thus the criterion controls both undersized and oversized products relative to the central-path value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every complementarity product must lie within a prescribed relative interval around the average complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i |x_i s_i/\mu-1|\leq\theta\).

children.title: Normwise Centrality Measures
children.top_down_role: Aggregate path-proximity measures expressed through vector norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Normwise Centrality Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized norm of the primal–dual complementarity residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,s\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), let \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(e=(1,\ldots,1)^\top\), and \(\mu=x^\top s/n\). For \(p\in[1,\infty]\), define the normwise centrality measure
\[
\delta_p(x,s)=\frac{\|XSe-\mu e\|_p}{\mu}.
\]
It is nonnegative, scale-free with respect to common multiplication of all complementarity products, and equals zero exactly when \(x_i s_i=\mu\) for every component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centrality is measured by the normalized p-norm deviation of componentwise complementarity products from their average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_p(x,s)=0\iff XSe=\mu e\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: normalized complementarity-residual norms are standard centrality measures
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized residual norm is a suitable definition, but the statement uses S without defining it in the statement itself, and no authoritative source with a specific locator supports the selected normalization.

children.title: Centrality-Measure Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relative strength and neighborhood implications of componentwise versus normwise measures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Neighborhood Equals the Infinity-Norm Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bridge between componentwise complementarity bounds and the normalized maximum-residual measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,s>0\), let \(\mu=n^{-1}x^{\mathsf T}s\) and \(r_i=x_i s_i/\mu-1\). For every \(\theta\ge0\), \[\|r\|_\infty\le\theta\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(1-\theta)\mu\le x_i s_i\le(1+\theta)\mu\quad\text{for every }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Componentwise relative complementarity bounds are exactly the infinity-norm centrality neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|XSe/\mu-e\|_\infty\le\theta\iff(1-\theta)\mu e\le XSe\le(1+\theta)\mu e\).
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Neighborhood Equals the Infinity-Norm Neighborhood
Centrality-Measure Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional comparisons among normalized complementarity-residual norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r=(XSe-\mu e)/\mu\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and set \(\delta_p=\|r\|_p\). For \(1\leq p\leq q\leq\infty\), finite-dimensional norm comparison gives
\[
\delta_q\leq\delta_p\leq n^{1/p-1/q}\delta_q.
\]
In particular, \(\delta_\infty\leq\delta_2\leq\sqrt n\,\delta_\infty\). Hence a radius-\(\theta\) neighborhood defined using \(\delta_p\) is contained in the radius-\(\theta\) neighborhood defined using \(\delta_q\), while the reverse inclusion requires the dimension factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normwise centrality measures are equivalent, but converting from a larger-index norm to a smaller-index norm incurs a dimension factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_q\leq\delta_p\leq n^{1/p-1/q}\delta_q\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct application of finite-dimensional norm equivalence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional norm inequalities and stated neighborhood inclusion are correct and fit a comparison property, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed sharpness claim for normalized complementarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(1\le p\le q\le\infty\), coordinate and all-ones vectors attain the constants in \(\|r\|_q\le\|r\|_p\le n^{1/p-1/q}\|r\|_q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proposed witnesses claim sharpness of the ambient-space norm constants for centrality residuals.
