children.title: Centrality Scaling Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of proximity assessments on component or norm scaling.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Formula for Unmatched Diagonal Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative transformation of normalized complementarity residuals when only one member of a primal-dual pair is diagonally scaled.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q=x\circ s\), \(\mu=n^{-1}e^{\mathsf T}q\), and \(r=q/\mu-e\). If \(\widehat x=Dx\), \(\widehat s=s\), and \(D=\operatorname{Diag}(d)\succ0\), then \[\widehat q=d\circ q,\qquad \widehat\mu=\frac1n e^{\mathsf T}(d\circ q),\qquad \widehat r=\frac{d\circ q}{\widehat\mu}-e.\] If \(q=\mu e\), then \(\widehat r=d/\bar d-e\), where \(\bar d=n^{-1}e^{\mathsf T}d\); the transformed pair is exactly central if and only if \(d\) is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unmatched diagonal scaling changes centrality according to the relative diagonal entries; exact centrality is preserved only by scalar scaling.
assumptions_latex: Centrality is normalized by the arithmetic mean of the complementarity products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q=\mu e\Longrightarrow\widehat r=d/\bar d-e.

notation.meaning: arithmetic mean of the diagonal scaling entries

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Formula for Unmatched Diagonal Scaling
Centrality Scaling Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance under reciprocal primal–dual diagonal scaling and sensitivity to unmatched scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a positive diagonal matrix and transform a primal–dual pair by \(\widehat x=Dx\) and \(\widehat s=D^{-1}s\). Then \(\widehat x_i\widehat s_i=x_i s_i\) for every \(i\), so \(\widehat\mu=\mu\) and every componentwise or normwise measure depending only on \(XSe-\mu e\) is unchanged. In contrast, scaling only one member of the pair generally changes the relative complementarity products and therefore changes these centrality measures unless the scaling is a positive scalar multiple of the identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocal diagonal scaling preserves complementarity-based centrality exactly; unmatched componentwise scaling generally does not.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_p(Dx,D^{-1}s)=\delta_p(x,s)\) for every \(p\in[1,\infty]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reciprocal primal-dual scaling preserves componentwise products algebraically
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-concordant Newton model and decrement
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be closed, strictly convex, three-times continuously differentiable, and have \(H(x)=\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional unconstrained or equality-reduced convex minimization in self-concordant barrier geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Self-concordant Newton theory applies to a strictly convex function whose third directional derivative is bounded by twice the three-halves power of its second directional derivative. The Hessian defines a local norm. The Newton step is the inverse-Hessian-scaled negative gradient, and its local norm is the Newton decrement. A Newton iteration uses a damped or full multiple of this step, with the decrement measuring both centrality and entry into the local fast-convergence region.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is open and convex and \(f\in C^3(D)\).
\(f\) is strictly convex and self-concordant, with \(\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\) throughout \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadruple \((\|\cdot\|_x,p_N,\lambda,x^+=x+tp_N)\) is the canonical affine-invariant Newton structure induced by a self-concordant objective or barrier.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Self-concordance is equivalent to requiring every univariate restriction \(t\mapsto f(x+th)\) to satisfy \(|\phi'''(t)|\leq2\phi''(t)^{3/2}\).
\(\lambda(x)^2=-\nabla f(x)^Tp_N(x)=p_N(x)^TH(x)p_N(x)\).
special_cases_latex: The logarithmic barrier \(-\sum_i\log(b_i-a_i^Tx)\) is self-concordant on its strict domain.
Linear and convex quadratic terms preserve self-concordance when combined with an appropriate self-concordant barrier.
immediate_consequences_latex: The definition and Newton decrement are invariant under nonsingular affine changes of coordinates.
When \(\lambda(x)\) is sufficiently small, the full Newton step remains in the domain and enters the quadratically convergent regime.
boundary_notes: Self-concordance alone does not assert strict convexity; positive-definite Hessians are imposed here so the Newton step is uniquely defined.
General \(\nu\)-self-concordant barriers additionally control the gradient and barrier parameter; that stronger notion is outside this slot.

notation.meaning: The \(k\)-th derivative as a multilinear form.

children.title: Damped-Newton Barrier Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Damped-Phase Iteration Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of analytic damped steps required to enter a prescribed local-decrement region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the update \(x^+=x+d/(1+\lambda)\), let \(\omega(u)=u-\log(1+u)\). If \(f_*:=\inf f> -\infty\) and \(\lambda(x_k)\geq\beta>0\) during the damped phase, then \(f(x_{k+1})\leq f(x_k)-\omega(\beta)\), so at most \[\left\lceil\frac{f(x_0)-f_*}{\omega(\beta)}\right\rceil\] such steps occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive decrement threshold gives uniform objective decrease and a finite bound on the damped phase.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_\beta\leq\left\lceil\frac{f(x_0)-f_*}{\beta-\log(1+\beta)}\right\rceil.

Damped-Newton Barrier Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Globally decreasing Newton update for a standard self-concordant barrier objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a standard self-concordant convex function \(f\) on an open convex domain, at \(x\) compute \(g=\nabla f(x)\), \(H=\nabla^2 f(x)\), the Newton direction \(d=-H^{-1}g\), and decrement \(\lambda=(g^\top H^{-1}g)^{1/2}\). When \(\lambda>0\), take
\[
x^+=x+\frac{1}{1+\lambda}d.
\]
Repeat until \(\lambda\) reaches a prescribed local-regime or termination threshold. The update remains in the domain and satisfies \(f(x^+)\leq f(x)-\lambda+\log(1+\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale the Newton direction by one over one plus the Newton decrement to obtain feasible global descent before entering the local regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^+\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(f(x^+)\leq f(x)-\lambda+\log(1+\lambda)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Damped-Newton regime for a self-concordant barrier
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be closed, strictly convex, and self-concordant, with Newton step \(p_N=-\nabla^2f(x)^{-1}\nabla f(x)\) and decrement \(\lambda=\lambda(x)\). Let Armijo parameters satisfy \(0<\alpha<1/2\) and \(0<\beta<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global-progress phase before entry into the full-step neighborhood of a self-concordant minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed threshold \(0<\eta\leq1/4\), the damped-Newton barrier regime is the set of iterates \(x\in D\) with \(\lambda(x)>\eta\). Its update is \(x^+=x+t p_N(x)\), where \(t\in(0,1]\) is selected by backtracking so that \(x+tp_N(x)\in D\) and \(f(x+tp_N(x))\leq f(x)+\alpha t\nabla f(x)^Tp_N(x)=f(x)-\alpha t\lambda(x)^2\). A canonical admissible scale is \(\widehat t=(1+\lambda(x))^{-1}\); backtracking accepts a step no smaller than \(\beta\widehat t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The damped-Newton barrier regime consists of points whose Newton decrement exceeds a fixed local threshold. From such a point, the method moves along the Newton direction with a step chosen by domain-preserving Armijo backtracking. The decrement determines a guaranteed damped trial scale, namely the reciprocal of one plus the decrement, and backtracking accepts at least a fixed fraction of that scale.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, bounded below, strictly convex, and self-concordant on \(D\).
The initial sublevel set is closed, and \(0<\alpha<1/2\), \(0<\beta<1\), \(0<\eta\leq1/4\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(x)>\eta\) identifies the damped phase, and its update uses a domain-feasible sufficient-decrease step \(t\geq\beta/(1+\lambda(x))\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Since \(\nabla f(x)^Tp_N(x)=-\lambda(x)^2\), the Armijo condition is \(f(x^+)\leq f(x)-\alpha t\lambda(x)^2\).
The explicit damped update \(x^+=x+p_N(x)/(1+\lambda(x))\) is a canonical self-concordant domain-preserving choice.
special_cases_latex: If backtracking accepts \(t=1\), the particular iteration is full even though the global algorithm permits damping.
For a logarithmic barrier objective, domain feasibility means every barrier argument remains strictly positive.
immediate_consequences_latex: While \(\lambda(x)>\eta\), accepted iterations decrease the objective by a positive amount depending only on \(\eta,\alpha,\beta\).
The damping prevents a Newton step from crossing the boundary where a barrier becomes infinite.
boundary_notes: This is a regime definition, not a claim that every iterate must use a strictly subunit step.
The threshold is analysis-dependent; different valid self-concordant Newton analyses use different numerical constants.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton-Decrement Suboptimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination certificate for standard self-concordant minimization in the damped regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be standard self-concordant, convex, and attain its minimum \(f^*\). If \(\lambda(x)<1\), then \[0\leq f(x)-f^*\leq\omega_*(\lambda(x)),\qquad \omega_*(u)=-u-\log(1-u).\] Thus a decrement threshold satisfying \(\omega_*(\lambda)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(\varepsilon\)-suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once the Newton decrement is below one, it quantitatively certifies objective accuracy.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is standard self-concordant and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)-f^*\leq-\lambda(x)-\log(1-\lambda(x)).
knowledge_statements.title: Newton-Decrement Suboptimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full Newton Is Not Globally Domain-Safe
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reason damping is required outside the local self-concordant region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-\log x+x^2/2\) on \((0,\infty)\), the Newton direction at \(x=2\) is \(d=-6/5\), which remains feasible, but scaling the linear term can produce points where the full Newton trial crosses the boundary while the damped step remains inside. More generally, self-concordance guarantees full-step domain preservation only under a local decrement condition; without it, damping or line search is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Self-concordance alone does not make arbitrary full Newton steps globally safe; domain preservation is a local guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda(x)\text{ unrestricted }\centernot\Rightarrow x-H^{-1}\nabla f(x)\in\operatorname{dom}f.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Doubly Exponential Local Decrement Decay
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration consequence of an invariant quadratic decrement recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\lambda_{k+1}\leq C\lambda_k^2\) and \(q=C\lambda_0<1\), then \[C\lambda_k\leq q^{2^k}.\] Thus the local iteration count needed for \(\lambda_k\leq\varepsilon\) is \(O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic decrement contraction produces doubly exponential local decay.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\lambda_k\leq(C\lambda_0)^{2^k}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Step Guarantees Are Local in the Decrement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scope boundary of the self-concordant full-Newton theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(\lambda(x)<1\) is sufficient for the standard full-step domain estimate, but self-concordance alone gives no corresponding full-step guarantee for unrestricted decrement. Moreover, quadratic iteration claims require an invariant smaller neighborhood in which the contraction coefficient is uniformly controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-step feasibility is local, and quadratic iteration bounds require a neighborhood that is invariant under the contraction estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda(x)\text{ unrestricted }\centernot\Rightarrow\text{full-step domain preservation or quadratic contraction}.
knowledge_statements.title: Full-Step Guarantees Are Local in the Decrement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Newton Decrement Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization-correct local full-step theorem for a standard self-concordant objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be standard self-concordant and convex, let \(
abla^2f(x)\succ0\), and let \(\lambda(x)<1\). For \(x^+=x-
abla^2f(x)^{-1}
abla f(x)\), \[x^+\in\operatorname{dom}f,\qquad \lambda(x^+)\leq\left( rac{\lambda(x)}{1-\lambda(x)}ight)^2.\] Consequently, any sufficiently small invariant decrement neighborhood has quadratic contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inside the local self-concordant region, a full Newton step stays in the domain and contracts the decrement quadratically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^+\in\operatorname{dom}f,\qquad\lambda(x^+)\leq\lambda(x)^2/(1-\lambda(x))^2.

Full-Newton Barrier Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic contraction of the Newton decrement for a standard self-concordant objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be standard self-concordant and convex, let \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\), and let \(\lambda=(\nabla f(x)^\top H^{-1}\nabla f(x))^{1/2}<1\). The full Newton iterate
\[
x^+=x-H^{-1}\nabla f(x)
\]
belongs to \(\operatorname{dom}f\), and its decrement obeys \(\lambda(x^+)\leq\lambda(x)^2/(1-\lambda(x))\). Consequently, on any neighborhood \(\lambda(x)\leq\beta<1\), repeated full steps exhibit quadratic decrement contraction while they remain in that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once the Newton decrement is below one, full Newton steps remain feasible and contract the decrement quadratically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^+\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\lambda(x^+)\leq\lambda(x)^2/(1-\lambda(x))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Newton regime for a self-concordant barrier
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be strictly convex and self-concordant with \(H(x)=\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\), Newton step \(p_N(x)=-H(x)^{-1}\nabla f(x)\), and decrement \(\lambda(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local fast-convergence phase near the minimizer or barrier center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a threshold \(0<\eta\leq1/4\), the full-Newton barrier regime is \(\mathcal Q_\eta=\{x\in D:\lambda(x)\leq\eta\}\). At every point in this regime the update is the unit Newton step \(x^+=x+p_N(x)\). The defining local property is that the unit step stays in \(D\), is accepted by the self-concordant sufficient-decrease test, and satisfies the decrement recurrence \(\lambda(x^+)\leq\lambda(x)^2/(1-\lambda(x))^2\); in particular, \(2\lambda(x^+)\leq(2\lambda(x))^2\) when \(\lambda(x)\leq1/4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full-Newton barrier regime is the neighborhood in which the Newton decrement is no larger than a fixed small threshold. The method then takes the entire Newton step. In this neighborhood the step remains inside the barrier domain, is accepted without damping, and the next decrement is bounded by the square of the current decrement divided by the squared distance from one. This is the local quadratic-convergence phase.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is closed, bounded below, strictly convex, and self-concordant on an open convex domain.
\(0<\eta\leq1/4\), with any sufficient-decrease parameters chosen so that the unit step is accepted throughout \(\mathcal Q_\eta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathcal Q_\eta\) implies \(x^+=x-\nabla^2f(x)^{-1}\nabla f(x)\in D\) and \(\lambda(x^+)\leq\lambda(x)^2/(1-\lambda(x))^2\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The regime is also called the pure-Newton or quadratically convergent phase.
For \(\lambda(x)\leq1/4\), the recurrence can be written \(2\lambda(x^+)\leq(2\lambda(x))^2\).
special_cases_latex: At a barrier center, \(\lambda(x)=0\), so \(p_N(x)=0\) and the full step leaves the point fixed.
For equality-constrained centering, the same definition applies after restricting the Newton equation and local norm to the feasible affine subspace.
immediate_consequences_latex: Once an iteration enters an invariant full-step threshold, subsequent iterates remain in the full-Newton regime.
The number of correct digits grows quadratically in the standard local interpretation.
boundary_notes: A unit step outside the decrement neighborhood is not part of this defined regime, even if it happens to be feasible.
The statement assumes exact Newton directions; controlled residuals require an inexact regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Loss of Descent at Unit Relative Tolerance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for the descent guarantee supplied by relative residual control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g\neq0\) and \(d=0\), then \(\|Hd+g\|_x^*=\|g\|_x^*\), so the relative residual condition holds with \(\eta=1\), but \(-g^Td=0\). Hence a tolerance at least one does not by itself certify a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At unit relative tolerance, the zero step is admissible and provides no descent, so the strict bound below one is essential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta=1\) permits \(d=0\) and therefore does not imply \(-g^Td>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Loss of Descent at Unit Relative Tolerance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual–Step-Error Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact local-norm relation between Newton-step error and the residual of an approximate Hessian solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\), \(g=\nabla f(x)\), \(n=-H^{-1}g\), \(r=Hd+g\), and \(\lambda=\|g\|_x^*\). Then \[r=H(d-n),\qquad \|r\|_x^*=\|d-n\|_x.\] Consequently, \(\|r\|_x^*\leq\eta\lambda\) is equivalent to \(\|d-n\|_x\leq\eta\lambda\), and it implies \[(1-\eta)\lambda\leq\|d\|_x\leq(1+\eta)\lambda,\qquad -g^Td\geq(1-\eta)\lambda^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local dual-norm solve residual equals the local-norm error in the Newton direction. Relative residual control therefore bounds the step and certifies descent when the tolerance is below one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|d-n\|_x\leq\eta\lambda\) and \(-g^Td\geq(1-\eta)\lambda^2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Residual–Step-Error Equivalence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Rate Regimes Under Inexact Self-Concordant Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Newton-decrement rates determined by the forcing sequence in the self-concordant local norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be standard self-concordant, let \(x_*\) be a minimizer, and suppose \(
abla^2f\succ0\) near \(x_*\). For sufficiently local full steps \(x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k\) satisfying \[\|
abla^2f(x_k)d_k+
abla f(x_k)\|_{x_k}^*\leq\eta_k\lambda_k,\qquad \lambda_k=\|
abla f(x_k)\|_{x_k}^*,\] one has \[\lambda_{k+1}=O(\lambda_k^2+\eta_k\lambda_k).\] Thus a sufficiently small uniform bound \(\eta_k\leq ar\eta<1\) gives local linear contraction, \(\eta_k	o0\) gives superlinear convergence, and \(\eta_k=O(\lambda_k)\) preserves quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a self-concordant minimizer, the next decrement is controlled by the exact Newton quadratic term plus the inexact-solve error. Fixed-small, vanishing, and decrement-proportional tolerances yield linear, superlinear, and quadratic local regimes.
assumptions_latex: the iterates remain in a sufficiently small full-step neighborhood
the displayed local-dual-norm residual condition holds
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{k+1}=O(\lambda_k^2+\eta_k\lambda_k)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local dual-norm residual condition for an approximate Newton direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a standard self-concordant convex function \(f\), write \(g=\nabla f(x)\), \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\), and \(\|v\|_x^*=(v^\top H^{-1}v)^{1/2}\). A direction \(d\) is an \(\eta\)-relative inexact Newton direction when

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-controlled inexact Newton regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be strictly convex and self-concordant, \(g=\nabla f(x)\), and \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\). An approximate Newton direction is denoted by \(p\), and its linear-system residual by \(r=Hp+g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-concordant barrier minimization when the Newton linear system is solved only approximately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inexact self-concordant Newton regime with forcing parameter \(\eta\in[0,1)\) consists of updates \(x^+=x+tp\) whose direction satisfies the relative residual condition \(\|Hp+g\|_2\leq\eta\|g\|_2\). Equivalently, \(p\) solves \(Hp=-g+r\) with \(\|r\|_2\leq\eta\|g\|_2\). The step length \(t\in(0,1]\) must preserve \(D\) and satisfy the chosen sufficient-decrease condition. A sequence \(\eta_k\) is called a forcing sequence; bounded forcing \(\eta_k\leq\bar\eta<1\) defines controlled inexactness, while \(\eta_k\to0\) defines asymptotically exact Newton solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact self-concordant Newton step solves the Hessian system only to a prescribed relative residual. The residual norm must be at most a forcing parameter times the gradient norm. The resulting direction is combined with a domain-preserving line search or, in the local region, a unit step. A forcing sequence bounded below one gives uniformly controlled solves, while a sequence converging to zero makes the Newton equations asymptotically exact.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is strictly convex and self-concordant, and \(H(x)\succ0\).
The accepted step remains in \(D\) and meets the globalization condition used by the method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_k\) is an admissible inexact Newton direction exactly when \(\|H_kp_k+g_k\|_2\leq\eta_k\|g_k\|_2\), with the forcing sequence quantifying computational accuracy.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(p=p_N+H^{-1}r\), inexactness is the perturbation of the exact Newton direction induced by the residual \(r\).
The exact regime is the special case \(\eta_k=0\), for which \(r_k=0\) and \(p_k=p_N(x_k)\).
special_cases_latex: A fixed \(\eta_k\leq\bar\eta<1\) is the standard linear-convergence forcing regime near a nonsingular minimizer.
If \(\eta_k\to0\), the generic inexact-Newton local theory permits superlinear convergence under its regularity hypotheses.
immediate_consequences_latex: The stopping tolerance for an iterative linear solver is coupled explicitly to the current nonlinear residual.
Decreasing forcing parameters allocate increasing linear-algebra accuracy only as the barrier iterate approaches its center.
boundary_notes: The Euclidean residual criterion is the cited standard form; local dual-norm criteria are related variants and require separately calibrated constants.
Self-concordance supplies barrier geometry, but local rate conclusions also require the regularity and step-acceptance hypotheses of inexact Newton theory.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-complexity interior-point family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathfrak I\) be a class of finite-dimensional convex optimization instances. For \(I\in\mathfrak I\), let \(d(I)\) denote its dimension parameters, \(L(I)\) its binary encoding length when applicable, and \(\epsilon\in(0,1)\) a requested optimality tolerance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case polynomial interior-point algorithms, including path-following and potential-reduction organizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial interior complexity family is a family of algorithms \(\{\mathcal A_I:I\in\mathfrak I\}\) that generates strictly interior iterates and for which there exists a polynomial \(p\), independent of \(I\) and \(\epsilon\), such that an \(\epsilon\)-solution is returned using at most \(p(d(I),L(I),\log(1/\epsilon))\) primitive operations in the declared computational model. An \(\epsilon\)-solution must satisfy the family’s stated feasibility-residual and duality-gap tolerances. The family may enforce a central-path neighborhood, decrease a logarithmic potential, or jointly reduce infeasibility and complementarity, provided the same worst-case polynomial bound holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial interior complexity family consists of interior-point algorithms whose worst-case work is bounded by one polynomial in the instance dimensions, the input encoding length when relevant, and the logarithm of the requested inverse accuracy. The algorithms keep inequality variables strictly interior and terminate at points meeting explicit residual and duality-gap tolerances. Path-following, potential-reduction, and infeasible-interior variants are different members when each has such a bound.
assumptions_latex: The instance class and the primitive-operation cost model are fixed before complexity is measured.
Every input has a finite size description in that model, and the requested tolerance satisfies \(0<\epsilon<1\).
The termination notion specifies quantitative primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and optimality or duality-gap requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\mathcal A_I\}\) is polynomial precisely when its declared worst-case operation count is bounded by \(p(d(I),L(I),\log(1/\epsilon))\) for one fixed polynomial \(p\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For rational data in the bit model, polynomiality means polynomial time in the binary input length and required output accuracy.
For an iteration analysis with polynomial work per iteration, it suffices that both the iteration count and per-iteration primitive-operation count are polynomial in the declared size parameters.
special_cases_latex: Short-step path-following methods for linear programming have bounds of order \(O(\sqrt n\log(1/\epsilon))\) iterations under standard assumptions.
A full-Newton method followed by exact rounding can yield polynomial exact solution procedures for rational linear programs.
immediate_consequences_latex: An iteration bound alone is not a complete computational bound unless the cost and numerical representation of each iteration are also declared.
Different centrality controls can define distinct polynomial families even when they share the same asymptotic iteration order.
boundary_notes: Observed practical speed does not establish worst-case polynomial complexity.
A bound polynomial in \(1/\epsilon\), rather than \(\log(1/\epsilon)\), is not polynomial in the usual encoded-accuracy measure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Central-Path Objective-Gap Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping certificate for a linear objective and a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Narrow Newton-Decrement Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-concordant neighborhood used by conservative short-step path following.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating short-step updates from unrestricted path-parameter changes.

Let \(x(t)=\arg\min_x\{t\langle c,xangle+F(x)\}\) for a \(

abla f_{t^+}(x)=

children.title: Long-Step Path Following
children.top_down_role: Aggressive path-following families based on wider neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Long-Step Gap Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration consequence of an order-\(1/n\) complementarity contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mu_{k+1}\leq(1-c/n)\mu_k\) for a dimension-independent \(c\in(0,n)\), then \(\mu_k\leq e^{-ck/n}\mu_0\), and \[k\geq\frac{n}{c}\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\] suffices for \(\mu_k\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order-one-over-dimension relative complementarity decrease yields an order-n-log-accuracy iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k=O\!\left(n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Long-Step Gap Complexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Wide Neighborhood Permits Large Upper Imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to two-sided centrality in the one-sided wide neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq2\), let normalized products satisfy \(p_1=n-(n-1)\gamma\) and \(p_i=\gamma\) for \(i\geq2\). Their average is one and every \(p_i\geq\gamma\), but \(p_1\) grows linearly with \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wide-neighborhood point can have one complementarity product much larger than the average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_i p_i=n-(n-1)\gamma.
knowledge_statements.title: Wide Neighborhood Permits Large Upper Imbalance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Wide Lower-Complementarity Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal–dual LP neighborhood characteristic of long-step path following.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\gamma<1\), define \(\mu=x^Ts/n\) and \[\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^Ty+s=c,\ x>0,\ s>0,\ x_is_i\geq\gamma\mu\ \forall i\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The wide neighborhood preserves strict primal–dual feasibility and imposes only a componentwise lower bound on complementarity products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,y,s)\in\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\iff Ax=b,\ A^Ty+s=c,\ x,s>0,\ \min_i x_is_i\geq\gamma x^Ts/n.
knowledge_statements.title: Wide Lower-Complementarity Neighborhood

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Complementarity Reduction for Feasible Newton Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact average-complementarity evolution along a feasible primal-dual LP direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\Delta x=0\), \(A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=0\), and \(s^T\Delta x+x^T\Delta s=-(1-\sigma)x^Ts\). Then \(\Delta x^T\Delta s=0\), and for every accepted \(\alpha\), \[\mu^+=\frac{(x+\alpha\Delta x)^T(s+\alpha\Delta s)}{n}=[1-\alpha(1-\sigma)]\mu.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible primal-dual Newton direction, average complementarity decreases affinely with the accepted step length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu^+=[1-\alpha(1-\sigma)]\mu.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Complementarity Reduction for Feasible Newton Directions
Long-Step Path Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual linear-programming path following within a wide complementarity neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a strictly positive primal–dual linear-programming iterate in \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\), choose a target \(\mu^+=\sigma\\mu\) with \(0<\sigma<1\), solve the primal–dual Newton equations with complementarity right-hand side \(\mu^+e-XSe\), and obtain direction \((\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\). Select the largest backtracked \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) for which \((x+\alpha\Delta x,s+\alpha\Delta s)\in\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\) and the chosen residual or complementarity progress test holds. Update the iterate and stop when feasibility residuals and \(x^\top s/n\) meet their tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Target a substantial complementarity reduction, then backtrack the primal–dual Newton step only enough to retain a wide neighborhood and progress.
assumptions_latex: the current primal–dual variables are strictly positive
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^+,s^+)\in\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\) with \((x^+,s^+)=(x,s)+\alpha(\Delta x,\Delta s)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Long-Step Geometric-Gap Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration consequence of the characteristic order-1/n complementarity reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose feasible iterates remain in \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\) and satisfy \(\mu_{k+1}\leq(1-c/n)\mu_k\) for a constant \(c\in(0,n)\). Then \(\mu_k\leq e^{-ck/n}\mu_0\), so \[k\geq \frac{n}{c}\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\] suffices for \(\mu_k\leq\varepsilon\). Thus this long-step progress regime has \(O(n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order-1/n relative complementarity decrease gives the characteristic linear-in-dimension long-step iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k=O\!\left(n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Long-Step Geometric-Gap Complexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Wide Neighborhood Does Not Bound Complementarity Imbalance Above
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp structural limitation of the one-sided long-step neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Membership in \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\) gives no dimension-independent upper bound on \(\max_i x_is_i/\mu\). Indeed, for any \(n\geq2\), products \(p_1=n-(n-1)\gamma\) and \(p_i=\gamma\) for \(i\geq2\) have average one and satisfy \(p_i\geq\gamma\), while \(p_1\) grows linearly with \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The wide neighborhood prevents tiny products but permits one product to be much larger than the average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)}\max_i\frac{x_is_i}{\mu}\geq n-(n-1)\gamma.
knowledge_statements.title: Wide Neighborhood Does Not Bound Complementarity Imbalance Above

children.title: Infeasible Path Following
children.top_down_role: Polynomial path-following families allowing feasibility residuals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fraction-to-the-Boundary Positivity Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Step-length rule preserving strict primal and dual positivity after an infeasible-start Newton direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x,s>0\), a direction \((\Delta x,\Delta s)\), and \(\eta\in(0,1)\), define \[\alpha_x^{\max}=\min\left\{1,\min_{\Delta x_i<0}-\frac{x_i}{\Delta x_i}\right\},\qquad \alpha_s^{\max}=\min\left\{1,\min_{\Delta s_i<0}-\frac{s_i}{\Delta s_i}\right\},\] taking a minimum over an empty set as \(1\), and set \(\alpha=\eta\min\{\alpha_x^{\max},\alpha_s^{\max}\}\). Then \(x+\alpha\Delta x>0\) and \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict fraction of the maximum primal and dual boundary steps preserves positivity of an infeasible path-following iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x+\alpha\Delta x>0,\qquad s+\alpha\Delta s>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Fraction-to-the-Boundary Positivity Step

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Floor for an Inconsistent Primal or Dual Affine System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Obstruction to feasibility-residual convergence in infeasible path following.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), every iterate satisfies \[\|Ax-b\|_2\geq\operatorname{dist}(b,\operatorname{range}A).\] Thus \(b\notin\operatorname{range}A\) gives a strictly positive primal-residual floor. Likewise, because \(\{A^Ty+s:y\in\mathbb R^m,\ s\geq0\}\) is a closed polyhedral set, if \(c\) is outside it then \[\inf_{y,\,s\geq0}\|A^Ty+s-c\|_2>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inconsistent primal or dual affine system imposes a positive residual floor, so ordinary infeasible path following cannot drive every feasibility residual to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b\notin\operatorname{range}A\implies\inf_x\|Ax-b\|_2>0.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from b to the range of A

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Floor for an Inconsistent Primal or Dual Affine System

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infeasible-Start Primal–Dual Newton System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton linearization simultaneously correcting primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementarity for a linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), \(A^Ty+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\), define \[r_p=Ax-b,\qquad r_d=A^Ty+s-c,\qquad \mu=\frac{x^Ts}{n},\qquad X=\operatorname{Diag}(x),\quad S=\operatorname{Diag}(s).\] Given \(\sigma\in[0,1]\), an infeasible-start primal–dual Newton direction solves \[A\Delta x=-r_p,\qquad A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=-r_d,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu e-Xs.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infeasible-start Newton system corrects primal residual, dual residual, and centered complementarity in one coupled direction.
assumptions_latex: The displayed Newton system is solvable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\Delta x=-r_p,\quad A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=-r_d,\quad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu e-Xs.
knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible-Start Primal–Dual Newton System

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Feasibility-Residual Contraction Along a Newton Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual evolution for a damped infeasible-start LP Newton direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(A\Delta x=-r_p\) and \(A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=-r_d\), where \(r_p=Ax-b\) and \(r_d=A^Ty+s-c\). For \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), \[r_p^+=(1-\alpha)r_p,\qquad r_d^+=(1-\alpha)r_d.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A damped infeasible-start Newton step contracts both affine feasibility residuals by exactly one minus the step length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_p^+=(1-\alpha)r_p,\qquad r_d^+=(1-\alpha)r_d.

notation.meaning: feasibility residuals after the damped Newton update

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Feasibility-Residual Contraction Along a Newton Step
Infeasible Path Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual homotopy that reduces feasibility residuals and complementarity together.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the linear-programming equations \(Ax=b\), \(A^\top y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\), start from positive \((x_0,y_0,s_0)\), possibly infeasible, with residuals \(r_p^0=Ax_0-b\) and \(r_d^0=A^\top y_0+s_0-c\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(0<\tau_{k+1}<\tau_k\), solve a primal–dual Newton system targeting
\[
r_p=\tau_{k+1}r_p^0,\qquad r_d=\tau_{k+1}r_d^0,
\]
and a centered complementarity equation, then shorten the step to preserve positivity and the selected neighborhood. Stop when both residual norms and \(x^\top s/n\) are below tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Follow a positive primal–dual homotopy that drives primal infeasibility, dual infeasibility, and complementarity toward zero together.
assumptions_latex: the primal–dual Newton systems are solvable
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|r_p^k\|\to0\), \(\|r_d^k\|\to0\), and \((x_k)^\top s_k/n\to0\) under the prescribed neighborhood and progress conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infeasible primal–dual path-following family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For the standard primal–dual linear programs, define \(r_b=Ax-b\), \(r_c=A^Ty+s-c\), \(\mu=x^Ts/n\), and assume only \(x^0>0\), \(s^0>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual linear-programming path following from equality-infeasible but strictly positive starting points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(0<\gamma<1\) and \(\beta\geq1\), define \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma,\beta)=\{(x,y,s):x>0,\ s>0,\ x_is_i\geq\gamma\mu\ \forall i,\ \|(r_b,r_c)\|\leq[\|(r_b^0,r_c^0)\|/\mu_0]\beta\mu\}\). An infeasible path-following method is an interior iteration that remains in this neighborhood and computes directions from the residual-correcting perturbed Newton system \(A\Delta x=-r_b\), \(A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=-r_c\), \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=-XSe+\sigma\mu e\), with step lengths chosen to preserve neighborhood membership and reduce \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infeasible path following starts from positive primal and slack variables without requiring the linear equality equations to hold. Its neighborhood balances every complementarity product and bounds the combined feasibility residual by a constant multiple of the duality measure. Each Newton direction targets primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and centered complementarity simultaneously, and the accepted step remains inside that extended neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The centering parameter and step-length rule are selected so the next iterate remains in \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma,\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family permits \((r_b,r_c)\neq0\) but couples \(\|(r_b,r_c)\|=O(\mu)\) with \(x_is_i\geq\gamma\mu\), so feasibility and complementarity are reduced together.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A full step in the first two Newton equations gives \(r_b^+=0\) and \(r_c^+=0\).
For a common step length \(\alpha\), the linear residuals satisfy \((r_b^+,r_c^+)=(1-\alpha)(r_b,r_c)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(r_b^0=r_c^0=0\), the method reduces to a feasible long-step path-following variant.
The symmetric initial point \((x^0,y^0,s^0)=(\zeta e,0,\zeta e)\) is used in the cited polynomial-complexity construction.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\mu_k\to0\) while all iterates remain in the neighborhood, then \(r_b^k\to0\) and \(r_c^k\to0\).
Strict positivity is maintained even though equality feasibility is not imposed at intermediate iterations.
boundary_notes: The term infeasible refers to equality residuals, not to violation of \(x>0\) or \(s>0\).
An infeasible path-following method need not by itself provide an infeasibility certificate for an inconsistent original problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infeasible-Iterate Primal–Dual Gap Identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decomposition showing why complementarity alone is not an objective-gap certificate before feasibility is restored.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r_p=Ax-b\) and \(r_d=A^Ty+s-c\), every \((x,y,s)\) satisfies \[c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts+y^Tr_p-x^Tr_d.\] Thus \(x^Ts\) equals the primal–dual objective gap only when the residual correction \(y^Tr_p-x^Tr_d\) vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an infeasible iterate, the objective gap equals complementarity plus explicit primal- and dual-residual correction terms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–dual logarithmic potential-reduction family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F^o\) be the strictly feasible primal–dual set of a standard-form linear program. For \((x,y,s)\in\mathcal F^o\), let \(\mu=x^Ts/n\) and choose \(\rho>n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal–dual linear-programming methods organized by descent of the Tanabe–Todd–Ye potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\Phi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^Ts)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_is_i)\) on \(\{(x,s):(x,y,s)\in\mathcal F^o\text{ for some }y\}\). A potential-reduction algorithm is an interior iteration that computes a primal–dual Newton direction, chooses a positive step preserving strict feasibility, and enforces \(\Phi_\rho(x^{k+1},s^{k+1})\leq\Phi_\rho(x^k,s^k)-\delta\) for a prescribed \(\delta>0\), or at least the decrease guaranteed by the family’s canonical parameter choice. Its progress measure is the potential itself rather than explicit membership in a fixed central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal–dual potential-reduction method assigns every strictly feasible point the Tanabe–Todd–Ye logarithmic potential. Each iteration takes a primal–dual Newton-type step, remains strictly feasible, and decreases that potential by a controlled amount. The potential combines reduction of the duality gap with a logarithmic penalty against unbalanced complementarity products, so the method need not explicitly maintain a named central-path neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: Every accepted step preserves \(x>0\), \(s>0\), and primal–dual equality feasibility.
The parameter and line-search rule guarantee a uniform positive potential decrease in the polynomial family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining progress condition is monotone controlled decrease of \(\Phi_\rho\), with \(\Phi_\rho\to-\infty\) forcing \(x^Ts\to0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\Phi_\rho=(\rho-n)\log(x^Ts)-\sum_i\log\bigl(x_is_i/(x^Ts/n)\bigr)+n\log n\).
The first term measures the duality gap and the remaining normalized term measures departure from complementarity balance.
special_cases_latex: The canonical primal–dual potential-reduction algorithm uses centering parameter \(\sigma=n/\rho\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Valid Lower-Bound Primal Gap Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality meaning of the bound-gap term in a primal potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(z^*=\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), \(z_L\leq z^*\), and \(x\) is primal feasible, then \[0\leq c^Tx-z^*\leq c^Tx-z_L.\] Hence \(c^Tx-z_L\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid lower bound turns the primal potential's objective-gap term into an optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^Tx-z_L\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow c^Tx-z^*\leq\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Valid Lower-Bound Primal Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invalid Lower Bound Destroys the Primal Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for primal logarithmic potentials using a supplied lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(z_L>z^*\), then \(c^Tx-z_L\) need not upper-bound primal suboptimality and may be nonpositive at feasible points, so \(\log(c^Tx-z_L)\) may be undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An overestimated lower bound can invalidate both the logarithmic potential and its stopping test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^Tx-z_L\not\geq c^Tx-z^*\text{ in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Lower Bound Destroys the Primal Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced Derivatives of the Primal Logarithmic Potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient, curvature, and null-space Newton equations for the classical primal potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(x)=c^Tx-z_L>0\), \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), and \(\Phi_q(x)=q\log g(x)-\sum_i\log x_i\). Then \[
abla\Phi_q(x)= rac{q}{g(x)}c-X^{-1}e,\qquad 
abla^2\Phi_q(x)=X^{-2}- rac{q}{g(x)^2}cc^T.\] If \(\operatorname{range}Z=\ker A\), a feasible Newton correction \(d=Zp\) satisfies \[(Z^T
abla^2\Phi_q(x)Z)p=-Z^T
abla\Phi_q(x)\] whenever the reduced matrix is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal potential has diagonal barrier curvature minus a rank-one gap term, and feasible Newton corrections restrict these derivatives to the constraint null space.
assumptions_latex: Z^T\nabla^2\Phi_q(x)Z\text{ is nonsingular for the displayed Newton equation}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ad=0,\qquad Z^T(\nabla^2\Phi_q(x)d+\nabla\Phi_q(x))=0.

Primal Potential Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential-decreasing method for a strictly feasible primal linear program with a known lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x>0\}\), and let \(z_L<c^\top x\) be a valid lower bound on the optimum. For \(q>n\), define
\[
\Phi_q(x)=q\log(c^\top x-z_L)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i.
\]
From a strictly feasible iterate, compute a feasible descent direction \(d\) with \(Ad=0\), using the gradient and Hessian of \(\Phi_q\) on the null space of \(A\). Choose \(\alpha>0\) so that \(x+\alpha d>0\) and \(\Phi_q(x+\alpha d)\leq\Phi_q(x)-\kappa\) for the prescribed progress constant; update and stop when \(c^\top x-z_L\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decrease a logarithmic potential combining the primal objective gap and distance from the nonnegative boundary while preserving primal feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax=b\) has a strictly positive feasible point
\(z_L\) is a valid strict lower bound
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax^+=b\), \(x^+>0\), and \(\Phi_q(x^+)\leq\Phi_q(x)-\kappa\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Objective-Scaling Equivariance of the Primal Potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization law under simultaneous scaling of the objective and supplied lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\beta>0\), replace \(c,z_L\) by \(\widetilde c=\beta c\), \(\widetilde z_L=\beta z_L\). Then \[\widetilde\Phi_q(x)=q\log(\widetilde c^Tx-\widetilde z_L)-\sum_i\log x_i=\Phi_q(x)+q\log\beta.\] Hence potential differences and descent comparisons are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling of the objective and lower bound adds only a constant to the primal logarithmic potential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde\Phi_q(x)-\widetilde\Phi_q(y)=\Phi_q(x)-\Phi_q(y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Primal Potential Iteration Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic iteration count from fixed potential decrease and a target-level lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a primal potential method satisfies \(\Phi_q(x^{k+1})\leq\Phi_q(x^k)-\kappa\), \(\kappa>0\), whenever \(c^Tx^k-z_L>\varepsilon\), and suppose \(\Phi_q(x)\geq L_\varepsilon\) on all generated points with that gap. Then it reaches \(c^Tx^k-z_L\leq\varepsilon\) within \(\lceil(\Phi_q(x^0)-L_\varepsilon)/\kappa\rceil\) accepted iterations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N\leq\left\lceil\frac{\Phi_q(x^0)-L_\varepsilon}{\kappa}\right\rceil.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible LP Gap Identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality certificate underlying feasible primal–dual potential reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Ax=b\), \(A^Ty+s=c\), and \(x,s\geq0\), then \[c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts\geq0.\] Hence \(x^Ts\leq\varepsilon\) certifies a primal–dual objective gap at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible primal–dual LP pair, total complementarity equals the objective gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible LP Gap Identity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Potential-Decrease-to-Gap Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap consequence of fixed decrease of the standard primal–dual logarithmic potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho>n\) and suppose \(\Phi_\rho(x^{k+1},s^{k+1})\leq\Phi_\rho(x^k,s^k)-\delta\). Since \(\Phi_\rho(x,s)\geq(\rho-n)\log(x^Ts)+n\log n\), \[(x^k)^Ts^k\leq n^{-n/(\rho-n)}\exp\!\left(\frac{\Phi_\rho(x^0,s^0)-k\delta}{\rho-n}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed decrease of the standard primal–dual potential gives an explicit exponentially decreasing upper bound on the feasible duality gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^k)^Ts^k\leq n^{-n/(\rho-n)}e^{(\Phi_0-k\delta)/(\rho-n)}.

Primal–Dual Potential Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming primal–dual potential method using strictly feasible iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal–dual pair \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\), choose \(\rho>n\) and define \(\Phi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^Ts)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_is_i)\). Starting from strictly feasible \((x^0,y^0,s^0)\), compute a primal–dual Newton or scaled-gradient direction preserving \(A\Delta x=0\) and \(A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=0\). Choose a positive step maintaining \(x^{k+1}>0\), \(s^{k+1}>0\), and satisfying \(\Phi_\rho(x^{k+1},s^{k+1})\leq\Phi_\rho(x^k,s^k)-\delta\) for a prescribed \(\delta>0\). Stop when \((x^k)^Ts^k\leq\varepsilon\), and output the primal–dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly take feasible interior directions and line-search for a fixed decrease of a primal–dual potential until the duality gap is at most the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
A strictly feasible primal–dual point exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^k)^Ts^k\leq\varepsilon\) at termination while primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and strict positivity are preserved.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural scaling law for the complementarity-product potential; canonically owned by the sibling potential-measure leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a positive diagonal matrix \(D\), set \(\widetilde x=Dx\) and \(\widetilde s=D^{-1}s\). Then \(\widetilde x_i\widetilde s_i=x_is_i\) and \(\widetilde x^T\widetilde s=x^Ts\), so \(\Phi_\rho(\widetilde x,\widetilde s)=\Phi_\rho(x,s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocal positive diagonal scaling leaves all complementarity products and the primal-dual logarithmic potential unchanged.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ is diagonal with positive diagonal entries}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi_\rho(Dx,D^{-1}s)=\Phi_\rho(x,s).
knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Diagonal-Scaling Invariance of the Primal–Dual Potential

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential-Decrease-to-Gap Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit conversion of fixed primal–dual potential decrease into a duality-gap estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho>n\) and suppose \(\Phi_\rho(x^{k+1},s^{k+1})\leq\Phi_\rho(x^k,s^k)-\delta\). Since \(\Phi_\rho(x,s)\geq(\rho-n)\log(x^Ts)+n\log n\), \[(x^k)^Ts^k\leq n^{-n/(\rho-n)}\exp\!\left(\frac{\Phi_\rho(x^0,s^0)-k\delta}{\rho-n}\right).\] Thus the gap is at most \(\varepsilon\) after \[k\geq\frac{\Phi_\rho(x^0,s^0)-n\log n-(\rho-n)\log\varepsilon}{\delta}.\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^k)^Ts^k\leq n^{-n/(\rho-n)}e^{(\Phi_0-k\delta)/(\rho-n)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Gap Convergence at Critical Potential Weight
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp parameter boundary for primal–dual potential reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(\rho=n\), the coefficient of \(\log(x^Ts)\) in the gap-plus-imbalance decomposition is zero. Consequently, even unbounded decrease or boundedness of the scale-invariant potential cannot by itself force \(x^Ts\to0\); a gap-convergence proof based solely on potential values requires \(\rho>n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At rho equal to n, the potential tracks balance but not gap scale, so potential progress alone cannot prove optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi_n\text{ control alone }\centernot\Rightarrow x^Ts\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical Weight Is Blind to Gap Scale
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary at potential weight \(\rho=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(\rho=n\), \(\Phi_n(tx,s)=\Phi_n(x,s)\) for every \(t>0\), although \((tx)^Ts=t\,x^Ts\). Thus an absolute value of \(\Phi_n\) cannot bound the duality-gap scale without an independent normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the critical weight, the potential measures imbalance but not the magnitude of the gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi_n(tx,s)=\Phi_n(x,s),\qquad (tx)^Ts=t x^Ts.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical Weight Is Blind to Gap Scale

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaling Law of the Primal–Dual Logarithmic Potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneity separating overall complementarity scale from imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Phi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^Ts)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_is_i)\) and \(a,b>0\), \[\Phi_\rho(ax,bs)=\Phi_\rho(x,s)+(\rho-n)\log(ab).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The excess weight rho minus n is exactly the potential's sensitivity to overall complementarity scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi_\rho(ax,bs)-\Phi_\rho(x,s)=(\rho-n)\log(ab).

notation.meaning: positive primal and dual scaling factors

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Law of the Primal–Dual Logarithmic Potential
Potential Progress Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic potential decomposition for positive primal–dual linear-programming iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), let \(\mu=x^Ts/n\), and for \(\rho\geq n\) define \(\Phi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^Ts)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_is_i)\). Then \[\Phi_\rho(x,s)=(\rho-n)\log(x^Ts)+n\log n-\sum_{i=1}^n\log\!\left(\frac{x_is_i}{\mu}\right).\] The imbalance term \(-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_is_i/\mu)\) is nonnegative because \(\prod_{i=1}^n(x_is_i/\mu)\leq1\). Hence \(\Phi_\rho\) combines a weighted duality-gap term with a nonnegative complementarity-imbalance term. When \(\rho>n\), uniform decrease of \(\Phi_\rho\), together with an upper bound on the imbalance term over the iterates under consideration, yields a corresponding upper bound on \(x^Ts\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal–dual potential is the sum of a weighted log-gap term and a nonnegative measure of complementarity imbalance. If that imbalance is bounded above, decreasing the potential controls the duality gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_\rho\) decomposes into a weighted log-gap term and a nonnegative complementarity-imbalance term; for \(\rho>n\), an upper bound on the latter permits potential bounds to be converted into bounds on \(x^Ts\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic decomposition of the standard primal–dual logarithmic potential

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical Weight Does Not Control the Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary at potential weight rho equals the dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(\rho=n\), the potential cannot by itself bound \(x^Ts\): for every \(t>0\), \(\Phi_n(tx,s)=\Phi_n(x,s)\), while \((tx)^Ts=t\,x^Ts\). Thus gap control from an absolute potential value requires \(\rho>n\) or an independent normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With weight rho equal to n, the potential measures only imbalance and is blind to the scale of the duality gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi_n(tx,s)=\Phi_n(x,s)\text{ for all }t>0\text{ while }(tx)^Ts=t x^Ts.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical Weight Does Not Control the Gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential-reduction progress specified without an explicit central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^k=(x^k,y^k,s^k)\) be strictly feasible primal–dual iterates and let \(\Phi\) be a potential defined on the strictly positive feasible set. knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Real-arithmetic and bit-complexity model pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an optimization instance have rational data encoded by a binary string of length \(L\), dimension parameters \(d\), and requested accuracy \(\epsilon\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two standard interpretations of polynomial complexity for interior-point algorithms on rational finite-dimensional inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The real-arithmetic model \(\mathsf M_{\mathbb R}\) counts each exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, comparison, and declared algebraic primitive at unit cost; its complexity is the number of such operations. The bit model \(\mathsf M_{\mathrm{bit}}\) encodes rational input and output in binary and charges for Boolean or machine-bit operations, including the dependence on operand lengths. An interior-point algorithm is polynomial in \(\mathsf M_{\mathbb R}\) when its arithmetic-operation count is polynomial in \(d\) and \(\log(1/\epsilon)\); it is polynomial in \(\mathsf M_{\mathrm{bit}}\) when its total bit-operation count and intermediate encoding lengths are polynomial in \(L\) and \(\log(1/\epsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The computational-model pair separates exact real-arithmetic accounting from binary bit accounting. The first assigns unit cost to each exact arithmetic primitive and measures only how many are used. The second represents rational quantities by binary strings and charges for operations according to their bit lengths, including growth of intermediate values. Consequently, a polynomial arithmetic-operation bound does not automatically constitute a polynomial bit-complexity bound.
assumptions_latex: The primitive operations counted by the real-arithmetic model are declared consistently.
For the bit model, all input data are rational and \(L\) is the length of their binary encoding.
The output accuracy or exact rounding requirement is part of the output specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathsf M_{\mathbb R},\mathsf M_{\mathrm{bit}})\) is the model pair distinguished by unit-cost exact arithmetic versus binary-length-sensitive computation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In \(\mathsf M_{\mathrm{bit}}\), polynomial time is polynomial in the length of the binary string encoding the instance.
An arithmetic iteration bound becomes a bit bound only after controlling numerical precision and the bit lengths of all computed quantities.
special_cases_latex: Gaussian elimination may be counted as a polynomial number of arithmetic operations in \(\mathsf M_{\mathbb R}\), while its bit cost additionally depends on coefficient growth and precision.
For integral data, an entry \(a\) requires a number of bits proportional to \(1+\lceil\log_2(1+|a|)\rceil\), including its sign.
immediate_consequences_latex: Complexity claims must state which model underlies the word polynomial.
Rounding a sufficiently accurate interior-point iterate to an exact rational solution can bridge an approximate arithmetic analysis and an exact bit-model result when encoding growth is controlled.
boundary_notes: Floating-point wall-clock cost is neither model without an explicit finite-precision analysis.
Iteration complexity is separate from both models because one iteration can contain many arithmetic or bit operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Complexity Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turing-model cost for rationally encoded interior-point computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the problem data are rational and encoded as a binary string of length \(L\). The bit complexity of an interior-point algorithm is the total number of elementary Boolean operations required to produce an output meeting a stated exact or approximate optimality criterion. Arithmetic on integers or rationals of bit length \(p\) is charged according to its bit-operation cost, rather than as one unit operation. A polynomial bit-complexity guarantee has the form \(T(L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\leq P(L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for some polynomial \(P\), and must include bounds on the encoding lengths of all intermediate quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bit complexity counts Boolean work on encoded rational data and must control both the number of arithmetic steps and the sizes of intermediate numbers.
assumptions_latex: Input coefficients and the requested accuracy are finitely encoded.
The output criterion and arithmetic representation are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomiality requires a bound polynomial in \(L\) and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), including intermediate precision costs.

children.title: Real-Arithmetic Complexity Models

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Arithmetic Complexity Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost exact-real operation model for interior-point algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the real-arithmetic model, each exact operation \(+\), \(-\), \(\times\), \(/\), and each permitted comparison on real operands has unit cost. The arithmetic complexity of an interior-point algorithm is the number of these operations needed to meet its stopping criterion. If the method performs \(N(n,m,\varepsilon)\) iterations and iteration \(k\) costs \(C_k(n,m)\) real operations, then its total cost is \(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}C_k(n,m)\). This model does not by itself charge for operand encoding, finite precision, rounding error, or growth of intermediate bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Real-arithmetic complexity treats every exact real operation as unit cost and therefore separates iteration and linear-algebra counts from finite-precision costs.
assumptions_latex: Exact real arithmetic and exact comparisons are available at unit cost.
The dimensions and stopping criterion are fixed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reported resource is a count of real operations, not a Turing bit-operation bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation-count model using exact real data and exact permitted operations without rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the real-arithmetic computation model, an idealized program-controlled computer can store countably many real numbers and perform exact operations on them, including the four basic arithmetic operations, comparisons, and evaluations of elementary functions such as \(\cos\) and \(\exp\). Stored values are actual reals rather than floating-point approximations, and the permitted operations incur no rounding error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real-arithmetic model idealizes an ordinary program-controlled computer by allowing exact real storage and exact arithmetic, comparisons, and elementary-function evaluations without floating-point approximation or rounding.

children.title: Input-Encoding Dependence
children.top_down_role: Influence of data representation length on polynomial complexity claims.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Encoding-Invariance Criterion for Polynomial Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualifier under which changing finite rational encodings preserves polynomial-time classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) be two encodings of the same rational instance class. If instances can be translated in both directions in polynomial time and there are polynomials \(P_{12},P_{21}\) such that \(|E_2(d)|\le P_{12}(|E_1(d)|)\) and \(|E_1(d)|\le P_{21}(|E_2(d)|)\) for every instance \(d\), then polynomial-time complexity with respect to one encoding is equivalent to polynomial-time complexity with respect to the other, up to polynomial composition. Without polynomial intertranslatability and polynomially related lengths, an exponentially more succinct encoding can change the complexity classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial complexity is invariant only between encodings that are efficiently intertranslatable and polynomially related in length.
assumptions_latex: \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) encode the same rational instance class
Translations in both directions take polynomial time
Encoded lengths are polynomially bounded in both directions
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial-time classification is preserved between \(E_1\) and \(E_2\); arbitrary or exponentially succinct encodings need not preserve it.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Invariance Criterion for Polynomial Complexity
Input-Encoding Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of polynomial-time claims on rational problem encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=(A,b,c)\) be rational problem data, and let \(L=\operatorname{len}(d)\) be the length of a fixed binary encoding containing coefficient signs, numerators, denominators, dimensions, and structural indices. A bit-polynomial interior-point bound must be polynomial in \(L\) and the encoded accuracy request. Bounds polynomial only in the dimensions \((m,n)\), or in numerical magnitudes without their encoding lengths, do not establish polynomial bit complexity. Equivalent rational encodings may change \(L\) polynomially; a representation permitting exponentially more succinct coefficients can correspondingly alter the complexity classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bit-complexity claim is meaningful only relative to a specified input encoding and must depend polynomially on its total binary length.
assumptions_latex: All numerical data are rational and finitely represented.
A concrete binary encoding convention is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial bit complexity is assessed as a function of the complete encoding length \(L\), not dimension alone.

children.title: Precision-Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Numerical precision requirements arising during interior-point computation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditioning-Driven Working-Precision Requirement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic precision requirement under an explicitly assumed stable linear-solve error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a computed solution of a nonsingular system \(Hd=r\), using unit roundoff \(u=2^{-p}\), satisfies \[\frac{\|\widehat d-d\|}{\|d\|}\le\frac{c\kappa(H)u}{1-c\kappa(H)u}\] whenever \(c\kappa(H)u<1\). To make this bound at most \(\eta>0\), it suffices that \[p\ge\log_2\!\left(\frac{c\kappa(H)(1+\eta)}{\eta}\right).\] Thus sufficient working precision grows as \(O(\log\kappa(H)+\log(1/\eta))\). It is polynomially bounded only when these logarithms are polynomially bounded in the encoded input length and requested accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated stable-solve bound, working precision grows with the logarithm of the condition number and the requested inverse accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The displayed forward-error bound holds in the selected norm
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\ge\log_2(c\kappa(H)(1+\eta)/\eta)\) suffices for relative forward error at most \(\eta\).

notation.meaning: condition number in the selected induced norm

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning-Driven Working-Precision Requirement
Precision-Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient finite-precision regime for converting arithmetic iteration bounds into bit bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an interior-point method take \(N\) iterations, and suppose every stored scalar and every arithmetic operation at iteration \(k\) uses at most \(p_k\) bits. A polynomial precision-growth regime requires a polynomial \(P\) such that \(N\leq P(L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\) and \(p_k\leq P(L,\log(1/\varepsilon),k)\) for all \(0\leq k<N\). If each iteration uses polynomially many arithmetic operations and \(p\)-bit arithmetic has polynomial cost in \(p\), these bounds imply polynomial total bit complexity. Uncontrolled condition numbers or exponentially shrinking tolerances may violate this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial bit complexity requires working precision to grow at most polynomially with input length, requested accuracy, and iteration index.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic and rounding procedures have polynomial cost in working precision.
Finite-precision iterates retain the algorithm's required invariants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial iteration count plus polynomial precision growth yields a polynomial bit-operation bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–dual interior Newton mechanism
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\). For an interior state \(z=(x,y,s)\) with \(x>0\), \(s>0\), define \(r_b=Ax-b\), \(r_c=A^Ty+s-c\), and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled primal–dual linear-programming mechanisms based on perturbed KKT Newton systems and positivity-preserving steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal–dual interior mechanism is an iteration that, for some centering parameter \(\sigma\in[0,1]\), computes \((\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) from \(\begin{bmatrix}0&A^T&I\\A&0&0\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-r_c\\-r_b\\-XSe+\sigma\mu e\end{bmatrix}\), then sets \((x^+,y^+,s^+)=(x,y,s)+\alpha(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) for \(0<\alpha\leq1\) chosen so that \(x^+>0\) and \(s^+>0\). A family is obtained by specifying rules for \(\sigma\), \(\alpha\), initialization, neighborhood or potential control, and termination or certificate extraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal–dual interior mechanism maintains positive primal and dual-slack variables, solves one coupled Newton system for feasibility and perturbed complementarity, and advances by a positivity-preserving step. Different centering choices, line searches, neighborhood controls, initializations, and termination or certificate rules define the individual algorithm families.
assumptions_latex: The displayed Newton system is solvable, possibly after an equivalent nonsingular reduction.
The step length is positive and preserves strict positivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled Newton equation plus the positivity-preserving update is the defining mechanism shared by primal–dual interior algorithm families.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The third block equation is \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=-XSe+\sigma\mu e\).
The cases \(\sigma=0\) and \(\sigma=1\) give affine-scaling and pure-centering targets, respectively.
special_cases_latex: With \(r_b=r_c=0\), the mechanism preserves primal and dual equality feasibility.
With nonzero residuals, the first two block equations target their elimination and define an infeasible-start mechanism.
immediate_consequences_latex: The centering parameter trades direct complementarity reduction against movement toward balanced products.
The fraction-to-boundary or line-search rule prevents finite iterates from reaching the boundary of the nonnegative orthant.
boundary_notes: This definition does not prescribe a particular predictor–corrector, neighborhood, or homogeneous embedding.
For nonlinear programs the KKT Jacobian contains derivatives of nonlinear constraints; the displayed system is the linear-programming canonical form.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible primal-dual potential-reduction interior-point algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-start primal-dual interior method with potential-minimizing step selection and relative-complementarity termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an interior primal-dual feasible point \((x_0,y_0,s_0)\), choose \(\rho\geq\sqrt n\) and set \(k=0\). At iteration \(k\), set \((x,s)=(x_k,s_k)\) and \(\gamma=n/(n+\rho)\), and compute \((d_x,d_y,d_s)\) from the specified primal-dual system. Choose \[\bar\alpha\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\alpha\geq0}\psi_{n+\rho}(x_k+\alpha d_x,s_k+\alpha d_s),\] and update \[(x_{k+1},y_{k+1},s_{k+1})=(x_k,y_k,s_k)+\bar\alpha(d_x,d_y,d_s).\] Increment \(k\) and stop if \[\frac{s_k^Tx_k}{s_0^Tx_0}\leq\varepsilon;\] otherwise repeat. The source asserts an iteration-complexity bound identical to that of its referenced linear-programming potential-reduction algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an interior primal-dual feasible point, compute the prescribed primal-dual direction, minimize the potential along that direction, update the primal, dual, and slack variables, and stop when complementarity has fallen to the specified fraction of its initial value. The source asserts the same iteration-complexity bound as its referenced linear-programming counterpart.
assumptions_latex: (d_x,d_y,d_s)\text{ is computed from the specified primal-dual system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar\alpha\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\alpha\geq0}\psi_{n+\rho}(x_k+\alpha d_x,s_k+\alpha d_s),\quad (x_{k+1},y_{k+1},s_{k+1})=(x_k,y_k,s_k)+\bar\alpha(d_x,d_y,d_s),\quad \frac{s_k^Tx_k}{s_0^Tx_0}\leq\varepsilon\text{ is the stopping test; the source asserts the referenced LP-identical iteration-complexity bound.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual and block representations of a primal–dual system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a standard-form primal–dual linear program, let \(z=(x,y,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\), \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), and \(e=(1,\ldots,1)^T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent organizations of primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementarity for linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal–dual residual representation is \(F_0(z)=(A^Ty+s-c,\ Ax-b,\ XSe)\), together with \(x\geq0\), \(s\geq0\). Its perturbed representation at parameter \(\tau\geq0\) is \(F_\tau(z)=(A^Ty+s-c,\ Ax-b,\ XSe-\tau e)\). Thus \(F_0(z)=0\) with nonnegativity represents the KKT system, while \(F_\tau(z)=0\), \(x>0\), \(s>0\), and \(\tau>0\) represents a central system. The corresponding Newton block representation uses the Jacobian \(J(z)=\begin{bmatrix}0&A^T&I\\A&0&0\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal–dual system can be represented as one residual map with three blocks: dual feasibility, primal feasibility, and componentwise complementarity. Subtracting a positive constant vector from the complementarity block gives the perturbed central system. Linearizing the residual map yields the standard three-by-three block Newton matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_0(z)=0\) encodes the primal–dual KKT equalities, \(F_\tau(z)=0\) encodes perturbed complementarity, and \(J(z)\) is their canonical Newton-system representation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(XSe=0\iff x_is_i=0\) for every \(i\).
\(XSe=\tau e\iff x_is_i=\tau\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\tau=0\), the perturbed map reduces to the KKT residual map.
On strictly positive states, \(X\) and \(S\) are nonsingular diagonal matrices, enabling standard block eliminations.
immediate_consequences_latex: The three residual blocks separate optimality error into dual feasibility, primal feasibility, and complementarity components.
Newton directions for feasible, infeasible, and centered methods arise by changing the right-hand side while retaining the same Jacobian structure.
boundary_notes: Nonnegativity must accompany \(F_0(z)=0\); otherwise the polynomial equations admit irrelevant sign-indefinite solutions.
The displayed map is for standard-form linear programming, not the full nonlinear-programming KKT map.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the residual map with respect to \((x,y,s)\).
