knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal versus primal–dual barrier Newton systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of Newton linearizations obtained from two equivalent formulations of nonlinear-programming barrier optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), \(Z=\operatorname{Diag}(z)\), and \(s_i>0\), the primal--dual formulation uses
\[
\Sigma_{pd}=S^{-1}Z,
\]
whereas direct Newton linearization of the primal barrier conditions uses
\[
\Sigma_p=\mu S^{-2}.
\]
The primal choice is obtained from the primal--dual choice by selecting \(Z=\mu S^{-1}\). Although the underlying optimality systems are equivalent, Newton's method applied to the two formulations generally produces different iterates. The derivatives in the primal--dual complementarity formulation remain bounded as slack components approach zero, whereas those in the eliminated primal formulation need not. Under some circumstances, the primal step can substantially violate \(s>0\) and \(z>0\), leading to slow progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal–dual Newton system uses Σ = S⁻¹Z, while direct Newton linearization of the primal barrier equations uses Σ = μS⁻². The latter is the specialization Z = μS⁻¹. Equivalent optimality systems generally yield different Newton iterates, and the primal formulation has a near-zero-slack derivative and positivity-violation failure boundary that motivates preferring the primal–dual system.
assumptions_latex: \text{The compared equation systems are equivalent formulations of the barrier optimality conditions.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Sigma_{pd}=S^{-1}Z,\qquad \Sigma_p=\mu S^{-2}=S^{-1}Z\ \text{when }Z=\mu S^{-1},\quad\text{but their Newton iterates generally differ.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linear-programming pair \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\), a feasible primal–dual interior system consists of \[Ax=b,\qquad A^Ty+s=c,\qquad x>0,\qquad s>0.\] A feasibility-preserving direction satisfies \[A\Delta x=0,\qquad A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=0.\] Consequently, every step \((x,y,s)+\alpha(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) that remains positive preserves both equality systems. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible interior primal–dual system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For the standard primal–dual linear programs, define \(\mathcal F^o=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^Ty+s=c,\ x>0,\ s>0\}\), \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior systems that preserve exact primal and dual equality feasibility while reducing complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible primal–dual interior system is a state \((x,y,s)\in\mathcal F^o\) together with a direction \((\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) satisfying \(A\Delta x=0\), \(A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=0\), and \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=-XSe+\sigma\mu e\) for some \(\sigma\in[0,1]\). An accepted update \((x^+,y^+,s^+)=(x,y,s)+\alpha(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) must satisfy \(x^+>0\), \(s^+>0\). The first two homogeneous direction equations ensure that every accepted iterate remains exactly primal and dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal–dual system starts at a strictly positive point satisfying both primal and dual linear equations. Its direction lies in the null spaces that preserve those equations and solves a centered linearization of complementarity. Any positive step that keeps the primal and slack variables positive therefore changes complementarity without introducing feasibility residuals.
assumptions_latex: \(0\leq\sigma\leq1\), and the block Newton equations admit a direction.
The step length preserves strict positivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_b=r_c=0\) and \(A\Delta x=0\), \(A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=0\) imply \(r_b^+=r_c^+=0\) for every accepted step.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The direction solves the general primal–dual Newton system with its first two right-hand-side blocks equal to zero.
Feasibility preservation is equivalent to \((x^+,y^+,s^+)\in\mathcal F^o\) whenever the positivity conditions hold.
special_cases_latex: \(\sigma=0\) gives the feasible affine-scaling direction.
\(\sigma=1\) gives a feasible centering direction toward products equal to the current average \(\mu\).
immediate_consequences_latex: No feasibility-restoration terms appear in the first two block equations.
The duality gap equals \(x^Ts=n\mu\) at every feasible interior state.

Feasible primal–dual systems require a strictly feasible initial point, which may be difficult to construct without reformulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible Primal–Dual Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual form of an infeasible-start primal–dual linear-programming system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r_p=b-Ax\), \(r_d=c-A^Ty-s\), and \(x,s>0\), an infeasible primal–dual Newton step toward target complementarity \(\sigma\mu\) solves \[A\Delta x=r_p,\qquad A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=r_d,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu e-XSe.\] With a common step length \(\alpha\), the new residuals satisfy \(r_p^+=(1-\alpha)r_p\) and \(r_d^+=(1-\alpha)r_d\). Thus feasibility residuals and complementarity are reduced jointly while positivity is enforced by the step-length rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible-start Newton system corrects primal residual, dual residual, and complementarity simultaneously; a common step contracts both feasibility residuals linearly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(0<\alpha\leq1\) preserving positivity, \(r_p^+=(1-\alpha)r_p\) and \(r_d^+=(1-\alpha)r_d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infeasible interior primal–dual system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a positive state \((x,y,s)\) with \(x>0\), \(s>0\), define \(r_b=Ax-b\), \(r_c=A^Ty+s-c\), \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior systems allowing nonzero primal and dual equality residuals and reducing them jointly with complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An infeasible primal–dual interior system is a positive state for which \((r_b,r_c)\) need not vanish, together with a direction satisfying \(A\Delta x=-r_b\), \(A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=-r_c\), and \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=-XSe+\sigma\mu e\), where \(\sigma\in[0,1]\). With a common step \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), the update remains interior and has residuals \(r_b^+=(1-\alpha)r_b\) and \(r_c^+=(1-\alpha)r_c\). A controlled system additionally requires residual size to remain coupled to the duality measure, typically \(\|(r_b,r_c)\|\leq C\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible primal–dual system keeps primal and slack variables strictly positive but permits violations of the primal and dual linear equations. Its Newton direction contains the negatives of both residuals, so a common partial step contracts each residual by the same factor and a full step eliminates them. Controlled infeasible systems also bound residual size by a constant multiple of the complementarity measure.
assumptions_latex: The residual-correcting Newton system is solvable.
The common step length satisfies \(0<\alpha\leq1\) and preserves positivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining residual dynamics are \((r_b^+,r_c^+)=(1-\alpha)(r_b,r_c)\), while the third block simultaneously targets centered complementarity.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The system is the Newton linearization of \((r_c,r_b,XSe-\sigma\mu e)=0\).
A full step \(\alpha=1\) produces exact primal and dual equality feasibility.
special_cases_latex: If \(r_b=r_c=0\), the system reduces to the feasible primal–dual system.
If \(\sigma=0\), the complementarity block is the infeasible affine-scaling equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: The method can start from arbitrary positive \(x^0,s^0\) without a separate feasibility phase.
If residuals remain \(O(\mu)\) and \(\mu\to0\), both feasibility residuals converge to zero.
boundary_notes: The word infeasible does not permit nonpositive primal or slack components.
Residual contraction alone does not ensure convergence of complementarity or boundedness of the iterates; centrality and step controls remain necessary.

notation.meaning: Constant coupling feasibility residuals to the duality measure.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Complementarity Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-path system for a primal–dual linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), the perturbed primal–dual complementarity system for the linear-programming pair is \[Ax=b,\qquad A^Ty+s=c,\qquad XSe=\mu e,\qquad x>0,\qquad s>0.\] Equivalently, every component satisfies \(x_is_i=\mu\). When solutions exist for all relevant \(\mu\), they form the primal–dual central path. Any accumulation point as \(\mu\downarrow0\) is primal feasible, dual feasible, nonnegative, and complementary, and hence is primal–dual optimal by weak duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The central system replaces exact complementarity by equal positive products; letting the perturbation vanish yields complementary primal–dual optimal limit points.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual linear programs have strictly feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite accumulation point as \(\mu\downarrow0\) satisfies \(Ax=b\), \(A^Ty+s=c\), \(x,s\geq0\), and \(XSe=0\).

notation.meaning: diagonal matrices formed from x and s

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbed primal–dual complementarity system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the standard primal–dual linear programs with variables \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(y\in\mathbb R^m\), and dual slack \(s\in\mathbb R^n\). Let \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), and \(e=(1,\ldots,1)^T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact central systems obtained by replacing complementary slackness with a common positive perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\tau>0\), the perturbed complementarity system is \(Ax=b\), \(A^Ty+s=c\), \(XSe=\tau e\), \(x>0\), and \(s>0\). Equivalently, \(x_is_i=\tau\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Its solution, when uniquely defined, is the central-path point \((x_\tau,y_\tau,s_\tau)\). Since \(x_\tau^Ts_\tau=n\tau\), its duality measure is exactly \(\mu_\tau=\tau\). The family over all \(\tau>0\) is the primal–dual central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbed complementarity system retains exact primal and dual feasibility but replaces zero complementary products by one common positive value. Strict positivity is imposed on both members of every complementary pair. A solution for a given perturbation parameter is a central-path point, and its average complementarity equals that parameter. Varying the parameter over positive values traces the primal–dual central path.
assumptions_latex: The primal–dual pair admits a strictly feasible point so the central system is defined.
For uniqueness, the standard linear-programming regularity stated in the source is assumed, including full row rank after preprocessing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C=\{(x_\tau,y_\tau,s_\tau):\tau>0\}\), where each point satisfies \(X_\tau S_\tau e=\tau e\) and \(\mu_\tau=\tau\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The system is \(F(x,y,s)=(0,0,\tau e)\) for the unperturbed KKT mapping \(F=(r_c,r_b,XSe)\).
It is the KKT system of the logarithmic-barrier problem \(\min\{c^Tx-\tau\sum_i\log x_i:Ax=b\}\), with \(s_i=\tau/x_i\).
special_cases_latex: As \(\tau\downarrow0\), the system approaches complementary slackness and any limit point is primal–dual optimal.
At \(\tau=	au_0>0\), all complementary products are identical, so the point lies in every standard centrality neighborhood with its exact-center parameter.
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal–dual gap at a central point is \(x_\tau^Ts_\tau=n\tau\).
Every perturbed-system solution is strictly interior and exactly primal and dual feasible.
boundary_notes: Replacing \(XSe=\tau e\) by approximate equality defines a centrality neighborhood, not the exact perturbed system.
When strict feasibility fails, this standard central path may not exist; homogeneous embeddings provide a different construction.

notation.meaning: Positive complementarity perturbation or central-path parameter.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Newton Direction Family for Standard-Form Linear Programming
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\). At an interior state \(x>0\), \(s>0\), set \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), \(r_p=Ax-b\), \(r_d=A^Ty+s-c\), \(\mu=x^Ts/n\), and let \(e\) be the all-ones vector.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional standard-form linear programming with exact solutions of the primal–dual Newton system; nonlinear and conic analogues require their corresponding KKT linearizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal–dual direction family at \((x,y,s)\) is the collection \(\mathcal D(x,y,s)=\{d(\sigma,q):\sigma\in[0,1],\ q\in\mathbb R^n\}\), where \(d(\sigma,q)=(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) solves \[\begin{bmatrix}A&0&0\\0&A^T&I\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-r_p\\-r_d\\-XSe+\sigma\mu e+q\end{bmatrix}.\] The parameter \(\sigma\) controls centering, while \(q\) supplies a trajectory or higher-order complementarity correction. The affine-scaling predictor is \(d(0,0)\); a centered Newton direction is \(d(\sigma,0)\) with \(\sigma>0\); and a corrected direction has \(q\neq0\). When the coefficient matrix is nonsingular, every pair \((\sigma,q)\) determines a unique direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a standard-form primal–dual linear program at a strictly positive state, a primal–dual direction family consists of the solutions of one common linearized KKT system. Its first two block equations reduce the primal and dual residuals, while its complementarity equation has right-hand side minus the current componentwise products plus a centering target and an optional correction. Setting both the centering parameter and correction to zero gives the affine-scaling predictor; a positive centering parameter gives a centered direction; and a nonzero correction represents predictor–corrector or higher-order path information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D(x,y,s)=\{d(\sigma,q):\sigma\in[0,1],\ q\in\mathbb R^n\}\) with \(d(\sigma,q)\) defined by the displayed primal–dual Newton system.
equivalent_formulations_latex: By linearity, whenever the Newton matrix is nonsingular, \(d(\sigma,q)=d(0,0)+\sigma d_c+d_q\), where the right-hand sides defining \(d_c\) and \(d_q\) are respectively \((0,0,\mu e)\) and \((0,0,q)\).
special_cases_latex: \(d(0,0)\) is the affine-scaling prediction direction.
\(d(1,0)\) is the full centering Newton direction under the stated convention.
Taking \(q=-\Delta X^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta S^{\mathrm{aff}}e\) incorporates the second-order complementarity product used by predictor–corrector methods.
immediate_consequences_latex: All members of the family share the same Newton coefficient matrix, so distinct right-hand sides can reuse one factorization.
If \(r_p=r_d=0\), then every family member is tangent to the primal and dual equality systems because \(A\Delta x=0\) and \(A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=0\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe a step length or guarantee that the updated variables remain positive.
If the Newton matrix is singular, the displayed equations define a set of directions rather than a unique member.

notation.meaning: Direction indexed by centering parameter and complementarity correction.
Diagonal matrices formed from the positive primal variables and dual slacks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Null-space positive-definiteness condition for a descent primal–dual step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient reduced-space curvature condition for an NLP primal–dual interior-point Newton direction, together with the nonminimizing-stationary-point failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
M=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_{xx}^{2}\mathcal L(x,y,z)&0\\0&\Sigma\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
C=\begin{bmatrix}A_E(x)&0\\A_I(x)&-I\end{bmatrix}.
\]
If \(M\) is positive definite on \(\ker C\), namely
\[
d^TMd>0\qquad\text{for every }d\in\ker C\setminus\{0\},
\]
then the direction defined by the primal--dual system is a descent direction. Without suitable curvature control, the primal--dual equations seek KKT points and can move toward a maximizer or another nonminimizing stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal–dual interior-point step is a descent direction if the block Hessian–complementarity matrix is positive definite on the null space of the linearized equality-and-slack constraints. KKT equations alone do not distinguish minimizers from maximizers or other stationary points, so an uncontrolled step need not be productive.
assumptions_latex: \Sigma=S^{-1}Z\ \text{is the complementarity block in the primal--dual system}
p\ \text{is the direction defined by the primal--dual Newton system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\ \text{is a descent direction.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modified KKT Residual and Primal–Dual Newton Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the modified KKT residual and its coupled Newton direction in the standard differentiable convex-program setting, including the central-path characterization and the conditional preservation of equality feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the standard convex program with inequalities \(f_i(x)\leq 0\) and equalities \(Ax=b\), and for \(t>0\), define
\[
r_t(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{bmatrix}r_{\mathrm{dual}}\\ r_{\mathrm{cent}}\\ r_{\mathrm{pri}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla f_0(x)+Df(x)^T\lambda+A^T\nu\\-\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)f(x)-t^{-1}\mathbf 1\\Ax-b\end{bmatrix}.
\]
If \(r_t(x,\lambda,\nu)=0\) and \(f(x)\prec0\), then \((x,\lambda,\nu)=(x^\star(t),\lambda^\star(t),\nu^\star(t))\); in particular, the variables are primal and dual feasible and their duality gap is \(m/t\). At a point satisfying \(f(x)\prec0\) and \(\lambda\succ0\), the primal–dual search direction is the Newton direction determined by
\[
\begin{bmatrix}H&Df(x)^T&A^T\\-\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)Df(x)&-\operatorname{diag}(f(x))&0\\A&0&0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x_{\mathrm{pd}}\\\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{pd}}\\\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{pd}}\end{bmatrix}
=-\begin{bmatrix}r_{\mathrm{dual}}\\r_{\mathrm{cent}}\\r_{\mathrm{pri}}\end{bmatrix},
\qquad H=\nabla^2f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla^2f_i(x).
\]
When the Newton matrix is nonsingular, this direction is unique. If \(Ax=b\), its last block equation gives \(A\Delta x_{\mathrm{pd}}=0\), and hence \(A(x+s\Delta x_{\mathrm{pd}})=b\) for every scalar \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The modified KKT residual has dual-stationarity, perturbed-complementarity, and equality-feasibility blocks. A strictly inequality-feasible zero is the corresponding central-path primal–dual point and has gap m/t. The primal–dual direction is obtained by jointly Newton-linearizing these blocks at a strictly inequality-feasible point with positive multipliers. If the current point satisfies the equality constraints, the primal direction lies in their nullspace and therefore preserves those equalities for every step length.
assumptions_latex: \text{The problem is in the standard differentiable convex form }\min f_0(x)\text{ s.t. }f_i(x)\leq0,\ Ax=b.
D r_t(x,\lambda,\nu)\ \text{is nonsingular when uniqueness of the Newton direction is asserted}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_t=0\ \wedge\ f(x)\prec0\Longrightarrow (x,\lambda,\nu)=(x^\star(t),\lambda^\star(t),\nu^\star(t)),\ \operatorname{gap}=m/t;\qquad Ax=b\Longrightarrow A\Delta x_{\mathrm{pd}}=0.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Scaling Prediction Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual affine-scaling predictor for linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an interior iterate \((x,y,s)\), define \(r_p=b-Ax\) and \(r_d=c-A^Ty-s\). The affine-scaling prediction direction is the solution of \[A\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}=r_p,\qquad A^T\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}}+\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}=r_d,\qquad S\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}+X\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}=-XSe.\] This is the primal–dual Newton direction for the unperturbed target \(XSe=0\). Choose the largest step fractions, possibly reduced by a safety factor, for which \(x+\alpha_p\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}>0\) and \(s+\alpha_d\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}>0\); the resulting trial point predicts achievable complementarity reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine predictor linearizes the system with zero target complementarity, then takes positivity-limited primal and dual steps to estimate gap reduction.
assumptions_latex: The displayed Newton system has a solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The direction targets zero complementarity to first order while correcting the current primal and dual residuals.

notation.meaning: positivity-limited primal and dual step lengths

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Affine-Scaling Predictor Direction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For the standard-form primal–dual pair, let \((x,y,s)\in\mathbb R^n_{++}\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n_{++}\), with residuals \(r_p=Ax-b\) and \(r_d=A^Ty+s-c\). Write \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), and \(e=(1,\ldots,1)^T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal–dual affine-scaling prediction for finite-dimensional linear programming, including feasible- and infeasible-interior states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-scaling prediction direction \(d^{\mathrm{aff}}=(\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}})\) is the pure Newton direction obtained by setting the complementarity target to zero: \[\begin{bmatrix}A&0&0\\0&A^T&I\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}\\\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}}\\\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-r_p\\-r_d\\-XSe\end{bmatrix}.\] Equivalently, it satisfies \(A\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}=-r_p\), \(A^T\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}}+\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}=-r_d\), and \(S\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}+X\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}=-XSe\). It predicts motion toward primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and zero complementarity without an explicit centering term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine-scaling predictor is the primal–dual Newton direction whose complementarity target is zero. Its linear equations cancel the current primal and dual residuals and linearize the condition that every primal variable–dual slack product should vanish. It contains no centering or second-order correction term. A full affine step would solve the linearized KKT equations exactly, although positivity generally limits the admissible step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^{\mathrm{aff}}\) is the solution of the displayed Newton system with centering parameter \(\sigma=0\) and no correction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The complementarity block is \(S\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}+X\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}=-Xs\).
For a feasible interior state, \(r_p=r_d=0\), so \(A\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}=0\) and \(A^T\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}}+\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}=0\).
special_cases_latex: If a unit affine step remains nonnegative, its linearized primal and dual residuals are zero.
The maximum affine primal and dual steps are obtained separately from the negative components of \(\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}\) and \(\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The predicted affine complementarity \(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}\) can be used to choose a subsequent centering parameter.
The omitted quadratic product \(\Delta X^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta S^{\mathrm{aff}}e\) is the complementarity-model error corrected in Mehrotra-type methods.
boundary_notes: Affine scaling alone does not control proximity to the central path.
The direction is distinct from the primal-only Dikin affine-scaling method.

knowledge_statements.title: Centering Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual Newton direction toward uniform positive complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an interior primal–dual iterate, let \(\mu=x^Ts/n\) and select \(\sigma\in(0,1]\). A centering direction solves the linearized system \[A\Delta x=r_p,\qquad A^T\Delta y+\Delta s=r_d,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu e-XSe.\] At a feasible iterate, \(r_p=r_d=0\), so the direction preserves the primal and dual equalities and moves the complementarity vector toward the uniform target \(\sigma\mu e\). Larger \(\sigma\) emphasizes restoration of centrality; smaller \(\sigma\) emphasizes reduction of the average complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A centering direction is a Newton step toward equal componentwise complementarity, balancing centrality restoration against reduction of the average gap.
assumptions_latex: The displayed Newton system is solvable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linearized complementarity vector is directed toward \(\sigma\mu e\), with equality feasibility preserved when the current residuals vanish.

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Centering Direction and Centering Component
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Use the standard-form primal–dual setting with \(x>0\), \(s>0\), \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), \(\mu=x^Ts/n\), and residuals \(r_p=Ax-b\), \(r_d=A^Ty+s-c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming centering directions defined by the primal–dual Newton equations; the centering target is the equal-product point \(x_is_i=\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The full centering direction \(d^{\mathrm{cen}}=(\Delta x^{\mathrm{cen}},\Delta y^{\mathrm{cen}},\Delta s^{\mathrm{cen}})\) is the primal–dual Newton direction with centering parameter one: \[\begin{bmatrix}A&0&0\\0&A^T&I\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}d^{\mathrm{cen}}=\begin{bmatrix}-r_p\\-r_d\\-XSe+\mu e\end{bmatrix}.\] The additive centering component \(d^c\) is defined by the same coefficient matrix and right-hand side \((0,0,\mu e)\). Thus, when the Newton system is nonsingular, \(d^{\mathrm{cen}}=d^{\mathrm{aff}}+d^c\). More generally, a partially centered direction is \(d(\sigma)=d^{\mathrm{aff}}+\sigma d^c\) for \(\sigma\in(0,1]\), targeting componentwise complementarity \(\sigma\mu e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A centering direction is a primal–dual Newton direction aimed at making the componentwise products of primal variables and dual slacks equal. With full centering, the target product is the current average complementarity. The direction can also be decomposed into the affine-scaling predictor plus a pure centering component. Multiplying that component by a parameter between zero and one interpolates between aggressive complementarity reduction and centrality restoration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The centering family is \(d(\sigma)=d^{\mathrm{aff}}+\sigma d^c\), where \(d^c\) has complementarity right-hand side \(\mu e\), and full centering is \(d(1)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The full direction satisfies \(S\Delta x^{\mathrm{cen}}+X\Delta s^{\mathrm{cen}}=-XSe+\mu e\).
The pure component satisfies \(A\Delta x^c=0\), \(A^T\Delta y^c+\Delta s^c=0\), and \(S\Delta x^c+X\Delta s^c=\mu e\).
special_cases_latex: At a point satisfying \(XSe=\mu e\), the full centering direction has zero complementarity-block right-hand side.
As \(\sigma\downarrow0\), the partially centered direction approaches the affine-scaling predictor.
immediate_consequences_latex: The centering component changes neither linearized primal nor linearized dual feasibility.
A positive \(\sigma\) counteracts dispersion among the products \(x_is_i\).
boundary_notes: Centering does not by itself specify a neighborhood or step acceptance rule.
Some texts reserve the phrase centering direction for the additive component \(d^c\); this record states both conventions explicitly.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Predictor–Corrector Direction Pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At an interior primal–dual state \((x,y,s)\), let \(M=\begin{bmatrix}A&0&0\\0&A^T&I\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\), \(r_p=Ax-b\), \(r_d=A^Ty+s-c\), and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-solve primal–dual predictor–corrector methods for standard-form linear programming, with a shared Newton matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal–dual predictor–corrector direction pair consists of a predictor \(d^p=(\Delta x^p,\Delta y^p,\Delta s^p)\) and a corrector \(d^c=(\Delta x^c,\Delta y^c,\Delta s^c)\) satisfying \[Md^p=\begin{bmatrix}-r_p\\-r_d\\-XSe+t^p\end{bmatrix},\qquad Md^c=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\t^c-\Delta X^p\Delta S^p e\end{bmatrix},\] where \(t^p,t^c\in\mathbb R^n\) are prescribed complementarity targets. The combined direction is \(d=d^p+d^c\). The correction leaves the predictor's linearized feasibility equations unchanged and compensates for the quadratic complementarity term generated by the predictor. In the common affine predictor case, \(t^p=0\); a scalar-centered corrector uses \(t^c=\sigma\mu e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A predictor–corrector method first computes a primal–dual Newton predictor and then solves another system with the same coefficient matrix. The second right-hand side has zero primal and dual feasibility components. Its complementarity component supplies a central target and subtracts the quadratic product of the predictor changes. Adding the two directions therefore preserves the predictor's linearized reduction of feasibility residuals while improving the second-order model of complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The combined predictor–corrector direction is \(d=d^p+d^c\) with the two directions defined by the displayed shared-matrix systems.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The combined complementarity equation is \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=-XSe+t^p+t^c-\Delta X^p\Delta S^p e\).
The corrector is feasibility-neutral: \(A\Delta x^c=0\) and \(A^T\Delta y^c+\Delta s^c=0\).
special_cases_latex: An affine predictor with \(t^p=0\) and a centered second-order corrector with \(t^c=\sigma\mu e\) yields the usual Mehrotra-type structure.
Setting \(t^c=0\) produces a pure second-order correction without explicit recentering.
immediate_consequences_latex: Only one factorization of \(M\) is required when the predictor and corrector are computed at the same state.
The construction separates complementarity prediction from centrality and trajectory-error correction.
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe how \(\sigma\), step lengths, or a central-path neighborhood are selected.
A corrector computed after changing the base state would not share the displayed matrix and is outside this definition.

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrices formed from the predictor changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Controlled Predictor–Correctors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Short-step primal–dual predictor–corrector scheme for a standard-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an interior primal–dual iterate \(z=(x,y,s)\), let \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\) and \(N_2(\theta)=\{z:x>0,\ s>0,\ \|Xs-\mu e\|_2\leq \theta\mu\}\). Compute an affine predictor from the primal–dual Newton equations with complementarity right-hand side \(-Xs\). Choose the largest trial step preserving membership in \(N_2(\bar\theta)\), select \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), and compute a corrector whose complementarity equation includes \(\sigma\mu e-\Delta X^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}\). Backtrack the combined step until the new iterate lies in \(N_2(\theta)\). Stop when the primal residual, dual residual, and \(\mu\) satisfy their prescribed tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute affine and centering corrections, then restrict the combined step so positivity and an explicit central-path neighborhood are preserved until residual and complementarity tolerances hold.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
The current iterate satisfies \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\).
The primal–dual Newton systems are nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^+\in N_2(\theta)\quad\text{and}\quad x^+>0,\ s^+>0\).

notation.meaning: All-ones vector in the complementarity space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the neighborhood-controlled predictor–corrector container, but no citation supports this particular neighborhood, predictor/corrector right-hand side, or acceptance sequence. The matrix notation \(\Delta X^{\mathrm{aff}}\) is not introduced, and the roles and required relation between \(\theta\) and \(\bar\theta\) are unspecified. An authoritative source with a section, theorem, or algorithm locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood-Controlled Predictor–Corrector Transition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), define \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(x,y,s):x>0,\ s>0,\ x_is_i\geq\gamma\mu\ \forall i\}\), where \(\mu=x^Ts/n\). A narrower feasible neighborhood may additionally require \(Ax=b\) and \(A^Ty+s=c\); an infeasible neighborhood may impose a residual bound proportional to \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form linear-programming predictor–correctors whose accepted step is explicitly constrained by a central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A neighborhood-controlled predictor–corrector is a predictor–corrector direction \(d=(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\), together with step lengths \(\alpha_p,\alpha_d\in(0,1]\), such that the accepted state \[(x^+,y^+,s^+)=(x+\alpha_p\Delta x,\ y+\alpha_d\Delta y,\ s+\alpha_d\Delta s)\] belongs to a prescribed neighborhood \(\mathcal N\). For \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\), this means \(x^+>0\), \(s^+>0\), and \(x_i^+s_i^+\geq\gamma\mu^+\) for every \(i\), with \(\mu^+=(x^+)^Ts^+/n\). In an infeasible regime one also requires \(\|(r_p^+,r_d^+)\|\leq C\mu^+\) for a fixed \(C\geq0\). The step-selection rule is the supremal admissible pair, or a prescribed fraction thereof, satisfying these inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A neighborhood-controlled predictor–corrector is not merely a two-stage direction calculation. It also includes an acceptance rule requiring the new positive primal and dual variables to remain in a specified central-path neighborhood. A common neighborhood places a lower bound, relative to the new average complementarity, on every componentwise primal–dual product. In infeasible methods, the new feasibility residuals are also bounded relative to complementarity. Step lengths are reduced until these conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transition is admissible exactly when the updated state satisfies positivity, the prescribed componentwise centrality inequalities, and any stated residual-to-complementarity bound.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a common step \(\alpha_p=\alpha_d=\alpha\), neighborhood control is the requirement \((x,y,s)+\alpha d\in\mathcal N\).
The condition \(x_i^+s_i^+\geq\gamma\mu^+\) is equivalent to \(\min_i x_i^+s_i^+/\mu^+\geq\gamma\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=0\), the residual bound reduces to primal–dual feasibility.
A backtracking rule that starts near the boundary step and decreases the step until \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\) is reached is neighborhood controlled.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every accepted state is strictly interior.
No complementarity pair can become arbitrarily small relative to the mean while the same \(\gamma>0\) is enforced.
boundary_notes: Neighborhood membership does not by itself specify the predictor or corrector right-hand sides.
Separate primal and dual steps require centrality to be checked using the actual mixed update.

notation.meaning: Fixed residual-to-complementarity bound in an infeasible neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.title: Mehrotra Predictor–Corrector Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical adaptive-centering form for standard-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: From an interior iterate \((x,y,s)\), solve the affine-scaling Newton system with target complementarity zero, obtaining \((\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}})\). Let \(\alpha_p^{\mathrm{aff}}\) and \(\alpha_d^{\mathrm{aff}}\) be the maximal positivity-preserving primal and dual steps, define \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\), \(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}=(x+\alpha_p^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}})^{\mathsf T}(s+\alpha_d^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}})/n\), and choose \(\sigma=(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}/\mu)^3\). Solve again with complementarity right-hand side \(-Xs-\Delta X^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}+\sigma\mu e\), then take fraction-to-boundary steps and stop at the prescribed KKT tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mehrotra’s family predicts the affine complementarity reduction, chooses centering adaptively, adds the second-order product correction, and takes safeguarded primal and dual steps.
assumptions_latex: The primal–dual Newton system admits the two required solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^+>0,\quad s^+>0,\quad \sigma=(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}/\mu)^3\in[0,1]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and overall algorithm match the Mehrotra family, but the precise cubic centering rule, separate affine step convention, second-order correction, and fraction-to-boundary implementation require a specific Mehrotra or authoritative textbook citation. Under the stated assumptions alone, the asserted bound \(\sigma\in[0,1]\) is not established.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mehrotra Adaptive-Centering Predictor–Corrector Direction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((x,y,s)\) be a strictly positive standard-form LP state, \(\mu=x^Ts/n\), and \(M\) the primal–dual Newton matrix. Let \(d^{\mathrm{aff}}\) solve the affine-scaling system. Define \(\alpha_p^{\mathrm{aff}}\) and \(\alpha_d^{\mathrm{aff}}\) as the maximum primal and dual affine steps in \([0,1]\) preserving nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The practical Mehrotra family for linear programming, using an affine predictor, adaptive centering, and one second-order correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute \[\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}=\frac{(x+\alpha_p^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}})^T(s+\alpha_d^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}})}{n},\qquad \sigma=\left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}}{\mu}\right)^p,\] where commonly \(p=3\). The centering-corrector direction \(d^{\mathrm{cc}}\) is defined by \[Md^{\mathrm{cc}}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\\sigma\mu e-\Delta X^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta S^{\mathrm{aff}}e\end{bmatrix}.\] The Mehrotra direction is \(d=d^{\mathrm{aff}}+d^{\mathrm{cc}}\). The next state uses positive fractions of the maximum primal and dual steps along \(d\). Thus the predicted effectiveness of affine scaling determines the amount of centering, while the product term supplies a second-order complementarity correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mehrotra's method first computes the affine-scaling predictor and estimates the complementarity that would remain at its maximum admissible primal and dual steps. The ratio of predicted to current complementarity, usually raised to the third power, determines an adaptive centering parameter. A second solve with the same matrix combines the resulting central target with a correction for the predictor's quadratic complementarity error. The affine and centering-corrector directions are added, after which primal and dual fraction-to-boundary steps are applied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d=d^{\mathrm{aff}}+d^{\mathrm{cc}}\), with \(\sigma=(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}/\mu)^p\) and the corrector right-hand side \(\sigma\mu e-\Delta X^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta S^{\mathrm{aff}}e\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The combined direction solves the primal–dual Newton equations with complementarity right-hand side \(-XSe+\sigma\mu e-\Delta X^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta S^{\mathrm{aff}}e\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}\ll\mu\), then \(\sigma\) is near zero and the step emphasizes complementarity reduction.
If \(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}\) is close to \(\mu\), then \(\sigma\) is larger and the step emphasizes centering.
Taking \(p=3\) gives the widely used cubic centering heuristic.
immediate_consequences_latex: The predictor and corrector need one matrix factorization and two substitutions.
The correction models complementarity to second order in the affine direction.
boundary_notes: The adaptive rule is heuristic; this definition does not assert global convergence without safeguards.
Implementations vary in the exponent, step fractions, and whether a curved or summed direction is used.

notation.meaning: Complementarity predicted at the affine boundary steps.
Positive exponent in the adaptive centering rule, commonly three.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Centrality Correctors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated centrality corrections following a primal–dual predictor step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute a predictor direction \(d^{(0)}\) and a tentative positivity-preserving step. For \(j=1,\ldots,q\), evaluate the tentative componentwise products \(w^{(j-1)}=(x+\Delta x^{(j-1)})\circ(s+\Delta s^{(j-1)})\). Choose a target vector \(t^{(j)}\) by projecting or clipping \(w^{(j-1)}\) into prescribed centrality bounds, solve the primal–dual Newton system with zero primal and dual residual right-hand sides and complementarity right-hand side \(t^{(j)}-w^{(j-1)}\), and add the resulting correction. Terminate corrections after \(q\) solves or when the centrality measure is below tolerance; then take a fraction-to-boundary step using the accumulated direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After prediction, repeatedly solve complementarity-only correction systems that move tentative products toward prescribed centrality bounds before accepting a safeguarded step.
assumptions_latex: Each correction uses the same nonsingular primal–dual Newton matrix.
The correction count \(q\in\mathbb N\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d=d^{(0)}+\sum_{j=1}^{q}d^{(j)}\quad\text{and the accepted iterate satisfies}\quad x^+>0,\ s^+>0\).

notation.meaning: Target complementarity vector for correction j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is appropriately an algorithm for multiple centrality correctors, but projecting or clipping tentative products does not identify a mathematically determinate corrector variant. The target bounds, projection rule, tentative-step convention, and stopping measure need an authoritative algorithm-level source and precise locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiple-Centrality-Corrector Direction Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M\) be the primal–dual Newton matrix at a fixed interior state, and let \(d^{(0)}\) be an initial predictor–corrector direction. For a trial step, let \(w^{(j)}\in\mathbb R^n\) denote its vector of predicted componentwise complementarity products.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gondzio-type multiple-correction families for standard-form linear programming; all corrections are computed at one base state and preserve the initial direction's linearized feasibility equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiple-centrality-corrector direction of order \(J\geq1\) is \[d^{[J]}=d^{(0)}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\delta d^{(j)},\qquad M\delta d^{(j)}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\q^{(j)}\end{bmatrix}.\] Each correction target \(q^{(j)}\) is selected from the current trial products \(w^{(j-1)}\) to reduce violations of a prescribed centrality interval \([\ell\mu^{(j-1)},u\mu^{(j-1)}]\), where \(0<\ell<1<u\). A canonical projection choice is \[q_i^{(j)}=\Pi_{[\ell\mu^{(j-1)},u\mu^{(j-1)}]}(w_i^{(j-1)})-w_i^{(j-1)}.\] Corrections are appended only while the resulting trial direction improves the admissible step or neighborhood measure and a prescribed correction limit has not been reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-centrality-corrector method starts with an ordinary predictor–corrector direction and adds one or more feasibility-neutral corrections. Every correction uses the same Newton matrix and changes only the complementarity right-hand side. A standard target clips predicted componentwise products into a centrality interval around their mean. The corrections are retained while they improve the admissible step or centrality and until a fixed maximum number has been computed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The order-\(J\) direction is \(d^{[J]}=d^{(0)}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\delta d^{(j)}\), where each correction has zero primal and dual residual blocks and a centrality-restoring complementarity block.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every correction satisfies \(A\delta x^{(j)}=0\) and \(A^T\delta y^{(j)}+\delta s^{(j)}=0\).
The projection target is zero for components already lying in the prescribed centrality interval.
special_cases_latex: \(J=1\) gives a single additional centrality correction.
Choosing \(u=+\infty\) yields a one-sided correction that only raises products below \(\ell\mu\).
immediate_consequences_latex: One factorization of \(M\) can serve all corrector substitutions.
The corrections can improve centrality or step length without altering linearized feasibility reduction.
boundary_notes: The exact centrality interval, stopping test, and trial step are implementation-dependent.
Additional corrections need not reduce total computation time even when they reduce iteration count.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Path Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative representation of higher-order directions along a smooth primal–dual central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the central path \(z(\mu)=(x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) be defined locally by \(F(z(\mu),\mu)=0\), where \(F\) contains primal feasibility, dual stationarity, and \(XSe-\mu e\). If \(F_z\) is nonsingular and \(F\) is \(p\)-times continuously differentiable, then derivatives \(z^{(k)}(\mu)\) for \(1\leq k\leq p\) are obtained recursively by differentiating \(F(z(\mu),\mu)=0\) exactly \(k\) times and solving a linear system with coefficient matrix \(F_z\). A path-following trial point is represented by \(z(\mu+h)=z(\mu)+\sum_{k=1}^{p}h^k z^{(k)}(\mu)/k!+O(|h|^{p+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order path directions are recursively computed derivatives of the smooth central path and form a truncated Taylor model for trial points.

notation.meaning: kth derivative of the central-path state.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the higher-order path-directions container, but the claimed \(O(|h|^{p+1})\) Taylor remainder does not follow merely from \(p\)-times continuous differentiability; stronger regularity such as a Lipschitz \(p\)th derivative or one additional derivative is normally needed. A source is also required for the interior-point specialization and recursive systems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Truncated Higher-Order Primal–Dual Trajectory Direction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(z=(x,y,s)\) and let \(F(z)=(Ax-b,\ A^Ty+s-c,\ XSe)\). Let \(\widehat z(\tau)\) be a sufficiently differentiable primal–dual trajectory with \(\widehat z(0)=z\), defined locally by prescribed residual and complementarity targets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-order Taylor directions for smooth primal–dual trajectories in linear programming; exact derivatives are obtained from repeated systems sharing the first-order Newton matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(p\geq2\), the order-\(p\) path displacement at parameter \(h\) is \[d_p(h)=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{h^j}{j!}\widehat z^{(j)}(0).\] The derivative vectors are defined by differentiating the trajectory equations through order \(p\). Their linear terms use the same Jacobian \(F'(z)\), while the right-hand side for order \(j\) contains products of derivatives of total order \(j\) arising from \(XSe\). An order-\(p\) higher-order path direction is any first-order representation of this displacement, or the curved update \(z^+=z+d_p(h)\), subject to positivity and any neighborhood constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-order path direction approximates a smooth primal–dual trajectory by retaining more than its first derivative. The update is the Taylor polynomial formed from the trajectory derivatives at the current state. Each derivative is obtained using the same first-order primal–dual Jacobian with a new right-hand side containing lower-order componentwise products. The resulting update may be treated as a curved step or collapsed into a single search displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The order-\(p\) trajectory displacement is \(d_p(h)=\sum_{j=1}^{p}h^j\widehat z^{(j)}(0)/j!\), with \(p\geq2\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(p=2\), \(d_2(h)=h\widehat z'(0)+h^2\widehat z''(0)/2\).
The higher derivatives may be computed by repeated back substitutions because their coefficient matrix is the trajectory Jacobian at \(z\).
special_cases_latex: The second-order truncation supplies the trajectory interpretation of a predictor plus one quadratic correction.
Taking \(p=1\) recovers an ordinary tangent or Newton path direction and is excluded from the higher-order class.
immediate_consequences_latex: Increasing \(p\) adds trajectory-curvature information without requiring a new coefficient-matrix factorization at the same state.
Positivity can restrict \(h\) even when the Taylor approximation is accurate locally.
boundary_notes: A Taylor truncation need not follow the path well through sharp turns.
The definition does not assert that increasing the order improves wall-clock performance or global convergence.

notation.meaning: Order-\(j\) derivative of the selected primal–dual trajectory.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Controlled Primal–Dual Interior-State Transition System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(z=(x,y,s)\) be a primal–dual state for a standard-form LP and let \(\mathcal I=\{(x,y,s):x>0,\ s>0\}\). Let \(\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal I\) be an optional centrality/residual neighborhood and let \(D(z)\) be an admissible direction set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal control-system view of positivity, neighborhood, direction, and initialization mechanisms for finite-dimensional primal–dual interior-point methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interior-state control system is a triple \((\mathcal Z,D,U)\) with state domain \(\mathcal Z\subseteq\mathcal I\), direction correspondence \(D(z)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n+m}\), and control set \[U(z,d)=\{(\alpha_p,\alpha_d):0<\alpha_p,\alpha_d\leq1,\ T(z,d,\alpha_p,\alpha_d)\in\mathcal Z\},\] where \[T(z,d,\alpha_p,\alpha_d)=(x+\alpha_p\Delta x,\ y+\alpha_d\Delta y,\ s+\alpha_d\Delta s).\] A generated sequence satisfies \(d^k\in D(z^k)\), \((\alpha_p^k,\alpha_d^k)\in U(z^k,d^k)\), and \(z^{k+1}=T(z^k,d^k,\alpha_p^k,\alpha_d^k)\). An initialization map is admissible when it returns \(z^0\in\mathcal Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior-state control system consists of an interior state domain, a set of allowable directions at every state, and a set of allowable primal and dual step lengths. The transition applies the selected steps and is admissible only when the resulting state remains in the domain, which may include positivity, centrality, and residual conditions. An initialization procedure belongs to the system when it returns a state in that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every controlled transition satisfies \(z^{k+1}=T(z^k,d^k,\alpha_p^k,\alpha_d^k)\in\mathcal Z\subseteq\mathcal I\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With a common step, restrict \(U\) to pairs \((\alpha,\alpha)\).
With \(\mathcal Z=\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\), admissibility is equivalent to positivity and the specified componentwise centrality inequalities after the update.
special_cases_latex: Fraction-to-the-boundary control is obtained by restricting the step lengths to fixed fractions of their boundary values.
A feasible-start system takes \(\mathcal Z\) inside the primal–dual equality manifold; an infeasible-start system permits nonzero residuals.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every state generated by the system remains strictly positive.
Initialization, direction choice, and step acceptance become separate mathematical components of the same transition model.
boundary_notes: This definition supplies no convergence claim.
Alternative sign conventions or nonlinear-programming KKT systems require corresponding changes to the state and transition.

notation.meaning: Admissible step-control pairs at state \(z\) along direction \(d\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fraction-to-the-Boundary Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise positivity safeguard for primal and dual interior variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x,s>0\), directions \(\Delta x,\Delta s\), and \(\tau\in(0,1)\), define \(\alpha_p^{\max}=\min\{1,\min_{i:\Delta x_i<0}(-x_i/\Delta x_i)\}\) and \(\alpha_d^{\max}=\min\{1,\min_{i:\Delta s_i<0}(-s_i/\Delta s_i)\}\), with an empty inner minimum interpreted as \(+\infty\). Set \(\alpha_p=\min\{1,\tau\alpha_p^{\max}\}\) and \(\alpha_d=\min\{1,\tau\alpha_d^{\max}\}\), and update \(x^+=x+\alpha_p\Delta x\) and \(s^+=s+\alpha_d\Delta s\). The safeguard may be combined with further merit-function or neighborhood backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale each primal and dual step to a fixed fraction of its maximal positivity-preserving length, leaving room before the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^+\in\mathbb R^n_{++}\quad\text{and}\quad s^+\in\mathbb R^n_{++}\).

notation.meaning: Maximal primal and dual positivity-preserving steps.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm belongs in the fraction-to-the-boundary container and its stated update preserves positivity. However, capping \(\alpha^{\max}\) at one and then multiplying it by \(\tau\) forces a step below one even when the full step is safely interior; this differs from the common convention that applies the cap after scaling the uncapped boundary ratio. A precise source is needed to establish the intended convention.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Fraction-to-the-Boundary Safeguard
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x>0\), \(s>0\), and let \((\Delta x,\Delta s)\) be a proposed primal–dual displacement. Let \(\tau_p,\tau_d\in(0,1)\) be prescribed safety fractions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise positivity safeguarding for finite-dimensional nonnegative primal variables and dual slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the maximum nonnegative primal and dual steps by \[\alpha_{p,\max}=\min\left\{1,\min_{i:\Delta x_i<0}\frac{-x_i}{\Delta x_i}\right\},\qquad \alpha_{d,\max}=\min\left\{1,\min_{i:\Delta s_i<0}\frac{-s_i}{\Delta s_i}\right\},\] with the inner minimum over an empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The fraction-to-the-boundary safeguarded steps are \(\alpha_p=\tau_p\alpha_{p,\max}\) and \(\alpha_d=\tau_d\alpha_{d,\max}\). Equivalently, they are the largest steps in \([0,1]\) satisfying \(x+\alpha_p\Delta x\geq(1-\tau_p)x\) and \(s+\alpha_d\Delta s\geq(1-\tau_d)s\), componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fraction-to-the-boundary safeguard first finds the largest primal and dual steps, capped at one, that do not cross a zero bound. It then takes fixed fractions of those boundary steps. Equivalently, the updated primal variables and dual slacks must retain prescribed positive fractions of their current values in every component threatened by the direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The safeguarded update satisfies \(x+\alpha_p\Delta x>0\) and \(s+\alpha_d\Delta s>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\alpha_{p,\max}=\sup\{\alpha\in[0,1]:x+\alpha\Delta x\geq0\}\), and analogously for \(\alpha_{d,\max}\).
The fraction condition is \(x_i+\alpha_p\Delta x_i\geq(1-\tau_p)x_i\) and \(s_i+\alpha_d\Delta s_i\geq(1-\tau_d)s_i\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: A common safeguard uses \(\tau_p=\tau_d=\tau\).
If every component of \(\Delta x\) is nonnegative, then \(\alpha_{p,\max}=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(\tau_p,\tau_d<1\), strict positivity is preserved.
The primal and dual boundary steps can be computed independently.
boundary_notes: The safeguard controls positivity but not centrality or residual reduction.
Choosing a safety fraction equal to one can place a component on the boundary and therefore does not ensure strict interiority.

notation.meaning: Maximum capped primal and dual steps to the nonnegative boundary.

children.title: Primal–Dual Step-Length Regimes
children.top_down_role: Shared and separate primal and dual step controls.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Step-Length Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of shared-step and separate-step primal–dual updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an interior state and a primal–dual direction, a shared-step regime chooses \(\alpha\leq\min\{\alpha_p^{\max},\alpha_d^{\max}\}\) and updates all variables by \((x^+,y^+,s^+)=(x,y,s)+\alpha(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\). A separate-step regime chooses \(\alpha_p\leq\alpha_p^{\max}\) and \(\alpha_d\leq\alpha_d^{\max}\), then sets \(x^+=x+\alpha_p\Delta x\), \(y^+=y+\alpha_d\Delta y\), and \(s^+=s+\alpha_d\Delta s\). Both regimes preserve strict positivity when their bounds are reduced by a fraction-to-boundary factor; separate steps need not preserve an affine primal–dual residual relation shared by a common step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared steps update the entire primal–dual state uniformly; separate steps can advance primal and dual blocks differently while retaining positivity safeguards.
assumptions_latex: The maximal step lengths are defined by componentwise positivity.
Accepted steps use a factor strictly below the relevant maximal boundary step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^+>0\quad\text{and}\quad s^+>0\) in either regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property matches the shared-versus-separate step-length container, but the assignment of the multiplier update to the dual step and the claim about loss of an affine residual relation are convention-dependent. These claims require a specific interior-point reference with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Step and Separate-Step Primal–Dual Regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(z=(x,y,s)\) be an interior primal–dual state and \(d=(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) a proposed direction. Let \(\alpha_{p,\max}\) and \(\alpha_{d,\max}\) denote the maximum primal and dual positivity-preserving steps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Step-length organization for standard-form LP primal–dual methods; dual multipliers and dual slacks share the dual step in the separate-step regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A common-step regime selects one \(\alpha\in(0,\min\{\alpha_{p,\max},\alpha_{d,\max}\}]\) and updates \[x^+=x+\alpha\Delta x,\quad y^+=y+\alpha\Delta y,\quad s^+=s+\alpha\Delta s.\] A separate-step regime selects \(\alpha_p\in(0,\alpha_{p,\max}]\) and \(\alpha_d\in(0,\alpha_{d,\max}]\) and updates \[x^+=x+\alpha_p\Delta x,\quad y^+=y+\alpha_d\Delta y,\quad s^+=s+\alpha_d\Delta s.\] Either regime may further restrict its steps through fraction-to-boundary or neighborhood conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common-step primal–dual method moves every primal and dual variable by the same scalar step, which cannot exceed either boundary step. A separate-step method moves the primal variables with one scalar and the dual multiplier and slack variables with another. Each scalar is limited by its own positivity boundary and may be reduced further to enforce centrality or other acceptance conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two regimes are distinguished by whether \(\alpha_p=\alpha_d\) is required or independent admissible values are permitted.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The common-step regime is the diagonal subset \(\{(\alpha_p,\alpha_d):\alpha_p=\alpha_d\}\) of the separate-step control set.
With fraction parameters \(\tau_p,\tau_d\), the separate steps are \(\alpha_p=\tau_p\alpha_{p,\max}\) and \(\alpha_d=\tau_d\alpha_{d,\max}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\alpha_{p,\max}=\alpha_{d,\max}\) and the same safety fraction is used, the separate-step update coincides with a common-step update.
Tightly coupled complementarity formulations may require a common step for all complementary variables.
immediate_consequences_latex: Separate steps can exploit a longer admissible move on one side of the primal–dual pair.
The actual updated complementarity in a separate-step regime must be evaluated using both \(\alpha_p\) and \(\alpha_d\).
boundary_notes: Separate steps do not preserve a single affine parameterization of the full primal–dual trajectory.
The definition does not select which regime is preferable for a given problem class.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual coupling under separate primal and dual QP interior-point steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex-QP specialization of shared-versus-separate primal-dual step control. The malformed final optimality-measure notation in the extract is excluded; the verified residual identities, failure boundary, and common fraction-to-the-boundary safeguard are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex-QP primal-dual Newton direction, let \[(x^+,y^+)=(x,y)+\alpha^{\mathrm{pri}}(\Delta x,\Delta y),\qquad \lambda^+=\lambda+\alpha^{\mathrm{dual}}\Delta\lambda,\] with step lengths preserving positivity. Then \[r_p^+=(1-\alpha^{\mathrm{pri}})r_p,\qquad r_d^+=(1-\alpha^{\mathrm{dual}})r_d+(\alpha^{\mathrm{pri}}-\alpha^{\mathrm{dual}})G\Delta x.\] Hence, if \(\alpha^{\mathrm{pri}}=\alpha^{\mathrm{dual}}=\alpha\in(0,1)\), both residuals satisfy \((r_p^+,r_d^+)=(1-\alpha)(r_p,r_d)\). With unequal steps, the additional Hessian-coupling term can increase \(r_d^+\) and may cause divergence. A safeguarded common step is \[\alpha=\min\{\alpha_\tau^{\mathrm{pri}},\alpha_\tau^{\mathrm{dual}}\},\] where \(\tau\in(0,1)\) and the two bounds are the largest \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) satisfying \(y+\alpha\Delta y\ge(1-\tau)y\) and \(\lambda+\alpha\Delta\lambda\ge(1-\tau)\lambda\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex-QP primal-dual Newton step, the primal residual is controlled by the primal step length, while unequal primal and dual lengths add a Hessian-dependent term to the new dual residual. Equal lengths contract both residuals by the same factor. Unequal lengths may be faster but can increase the dual residual and even cause divergence, so a common fraction-to-the-boundary step provides a safeguard.
assumptions_latex: (\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta\lambda)\ \text{satisfies the convex-QP primal-dual Newton equations}
\alpha^{\mathrm{pri}},\alpha^{\mathrm{dual}}\ \text{preserve positivity of the updated slack and multiplier}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha^{\mathrm{pri}}=\alpha^{\mathrm{dual}}=\alpha\in(0,1)\Rightarrow(r_p^+,r_d^+)=(1-\alpha)(r_p,r_d),\qquad \alpha^{\mathrm{pri}}\ne\alpha^{\mathrm{dual}}\Rightarrow r_d^+\text{ may increase.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible-Start and Infeasible-Start Interior Regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a standard-form primal–dual LP state \(z^0=(x^0,y^0,s^0)\) with \(x^0>0\) and \(s^0>0\), define \(r_p^0=Ax^0-b\), \(r_d^0=A^Ty^0+s^0-c\), and \(\mu_0=(x^0)^Ts^0/n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by the initial equality residuals; both regimes require strict positivity of the complementary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The feasible-start interior regime is the set \[\mathcal I_F=\{(x^0,y^0,s^0):x^0>0,\ s^0>0,\ r_p^0=0,\ r_d^0=0\}.\] The infeasible-start interior regime is \[\mathcal I_I=\{(x^0,y^0,s^0):x^0>0,\ s^0>0,\ (r_p^0,r_d^0)\neq(0,0)\}.\] A residual-controlled infeasible start additionally satisfies \(\|(r_p^0,r_d^0)\|\leq C\mu_0\) for a prescribed \(C>0\). Algorithms in the feasible regime normally choose tangent directions that retain zero residuals, whereas infeasible-interior directions include equations that reduce the nonzero residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An initial interior point is in the feasible-start regime when both primal and dual equality residuals vanish and the primal variables and dual slacks are strictly positive. It is in the infeasible-start regime when positivity holds but at least one equality residual is nonzero. A controlled infeasible start also bounds the residual norm relative to its initial complementarity measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every strictly positive initial state belongs to exactly one of \(\mathcal I_F\) or \(\mathcal I_I\), according to whether \((r_p^0,r_d^0)=(0,0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(z^0\in\mathcal I_F\) exactly when it is strictly primal–dual feasible.
\(z^0\in\mathcal I_I\) exactly when it is strictly interior with respect to nonnegativity but infeasible for at least one equality system.
special_cases_latex: A primal-feasible but dual-infeasible state, with \(r_p^0=0\) and \(r_d^0\neq0\), belongs to \(\mathcal I_I\).
A dual-feasible but primal-infeasible state also belongs to \(\mathcal I_I\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Feasible-start tangent steps preserve equality feasibility when their first two Newton right-hand sides are zero.
Infeasible-start methods must explicitly include residual-reduction terms.
boundary_notes: Strict positivity is independent of equality feasibility.
A point on the nonnegative boundary belongs to neither interior regime.

children.title: Feasible-Start Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interior-point regimes initialized with the required primal or primal–dual feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Start Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly feasible initialization for standard-form primal–dual linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal–dual pair \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\), a feasible-start regime initializes \((x^0,y^0,s^0)\) so that \(Ax^0=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y^0+s^0=c\), \(x^0>0\), and \(s^0>0\). Consequently, any Newton direction satisfying the homogeneous linearized feasibility equations \(A\Delta x=0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0\) preserves primal and dual feasibility for every accepted step, while positivity is maintained separately by step-length control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible-start method begins strictly inside both feasible regions, so homogeneous Newton feasibility equations preserve zero primal and dual residuals.
assumptions_latex: A strictly primal–dual feasible point exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_p^0=b-Ax^0=0\quad\text{and}\quad r_d^0=c-A^{\mathsf T}y^0-s^0=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriate for the feasible-start container, but the record provides no citation at all. Supply an authoritative interior-point or linear-programming source with a specific section, definition, or page locator.

children.title: Infeasible-Start Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interior-point regimes permitting nonzero initial feasibility residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible-Start Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive but not necessarily feasible primal–dual initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a standard-form primal–dual linear program, an infeasible-start regime permits initial variables \((x^0,y^0,s^0)\) satisfying \(x^0>0\) and \(s^0>0\) without requiring \(Ax^0=b\) or \(A^{\mathsf T}y^0+s^0=c\). At iteration \(k\), the Newton equations include the nonzero residual right-hand sides \(r_p^k=b-Ax^k\) and \(r_d^k=c-A^{\mathsf T}y^k-s^k\), together with a perturbed complementarity equation. Step lengths preserve positivity, and termination requires simultaneous reduction of scaled primal infeasibility, scaled dual infeasibility, and complementarity below their prescribed tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible-start method requires positive primal and slack variables but allows nonzero feasibility residuals, which are explicitly reduced by each Newton system.
assumptions_latex: The primal–dual Newton equations are consistently defined at each iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k>0,\ s^k>0\quad\text{while}\quad \|r_p^k\|\to0,\ \|r_d^k\|\to0,\ \mu_k\to0\) is the target regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes an infeasible-start regime and fits the terminal container. No source is cited, however, and the displayed convergence language must be supported or clearly treated only as a termination target rather than a convergence guarantee. A precise algorithm or textbook locator is required.

children.title: Residual-Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Progress from initially infeasible iterates toward a feasible interior trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for switching from infeasible-start control to a near-feasible local regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_p^k\), \(r_d^k\), and \(\mu_k\) denote the primal residual, dual residual, and average complementarity. For fixed tolerances \(\eta_p,\eta_d>0\) and scaling factors \(D_p,D_d>0\), define the transition predicate \(T_k\) by \(\|r_p^k\|/D_p\leq\eta_p\mu_k\) and \(\|r_d^k\|/D_d\leq\eta_d\mu_k\). An infeasible-start iteration may enter a near-feasible path-following regime only when \(T_k\) holds; thereafter, acceptance rules must retain these residual-to-complementarity bounds or revert to the residual-reduction regime. This predicate distinguishes approximate centrality with controlled feasibility from complementarity reduction alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Switch to near-feasible path following only when scaled primal and dual residuals are bounded proportionally to current complementarity; revert if those bounds fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_k\iff \frac{\|r_p^k\|}{D_p}\leq\eta_p\mu_k\ \text{and}\ \frac{\|r_d^k\|}{D_d}\leq\eta_d\mu_k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the residual-transition container, but this particular proportional residual predicate, its scaling factors, and the mandatory switch/reversion policy are algorithm-dependent rather than canonical. No evidence supports the claim that entry may occur only under this predicate; a precise source is required.

children.title: Auxiliary Initialization Calculus
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary constructions for locating an interior start or diagnosing feasibility.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Least-Norm Shifted Interior Initialization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Assume \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank. Consider the standard-form primal and dual equality systems \(Ax=b\) and \(A^Ty+s=c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete auxiliary initialization construction for linear programming; it creates positive primal and slack variables from least-norm equality solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute auxiliary least-norm points \[\widetilde x\in\arg\min\{\|x\|_2^2:Ax=b\},\qquad (\widetilde y,\widetilde s)\in\arg\min\{\|s\|_2^2:A^Ty+s=c\}.\] Choose shifts \(\delta_x>\max\{0,-\min_i\widetilde x_i\}\) and \(\delta_s>\max\{0,-\min_i\widetilde s_i\}\), and define \[x^0=\widetilde x+\delta_xe,\qquad y^0=\widetilde y,\qquad s^0=\widetilde s+\delta_se.\] This auxiliary calculus guarantees \(x^0>0\) and \(s^0>0\). Its equality residuals are \(r_p^0=\delta_xAe\) and \(r_d^0=\delta_se\), so the shifted point is generally an infeasible-interior start unless the shifts are compensated by additional projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The auxiliary initialization first solves two least-norm equality problems, one for the primal variables and one for the dual slack. Because either least-norm vector may contain nonpositive components, positive multiples of the all-ones vector are added until every primal variable and dual slack is strictly positive. The resulting state is an interior starting point. The shifts usually reintroduce equality residuals, which are stated explicitly and are handled by an infeasible-interior method or by further correction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The shifted auxiliary state satisfies \(x^0>0\), \(s^0>0\), \(r_p^0=\delta_xAe\), and \(r_d^0=\delta_se\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(A\) has full row rank, \(\widetilde x=A^T(AA^T)^{-1}b\).
The least-norm dual slack is obtained by orthogonally projecting \(c\) onto the null space complementary to \(\operatorname{Range}(A^T)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\widetilde x>0\) and \(\widetilde s>0\), the shifts may be omitted and the least-norm point is strictly feasible.
Additional positive shifts may be chosen to improve balance among the products \(x_i^0s_i^0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The construction always supplies strict bound interiority once the least-norm subproblems are solvable.
The residuals introduced by the positivity shifts are known analytically.
boundary_notes: The construction is a starting-point heuristic, not a certificate that the original primal and dual problems are feasible.
Large shifts may yield poor residual-to-complementarity scaling.

notation.meaning: Positive component shifts used to obtain strict interiority.

children.title: Phase-I Auxiliary Models
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary optimization models used to seek an interior starting regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Phase-I Auxiliary Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex Phase-I model for finding a strictly feasible inequality point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(g_i(x)<0\), choose any \(x^0\) in the domain of every \(g_i\) and a scalar \(t^0>\max_i g_i(x^0)\). Solve the auxiliary convex problem \(\min_{x,t} t\) subject to \(g_i(x)\leq t\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), initialized at the strictly feasible point \((x^0,t^0)\). Stop when either a point with \(t<0\) is obtained or the auxiliary optimality tolerance is reached. Output \(x\) as a strict interior start when \(t<0\); if the certified optimal value is positive, report that the original strict inequalities have no common solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a common constraint-violation bound from an easily constructed interior auxiliary point; a negative result supplies a strict interior start.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex on a common convex domain.
An initial \(x^0\) belongs to that common domain.
The auxiliary problem is solved with a valid optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t<0\Longrightarrow g_i(x)<0\ \text{for every}\ i\).

notation.meaning: Common upper bound on all inequality values.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Phase-I formulation and negative-\(t\) implication are appropriate for the container. The infeasibility diagnosis from a positive certified optimum depends on attainment, solution accuracy, and the meaning of the certificate, none of which is sourced or fully specified. Provide an authoritative convex-optimization source with a precise Phase-I locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Phase-I Interior-Point Auxiliary Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior-start construction that updates violated and satisfied constraint sets, with a conditional dual infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(g_i(x)\geq0\), define \(S=\{s:g_s(x)\leq0\}\) and \(T=\{t:g_t(x)>0\}\). For a strictly decreasing null sequence \(r_k\downarrow0\), minimize \(U(x,r_k)=-\sum_{s\in S}g_s(x)+r_k\sum_{t\in T}I_t(g_t(x))\). Whenever a previously violated constraint becomes strictly satisfied, move its index from \(S\) to \(T\) and update the auxiliary problem. If \(S=\varnothing\), a strictly feasible point has been obtained. The procedure declares infeasibility if an auxiliary problem is solved with \(S\ne\varnothing\). When the constraints are concave, the auxiliary problem is convex; under the cited dual framework, \(G^k>0\) at an unconstrained auxiliary minimum is a sufficient infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the negative sum of currently violated constraint values while protecting already strictly satisfied constraints with interior penalty terms. Transfer an index to the satisfied set whenever its constraint becomes strictly positive. An empty violated set supplies the required interior start. Remaining violations at a solved auxiliary problem trigger the procedure's infeasibility declaration, while the rigorous early certificate stated in the extract additionally requires concave constraints and the source's dual quantity to satisfy G^k>0. Constraints reserved for exterior penalties are ignored until an interior point is found.
assumptions_latex: x^0\text{ is given but is not strictly feasible for every constraint}
\text{for convexity and the dual certificate, every }g_i\text{ is concave and the cited dual framework applies}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\varnothing\Longrightarrow g_i(x)>0\ \forall i;\qquad S\ne\varnothing\text{ at an auxiliary solution triggers declared infeasibility};\qquad G^k>0\Longrightarrow\text{infeasibility under the concave-constraint dual assumptions}.
