knowledge_statements.statement_title: First- and second-order stationarity targets for nonconvex NLP
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c_E(x)=0\) and \(c_I(x)\ge0\), with twice continuously differentiable data. Let \(L(x,y,z)=f(x)-y^Tc_E(x)-z^Tc_I(x)\), and let \(\mathcal C(x,y,z)\) denote the KKT critical cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and approximate stationarity for smooth finite-dimensional nonconvex nonlinear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A primal-dual point \((x,y,z)\) is a first-order stationarity target when \[c_E(x)=0,\quad c_I(x)\ge0,\quad z\ge0,\quad z_i c_{I,i}(x)=0,\quad 
abla_xL(x,y,z)=0.\] It is a second-order stationarity target when it is first-order stationary and additionally \[d^T
abla_{xx}^2L(x,y,z)d\ge0\quad	ext{for every }d\in\mathcal C(x,y,z).\] For tolerances \(\epsilon_p,\epsilon_d,\epsilon_c,\epsilon_H\ge0\), an approximate target replaces feasibility, dual residual, and complementarity equalities by residual bounds and requires \[\min_{d\in\mathcal C_\epsilon,\ \|d\|=1}d^T
abla_{xx}^2L(x,y,z)d\ge-\epsilon_H,\] for an explicitly specified approximate critical cone \(\mathcal C_\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth nonconvex nonlinear program, the first-order stationarity target is a primal-dual KKT point: it is feasible, has nonnegative inequality multipliers, satisfies complementarity, and has zero Lagrangian gradient. A second-order target also requires the Lagrangian Hessian to have nonnegative curvature along every critical direction. Approximate targets bound the primal, dual, and complementarity residuals and permit the least critical-cone curvature to be mildly negative by a stated tolerance. The critical cone and all residual norms must be specified when an approximate target is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: First-order targets satisfy the KKT system; second-order targets additionally satisfy \(d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(x,y,z)d\ge0\) for all \(d\in\mathcal C(x,y,z)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(Z_C\) spans a linear critical subspace, the curvature condition is equivalent to \(Z_C^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(x,y,z)Z_C\succeq0\).
special_cases_latex: Under strict complementarity and LICQ, the critical cone reduces to the null space of the active-constraint Jacobian.
For unconstrained optimization, the targets reduce to \(\nabla f(x)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A strict negative-curvature direction in the critical cone rules out exact second-order stationarity.
boundary_notes: Second-order stationarity is necessary for a regular local minimizer but is not generally sufficient without a strict curvature condition.
At degenerate points, the critical cone need not be a linear subspace.

notation.meaning: Critical cone at a KKT point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of an NLP interior-point sequence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(v_k=(x_k,s_k,y_k,z_k)\) be primal-dual iterates for a smooth nonlinear program, with \(s_k,z_k>0\), barrier parameters \(\mu_k>0\), and perturbed KKT residual \(F_{\mu_k}(v_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A taxonomy-level definition covering global subsequential convergence and local primal-dual convergence; it does not itself assert that a particular algorithm has these properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An NLP interior-point sequence is convergent to a primal-dual solution \(v_*=(x_*,s_*,y_*,z_*)\) when \[\mu_k\to0,\qquad \|F_{\mu_k}(v_k)\|\to0,\qquad v_k\to v_*,\] so that \(v_*\) satisfies the unperturbed KKT conditions. It has global feasibility-stationarity convergence when every accumulation point, or at least one accumulation point under the algorithm's stated compactness assumptions, is feasible and KKT stationary. It has local primal-dual convergence when all iterates started in a neighborhood of a regular solution remain in that neighborhood and converge to it. Its local rate is Q-linear, Q-superlinear, or Q-quadratic according as the error sequence \(e_k=\|v_k-v_*\|\) satisfies \(e_{k+1}\le\rho e_k\) eventually for some \(\rho<1\), \(e_{k+1}/e_k\to0\), or \(e_{k+1}\le Ce_k^2\) eventually.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence of an NLP interior-point sequence means that the barrier parameter and perturbed KKT residual both tend to zero and the primal-dual iterates approach a point satisfying the original KKT conditions. Global feasibility-stationarity convergence concerns KKT properties of accumulation points from the algorithm's admissible starting set. Local primal-dual convergence concerns iterates initialized near a regular solution. Linear, superlinear, and quadratic rates are defined through the norm of the full primal-dual error. These properties are distinct: vanishing barrier parameters alone do not imply convergence, and convergence of objective values alone does not imply feasibility or stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence requires \(\mu_k\to0\), \(F_{\mu_k}(v_k)\to0\), and \(v_k\to v_*\) with \(F_0(v_*)=0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(v_k\to v_*\) and \(F_\mu\) is continuous at \((v_*,0)\), then \(\mu_k\to0\) and \(F_{\mu_k}(v_k)\to0\) imply \(F_0(v_*)=0\).
special_cases_latex: For a feasible primal-dual sequence, convergence can be monitored through stationarity and complementarity residuals.
A fixed reduction \(\mu_{k+1}=\sigma\mu_k\), \(0<\sigma<1\), is associated with a linear barrier-parameter rate.
immediate_consequences_latex: At a finite limit, \(s_{*,i}z_{*,i}=0\) follows from \(S_kz_k-\mu_ke\to0\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not guarantee uniqueness of the limiting multiplier.
Divergent iterates may still have \(\mu_k\to0\), so residual and iterate conditions are essential.

notation.meaning: Norm of the full primal-dual error.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global feasibility-stationarity convergence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an interior-point algorithm generate \(v_k=(x_k,s_k,y_k,z_k)\) with \(s_k,z_k>0\) for \(c_E(x)=0\), \(c_I(x)-s=0\), and let \(R_p(v)=(c_E(x),c_I(x)-s)\), \(R_d(v)=\nabla_xL(x,y,z)\), and \(R_c(v)=Sz\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global means convergence from the algorithm's prescribed admissible starting set, usually in the subsequential sense; it does not mean convergence to a globally optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interior-point algorithm has global feasibility-stationarity convergence on a starting set \(\mathcal V_0\) if, for every \(v_0\in\mathcal V_0\), either it terminates at a KKT point or the generated sequence has an accumulation point \(v_*\) satisfying \[R_p(v_*)=0,\qquad R_d(v_*)=0,\qquad s_*,z_*\ge0,\qquad R_c(v_*)=0.\] A stronger all-limit-points form requires every accumulation point to satisfy these relations. A residual form requires \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}\max\{\|R_p(v_k)\|,\|R_d(v_k)\|,\|S_kz_k\|\}=0,\] together with boundedness sufficient to extract a convergent subsequence. The precise definition must state whether it concerns one accumulation point, all accumulation points, or convergence of the entire sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global feasibility-stationarity convergence means that, from every allowed initial point, the algorithm either stops at a KKT point or produces an accumulation point that is primal feasible, dual stationary, nonnegative in the slack and inequality-multiplier variables, and complementary. A stronger version requires every accumulation point to have these properties. An equivalent residual-oriented formulation uses a vanishing lower limit of the maximum primal, dual, and complementarity residual, plus boundedness that yields a convergent subsequence. In this terminology, global refers to the starting region of the algorithm and not to global optimality of the limit point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every asserted limiting point satisfies primal feasibility, Lagrangian stationarity, multiplier nonnegativity, and complementarity.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under boundedness and continuity, a subsequence with \(R_p(v_{k_j}),R_d(v_{k_j}),S_{k_j}z_{k_j}\to0\) converges along a further subsequence to a KKT point.
special_cases_latex: Whole-sequence convergence is obtained when the sequence has a unique accumulation point.
For equality-only problems, the complementarity and nonnegativity conditions disappear.
immediate_consequences_latex: A limiting point satisfying these relations is first-order stationary but need not be a local minimizer in a nonconvex problem.
boundary_notes: A line-search primal-dual iteration for nonlinear programming may require safeguards beyond those sufficient in linear programming.
Compactness, constraint qualifications, and bounded multipliers are algorithm-dependent hypotheses, not part of the bare definition.

notation.meaning: Primal, dual, and complementarity residual maps.
Admissible set of initial primal-dual points.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Feasibility Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility inherited by accumulation points from vanishing global constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{x_k\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) be iterates for constraints \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\geq0\), and define \(\theta(x)=\|h(x)\|+\|\min\{g(x),0\}\|\), with the minimum taken componentwise. If \(\theta(x_k)\to0\) and a subsequence \(x_{k_j}\to\bar x\), continuity gives \(h(\bar x)=0\) and \(g(\bar x)\geq0\). Thus every finite accumulation point is feasible. This conclusion neither asserts existence of an accumulation point nor prevents the full sequence from being unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If constraint violation tends to zero, every finite accumulation point is feasible; the claim does not ensure bounded iterates or existence of a limit point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accumulation point \(\bar x\) of \(\{x_k\}\) satisfies \(h(\bar x)=0\) and \(g(\bar x)\geq0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Global Stationarity Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT stationarity inherited from convergent primal–dual residual subsequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L(x,y,z)=f(x)+y^{\mathsf T}h(x)-z^{\mathsf T}g(x)\), let \((x_{k_j},y_{k_j},z_{k_j})\to(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\). If \(h(x_{k_j})\to0\), \(\min\{g(x_{k_j}),0\}\to0\), \(z_{k_j}\geq0\), \(\nabla_xL(x_{k_j},y_{k_j},z_{k_j})\to0\), and \(z_{k_j}\circ g(x_{k_j})\to0\), then continuity implies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, Lagrangian stationarity, and complementarity at \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\). Hence the limiting triple satisfies the first-order KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent primal–dual subsequence whose feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity residuals vanish has a KKT limit.
assumptions_latex: \(f\), \(h\), and \(g\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
The displayed primal–dual subsequence converges finitely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(\bar x)=0\), \(g(\bar x)\geq0\), \(\bar z\geq0\), \(\nabla_xL(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)=0\), and \(\bar z\circ g(\bar x)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limit Outcomes for the Complete Trust-Region Interior-Point Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded limiting alternatives for the complete nonlinear trust-region interior-point method, conditional on the hypotheses invoked from Theorems 19.1 and 19.2.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the hypotheses invoked by Theorems 19.1 and 19.2 for the complete Algorithm 19.4 applied to nonlinear program (19.43). For some barrier parameter \(\mu\) generated by the algorithm, either \(\lVert c_k-s_k\rVert\leq\epsilon_\mu\) is never satisfied, in which case stationarity for minimizing \(h(x)\) holds in the limit, or \(c_k-s_k\to0\), in which case \(\{(c_k,A_k)\}\) has a limit point \((\bar c,\bar A)\) that fails LICQ. Moreover, if a primal limit point \(\hat x\) satisfies LICQ, then the first-order necessary conditions for problem (19.43) hold at \(\hat x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the hypotheses carried over from Theorems 19.1 and 19.2, the complete nonlinear trust-region interior-point method has the stated alternatives: persistent failure to meet a barrier feasibility tolerance yields limiting stationarity of the infeasibility measure, while vanishing constraint-slack residuals can yield a constraint-data limit point that fails LICQ. Any primal limit point satisfying LICQ satisfies the original nonlinear program's first-order necessary conditions.
assumptions_latex: \text{The complete Algorithm 19.4 is applied to nonlinear program (19.43).}
\text{The hypotheses invoked from Theorems 19.1 and 19.2 hold.}
\mu\text{ is a barrier parameter generated by the algorithm.}
\hat x\text{ is a primal limit point when the LICQ-conditioned conclusion is invoked.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\lVert c_k-s_k\rVert\leq\epsilon_\mu\text{ is never satisfied}\Rightarrow\text{stationarity of }h\text{ holds in the limit}\right]\ \lor\ \left[(c_k-s_k)\to0\Rightarrow\exists(\bar c,\bar A)\text{ failing LICQ}\right],\qquad \hat x\text{ satisfies LICQ}\Rightarrow\hat x\text{ satisfies the first-order necessary conditions for (19.43)}.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Limit-Point Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous feasibility and KKT convergence along bounded primal–dual barrier subsequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\geq0\). Then \(\bar x\) is feasible and \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\) satisfies the first-order KKT conditions. If every accumulation triple satisfies these hypotheses, every primal accumulation point paired with its multiplier limit is KKT.

The joint residual \(R_k\) tends to zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Convergence Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Missing feasibility, residual control, or a finite accumulation subsequence blocks global KKT conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Vanishing barrier parameters alone do not imply a feasible or stationary accumulation point. For the infeasible problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}0\) subject to \(x^2+1=0\), the equality violation satisfies \(|x^2+1|\geq1\) for every \(x\), so no algorithm can produce a feasible limit. Separately, even when feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity residuals tend to zero, a sequence with no finite convergent primal–dual subsequence has no finite limit at which those residuals can imply the KKT conditions. Therefore a global KKT limit conclusion requires both joint residual decay along a subsequence and existence of a finite primal–dual limit for that subsequence; boundedness or compactness assumptions are common sufficient conditions for obtaining such a subsequence but are not themselves necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing barrier parameter cannot overcome infeasibility or missing residual decay, and residual decay yields no finite KKT limit unless a finite convergent primal–dual subsequence exists. Boundedness or compactness is sufficient, but not necessary, for obtaining such a subsequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without feasibility attainability, joint residual decay along a subsequence, and a finite primal–dual limit for that subsequence, convergence to a KKT triple is not guaranteed.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Primal–Dual Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Newton convergence for a fixed positive barrier parameter near a regular primal–dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\mu>0\) and let \(F_\mu:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^q\) be the primal–dual perturbed KKT map. Suppose \(F_\mu(w_\mu)=0\), its Jacobian \(J_\mu(w_\mu)\) is nonsingular, and \(J_\mu\) is Lipschitz continuous near \(w_\mu\). Then there is a neighborhood \(U\) such that, for every \(w_0\in U\), the exact Newton iteration \(J_\mu(w_k)d_k=-F_\mu(w_k)\), \(w_{k+1}=w_k+d_k\), is well defined, remains in \(U\), and converges to \(w_\mu\). Moreover, for some \(C>0\), \(\|w_{k+1}-w_\mu\|\leq C\|w_k-w_\mu\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a regular fixed-parameter primal–dual solution, exact Newton steps remain local and converge quadratically to that solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact primal–dual Newton iteration converges locally and quadratically to \(w_\mu\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the perturbed KKT map
regular primal–dual solution at fixed barrier parameter

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local primal-dual convergence near a regular NLP solution
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(v_*=(x_*,s_*,y_*,z_*)\) satisfy the KKT conditions for a twice continuously differentiable NLP, and let \(T\) be the iteration map, including its barrier-parameter and step-acceptance rules.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convergence of the full primal-dual sequence near a regular constrained solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The iteration has local primal-dual convergence to \(v_*\) if there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(v_*\) and a barrier threshold \(\bar\mu>0\) such that, for every admissible \(v_0\in U\) and \(0<\mu_0\le\bar\mu\), all iterates are well defined, remain in \(U\), preserve \(s_k,z_k>0\), and satisfy \[v_k\to v_*,\qquad \mu_k\to0,\qquad F_{\mu_k}(v_k)\to0.\] In the regular regime, \(v_*\) is normally assumed to satisfy LICQ, strict complementarity, and the second-order sufficient conditions, with locally Lipschitz second derivatives. The convergence is primal-dual because it includes \(x_k,s_k,y_k,z_k\), rather than only the primal variables or objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local primal-dual convergence means that there is a neighborhood of a KKT solution such that every admissible sufficiently close primal-dual starting point, with a sufficiently small positive barrier parameter, generates a well-defined interior sequence that remains nearby and converges in all primal, slack, equality-multiplier, and inequality-multiplier components. The barrier parameter and perturbed KKT residual also tend to zero. Standard fast local theory assumes linear independence of active constraint gradients, strict complementarity, second-order sufficiency, and locally Lipschitz second derivatives. Convergence of the primal variables alone is weaker and does not satisfy this definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(U\) and \(\bar\mu>0\) such that every admissible \((v_0,\mu_0)\in U\times(0,\bar\mu]\) generates \(v_k\to v_*\) while preserving strict interiority.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If the local iteration is represented by a contraction \(T\) on a closed neighborhood of \(v_*\), the definition is equivalent to \(T^k(v_0)\to v_*\) for every admissible \(v_0\) in that neighborhood.
special_cases_latex: With exact Newton steps and a fixed sufficiently small barrier parameter, the local target is the corresponding central-path point rather than \(v_*\).
When \(\mu_k\to0\), the local targets approach the original KKT solution.
immediate_consequences_latex: Local convergence implies boundedness and eventual uniqueness of the nearby primal-dual branch under the stated regularity conditions.
boundary_notes: Without strict complementarity or LICQ, the primal-dual Jacobian may be singular and this regular local definition may not apply.
Globalization may be inactive locally but is essential outside the neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fast local barrier rate regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(v_k=(x_k,s_k,y_k,z_k)\to v_*\) be a local primal-dual sequence, let \(e_k=\|v_k-v_*\|\), and let \(E(v;\mu)\) measure the perturbed KKT residual.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular smooth NLP solutions satisfying the hypotheses needed for nonsingular primal-dual Newton steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fast local barrier rate regime is a local primal-dual regime in which full steps are eventually accepted and \[\frac{e_{k+1}}{e_k}\to0.\] A canonical superlinear parameter schedule chooses, for fixed \(\theta>0\), \(0<\delta<1\), and \(\beta>\delta\), \[\epsilon_{\mu_k}=\theta\mu_k,\qquad \mu_{k+1}=\mu_k^{1+\delta},\qquad \tau_k=1-\mu_k^{\beta},\] where \(E(v_k;\mu_k)\le\epsilon_{\mu_k}\) is the inner accuracy condition and \(\tau_k\) is the fraction-to-the-boundary parameter. A quadratic regime additionally satisfies \(e_{k+1}\le Ce_k^2\) eventually. Inexact derivatives or linear solves belong to the fast regime only when their errors vanish rapidly enough not to dominate the Newton error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fast local barrier rate regime is a local primal-dual convergence regime whose full steps are eventually accepted and whose error ratio tends to zero. One standard superlinear schedule solves each barrier system to an accuracy proportional to the current barrier parameter, decreases that parameter by a power greater than one, and lets the fraction-to-the-boundary parameter approach one faster than the barrier reduction exponent requires. A quadratic regime further bounds the next error by a constant times the square of the current error. Approximate derivatives and linear solves are compatible only if their errors decay rapidly enough to preserve the stated rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining fast-rate condition is \(e_{k+1}/e_k\to0\); the displayed parameter schedule is a canonical superlinear realization.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Q-superlinear convergence is equivalent to \(e_{k+1}=o(e_k)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\mu_{k+1}=\sigma\mu_k\) with fixed \(0<\sigma<1\), the associated barrier regime is generally only linearly convergent.
No reduction faster than quadratic can improve an overall Newton iteration beyond quadratic order.
immediate_consequences_latex: Eventually unit primal and dual steps eliminate backtracking as the rate-limiting mechanism.
boundary_notes: The parameter schedule alone does not establish the rate without regularity, accurate Newton systems, and eventual inactivity of the globalization mechanism.
Degenerate solutions generally require different local analysis.

children.title: Superlinear Local Regimes
children.top_down_role: Fast local barrier behavior exceeding linear convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear Local Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Superlinear convergence under vanishing relative linear-solve or model error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(w_*)=0\), let \(J=F'\) be continuous near \(w_*\), and suppose \(J(w_*)\) is nonsingular. Consider inexact primal–dual Newton steps satisfying \(J(w_k)d_k=-F(w_k)+r_k\) and \(w_{k+1}=w_k+d_k\). If \(w_k\to w_*\) and \(\|r_k\|/\|F(w_k)\|\to0\), then \(\|w_{k+1}-w_*\|/\|w_k-w_*\|\to0\). Thus the local convergence is superlinear. The same conclusion applies to a barrier sequence only when perturbations caused by changing barrier parameters are also asymptotically negligible relative to the current primal–dual error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent inexact primal–dual Newton iteration is superlinear when relative solve errors and any barrier-parameter perturbations vanish compared with the current error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \frac{\|w_{k+1}-w_*\|}{\|w_k-w_*\|}\to0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Local Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic local convergence with an exact Jacobian and second-order residual accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(w_*)=0\), suppose \(J(w_*)=F'(w_*)\) is nonsingular, and assume \(J\) is Lipschitz continuous near \(w_*\). If steps satisfy \(J(w_k)d_k=-F(w_k)+r_k\), \(w_{k+1}=w_k+d_k\), and \(\|r_k\|\leq c\|F(w_k)\|^2\), then all sufficiently close initial points generate iterates satisfying \(\|w_{k+1}-w_*\|\leq C\|w_k-w_*\|^2\). For a varying barrier parameter, quadratic convergence to the unperturbed KKT point additionally requires the parameter-induced residual to be \(O(\|w_k-w_*\|^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lipschitz derivatives and second-order-accurate Newton solves yield quadratic local convergence; a changing barrier parameter must contribute only second-order residual error.
assumptions_latex: \(J(w_*)\) is nonsingular and \(J\) is locally Lipschitz.
The initial point is sufficiently close to \(w_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(C>0\) such that \(\|w_{k+1}-w_*\|\leq C\|w_k-w_*\|^2\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rate-Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local rate determined by Newton error, barrier forcing, and derivative-solve accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e_k=\|w_k-w_*\|\), and suppose a local primal–dual iteration satisfies \(e_{k+1}\leq C(e_k^2+\mu_{k+1}+\eta_k e_k)\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), where \(C>0\), \(e_k\to0\), \(\mu_{k+1}\geq0\) measures the next barrier perturbation, and \(\eta_k\geq0\) measures relative derivative or solve error. If \(\mu_{k+1}=O(e_k)\) and \(\eta_k=O(1)\), the recursion gives only \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k)\); Q-linear convergence follows when \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}C(\mu_{k+1}/e_k+\eta_k)<1\). If \(\mu_{k+1}=o(e_k)\) and \(\eta_k\to0\), then \(e_{k+1}/e_k\to0\), so the convergence is Q-superlinear. If \(\mu_{k+1}=O(e_k^2)\) and \(\eta_k=O(e_k)\), then \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k^2)\), so the convergence is Q-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First-order-sized barrier and derivative errors give only a first-order error bound, with linear convergence requiring an actual contraction coefficient. Errors negligible relative to the current error yield superlinear convergence, while second-order barrier error and first-order relative solve error yield quadratic convergence.
assumptions_latex: The displayed local error recursion holds with a constant \(C>0\) independent of all sufficiently large \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic sizes of \(\mu_{k+1}\) and \(\eta_k\), together with the first-order contraction coefficient when applicable, determine the stated Q-linear, Q-superlinear, or Q-quadratic regime.

children.top_down_role: Derivative approximation regimes that limit attainable local convergence rates.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Quality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative approximation accuracy separating linear, superlinear, and quadratic primal–dual rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(w_*)=0\) with nonsingular \(J_*=F'(w_*)\), and let \(B_kd_k=-F(w_k)\), \(w_{k+1}=w_k+d_k\). Along nonzero steps, the Dennis–Moré condition is \(\|(B_k-J_*)d_k\|/\|d_k\|\to0\); together with local convergence and standard smoothness, it is the derivative-quality threshold for superlinear convergence. A uniform bound \(\|B_k-J(w_k)\|\leq c\|w_k-w_*\|\), with locally Lipschitz \(J\), supports quadratic convergence. Merely bounded approximation error generally supports at most a linear local rate and need not yield superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing derivative error along steps marks the superlinear threshold; error proportional to distance supports quadratic convergence, while merely bounded error generally permits only linear convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable and \(J_*\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed Dennis–Moré and first-order matrix-error predicates separate the superlinear and quadratic derivative-quality regimes.

children.title: Degenerate NLP Barrier Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence regimes without strict complementarity or full regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate NLP Barrier Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of strict complementarity can singularize the limiting primal–dual system and reduce barrier-path rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\geq0}x^2\). Its solution is \(x_*=0\) with multiplier \(z_*=0\), so strict complementarity fails. The perturbed KKT equations \(2x-z=0\) and \(xz=\mu\) have the positive solution \(x_\mu=\sqrt{\mu/2}\), \(z_\mu=\sqrt{2\mu}\). Hence the central-path error is \(\Theta(\sqrt\mu)\), not \(O(\mu)\). Moreover, the Jacobian \(\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\z&x\end{pmatrix}\) tends to a singular matrix as \(\mu\downarrow0\). Thus ordinary nonsingular-Jacobian arguments do not guarantee quadratic convergence at this degenerate KKT point, although the barrier path still converges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without strict complementarity, the central path may approach only at square-root order and its limiting primal–dual Jacobian may become singular, invalidating standard quadratic-rate arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For this degenerate problem, \(\|(x_\mu,z_\mu)-(0,0)\|=\Theta(\sqrt\mu)\), and the limiting perturbed-KKT Jacobian is singular.

notation.meaning: multiplier for the constraint x nonnegative

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate NLP barrier-convergence regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(v_*=(x_*,s_*,y_*,z_*)\) be a KKT point of a smooth NLP. Degeneracy means that at least one regularity property used by standard primal-dual local theory fails, such as LICQ, strict complementarity, multiplier uniqueness, or nonsingularity of the primal-dual KKT Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the regime; no universal rate or convergence guarantee is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A degenerate NLP barrier-convergence regime is a sequence \(v_k=(x_k,s_k,y_k,z_k)\), \(s_k,z_k>0\), with \(\mu_k\downarrow0\) and \(F_{\mu_k}(v_k)\to0\), whose limiting KKT set contains a degenerate point. Failure of strict complementarity occurs when some active inequality satisfies \[c_{I,i}(x_*)=0,\qquad z_{*,i}=0.\] Failure of LICQ occurs when the gradients of the active constraints are linearly dependent. Because multipliers or central-path branches may be nonunique, convergence may be stated setwise as \[\operatorname{dist}(v_k,\mathcal S_*)\to0,\] where \(\mathcal S_*\) is the relevant local primal-dual solution set, rather than as convergence to a unique vector. Any claimed pointwise rate must specify an error bound or alternative regularity condition replacing the failed assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate NLP barrier-convergence regime is an interior primal-dual sequence with vanishing barrier parameter and perturbed KKT residual whose limiting solution fails at least one of the regularity properties underlying standard local theory. Examples include linearly dependent active constraint gradients, a nonunique multiplier, a singular primal-dual Jacobian, or an active inequality with zero multiplier. Since the local solution or central-path branch can be nonunique, convergence may be defined by distance to a local primal-dual solution set rather than convergence to one multiplier vector. Any stronger pointwise rate requires an explicitly stated replacement such as an error bound or another stability condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degenerate convergence permits \(\operatorname{dist}(v_k,\mathcal S_*)\to0\) even when no unique regular primal-dual limit or nonsingular Newton Jacobian exists.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strict-complementarity failure is characterized by an index with both active slack and associated limiting multiplier equal to zero.
special_cases_latex: Primal convergence \(x_k\to x_*\) may coexist with nonconvergence or nonuniqueness of \((y_k,z_k)\).
A constant-rank but non-LICQ solution is a distinct degenerate subregime.
immediate_consequences_latex: The regular superlinear parameter schedule cannot be invoked without additional assumptions that control the singular or set-valued local behavior.
boundary_notes: Degeneracy is not synonymous with failure of convergence.
No inspected supplied source provided a unified barrier-convergence definition covering all failures of LICQ and strict complementarity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior-point linear algebra stack
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At each interior-point iteration, Newton linearization produces a sparse block system \(K_kp_k=-r_k\), where \(p_k\) contains primal, slack, equality-multiplier, and inequality-multiplier steps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional primal-dual interior-point implementations; the definition covers representations, solvers, stabilization, scaling, and recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interior-point linear algebra stack is the collection \[\mathfrak L_k=(K_k,\mathcal R_k,\mathcal S_k,\mathcal P_k,\mathcal T_k,\mathcal C_k)\] that maps a primal-dual residual \(r_k\) to a computed step. Here \(K_k\) is the full Newton matrix; \(\mathcal R_k\) is an algebraically equivalent full, augmented, normal-equation, or Schur-complement representation; \(\mathcal S_k\) is a direct or iterative solver; \(\mathcal P_k\) is scaling or preconditioning; \(\mathcal T_k\) is regularization, pivoting, or inertia control; and \(\mathcal C_k\) recovers eliminated variables and evaluates the original-system residual. The stack is algebraically consistent when, in exact arithmetic and under the required nonsingularity assumptions, solving the reduced system and applying \(\mathcal C_k\) yields a vector \(p_k\) satisfying \(K_kp_k=-r_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interior-point linear algebra stack is the complete mathematical mechanism that turns a primal-dual Newton residual into a step. It includes the original block matrix, a selected equivalent representation such as a full, augmented, normal-equation, or Schur-complement system, the direct or iterative solver, scaling or preconditioning, stabilization or inertia control, and the formulas used to recover eliminated variables and check the residual in the original system. Exact algebraic consistency means that solving the reduced system and recovering the omitted components produces a solution of the full Newton equations whenever the eliminations are valid. The stack is broader than a factorization alone because representation, stabilization, and recovery affect the step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact stack satisfies \(K_k\mathcal C_k(\widehat p_k)=-r_k\) whenever \(\widehat p_k\) solves the selected reduced representation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The stack may be viewed as a composition \(r_k\mapsto\widehat r_k\mapsto\widehat p_k\mapsto p_k\), consisting of reduction, solution, and recovery maps.
special_cases_latex: A sparse normal-equation stack uses Cholesky factorization followed by back-substitution for eliminated variables.
An augmented-system stack uses symmetric-indefinite factorization and retains primal and multiplier blocks.
immediate_consequences_latex: Residual certification in the full system permits comparison of steps produced by different algebraically equivalent representations.
boundary_notes: Algebraic equivalence does not imply equal conditioning in floating-point arithmetic.
Matrix-free stacks may represent \(K_k\) only through operator products.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent interior-point linear-system forms
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Kp=b\) be a primal-dual Newton system partitioned into retained variables \(u\) and eliminable variables \(w\): \(K=\begin{bmatrix}K_{uu}&K_{uw}\\K_{wu}&K_{ww}\end{bmatrix}\), with \(K_{ww}\) nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block and reduced representations obtained by exact elimination of primal-dual Newton equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interior-point linear-system form is a system obtained from the full Newton equations by a nonsingular permutation, symmetric scaling, or exact block elimination, together with recovery equations for every eliminated variable. Eliminating \(w\) gives the Schur-complement form \[\bigl(K_{uu}-K_{uw}K_{ww}^{-1}K_{wu}\bigr)u=b_u-K_{uw}K_{ww}^{-1}b_w,\qquad w=K_{ww}^{-1}(b_w-K_{wu}u).\] Full primal-dual, augmented KKT, normal-equation, and constraint-space or null-space systems are distinct forms according to which variable classes are retained. Two forms are equivalent when their solution and recovery maps are bijective on the solution set under the stated invertibility assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior-point linear-system form is a full or reduced representation of the primal-dual Newton equations obtained by valid permutations, symmetric scalings, or exact block eliminations. Every reduced form includes formulas that recover all eliminated step components. In the generic two-block case, the retained variables solve the Schur-complement system and the eliminated variables are then recovered by back-substitution. Full primal-dual, augmented KKT, normal-equation, Schur-complement, range-space, and null-space systems differ by the variables retained and the blocks inverted. They are mathematically equivalent only when the relevant inverses exist and the recovery map is one-to-one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reduced form is defined by its Schur complement and a recovery map that reconstructs a solution of the full system.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Block Gaussian elimination and Schur-complement reduction define the same exact reduced system.
A permutation or nonsingular symmetric scaling changes the representation without changing the underlying Newton direction after inverse transformation.
special_cases_latex: Eliminating complementarity variables first yields a symmetric augmented KKT system.
Further eliminating primal variables can yield a positive-definite normal equation under suitable rank and definiteness assumptions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different exact forms generate the same Newton direction in exact arithmetic.
boundary_notes: The forms can have substantially different sparsity and conditioning.
An elimination is invalid if its pivot block is singular or numerically unusable without stabilization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual KKT residual and Newton system for standard-form linear programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming specialization of an interior-point Newton-system representation, including its positivity-preserving step boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{b^T\lambda:A^T\lambda+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), a tuple \((x,\lambda,s)\) is primal-dual optimal if and only if \(A^T\lambda+s=c\), \(Ax=b\), \(XSe=0\), and \((x,s)\ge0\). Define \[F(x,\lambda,s)=\begin{bmatrix}A^T\lambda+s-c\\Ax-b\\XSe\end{bmatrix}.\] At an equality-feasible point with \(x>0\) and \(s>0\), its pure Newton direction satisfies \[\begin{bmatrix}0&A^T&I\\A&0&0\\S&0&X\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta\lambda\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\-XSe\end{bmatrix}.\] A step length \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) must preserve \(x+\alpha\Delta x>0\) and \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\); the full Newton step need not do so and the admissible step may be small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard-form LP optimality is equivalent to primal feasibility, dual feasibility, componentwise complementarity, and nonnegativity. Linearizing this residual system at a strictly primal-dual feasible point gives the displayed block Newton system. The step length must preserve strict positivity, and a full pure-Newton step can be inadmissible or allow little progress.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb R^m,\quad c,x,s\in\mathbb R^n,\quad \lambda\in\mathbb R^m
Ax=b,\quad A^T\lambda+s=c,\quad x>0,\quad s>0\quad\text{for the displayed Newton system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,\lambda,s)\text{ is primal-dual optimal}\iff A^T\lambda+s=c,\ Ax=b,\ XSe=0,\ (x,s)\ge0;\qquad J_F\Delta=-F.

knowledge_statements.title: Full Primal–Dual KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unreduced Newton system for equality constraints, inequality slacks, and primal–dual complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the Newton increments be \(\Delta x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta y\in\mathbb R^m\), \(\Delta z,\Delta s\in\mathbb R^p\). With \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), \(Z=\operatorname{Diag}(z)\), the full primal–dual system is
\[
\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}&G^{\mathsf T}&0\\A&0&0&0\\G&0&0&I\\0&0&S&Z\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\\\Delta z\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}r_d\\r_e\\r_i\\r_c\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Here \(H\) is the Lagrangian Hessian or a symmetric approximation, while \(A\) and \(G\) are equality- and inequality-constraint Jacobians. The four block rows respectively encode linearized stationarity, equality feasibility, slack feasibility, and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full Newton system retains primal, equality-multiplier, inequality-multiplier, and slack increments, coupling stationarity, feasibility, and complementarity without block elimination.
assumptions_latex: \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(G\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed block system simultaneously determines \((\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z,\Delta s)\) whenever its coefficient matrix is nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full primal-dual KKT Newton system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c_E(x)=0\), \(c_I(x)-s=0\), \(s\ge0\), let \(y,z\) be multipliers, \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), \(Z=\operatorname{Diag}(z)\), and \(L=f-y^Tc_E-z^Tc_I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unreduced smooth-NLP primal-dual Newton equations retaining primal, slack, and both multiplier step classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The full primal-dual KKT system at \((x,s,y,z)\), for barrier parameter \(\mu>0\), is the Newton linearization \[\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_{xx}^2L&0&-A_E^T&-A_I^T\\0&Z&0&S\\A_E&0&0&0\\A_I&-I&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p_x\\p_s\\p_y\\p_z\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_xL\\Sz-\mu e\\c_E(x)\\c_I(x)-s\end{bmatrix}.\] It is full because none of the four principal step classes is eliminated before solution. A centering or predictor-corrector variant changes the complementarity right-hand side but retains the same block-variable interpretation. Strict interiority \(s,z>0\) makes \(S\) and \(Z\) positive diagonal, while nonsingularity of the entire coefficient matrix is a separate condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full primal-dual KKT system is the unreduced Newton linearization of stationarity, perturbed complementarity, equality feasibility, and slack-form inequality feasibility. Its unknown vector retains the primal step, slack step, equality-multiplier step, and inequality-multiplier step. The Hessian of the Lagrangian occupies the primal block, the constraint Jacobians couple primal and multiplier variables, and the positive diagonal slack and multiplier matrices form the complementarity block. Centering and predictor-corrector choices may alter the complementarity right-hand side without changing the classification as a full system. Strict positivity of slacks and inequality multipliers does not by itself guarantee that the whole KKT matrix is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed four-by-four block Newton equation is the full primal-dual KKT system, with all principal variable classes retained.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Multiplying selected block rows by nonsingular diagonal matrices or applying a consistent permutation gives an equivalent full form.
special_cases_latex: For a linear program, \(\nabla_{xx}^2L=0\) and the Jacobians are constant.
For equality-only problems, the slack, inequality-multiplier, and complementarity blocks disappear.
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact solution of the system gives the Newton correction for the perturbed KKT residual.
boundary_notes: The displayed sign convention follows \(L=f-y^Tc_E-z^Tc_I\); other consistent multiplier conventions change block signs.
Reduced systems are not full systems even when they recover the same direction.

notation.meaning: Primal, slack, equality-multiplier, and inequality-multiplier Newton steps.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Scaling of the Full Primal–Dual System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent symmetric full-space representation obtained without eliminating any primal–dual variable class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the full system
\[
\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}&G^{\mathsf T}&0\\A&0&0&0\\G&0&0&I\\0&0&S&Z\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\\\Delta z\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}r_d\\r_e\\r_i\\r_c\end{bmatrix},
\]
where \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\) and \(S\) and \(Z\) are diagonal. If \(S\) is nonsingular, multiplying only the complementarity block row by \(S^{-1}\) gives the equivalent symmetric system
\[
\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}&G^{\mathsf T}&0\\A&0&0&0\\G&0&0&I\\0&0&I&D\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\\\Delta z\\\Delta s\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}r_d\\r_e\\r_i\\S^{-1}r_c\end{bmatrix},
\qquad D=S^{-1}Z.
\]
For positive slacks and multipliers, \(D\succ0\). No unknown has been eliminated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling the complementarity row by the inverse slack matrix converts the full four-variable-class Newton system to an equivalent symmetric block system while retaining all increments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled coefficient matrix is symmetric and has exactly the same solution as the unscaled full system.

notation.meaning: diagonal complementarity scaling in the symmetric full-space representation

knowledge_statements.title: Augmented KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric saddle-point reduction obtained by eliminating slack and inequality-multiplier increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the full primal–dual system, eliminate \(\Delta s\) and \(\Delta z\), and define \(D=S^{-1}Z\) and \(W=H+G^{\mathsf T}DG\). The remaining increments satisfy
\[
\begin{bmatrix}W&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}r_d-G^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}(r_c-Zr_i)\\r_e\end{bmatrix}.
\]
After solving this symmetric-indefinite augmented KKT system, recover
\[
\Delta s=r_i-G\Delta x,\qquad
\Delta z=S^{-1}(r_c-Z\Delta s).
\]
Thus block elimination preserves the primal and equality-multiplier variables while absorbing complementarity curvature into \(W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating slack and inequality-multiplier steps produces a symmetric saddle-point system in the primal and equality-multiplier steps, followed by explicit back-substitution.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is nonsingular; in an interior-point iterate, \(S\succ0\) and \(Z\succ0\).
The full system uses the block and residual conventions of the prerequisite record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced solution and stated back-substitutions solve the full primal–dual equations exactly in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmented KKT system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the linear-programming primal-dual step equations with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(x,s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), and \(D=S^{-1/2}X^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical symmetric-indefinite reduction obtained by eliminating the complementarity-variable step from a primal-dual system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The augmented KKT system is the symmetric two-block system \[\begin{bmatrix}-D^{-2}&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta\lambda\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-r_c+X^{-1}r_{xs}\\-r_b\end{bmatrix},\] obtained from the full equations by eliminating \(\Delta s\). The eliminated step is recovered from \[\Delta s=-X^{-1}r_{xs}-X^{-1}S\Delta x.\] More generally, an augmented KKT form is a symmetric-indefinite system retaining a primal block and a constraint-multiplier block, \(\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\), after other primal-dual variables have been eliminated. Its defining features are retention of both variable classes, symmetry, and indefiniteness rather than positive definiteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The augmented KKT system is a symmetric-indefinite reduction of the full primal-dual equations that retains the primal step and a constraint-multiplier step while eliminating the complementarity-variable step. In the canonical linear-programming form, the primal diagonal block is minus the inverse scaling matrix, the off-diagonal blocks are the constraint matrix and its transpose, and the multiplier diagonal block is zero. After solving this two-block system, the eliminated dual-slack step is recovered by back-substitution. More generally, any system with a primal curvature block, constraint Jacobian blocks, and a zero multiplier block is an augmented KKT form when it arises from valid elimination of the remaining primal-dual variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented system retains \((\Delta x,\Delta\lambda)\) in a symmetric-indefinite KKT matrix and recovers \(\Delta s\) by back-substitution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(H=-D^{-2}\), the matrix has the generic KKT form \(\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\).
special_cases_latex: Regularization replaces the zero multiplier block by a negative diagonal block and may perturb the primal block.
Free variables can be represented directly in an augmented formulation without forming a normal equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: The augmented form avoids explicitly forming \(AD^2A^T\).
boundary_notes: The coefficient matrix is generally indefinite and therefore is not factored by ordinary Cholesky.
Equivalence to the full system requires \(X\) and the eliminated pivot blocks to be nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inertia of a Positive-Definite Augmented KKT Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definiteness and nonsingularity structure of the symmetric augmented system when its primal block is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W=W^{\mathsf T}\succ0\) and let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank. Then
\[
K=\begin{bmatrix}W&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}
\]
is nonsingular and has inertia
\[
\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0),
\]
meaning \(n\) positive, \(m\) negative, and no zero eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite primal block and independent constraint rows make the augmented KKT matrix nonsingular, with one negative eigenvalue per constraint and all remaining eigenvalues positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0)\), so \(K\) is symmetric indefinite and nonsingular.

notation.meaning: numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Equation Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite multiplier reduction of a symmetric augmented KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W=W^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). For increments \(\Delta x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\Delta y\in\mathbb R^m\), consider
\[
W\Delta x+A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y=q,\qquad A\Delta x=b.
\]
If \(W\succ0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), eliminating \(\Delta x\) gives
\[
(AW^{-1}A^{\mathsf T})\Delta y=AW^{-1}q-b,
\]
where \(AW^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\) is symmetric positive definite. After solving this normal equation, recover
\[
\Delta x=W^{-1}(q-A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the primal block is positive definite and the constraint Jacobian has full row rank, eliminating the primal step yields a symmetric positive-definite multiplier normal equation, followed by primal back-substitution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normal matrix \(AW^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\) is symmetric positive definite, and back-substitution recovers the augmented-system solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior-point normal-equation system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(x,s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), and set \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), and \(D=S^{-1/2}X^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite multiplier-space reduction of the primal-dual linear-programming step equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The interior-point normal-equation system is \[AD^2A^T\Delta\lambda=-r_b-AXS^{-1}r_c+AS^{-1}r_{xs}.\] It is obtained by eliminating \(\Delta s\) and \(\Delta x\) from the full primal-dual system. After solving it, the remaining steps are recovered by \[\Delta s=-r_c-A^T\Delta\lambda,\qquad \Delta x=-S^{-1}r_{xs}-XS^{-1}\Delta s.\] Since \(D^2\succ0\), the coefficient matrix \(AD^2A^T\) is symmetric positive definite exactly when \(A\) has full row rank. It is called a normal equation because it is the Gram matrix of \(DA^T\): \(AD^2A^T=(DA^T)^T(DA^T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interior-point normal equation is the multiplier-space system obtained after eliminating the slack and primal steps from the full primal-dual equations. Its coefficient matrix is the weighted Gram matrix A times D squared times A transpose. Once the multiplier step is computed, the eliminated dual-slack and primal steps are recovered by explicit back-substitution. Because the diagonal scaling is positive definite, the normal-equation matrix is symmetric positive definite precisely when the constraint matrix has full row rank. The form supports Cholesky factorization but can magnify conditioning problems and create fill through the weighted matrix product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under \(D^2\succ0\) and full row rank of \(A\), \(AD^2A^T\succ0\), and the normal equation uniquely determines \(\Delta\lambda\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(AD^2A^T=(DA^T)^T(DA^T)\), so the system is a weighted least-squares normal equation.
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is rank deficient, the normal-equation matrix is positive semidefinite and singular.
Sparse Cholesky is the canonical direct solver when the matrix is sufficiently well conditioned.
immediate_consequences_latex: The full primal-dual direction is recovered without factoring the larger indefinite KKT matrix.
Dense columns of \(A\) may make \(AD^2A^T\) dense.
boundary_notes: Forming a Gram matrix can worsen the condition number relative to an augmented formulation.
Near a solution, entries of \(D^2\) may become extremely large or small, causing ill conditioning.

notation.meaning: Constraint-multiplier Newton step retained by the reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Schur-Complement Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General block elimination and recovery formula for an invertible principal block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), \(E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(f\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(g\in\mathbb R^m\). For \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), consider
\[
\begin{bmatrix}B&E^{\mathsf T}\\E&-C\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}f\\g\end{bmatrix}.
\]
If \(B\) is nonsingular, eliminating \(u\) yields
\[
(C+EB^{-1}E^{\mathsf T})v=EB^{-1}f-g,
\]
with recovery formula
\[
u=B^{-1}(f-E^{\mathsf T}v).
\]
The matrix \(S_C=C+EB^{-1}E^{\mathsf T}\) is the signed Schur-complement matrix for this equation. If \(B\succ0\), \(C\succeq0\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(E)=m\), then \(S_C\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating an invertible principal block yields a smaller signed Schur-complement system. It is positive definite when the principal block is positive definite, the lower regularization block is positive semidefinite, and the coupling block has full row rank.
assumptions_latex: For the definiteness conclusion, \(B\succ0\), \(C\succeq0\), and \(E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Solving the Schur-complement equation and applying \(u=B^{-1}(f-E^{\mathsf T}v)\) is algebraically equivalent to solving the original block system.

notation.meaning: principal, lower regularization, and coupling blocks

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Schur-Complement Reduction of a Primal–Dual Block System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), and consider \(K(u,v)=(f,g)\) with \(K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&-C\end{bmatrix}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact block elimination. The definition covers symmetric interior-point augmented systems when \(H\) and \(C\) are symmetric; numerical approximation and singular leading blocks are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Schur-complement system obtained by eliminating \(u\) is defined by \[S_Hv=AH^{-1}f-g,\qquad S_H:=C+AH^{-1}A^T.\] Once \(v\) is determined, the eliminated variable is recovered by \[u=H^{-1}(f-A^Tv).\] Thus a Schur-complement solve consists of forming or applying \(S_H\), solving its reduced equation in the constraint-space variable \(v\), and applying the stated recovery map. For the primal–dual augmented matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}0&A\\A^T&-D^{-2}\end{bmatrix}\), elimination of the second block gives the positive-semidefinite normal-equation coefficient \(AD^2A^T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a two-by-two block system with invertible primal block \(H\), a Schur-complement system is the reduced equation with coefficient \(S_H=C+AH^{-1}A^T\). Its right-hand side is \(AH^{-1}f-g\), and the eliminated variable is recovered as \(u=H^{-1}(f-A^Tv)\). In the standard primal–dual interior-point augmented form, this reduction yields the normal-equation matrix \(AD^2A^T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S_H=C+AH^{-1}A^T,\qquad S_Hv=AH^{-1}f-g,\qquad u=H^{-1}(f-A^Tv).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is nonsingular if and only if \(S_H\) is nonsingular, provided \(H\) is nonsingular.
With \(H=D^{-2}\succ0\) and \(C=0\), the reduced coefficient is \(S_H=AD^2A^T\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has full row rank and \(H\succ0\), then \(AH^{-1}A^T\succ0\).
If \(C\succeq0\) and \(H\succ0\), then \(S_H\succeq0\), with strict definiteness when its null space is trivial.
immediate_consequences_latex: The full solution is uniquely determined by one reduced solve and applications of \(H^{-1}\).
The reduced dimension is \(m\), which is advantageous when the constraint block is smaller than the primal block.
boundary_notes: If \(H\) is singular, this definition does not authorize using \(H^{-1}\); generalized Schur complements require additional range conditions.
Explicitly forming \(AH^{-1}A^T\) may increase density or worsen conditioning even when the algebraic reduction is valid.

notation.meaning: Schur complement of the leading block, with sign chosen to give a positive normal-equation matrix in the interior-point specialization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Determinant and Inertia Identities for the Signed Schur Complement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural identities relating the full symmetric block matrix to its Schur complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
M=\begin{bmatrix}B&E^{\mathsf T}\\E&-C\end{bmatrix},
\qquad S_C=C+EB^{-1}E^{\mathsf T},
\]
where \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\) is nonsingular and \(C=C^{\mathsf T}\). Then \(M\) is congruent to \(\operatorname{diag}(B,-S_C)\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{inertia}(M)=\operatorname{inertia}(B)+\operatorname{inertia}(-S_C),
\]
\[
\det M=\det(B)\det(-S_C)=(-1)^m\det(B)\det(S_C),
\]
and \(M\) is nonsingular if and only if \(S_C\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block congruence separates the full symmetric matrix into its eliminated principal block and the negative signed Schur complement, giving exact inertia, determinant, and nonsingularity identities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\sim_{\mathrm{cong}}\operatorname{diag}(B,-S_C)\), with the stated determinant, inertia, and nonsingularity consequences.

notation.meaning: matrix congruence by a nonsingular change of variables
order of the lower block and of the Schur complement

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Null-Space and Range-Space Constraint Reductions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H=H^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, and consider \(Hp+A^T\lambda=f\), \(Ap=b\). Let \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) satisfy \(AZ=0\) and have full column rank, and choose \(Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) with \(AY=I_m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional reductions of a full-row-rank equality-constrained KKT system. The range-space member additionally requires invertible \(H\); the null-space member requires a nonsingular reduced Hessian for unique recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The constraint-space reduction pair comprises two algebraically equivalent reduced descriptions. The null-space reduction writes \[p=Yb+Zq,\qquad (Z^THZ)q=Z^T(f-HYb),\] followed by recovery of \(\lambda\) from \(A^T\lambda=f-Hp\). The range-space reduction, when \(H\) is nonsingular, solves \[(AH^{-1}A^T)\lambda=AH^{-1}f-b,\qquad p=H^{-1}(f-A^T\lambda).\] The first system evolves in the null space of the constraints and has dimension \(n-m\); the second evolves in the multiplier or constraint range space and has dimension \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint-space reduction pair consists of the null-space and range-space reductions of the same KKT equations. The null-space form parameterizes every feasible primal step as \(p=Yb+Zq\) and solves with \(Z^THZ\). The range-space form eliminates the primal step and solves with \(AH^{-1}A^T\), then recovers \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p=Yb+Zq,\quad Z^THZq=Z^T(f-HYb),\qquad AH^{-1}A^T\lambda=AH^{-1}f-b.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: With orthogonal matrices \([Y\ Z]\), the decomposition separates range and null-space coordinates without changing Euclidean norms.

If both reduced matrices are nonsingular, either member of the pair produces the unique solution of \(\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p\\\lambda\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}f\\b\end{bmatrix}\).
special_cases_latex: When \(H\succ0\), both \(Z^THZ\succ0\) and \(AH^{-1}A^T\succ0\).
When \(m\ll n\), the range-space system is typically the smaller member; when \(n-m\ll n\), the null-space system is typically smaller.
immediate_consequences_latex: The null-space coordinate automatically preserves \(Ap=b\).
The two reductions expose complementary opportunities for exploiting constraint rank, sparsity, and available inverse applications.
boundary_notes: Rank-deficient \(A\) requires removal of redundant constraints or generalized inverses.
An indefinite \(H\) may still admit a nonsingular KKT matrix even when the range-space reduction through \(H^{-1}\) is unsuitable.

children.title: Null-Space Reductions
children.top_down_role: Interior-point system reductions expressed through constraint null spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Space Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-space reduction of an equality-constrained symmetric KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W=W^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), where \(A\) has rank \(m\). Consider \(p\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
Wp+A^{\mathsf T}y=q,\qquad Ap=b.
\]
Choose \(p_0\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(Ap_0=b\), and let \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) have full column rank with \(\operatorname{range}(Z)=\ker A\). Every feasible \(p\) has a unique representation \(p=p_0+Zw\), where \(w\in\mathbb R^{n-m}\). The reduced equation is
\[
(Z^{\mathsf T}WZ)w=Z^{\mathsf T}(q-Wp_0).
\]
If \(Z^{\mathsf T}WZ\) is nonsingular, this equation uniquely determines \(w\) and \(p\); the unique multiplier \(y\) then satisfies
\[
A^{\mathsf T}y=q-Wp.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible particular step plus a basis of the constraint null space converts the KKT equations into a reduced primal system of order equal to the constraint nullity, after which the multiplier is recovered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The null-space equation is equivalent to the KKT system and has order \(n-m\).

notation.meaning: particular solution of the linearized constraints

source_refs.locator: 4.4.2 Projections, Range-, and Null-Space Bases p. 71

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis Invariance of the Reduced Hessian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate invariance and curvature interpretation of the null-space reduced matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank and let \(Z,\widetilde Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) be bases of \(\ker A\). There is a nonsingular matrix \(T\) such that \(\widetilde Z=ZT\), and hence
\[
\widetilde Z^{\mathsf T}W\widetilde Z=T^{\mathsf T}(Z^{\mathsf T}WZ)T.
\]
Consequently, rank, inertia, nonsingularity, and positive definiteness of the reduced Hessian are independent of the chosen null-space basis. Moreover,
\[
Z^{\mathsf T}WZ\succ0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d^{\mathsf T}Wd>0\quad\text{for every }0\ne d\in\ker A.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing the null-space basis changes the reduced Hessian only by congruence, so its inertia and definiteness are intrinsic to curvature on feasible directions.
assumptions_latex: The columns of \(Z\) and \(\widetilde Z\) are bases of \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reduced-Hessian inertia is basis independent, and positive definiteness is equivalent to positive curvature on every nonzero null-space direction.

notation.meaning: nonsingular change-of-basis matrix between null-space coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Invariance of the Reduced Hessian

children.title: Range-Space Reductions
children.top_down_role: Interior-point system reductions expressed through constraint ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Range-Space Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier-space reduction obtained by eliminating the primal variable from a KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W=W^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). For \(p\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(y\in\mathbb R^m\), consider
\[
Wp+A^{\mathsf T}y=q,\qquad Ap=b.
\]
If \(W\) is nonsingular, eliminating \(p\) gives
\[
(AW^{-1}A^{\mathsf T})y=AW^{-1}q-b,
\]
with recovery formula
\[
p=W^{-1}(q-A^{\mathsf T}y).
\]
If \(AW^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\) is nonsingular, the reduced equation and recovery formula uniquely determine \((p,y)\). If additionally \(W\succ0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), then \(AW^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\succ0\). The reduced equation has order \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating a nonsingular primal block produces a multiplier-space system of order equal to the number of constraints. The reduced matrix is positive definite when the primal block is positive definite and the constraint Jacobian has full row rank.
assumptions_latex: For positive definiteness, \(W\succ0\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(AW^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\) is nonsingular, the range-space equation and primal back-substitution are equivalent to the original KKT system.

children.title: Reduction-Dimension Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural cost differences driven by primal, dual, or constraint dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Dimension Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension criterion for choosing between null-space and range-space KKT reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank with \(m\le n\). A null-space reduction forms a system of order \(n-m\), whereas a range-space reduction forms a system of order \(m\). Consequently, measured only by dense factorization arithmetic, their leading costs scale respectively as
\[
O((n-m)^3)\qquad\text{and}\qquad O(m^3).
\]
This dimension comparison is not a complete sparse-solver selection rule: the cost of constructing bases or applying \(W^{-1}\), the sparsity and conditioning of the reduced matrices, and back-substitution can dominate. Thus smaller reduced dimension is a useful criterion only after structural costs are considered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Null-space and range-space reductions have orders equal to constraint nullity and constraint count; the smaller order may be cheaper, but sparsity, conditioning, and operator costs can reverse the choice.
assumptions_latex: The stated cubic comparison uses dense direct factorization arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dimension alone favors null-space reduction when \(n-m<m\) and range-space reduction when \(m<n-m\), subject to structural costs.

children.title: Rank-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Effects of deficient or nearly deficient constraint representations on both reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of uniqueness in an equality-constrained KKT system when constraint rank or reduced curvature is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W=W^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\le n\), and
\[
K=\begin{bmatrix}W&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
When \(A\) has full row rank, let \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) have full column rank and satisfy \(\operatorname{range}(Z)=\ker A\). Then \(K\) is nonsingular if and only if \(A\) has full row rank and \(Z^{\mathsf T}WZ\) is nonsingular. Thus loss of constraint row rank or loss of nonsingularity of the reduced Hessian marks a boundary at which the unregularized KKT system does not have a unique solution for every right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality-constrained KKT matrix is nonsingular exactly when the constraint Jacobian has full row rank and the Hessian restricted to its null space is nonsingular. Failure of either condition destroys general unique solvability.
assumptions_latex: When \(A\) has full row rank, the columns of \(Z\) form a basis of \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matrix \(K\) is nonsingular if and only if \(A\) has full row rank and \(Z^{\mathsf T}WZ\) is nonsingular.

notation.meaning: basis matrix for the null space of the constraint Jacobian

source_refs.locator: 4.4.2 Projections, Range-, and Null-Space Bases p. 71

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independent Witnesses for the Two Singularity Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal examples separating constraint-rank loss from loss of reduced curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The two hypotheses in the KKT nonsingularity criterion fail independently. First, with \(n=m=1\), \(W=[1]\), and \(A=[0]\), the constraint row is rank deficient and
\[
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}
\]
is singular although \(W\succ0\). Second, with \(n=2\), \(m=1\),
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad W=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},
\]
\(A\) has full row rank, but for \(Z=(0,1)^{\mathsf T}\) one has \(Z^{\mathsf T}WZ=0\), and
\[
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&0&0\\1&0&0\end{bmatrix}
\]
is singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One example shows that a positive-definite primal block cannot compensate for dependent constraint rows; another shows that independent rows cannot compensate for zero curvature along a feasible direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constraint-rank loss and reduced-curvature singularity are distinct sufficient mechanisms for singularity of the unregularized KKT matrix.

notation.meaning: basis vector for the null space of the full-row-rank constraint matrix in the second example

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Direct Solver for an Interior-Point Newton System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At an interior-point iteration let \(K_\mu z=r\) denote a finite-dimensional primal–dual, augmented, or normal-equation system. The coefficient matrix may be symmetric positive definite or symmetric indefinite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic definition of factorization-based solvers, with sparse permutations allowed. Floating-point pivot thresholds and iterative methods are not part of the defining core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direct interior-point linear solver is a mapping that computes a permutation and a finite factorization of \(K_\mu\), then obtains \(z\) by a fixed number of triangular or block-diagonal solves. In the positive-definite case it has the form \[PK_\mu P^T=LL^T,\qquad LL^T(Pz)=Pr.\] In the symmetric-indefinite case it has the form \[PK_\mu P^T=LBL^T,\] where \(L\) is unit lower triangular and \(B\) is block diagonal with nonsingular \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) blocks. The defining exactness condition is \(K_\mu z=r\); permutation, symbolic analysis, numerical factorization, and substitutions together constitute the direct solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct interior-point linear solver solves an interior-point Newton system by explicitly factorizing an equivalent coefficient matrix and performing triangular substitutions. Positive-definite reductions use Cholesky factors, whereas symmetric-indefinite augmented or full KKT systems use a pivoted block \(LBL^T\) factorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[PK_\mu P^T=LL^T\quad\text{or}\quad PK_\mu P^T=LBL^T,\qquad K_\mu z=r.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Factoring a symmetrically permuted matrix and unpermuting the solution is algebraically equivalent to factoring \(K_\mu\) itself.
A direct solve may be applied to the full primal–dual system or to an exactly equivalent augmented, normal-equation, or Schur-complement form.
special_cases_latex: For \(K_\mu=AD^2A^T\succ0\), sparse Cholesky is the canonical direct method.
For a symmetric-indefinite augmented KKT matrix, pivoted \(LBL^T\) is the canonical direct method.
immediate_consequences_latex: Multiple right-hand sides can reuse the same factors while \(K_\mu\) is unchanged.
The permutation may be selected to limit fill without altering the exact solution.
boundary_notes: A stationary iterative scheme or Krylov method without a completed factorization is not a direct solver under this definition.
Near singularity can require regularization or rank-revealing treatment before the defining nonsingular factorization exists.

notation.meaning: Interior-point linear-system matrix at barrier parameter \(\mu\).
Nonsingular block-diagonal pivot matrix in a symmetric-indefinite factorization.

children.title: Sparse Cholesky Methods
children.top_down_role: Direct solution families for positive-definite reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Cholesky Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct sparse solution of symmetric positive-definite normal or Schur-complement systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a sparse matrix \(M=M^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) with \(M\succ0\), a right-hand side \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), and a permutation matrix \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Determine the symbolic nonzero pattern and compute a lower triangular matrix \(L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) with positive diagonal such that
\[
PMP^{\mathsf T}=LL^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Compute \(w,z\in\mathbb R^n\) from
\[
Lw=Pb,\qquad L^{\mathsf T}z=w,
\]
and return
\[
x=P^{\mathsf T}z.
\]
Report factorization failure if a nonpositive pivot is encountered. In exact arithmetic, successful completion returns \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(Mx=b\). The permutation can change fill and arithmetic work but not the represented system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetrically permute a sparse positive-definite system, compute its Cholesky factor, perform two triangular solves, and undo the permutation. Ordering changes fill and work but not the exact solution.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is a permutation matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On successful factorization, the returned vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) solves \(Mx=b\) in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Cholesky Factorization and Solve Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic and storage for scalar sparse Cholesky expressed through symbolic factor column counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be the symbolic Cholesky factor after a fixed symmetric permutation and let \(c_j=\operatorname{nnz}(L_{j:n,j})\). A conventional scalar sparse Cholesky factorization uses \(O(\sum_{j=1}^n c_j^2)\) arithmetic and \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(L))\) factor storage. Each subsequent forward-and-backward solve costs \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(L))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse Cholesky storage is proportional to factor nonzeros, scalar factorization work is controlled by squared column counts, and each new right-hand side costs linear work in factor nonzeros.
assumptions_latex: The matrix is symmetric positive definite.
The permutation and symbolic factor pattern are fixed.
A conventional scalar sparse Cholesky implementation is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{storage}=\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(L)),\quad \mathrm{factor\ work}=O\!\left(\sum_jc_j^2\right),\quad \mathrm{solve\ work}=O(\operatorname{nnz}(L)).

notation.meaning: number of structural entries in column j of the lower factor
