knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Cholesky Solution of a Positive-Definite Interior-Point Reduction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M=M^T\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be sparse and positive definite, typically \(M=AD^2A^T\) with \(D\succ0\) diagonal and \(A\) of full row rank.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sparse symmetric positive-definite systems. The defining factorization is exact; sparsity refers to structural nonzeros after a symmetric permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sparse Cholesky method chooses a permutation matrix \(P\) and computes the unique lower-triangular matrix \(L\) with positive diagonal satisfying \[PMP^T=LL^T.\] For \(Mz=r\), it solves \[Ly=Pr,\qquad L^Tw=y,\qquad z=P^Tw.\] The method is called sparse when \(P\) is chosen from the structural graph of \(M\) so that the number and arrangement of nonzeros in \(L\), including fill created by elimination, remain tractable. Symbolic analysis determines the factor pattern; numerical Cholesky supplies its values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse Cholesky method solves a sparse positive-definite interior-point reduction by symmetrically permuting it, factoring the result as \(LL^T\), and applying two triangular solves. Sparsity is measured in the factor, including fill-in, rather than only in the original matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[PMP^T=LL^T,\qquad Ly=Pr,\qquad L^Tw=y,\qquad z=P^Tw.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(R=L^T\) gives the equivalent upper-triangular factorization \(PMP^T=R^TR\).
For \(M=AD^2A^T\), the factor is also related to a QR factorization of \(DA^TP^T\) with compatible diagonal conventions.
special_cases_latex: If \(P=I\), the method is unpermuted sparse Cholesky.
For several interior-point iterations with an unchanged structural pattern, symbolic analysis and the elimination structure may be reused.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive definiteness guarantees nonzero positive pivots in exact arithmetic.
The exact solution is independent of the chosen symmetric permutation, although storage and arithmetic costs are not.
boundary_notes: Positive-semidefinite or rank-deficient normal equations need regularization, rank detection, or a different factorization.
Forming normal equations can square a condition number and can create structural density.

notation.meaning: Lower-triangular Cholesky factor with positive diagonal.

children.title: Symmetric-Indefinite LDL Methods
children.top_down_role: Pivoted direct methods for augmented and full KKT systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric-Indefinite LDL Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pivoted direct factorization for symmetric-indefinite augmented or full KKT matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a sparse symmetric nonsingular matrix \(K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), a right-hand side \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), and a symmetric pivoting rule. Compute a permutation matrix \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), a unit lower triangular matrix \(L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and a block diagonal matrix \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), with diagonal blocks of order one or two, such that
\[
PKP^{\mathsf T}=LDL^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Compute \(w,z,u\in\mathbb R^n\) from
\[
Lw=Pb,\qquad Dz=w,\qquad L^{\mathsf T}u=z,
\]
and return
\[
x=P^{\mathsf T}u.
\]
Accept a pivot only when the selected rule's stability test holds; otherwise perform a symmetric interchange or report numerical factorization failure. In exact arithmetic, any successful factorization returns \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(Kx=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric-indefinite direct solver uses stable one-by-one or two-by-two pivots to form a block-LDL factorization, followed by triangular and block-diagonal solves.
assumptions_latex: The pivoting rule uses symmetric row-and-column permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A successful factorization and substitution sequence returns \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(Kx=b\) in exact arithmetic.

notation.meaning: block diagonal factor with one-by-one and two-by-two pivots

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Quasi-Definite Block LDL Factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pivot-free block factorization for a structured symmetric-indefinite system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\succ0\), \(R\succ0\), and \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Then \[K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&-R\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\AH^{-1}&I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}H&0\\0&-(R+AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T})\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I&H^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\\0&I\end{bmatrix}.\] Consequently, \(K\) is nonsingular and has inertia \((n,m,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric quasi-definite saddle matrix has a pivot-free block LDL factorization with positive- and negative-definite diagonal blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is nonsingular, admits the displayed factorization, and has inertia \((n,m,0)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pivoted Symmetric-Indefinite Block LDL Factorization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K=K^T\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}\) be a nonsingular, possibly indefinite, augmented or full primal–dual KKT matrix.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional symmetric-indefinite factorization with symmetric pivoting. The block form permits both \(1\times1\) and \(2\times2\) pivots for numerical stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric-indefinite LDL method computes a permutation matrix \(P\), a unit lower-triangular matrix \(L\), and a block-diagonal matrix \(B\) such that \[PKP^T=LBL^T,\qquad B=\operatorname{blkdiag}(B_1,\ldots,B_q),\] where every \(B_i\) is a nonsingular symmetric \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) block. For \(Kz=r\), the solution is defined by \[Ly=Pr,\qquad Bw=y,\qquad L^Tv=w,\qquad z=P^Tv.\] Pivot selection is symmetric and may depend on numerical values because it must control element growth as well as sparse fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric-indefinite LDL method factors a symmetrically permuted KKT matrix as \(LBL^T\), where \(L\) is unit lower triangular and \(B\) contains nonsingular one-by-one or two-by-two symmetric pivot blocks. It solves by forward substitution, block-diagonal solution, backward substitution, and inverse permutation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[PKP^T=LBL^T,\qquad Kz=r\] with nonsingular symmetric \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) blocks in \(B\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: When every pivot block is \(1\times1\), \(B\) is diagonal and the factorization is conventionally written \(LDL^T\).
The inertia of \(K\) equals the sum of the inertias of the blocks of \(B\).
special_cases_latex: Bunch–Parlett and Bunch–Kaufman methods are pivot-selection realizations of this factorization class.
For quasi-definite primal–dual matrices, specialized pivot orders may avoid or reduce delayed pivots.
immediate_consequences_latex: The factorization directly exposes positive, negative, and zero eigenvalue counts through \(B\).
Unlike Cholesky, it can represent nonsingular indefinite augmented KKT systems without changing their signs.
boundary_notes: A zero or numerically unacceptable pivot requires a different pivot, perturbation, or rank treatment.
Using only diagonal pivots without stability safeguards need not yield a stable factorization of a general indefinite matrix.

notation.meaning: Symmetric pivot block of order one or two.
Inertia: the triple of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalue counts.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LDL Factorization and Solve Residual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based numerical checks for a computed symmetric-indefinite factorization and solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For computed \(P,L,D\), define \(E=PKP^{\mathsf T}-LDL^{\mathsf T}\). If \[\|E\|\le\eta\|K\|\] in a declared subordinate norm, then \(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) exactly factors the nearby symmetric matrix \(P(K-P^{\mathsf T}EP)P^{\mathsf T}\), whose relative perturbation is at most \(\eta\). A returned solution \(\widehat x\) passes the normalized residual test when \[\frac{\|b-K\widehat x\|}{\|K\|\|\widehat x\|+\|b\|}\le\tau.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factorization residual and normalized system residual provide checkable backward-accuracy diagnostics for an indefinite LDL solve.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) has nonsingular one-by-one or two-by-two diagonal blocks.
A declared consistent norm is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The factor residual certifies an exact factorization of a nearby symmetric matrix, and the normalized system residual certifies the returned solve residual.
knowledge_statements.title: LDL Factorization and Solve Residual Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Breakdown of Unguarded Diagonal Pivoting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsingular symmetric-indefinite family motivating guarded one-by-one and two-by-two pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0\le\varepsilon<1\), let \[K_\varepsilon=\begin{bmatrix}\varepsilon&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}.\] Since \(\det K_\varepsilon=-1\), every member is nonsingular. For \(\varepsilon>0\), elimination using the first diagonal entry produces multiplier \(1/\varepsilon\) and Schur complement \(-1/\varepsilon\), both unbounded as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). At \(\varepsilon=0\), diagonal pivoting breaks down immediately although the full \(2\times2\) block is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular two-by-two indefinite matrix can defeat diagonal-only elimination and cause unbounded element growth, while a two-by-two pivot remains valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stable symmetric-indefinite factorization cannot rely on unguarded diagonal pivots alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Breakdown of Unguarded Diagonal Pivoting

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LDL Factorization Backward-Error Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based numerical certificate for a computed symmetric-indefinite factorization and solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given computed \(P,L,D\), define \(E=PKP^{\mathsf T}-LDL^{\mathsf T}\). If \[\|E\|\le\eta\|K\|\] in a declared subordinate norm, then the factors are the exact block-LDL factors of the nearby symmetric matrix \(K-P^{\mathsf T}EP\), whose relative perturbation is at most \(\eta\). A returned solution \(\widehat x\) additionally satisfies a normwise solve certificate when \[\frac{\|b-K\widehat x\|}{\|K\|\|\widehat x\|+\|b\|}\le\tau.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factorization residual and normalized linear-system residual certify backward accuracy of an indefinite LDL solve.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is block diagonal with nonsingular one-by-one or two-by-two blocks.
The same declared norm is used throughout.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The factors and solution solve a nearby symmetric problem with quantified residuals.

children.title: Sparse Factorization Fill Control
children.top_down_role: Symbolic ordering families controlling factorization cost.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fill-In and Fill-Controlling Elimination Ordering
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M=M^T\) be structurally sparse. Its undirected adjacency graph \(G(M)=(V,E)\) has \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\{i,j\}\in E\) when \(i\ne j\) and \(M_{ij}\) is structurally nonzero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symbolic symmetric elimination for Cholesky or symmetric-indefinite factors. Numerical cancellation is ignored when defining structural fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an elimination ordering \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), eliminating \(v_k\) removes that vertex and joins every pair of its current neighbors. A newly inserted edge is a fill edge. The filled graph \(G_\pi^+=(V,E\cup F_\pi)\) and the corresponding factor pattern define the fill generated by \(\pi\). A fill-control rule is a mapping from the current elimination graph to a next pivot or pivot block, chosen to reduce a structural cost such as \[|F_\pi|,\qquad \operatorname{nnz}(L),\qquad\text{or an elimination-work estimate}.\] Minimum degree chooses a current vertex of least degree; minimum local fill chooses a vertex predicted to introduce the fewest new edges; nested dissection recursively orders separator vertices after the separated subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse factorization fill control is the choice of a symmetric elimination ordering using the matrix adjacency graph. Eliminating a vertex makes its remaining neighbors mutually adjacent; edges created by this operation are fill. Minimum-degree, minimum-local-fill, and nested-dissection rules select orderings intended to limit factor storage or work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G_\pi^+=(V,E\cup F_\pi),\qquad F_\pi:=\{\text{edges created by elimination under }\pi\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A structural fill edge corresponds to a factor position that can become nonzero although the matching entry of the original matrix is structurally zero.
Minimizing \(|F_\pi|\) is equivalent to minimizing the number of off-diagonal structural nonzeros added to the symmetric factor pattern.
special_cases_latex: A perfect elimination ordering has \(F_\pi=\varnothing\).
Supernodes group consecutive columns with identical relevant sparsity structure so their symbolic and numerical work can be aggregated.
immediate_consequences_latex: A fill-reducing permutation changes computational cost but not the exact solution of the permuted linear system.
When the sparsity pattern is fixed across interior-point iterations, the symbolic ordering can be reused.
boundary_notes: Finding a globally minimum-fill ordering is generally intractable, so practical rules are heuristics.
For indefinite factorization, stability-driven numerical pivoting can alter a previously chosen symbolic ordering.

notation.meaning: Set of structural fill edges generated by ordering \(\pi\).
Number of structural nonzeros in the factor.

children.title: Sparse Ordering Families
children.top_down_role: Permutation strategies for sparse interior-point factorizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Ordering Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-based symmetric permutations used to control sparse-factorization fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) have a structurally symmetric sparsity pattern. Its undirected graph \(G(M)\) has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with an edge between distinct vertices \(i\) and \(j\) when \(M_{ij}\) is structurally nonzero. A symmetric ordering is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), represented by a permutation matrix \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and applied as \(PMP^{\mathsf T}\). Symbolic elimination in this order connects the current higher-numbered neighbors of each eliminated vertex, producing the filled elimination graph. Minimum-degree families select vertices of small current degree. Nested-dissection families recursively order separated subgraphs before their graph separators. Both families seek to reduce factor nonzeros and arithmetic work relative to poor orderings, but neither guarantees a globally minimum-fill permutation for a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-degree and nested-dissection families use the structural graph to symmetrically permute a sparse matrix, seeking less elimination fill and factorization work without changing the represented linear system.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) has a structurally symmetric sparsity pattern.
Ordering decisions use structural nonzeros and ignore accidental numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each ordering family produces a symmetric permutation \(P\) that preserves algebraic equivalence while changing the symbolic filled factor graph.

notation.meaning: undirected structural sparsity graph of the matrix
permutation of the variable indices and its permutation matrix

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Fill and Perfect Elimination Orderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph characterization of symmetric orderings that introduce no fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ordering \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) of an undirected graph produces no elimination fill if and only if, for every \(i\), the neighbors of \(v_i\) among \(\{v_{i+1},\ldots,v_n\}\) form a clique. Such an ordering is a perfect elimination ordering. A graph admits a perfect elimination ordering if and only if it is chordal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordering has zero fill exactly when every vertex's later neighbors form a clique; such an ordering exists exactly for chordal graphs.
assumptions_latex: The graph represents a structurally symmetric matrix pattern.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(\pi)=0\iff\pi\text{ is a perfect elimination ordering},\qquad \exists\pi:F(\pi)=0\iff G\text{ is chordal}.

notation.meaning: symbolic fill count under ordering pi

children.title: Fill-Reduction Objectives
children.top_down_role: Structural objectives used to limit factor memory and arithmetic cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Fill-Reduction Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial fill and column-count work objectives for symmetric sparse-factorization orderings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) have a structurally symmetric sparsity pattern, and let \(\pi\) be a permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with permutation matrix \(P_\pi\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Let \(L_\pi\) be the symbolic lower factor obtained by Cholesky elimination of the pattern of \(P_\pi MP_\pi^{\mathsf T}\), ignoring numerical cancellation. Define the symbolic fill count by
\[
F(\pi)=\operatorname{nnz}(L_\pi)-\operatorname{nnz}(\operatorname{tril}(P_\pi MP_\pi^{\mathsf T})).
\]
For each column \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define
\[
\ell_j(\pi)=\#\{i\in\{j+1,\ldots,n\}:(L_\pi)_{ij}\ne0\},
\]
and define the column-count work proxy
\[
C(\pi)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1+\ell_j(\pi))^2.
\]
A minimum-fill ordering minimizes \(F\), while an ordering based on this work proxy minimizes \(C\). The two objectives need not have the same minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fill objective counts new symbolic lower-factor entries, while a column-count objective estimates factorization work. These objectives can select different symmetric permutations.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) has a structurally symmetric sparsity pattern.
Symbolic factorization ignores accidental numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordering problems are \(\min_{\pi}F(\pi)\) and \(\min_{\pi}C(\pi)\), and their minimizers may differ.

notation.meaning: number of added lower-triangular symbolic factor entries
number of symbolic subdiagonal entries in column \(j\) of the factor

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-Fill Optimization Is NP-Complete
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational boundary for exact optimization of the symbolic fill objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph \(G\) and integer \(k\), deciding whether an elimination ordering exists whose chordal completion adds at most \(k\) edges is NP-complete. Consequently, globally minimizing symbolic Cholesky fill over all permutations is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deciding whether an ordering with at most a prescribed amount of fill exists is NP-complete, so exact global minimum-fill ordering is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: Fill is structural and is defined equivalently by graph elimination or chordal completion.
The graph and integer bound have finite encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \textsc{Minimum Fill-In}\text{ is NP-complete, and }\min_\pi F(\pi)\text{ is NP-hard}.

notation.meaning: symbolic fill count under ordering pi

children.title: Symbolic Factorization Reuse
children.top_down_role: Reuse of symbolic structure across related interior-point systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Symbolic Factorization Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reuse criterion for repeated sparse direct solves with fixed ordering and sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be a sequence of sparse matrices with \(\operatorname{pat}(K_k)=\mathcal{S}\), and fix a symmetric permutation \(P\). If every factorization uses the same elimination rule without numerical pivoting that changes the permutation, then the elimination tree and the structural nonzero pattern of the factors of \(P K_k P^{T}\) depend only on \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(P\). Hence symbolic analysis, storage allocation, and the elimination schedule may be computed once and reused for every \(k\); only numerical factorization must be repeated when matrix values change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed sparsity pattern, ordering, and pivot policy permit reuse of the elimination tree, factor structure, storage layout, and schedule across interior-point iterations.
assumptions_latex: The permutation \(P\) and structural elimination rule are fixed.
Numerical pivoting does not alter the symbolic permutation or factor pattern.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symbolic factorization of \(P K_kP^{T}\) is reusable for all \(k\).

notation.meaning: structural nonzero pattern of a sparse matrix

children.title: Ordering Breakdown Regimes
children.top_down_role: Matrix structures where standard sparse orderings produce excessive fill.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Breakdown Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which a reference sparse ordering or symbolic factorization no longer predicts the factor structure used by a direct solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be an ordering selected for a reference sparsity pattern \(\mathcal{S}_0\). If \(\operatorname{pat}(K_k)\neq\mathcal{S}_0\), symbolic analysis based on \(\mathcal{S}_0\) does not in general predict the factor structure of \(P K_kP^{T}\). Even when \(\operatorname{pat}(K_k)=\mathcal{S}_0\), the predicted structure is not guaranteed to be the structure actually used if threshold pivoting, delayed pivots, rank detection, or another numerical-stability mechanism changes the permutation or admits additional fill. Changes in numerical values alone do not alter the structural factorization under a fixed no-pivoting elimination rule; small pivots matter here only when they trigger a structurally consequential solver decision. When pattern or pivot-policy invariance fails, renewed symbolic analysis, conservative storage, or dynamic solver accommodation may be needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordering or symbolic reuse can fail when the matrix pattern changes or when numerical stabilization changes the permutation, delays pivots, or creates fill beyond the reference prediction; value changes alone do not change a fixed no-pivoting symbolic factorization.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) was computed from a reference pattern \(\mathcal{S}_0\).
The direct solver may use numerical pivoting or another stabilization mechanism that changes the realized elimination structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the sparsity pattern or the structurally relevant pivot policy is not invariant, the reference fill prediction and symbolic storage are not guaranteed to remain valid.

children.title: Structured Dense Factorization Updates
children.top_down_role: Special treatments for dense columns and low-rank structure.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Low-Rank Correction of a Sparse Interior-Point Factorization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M=M_s+UCV^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), where \(M_s\) is nonsingular and admits a sparse direct factorization, \(U,V\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), and \(C\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\) is nonsingular with \(p\ll n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact structured treatment of a small number of dense columns or a low-rank modification. The small correction matrix must be nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structured dense factorization update solves with \(M\) by retaining factors of the sparse core \(M_s\) and representing the omitted dense contribution as a rank-\(p\) correction. Its inverse action is defined by \[M^{-1}r=M_s^{-1}r-M_s^{-1}U\bigl(C^{-1}+V^TM_s^{-1}U\bigr)^{-1}V^TM_s^{-1}r.\] Equivalently, it solves a bordered system whose Schur complement is \(C^{-1}+V^TM_s^{-1}U\). For an interior-point normal matrix \(AD^2A^T\), columns designated dense are omitted from the sparse partial sum, then restored through their outer-product low-rank correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured dense factorization update separates a matrix into a factorizable sparse core and a low-rank term representing dense columns or other structured changes. Solves reuse the sparse factors and correct the result through a small dense Schur-complement system using the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury formula.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The low-rank inverse formula is equivalent to block elimination in \(\begin{bmatrix}M_s&U\\-V^T&C^{-1}\end{bmatrix}\).
For symmetric outer-product updates, one may take \(V=U\) and symmetric \(C\).
special_cases_latex: For one dense column, \(p=1\) and the correction system is scalar.
For \(p\) dense columns, one sparse factorization and multiple triangular substitutions supply the required inverse applications.
immediate_consequences_latex: The dense columns need not be included in the sparse matrix product that determines the core factor pattern.
Factor reuse is possible while only \(U\), \(V\), or \(C\) changes.
boundary_notes: If the sparse partial sum is poorly conditioned, the correction formula can be numerically unreliable despite exact algebraic validity.
This definition assumes genuinely low rank; a large dense block may require a different structured factorization.

notation.meaning: Rank or number of separately treated dense columns.

children.title: Dense-Column Handling
children.top_down_role: Special factorization treatment for dense columns embedded in sparse systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Column Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition-and-update treatment of a small set of dense columns in an otherwise sparse positive-definite reduced system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=[A_s\;A_d]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times(n_s+r)}\), where \(A_s\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n_s}\) is sparse and \(A_d\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\) is dense, and let \(D=\operatorname{diag}(D_s,D_d)\) with positive diagonal blocks \(D_s\in\mathbb{R}^{n_s\times n_s}\) and \(D_d\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\). Given \(H=H^{T}\succ0\), form and sparsely factor \(S_s=H+A_sD_sA_s^{T}\), and retain \(U=A_dD_d^{1/2}\) separately. To solve \((S_s+UU^{T})y=b\), compute \(q=S_s^{-1}b\) and \(W=S_s^{-1}U\), solve \((I_r+U^{T}W)z=U^{T}q\), and return \(y=q-Wz\). In finite precision, accept the result when its residual meets the prescribed linear-solve tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate the few dense columns, factor the positive-definite sparse core, and incorporate the dense contribution through an r-by-r Woodbury correction system.
assumptions_latex: The number \(r\) of dense columns is small relative to \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In exact arithmetic, the returned vector satisfies \((S_s+UU^{T})y=b\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Definite Woodbury Correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solvability certificate for the compact dense-column correction system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S_s\succ0\), then for every \(U\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\), \(I_r+U^{\mathsf T}S_s^{-1}U\succ0\). Hence the dense correction system has a unique solution and admits Cholesky factorization; moreover \(S_s+UU^{\mathsf T}\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite sparse core guarantees that both the updated matrix and the small Woodbury correction matrix are positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I_r+U^{\mathsf T}S_s^{-1}U\succ0\quad\text{and}\quad S_s+UU^{\mathsf T}\succ0.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Woodbury Correction

children.title: Dense-Coupling Schur Isolation
children.top_down_role: Isolation of compact dense coupling through reduced Schur structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Coupling Schur Isolation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block elimination representation isolating a small dense coupling block from a sparse core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\begin{pmatrix}S&U\\ U^{T}&D\end{pmatrix}\), where \(S\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a nonsingular sparse core and \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\) is a small dense block. For \(K\binom{x}{z}=\binom{b}{c}\), define the dense Schur complement \(C=D-U^{T}S^{-1}U\). If \(C\) is nonsingular, then \(z=C^{-1}(c-U^{T}S^{-1}b)\) and \(x=S^{-1}(b-Uz)\). Thus the large computation consists of solves with the sparse factorization of \(S\), while dense factorization is confined to the \(r\)-dimensional matrix \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block elimination confines dense coupling to a small Schur complement while retaining sparse solves with the large core matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Solving the block system is equivalent to solving the reduced dense system in \(C\) followed by sparse back-substitution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Schur Determinant and Inertia Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsingularity and inertia certificates for dense-coupling isolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric \(K=\begin{bmatrix}S&U\\U^{\mathsf T}&D\end{bmatrix}\) with nonsingular symmetric \(S\), let \(C=D-U^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}U\). Block congruence gives \(K\sim_{\mathrm{cong}}\operatorname{diag}(S,C)\). Consequently, \(\det K=\det S\det C\), \(K\) is nonsingular if and only if \(C\) is nonsingular, and \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(S)+\operatorname{inertia}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block congruence splits determinant and inertia between the sparse core and the small dense Schur complement, so the latter certifies nonsingularity once the core is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \det K=\det S\det C,\quad K\text{ nonsingular}\iff C\text{ nonsingular},\quad \operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(S)+\operatorname{inertia}(C).

children.title: Low-Rank Factor Updates
children.top_down_role: Reuse or modification of factorizations under low-rank system changes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Low-Rank Determinant and Nonsingularity Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small-matrix nonsingularity certificate for a low-rank modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(C\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}\) be nonsingular, with \(U,V\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\). Then \[\det(A+UCV^{\mathsf T})=\det(A)\det(C)\det(C^{-1}+V^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}U).\] Hence \(A+UCV^{\mathsf T}\) is nonsingular if and only if \(C^{-1}+V^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}U\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsingularity of a low-rank modification reduces exactly to nonsingularity of its small correction matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A+UCV^{\mathsf T}\) is nonsingular exactly when \(C^{-1}+V^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}U\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Determinant and Nonsingularity Test
Low-Rank Factor Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Woodbury representation for solving after a low-rank modification of a factored matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\) be nonsingular, with a factorization of \(A\) available, and let \(U,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\). If \(M=C^{-1}+V^{T}A^{-1}U\) is nonsingular, then
\[(A+UCV^{T})^{-1}=A^{-1}-A^{-1}U M^{-1}V^{T}A^{-1}.\]
Consequently, solving with the updated matrix requires solves using the existing factors of \(A\), formation and factorization of only the \(r\times r\) matrix \(M\), and low-rank matrix-vector products. For a symmetric update, take \(V=U\) and symmetric \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r matrix change can be handled using the original factors plus a small r-by-r correction system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed Woodbury formula represents the inverse of \(A+UCV^{T}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: QR-Based Cholesky Rank-r Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct factor update for an additive positive-semidefinite low-rank modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=LL^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), with \(L\) lower triangular, and let \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\). Retriangularize \[\begin{bmatrix}L^{\mathsf T}\\U^{\mathsf T}\end{bmatrix}=QR\] by orthogonal transformations, choosing the diagonal of the upper-triangular \(R\) positive. Then \[A+UU^{\mathsf T}=R^{\mathsf T}R.\] Exploiting the triangular first block takes \(O(n^2r+nr^2)\) arithmetic and \(O(nr)\) auxiliary storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Append the low-rank rows to the transposed Cholesky factor and retriangularize to obtain the updated factor without a full dense refactorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R^{\mathsf T}R=A+UU^{\mathsf T}.

children.title: Update-Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditioning regimes where low-rank updates become unstable or uneconomical.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Semidefinite Update Safe Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definiteness behavior of an additive positive-semidefinite low-rank update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A\succ0\) and \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\), then \[A+UU^{\mathsf T}\succ0,\qquad I+U^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}U\succeq I.\] Thus the correction matrix is positive definite and has \(\lambda_{\min}\ge1\), although it may still be ill-conditioned when its largest eigenvalue is large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite low-rank addition preserves positive definiteness and cannot make its correction matrix singular, though that matrix may still be poorly conditioned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A+UU^{\mathsf T}\succ0\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(I+U^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}U)\ge1\).

notation.meaning: Correction matrix for the additive update.

Update-Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning and definiteness limits for low-rank factor updates and downdates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B=A+UCV^{T}\), the Woodbury-based update is numerically unsafe when the correction matrix \(M=C^{-1}+V^{T}A^{-1}U\) is singular or severely ill-conditioned, because errors in solves with \(A\) and in forming \(M\) are amplified by \(\lVert M^{-1}\rVert\). In the symmetric positive-definite downdate \(B=A-UU^{T}\), positive definiteness holds exactly when \(I-U^{T}A^{-1}U\succ0\). If its smallest eigenvalue approaches zero, the updated matrix approaches singularity; if that eigenvalue is nonpositive, a positive-definite factor downdate cannot produce a valid Cholesky factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low-rank updates become unstable near a singular correction matrix, and Cholesky downdates fail when the updated matrix loses positive definiteness.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is nonsingular for the general update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Safe updating requires a well-conditioned correction system and, for Cholesky downdates, \(I-U^{T}A^{-1}U\succ0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Rank-One Downdate Singularity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized family exposing the conditioning and definiteness transition of a Cholesky downdate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=I_n\), \(U_\delta=\sqrt{1-\delta}\,e_1\), and \(B_\delta=A-U_\delta U_\delta^{\mathsf T}\), where \(\delta\le1\). Then \[B_\delta=\operatorname{diag}(\delta,1,\ldots,1),\qquad I-U_\delta^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}U_\delta=[\delta].\] For \(0<\delta\le1\), \(B_\delta\succ0\) and \(\kappa_2(B_\delta)=1/\delta\); at \(\delta=0\), both matrices are singular; for \(\delta<0\), \(B_\delta\) is indefinite and has no real Cholesky factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-one downdate becomes arbitrarily ill-conditioned, then singular, and finally indefinite exactly as its scalar correction crosses zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta>0\), \(\delta=0\), and \(\delta<0\) give the positive-definite, singular, and indefinite regimes, respectively.

notation.meaning: Distance from the singular downdate boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Semidefinite Updates Avoid the Downdate Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definiteness and correction-system behavior for additive positive-semidefinite low-rank changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(A\succ0\) and \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\), then
\[A+UU^{\mathsf T}\succ0,\qquad I+U^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}U\succeq I.\]
Hence the Woodbury correction matrix for this additive update is positive definite with \(\lambda_{\min}\ge1\); loss of positive definiteness through the small correction system is a downdate phenomenon, not an additive positive-semidefinite-update phenomenon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a positive-semidefinite low-rank term preserves positive definiteness and leaves the small correction matrix bounded away from singularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A+UU^{\mathsf T}\succ0\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(I+U^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}U)\ge1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Operator-Based Solve of an Interior-Point Linear System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K_\mu:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^N\) be a linear primal–dual, augmented, or normal-equation operator and let \(M_\mu\) be a nonsingular preconditioning operator with inexpensive inverse action.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional iterative solution using operator applications. Explicit storage or factorization of the full coefficient matrix is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operator-based interior linear solver is an iterative mapping that accesses the system through evaluations of \(v\mapsto K_\mu v\), optional transpose evaluations, vector operations, inner products, and applications of \(M_\mu^{-1}\). Starting from \(z_0\), its \(k\)-th approximation belongs to a preconditioned Krylov affine space such as \[z_k\in z_0+\mathcal K_k(M_\mu^{-1}K_\mu,M_\mu^{-1}r_0),\qquad r_0=b-K_\mu z_0,\] and terminates when a prescribed residual condition is met. The operator may be evaluated from constituent Jacobian, Hessian, diagonal-scaling, and constraint products without assembling \(K_\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator-based interior linear solver computes an approximate solution using products with the interior-point system operator and applications of a preconditioner, rather than requiring a complete direct factorization. Its iterates lie in a Krylov space generated from the preconditioned operator and initial residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[z_k\in z_0+\mathcal K_k(M_\mu^{-1}K_\mu,M_\mu^{-1}r_0),\qquad r_k=b-K_\mu z_k.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Left preconditioning uses \(M_\mu^{-1}K_\mu z=M_\mu^{-1}b\); right or symmetric preconditioning gives an equivalent transformed system when the transformations are nonsingular.
A matrix-free implementation is an operator-based implementation in which the full entries of \(K_\mu\) are never assembled.
special_cases_latex: Conjugate gradients applies to a positive-definite normal-equation operator.
MINRES or related symmetric Krylov methods apply to a symmetric-indefinite augmented operator.
immediate_consequences_latex: Only the actions required by the chosen Krylov recurrence must be implemented.
The solve can exploit problem-specific fast products even when explicit factorization would be prohibitively dense.
boundary_notes: A small residual in a poorly conditioned system need not imply a small solution error.
Nonsymmetric preconditioning can destroy symmetry required by methods such as MINRES.

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov Methods for Augmented Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preconditioned MINRES for symmetric-indefinite primal-dual augmented systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a symmetric nonsingular augmented matrix \(K\), right-hand side \(b\), initial vector \(z_0\), and symmetric positive-definite preconditioner \(P\), apply MINRES to \(P^{-1/2}KP^{-1/2}w=P^{-1/2}b\) with \(z=P^{-1/2}w\). Starting from \(r_0=b-Kz_0\), construct Lanczos vectors in successive Krylov spaces \(\mathcal{K}_j(P^{-1}K,P^{-1}r_0)\) and choose \(z_j\) to minimize the corresponding preconditioned residual norm. Stop at the first \(j\) satisfying \(\lVert b-Kz_j\rVert_{P^{-1}}\leq\tau\lVert b\rVert_{P^{-1}}\), and return \(z_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preconditioned MINRES solves a symmetric-indefinite augmented system using Lanczos iterations and a residual-based stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the first MINRES iterate meeting the prescribed preconditioned relative-residual tolerance.

notation.meaning: jth Krylov subspace generated by T and v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Krylov Iteration for an Augmented KKT System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K=K^T\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}\) be a nonsingular symmetric-indefinite augmented interior-point matrix, let \(Kz=b\), and let \(z_0\) have residual \(r_0=b-Kz_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric-indefinite augmented systems. The defining approximation is residual-minimizing over a Krylov space; symmetry-compatible preconditioning is allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Krylov method for the augmented system generates approximations \[z_k\in z_0+\mathcal K_k(K,r_0),\qquad \mathcal K_k(K,r_0)=\operatorname{span}\{r_0,Kr_0,\ldots,K^{k-1}r_0\}.\] In the MINRES realization, \(z_k\) is selected by \[\|b-Kz_k\|_2=\min_{z\in z_0+\mathcal K_k(K,r_0)}\|b-Kz\|_2.\] With an SPD preconditioner \(M=CC^T\), the same definition is applied to the symmetric transformed system \(C^{-1}KC^{-T}y=C^{-1}b\), followed by \(z=C^{-T}y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Krylov method for an augmented interior-point system searches successive affine spaces generated by the symmetric-indefinite matrix and the initial residual. In the MINRES form, each iterate minimizes the Euclidean residual norm over its current Krylov space. SPD preconditioning is introduced through a symmetry-preserving congruence transformation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[z_k\in z_0+\mathcal K_k(K,r_0),\qquad \|b-Kz_k\|_2=\min_{z\in z_0+\mathcal K_k(K,r_0)}\|b-Kz\|_2.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A symmetry-preserving preconditioned solve is an unpreconditioned symmetric Krylov solve for \(C^{-1}KC^{-T}\).
Other symmetric-indefinite Krylov recurrences may use different orthogonality or quasi-minimality conditions while retaining the same operator domain.
special_cases_latex: If \(K\succ0\), the system also lies in the domain of conjugate gradients.
QMR with an incomplete symmetric-indefinite factorization is a nearby augmented-system variant, though its defining optimality condition differs from MINRES.
immediate_consequences_latex: No normal-equation product \(AH^{-1}A^T\) must be formed.
The method preserves direct access to both primal and constraint blocks of the augmented system.
boundary_notes: CG is not generally valid for an indefinite augmented matrix.
A nonsymmetric or indefinite preconditioner does not yield the stated symmetric transformed problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov Methods for Normal Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preconditioned conjugate gradients for positive-definite normal-equation reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(N=N^{T}\succ0\), \(g\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), an initial vector \(y_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), a preconditioner \(P=P^{T}\succ0\), and \(\tau\in(0,1)\), set \(r_0=g-Ny_0\), solve \(Ps_0=r_0\), and set \(p_0=s_0\). For \(j=0,1,\ldots\), first return \(y_j\) if \(\lVert r_j\rVert_{P^{-1}}\leq\tau\lVert g\rVert_{P^{-1}}\). Otherwise compute \(\alpha_j=(r_j^{T}s_j)/(p_j^{T}Np_j)\), \(y_{j+1}=y_j+\alpha_jp_j\), and \(r_{j+1}=r_j-\alpha_jNp_j\). Solve \(Ps_{j+1}=r_{j+1}\); if the residual test is not satisfied, set \(\beta_j=(r_{j+1}^{T}s_{j+1})/(r_j^{T}s_j)\) and \(p_{j+1}=s_{j+1}+\beta_jp_j\), and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preconditioned conjugate gradients solves a positive-definite normal equation using matrix-vector products and preconditioner solves, testing the relative residual before performing any recurrence that could divide by a zero residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In exact arithmetic, each recurrence executed before convergence is well-defined, and the returned iterate satisfies the stated residual tolerance.

notation.meaning: preconditioned residual norm defined by the positive-definite matrix P inverse

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate-Gradient Krylov Solve of Interior-Point Normal Equations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(N=AD^2A^T\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), where \(D\succ0\) is diagonal and \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank. Then \(N\succ0\). Consider \(Ny=h\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional positive-definite normal equations. Exact-arithmetic CG characterization is used; preconditioned variants require an SPD preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Krylov method for the normal equations, in its conjugate-gradient form, generates \[y_k\in y_0+\mathcal K_k(N,r_0),\qquad r_0=h-Ny_0,\] and selects the unique iterate satisfying either equivalent condition \[y_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in y_0+\mathcal K_k(N,r_0)}\tfrac12y^TNy-h^Ty,\qquad r_k\perp\mathcal K_k(N,r_0).\] With \(M\succ0\), preconditioned CG applies the same construction to \(M^{-1/2}NM^{-1/2}\) and transformed right-hand side. Products may be evaluated as \(Nv=A(D^2(A^Tv))\) without forming \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Krylov method for interior-point normal equations uses conjugate gradients on the positive-definite matrix \(N=AD^2A^T\). Each iterate lies in the affine Krylov space, minimizes the associated quadratic there, and has a residual orthogonal to that Krylov space. An SPD preconditioner may be applied through a symmetric transformation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y_k\in y_0+\mathcal K_k(N,r_0),\qquad y_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y}\{\tfrac12y^TNy-h^Ty:y-y_0\in\mathcal K_k(N,r_0)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The energy minimization condition is equivalent to \(r_k\perp\mathcal K_k(N,r_0)\).
LSQR applied to the associated least-squares system is equivalent in exact arithmetic to CG on the normal equations under the standard correspondence.
special_cases_latex: For \(M=I\), the method is unpreconditioned CG.
Network-structured normal equations may use a problem-specific SPD preconditioner.
immediate_consequences_latex: Each product with \(N\) can be computed using one product with \(A^T\), diagonal scaling, and one product with \(A\).
The method avoids Cholesky fill at the cost of an iteration count governed by the preconditioned spectrum.
boundary_notes: If \(A\) is row-rank deficient, \(N\) is only semidefinite and standard SPD CG assumptions fail.
Extreme entries of \(D\) can make the normal equations severely ill conditioned.

children.title: Matrix-Free Primal–Dual Operators
children.top_down_role: Operator-based system application without explicit KKT assembly.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Primal–Dual Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block operator application for a primal-dual Newton system without explicit KKT assembly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a primal-dual Newton matrix
\[K=\begin{pmatrix}H&A^{T}&-G^{T}\\ A&0&0\\ ZG&0&S\end{pmatrix},\]
its action on \(v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)\) is
\[Kv=\bigl(Hv_x+A^{T}v_y-G^{T}v_z,\;Av_x,\;ZGv_x+Sv_z\bigr).\]
Here \(H\) is the Lagrangian Hessian, \(A\) and \(G\) are equality- and inequality-constraint Jacobians, and \(S,Z\) are diagonal slack and multiplier matrices. Therefore a Krylov method can apply \(K\) using Hessian-vector products, Jacobian products, transposed-Jacobian products, and diagonal scaling, without forming or storing the assembled block matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual KKT matrix can be applied through Hessian and Jacobian products plus diagonal scaling, avoiding explicit block-matrix assembly.
assumptions_latex: All displayed linear operators have compatible finite-dimensional domains.
The required forward and transpose Jacobian products are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed operator action equals multiplication by the assembled primal-dual matrix \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix-Free Action of the Primal–Dual Newton Operator
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\) and \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\) with \(x,s>0\), and let the primal–dual increment be \(q=(q_\lambda,q_x,q_s)\in\mathbb R^{m+2n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming primal–dual Newton operator with diagonal complementarity blocks. The definition extends to nonlinear programming by replacing zero curvature with a Hessian action, but that extension is not asserted here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The matrix-free primal–dual operator is the linear map \[\mathcal K(q_\lambda,q_x,q_s)=\bigl(Aq_x,\ A^Tq_\lambda+q_s,\ Sq_x+Xq_s\bigr).\] An implementation is matrix-free when it evaluates this triple using routines for \(Aq_x\), \(A^Tq_\lambda\), and componentwise products with \(x\) and \(s\), without storing the block matrix \[\begin{bmatrix}0&A&0\\A^T&0&I\\0&S&X\end{bmatrix}.\] A matrix-free linear solver seeks \(q\) satisfying \(\mathcal Kq=r\), or a prescribed residual tolerance, using only such operator evaluations and auxiliary preconditioner actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-free primal–dual operator maps multiplier, primal, and dual-slack increments to the three residual blocks using products with \(A\), products with \(A^T\), and diagonal scaling by the current primal and slack vectors. The equivalent block KKT matrix is not assembled or stored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal K(q_\lambda,q_x,q_s)=(Aq_x,\ A^Tq_\lambda+q_s,\ Sq_x+Xq_s).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Applying the displayed block matrix to \((q_\lambda,q_x,q_s)\) gives exactly \(\mathcal K(q_\lambda,q_x,q_s)\).
Eliminated augmented or normal-equation operator actions can also be matrix-free when inverse diagonal scalings and products with \(A\) and \(A^T\) are applied compositionally.
special_cases_latex: The normal-equation action is \(v\mapsto A(D^2(A^Tv))\).
The augmented action is \((u,v)\mapsto(Av,A^Tu-D^{-2}v)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Storage of the full KKT coefficient matrix is unnecessary.
Automatic differentiation or structured Jacobian routines can supply the required products in broader primal–dual models.
boundary_notes: Matrix-free evaluation does not itself specify convergence or a stopping rule for the iterative solver.
A preconditioner may still use explicitly assembled approximations or partial factors.

notation.meaning: Positive diagonal matrices formed from the current primal and slack variables.

children.title: Interior-Point Preconditioning

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Preconditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier-robust spectral criterion for preconditioners of reduced symmetric positive-definite interior-point systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N_\mu=N_\mu^{T}\succ0\) be a normal-equation matrix for barrier parameter \(\mu>0\), and let \(P_\mu=P_\mu^{T}\succ0\) be a preconditioner. Suppose constants \(0<c\leq C<\infty\), independent of \(\mu\), satisfy \[c\,v^{T}P_\mu v\leq v^{T}N_\mu v\leq C\,v^{T}P_\mu v\qquad\text{for every }v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.\] Then the symmetric preconditioned matrix \(Q_\mu=P_\mu^{-1/2}N_\mu P_\mu^{-1/2}\) has spectrum in \([c,C]\) and satisfies \(\kappa_2(Q_\mu)\leq C/c\). Because \(P_\mu^{-1}N_\mu\) is similar to \(Q_\mu\), it has the same eigenvalues. Consequently, the standard preconditioned conjugate-gradient convergence estimate is uniform as \(\mu\downarrow0\); this uniform spectral equivalence formalizes barrier robustness for the reduced system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduced-system preconditioner is barrier-robust when its symmetric preconditioned matrix remains uniformly spectrally equivalent to the reduced matrix, yielding a barrier-independent condition-number bound and PCG estimate.
assumptions_latex: The spectral-equivalence constants \(c\) and \(C\) are independent of \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(Q_\mu)\subseteq[c,C]\) and \(\kappa_2(Q_\mu)\leq C/c\), uniformly in \(\mu\), where \(Q_\mu=P_\mu^{-1/2}N_\mu P_\mu^{-1/2}\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean spectral condition number of a symmetric positive-definite matrix

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Preconditioner for a Barrier-Dependent Linear System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K_\mu z=b\) be an interior-point linear system indexed by \(\mu>0\), and let \(M_\mu\) be a nonsingular matrix or linear operator whose inverse can be applied substantially more cheaply than \(K_\mu^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional left, right, or symmetric preconditioning. A barrier-robust condition is included for positive-definite reductions; indefinite systems require an analogous spectral or field-of-values criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interior-point preconditioner is a family \(\{M_\mu\}_{\mu>0}\) used to replace \(K_\mu z=b\) by an equivalent transformed system, for example \[M_\mu^{-1}K_\mu z=M_\mu^{-1}b.\] For symmetric positive-definite \(K_\mu\) and \(M_\mu\), it is barrier-robust on an index set \(I\) when constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), independent of \(\mu\in I\), satisfy \[c\,v^TM_\mu v\le v^TK_\mu v\le C\,v^TM_\mu v\qquad\forall v.\] Equivalently, every eigenvalue of \(M_\mu^{-1/2}K_\mu M_\mu^{-1/2}\) lies in \([c,C]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior-point preconditioner is an inexpensive invertible approximation to a barrier-dependent system matrix, used to transform the linear equations while preserving their solution. In the SPD case, it is barrier-robust when the preconditioned eigenvalues remain uniformly bounded above and away from zero as the barrier parameter varies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[M_\mu^{-1}K_\mu z=M_\mu^{-1}b,\qquad cM_\mu\preceq K_\mu\preceq CM_\mu.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For SPD systems, uniform spectral equivalence is equivalent to \(\sigma(M_\mu^{-1/2}K_\mu M_\mu^{-1/2})\subset[c,C]\).
If \(M_\mu=C_\mu C_\mu^T\), symmetric preconditioning solves \(C_\mu^{-1}K_\mu C_\mu^{-T}y=C_\mu^{-1}b\) and sets \(z=C_\mu^{-T}y\).
special_cases_latex: Incomplete Cholesky supplies an SPD preconditioner for normal equations.
Block-diagonal, constraint, and approximate Schur-complement preconditioners target augmented KKT systems.
immediate_consequences_latex: Uniformly clustered preconditioned spectra can prevent Krylov iteration counts from deteriorating solely because \(\mu\) decreases.
The preconditioner may reuse sparse factors of a simplified or slowly varying system.
boundary_notes: Spectral equivalence in the displayed Loewner form applies only to SPD matrices.
A very accurate preconditioner may still be unattractive if its construction or inverse application is too expensive.

children.title: Inexact Linear-Solve Forcing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Accuracy control linking iterative solves with outer convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Linear-Solve Forcing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual forcing conditions coupling Krylov accuracy to local inexact-Newton convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be continuously differentiable near a solution \(w_*\), with nonsingular \(F'(w_*)\). An inexact Newton step \(d_k\) satisfies the forcing condition
\[\lVert F(w_k)+F'(w_k)d_k\rVert\leq\eta_k\lVert F(w_k)\rVert,\qquad 0\leq\eta_k<1.\]
Under the standard local assumptions for inexact Newton iteration, a uniform bound \(\eta_k\leq\bar\eta<1\) gives local linear convergence; \(\eta_k\to0\) gives superlinear convergence; and, when \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz, \(\eta_k=O(\lVert F(w_k)\rVert)\) gives quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linear residual is controlled by a forcing term: bounded forcing gives linear convergence, vanishing forcing superlinear convergence, and residual-proportional forcing quadratic convergence.
assumptions_latex: For the quadratic regime, \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic behavior of \(\eta_k\) determines the stated local convergence regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forcing-condition formulation and convergence regimes are standard and fit the terminal container, but this theorem-level local convergence claim has no citation. An authoritative inexact-Newton theorem locator is required, particularly to confirm the complete neighborhood and regularity hypotheses for the quadratic regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Forcing Sequence for Inexact Interior Newton Steps
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F(w)=0\) denote the nonlinear primal–dual residual equations and let \(J_k=F'(w_k)\). An approximate Newton step \(p_k\) has linear residual \(e_k:=J_kp_k+F(w_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-dimensional inexact Newton forcing measured in a fixed norm. Globalization and feasibility safeguards are outside the defining condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact linear-solve forcing regime is a sequence \(\{\eta_k\}\subset[0,1)\) for which each computed step satisfies \[\|J_kp_k+F(w_k)\|\le\eta_k\|F(w_k)\|.\] A fixed-accuracy regime has \(\eta_k\le\bar\eta<1\). A vanishing regime has \(\eta_k\to0\). A residual-proportional regime has \(\eta_k=O(\|F(w_k)\|)\). More generally, the tolerance may combine an upper safeguard with a residual-dependent term, such as \(\eta_k=\min\{\bar\eta,c\|F(w_k)\|^\alpha\}\), where \(c>0\) and \(0<\alpha\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact linear-solve forcing regime prescribes a relative bound on the residual of each approximate primal–dual Newton equation. Fixed forcing keeps the relative residual below a constant less than one, vanishing forcing drives that relative tolerance to zero, and residual-proportional forcing makes it decrease at the scale of the nonlinear residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|J_kp_k+F(w_k)\|\le\eta_k\|F(w_k)\|,\qquad 0\le\eta_k<1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For the linear system \(J_kp_k=b_k\) with \(b_k=-F(w_k)\), the condition is \(\|b_k-J_kp_k\|\le\eta_k\|b_k\|\).
If a consistently transformed norm is used, the same definition applies to a preconditioned residual.
special_cases_latex: \(\eta_k=0\) specifies an exact linear solve.
\(\eta_k=\min\{0.5,\sqrt{\|F(w_k)\|}\}\) is a standard vanishing-forcing pattern.
\(\eta_k=O(\|F(w_k)\|)\) is the classical quadratic-accuracy regime under the usual local smoothness assumptions.
immediate_consequences_latex: The inner iteration can terminate as soon as its residual meets the outer-method tolerance.
Early outer iterations may use looser solves while later iterations demand greater accuracy.
boundary_notes: The residual norm and any scaling must be specified consistently; raw componentwise residuals can be misleading in poorly scaled KKT systems.
The definition alone does not guarantee global or local convergence of a particular interior-point algorithm.

notation.meaning: Relative forcing parameter for the \(k\)-th inexact Newton solve.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stabilized Interior-Point Linear-System Construction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K_\mu z=b\) be a symmetric interior-point Newton system that may be singular, have unsuitable inertia, or become poorly scaled as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional stabilization by congruent scaling, primal–dual diagonal regularization, and residual correction. These operations define a stabilized solve, not a convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear-system stabilization stack is a parameterized composition \((E_\mu,R_\mu,\mathcal C_\mu)\) consisting of an invertible scaling \(E_\mu\), a symmetric regularization \(R_\mu\), and an optional residual-correction map. The stabilized coefficient is \[\widehat K_\mu=E_\mu(K_\mu+R_\mu)E_\mu^T.\] One first solves \(\widehat K_\mu y=E_\mu b\) and sets \(z_0=E_\mu^Ty\). A residual-correction step may then solve \[(K_\mu+R_\mu)d_j=b-K_\mu z_j,\qquad z_{j+1}=z_j+d_j.\] The parameters are admissible when \(\widehat K_\mu\) is nonsingular and has the inertia required by the primal–dual model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-system stabilization stack combines invertible scaling, symmetric regularization, and optional residual correction. It replaces the difficult interior-point matrix by a nonsingular, suitably signed scaled matrix, solves that system, and may refine the result against the original residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat K_\mu=E_\mu(K_\mu+R_\mu)E_\mu^T,\qquad \widehat K_\mu y=E_\mu b,\qquad z_0=E_\mu^Ty.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Diagonal equilibration is the case in which \(E_\mu\) is diagonal.
Primal–dual regularization is obtained when \(R_\mu\) adds a positive shift to the primal block and a negative shift to the multiplier block.
special_cases_latex: With \(E_\mu=I\) and no correction, the stack reduces to regularization alone.
With \(R_\mu=0\), the stack reduces to congruent scaling and optional refinement.
immediate_consequences_latex: Congruent scaling preserves inertia when \(E_\mu\) is nonsingular.
Regularization can remove zero eigenvalues or correct an unsuitable signature before factorization.
boundary_notes: A stabilized solution generally solves the perturbed system exactly, not the original system, unless correction or perturbation control is imposed.
Excessive regularization can erase useful curvature information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal and Dual Diagonal Regularization of a KKT Matrix
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H=H^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(K=\begin{bmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\). Let \(\delta,\gamma\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric saddle-point systems. The primal shift targets curvature and inertia; the dual shift targets constraint-rank singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal–dual regularization pair is the ordered pair \((\delta,\gamma)\) defining the perturbed KKT matrix \[K_{\delta,\gamma}=\begin{bmatrix}H+\delta I_n&A^T\\A&-\gamma I_m\end{bmatrix}.\] The primal regularization \(\delta I_n\) shifts curvature eigenvalues upward and is selected to obtain the required positive definiteness on the constraint null space or the required KKT inertia. The dual regularization \(-\gamma I_m\) supplies negative curvature in the multiplier block and removes singularity associated with dependent or nearly dependent constraint rows. A regularized step is any \((p,\lambda)\) satisfying \(K_{\delta,\gamma}(p,\lambda)=(f,g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal–dual regularization pair adds a positive diagonal shift to the primal curvature block and a negative diagonal shift to the multiplier block of a symmetric KKT matrix. The primal parameter controls curvature and inertia, while the dual parameter protects against singular or rank-deficient constraint blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K_{\delta,\gamma}=\begin{bmatrix}H+\delta I_n&A^T\\A&-\gamma I_m\end{bmatrix},\qquad K_{\delta,\gamma}\begin{bmatrix}p\\\lambda\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}f\\g\end{bmatrix}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Eliminating \(p\), when \(H+\delta I\) is invertible, gives the regularized Schur matrix \(\gamma I+A(H+\delta I)^{-1}A^T\).
The unregularized KKT system is recovered at \((\delta,\gamma)=(0,0)\).
special_cases_latex: Primal-only regularization has \(\gamma=0\).
Dual-only rank stabilization has \(\delta=0\) and \(\gamma>0\).
In nonlinear interior-point systems, the same pair appears within the larger primal–slack–multiplier matrix.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(H+\delta I\succ0\) and \(\gamma>0\), then the displayed Schur complement is positive definite.
The two parameters can be varied independently because they address different failure modes.
boundary_notes: The regularized step is biased relative to the unperturbed Newton step.
A parameter rule must balance nonsingularity and inertia against distortion of the original second-order model.

children.title: Primal-Block Regularization
children.top_down_role: Stabilization applied to primal curvature or variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Block Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive diagonal stabilization of the primal block in a saddle-point Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a symmetric saddle-point matrix \(K=\begin{pmatrix}H&A^{T}\\ A&-D\end{pmatrix}\), its primal-block regularization with parameter \(\delta_p>0\) is
\[K_{\delta_p}=\begin{pmatrix}H+\delta_p I&A^{T}\\ A&-D\end{pmatrix}.\]
More generally, \(\delta_p I\) may be replaced by a symmetric matrix \(R_p\succ0\). The modification acts only on primal variables and satisfies \(v^{T}(H+R_p)v=v^{T}Hv+v^{T}R_pv\). Thus it raises primal curvature in every direction; when \(H\succeq0\), the regularized primal block is positive definite and has smallest eigenvalue at least \(\lambda_{\min}(R_p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal-block regularization adds a positive-definite matrix to the primal Hessian block, increasing curvature while leaving constraint couplings unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regularized primal block is \(H+R_p\); if \(H\succeq0\), then \(H+R_p\succ0\).

children.title: Dual-Block Regularization
children.top_down_role: Stabilization applied to multiplier or constraint blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Block Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual diagonal stabilization of a symmetric primal–dual Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=H^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(\delta_d\ge 0\). Dual-block regularization replaces the zero dual diagonal of a saddle-point matrix by a negative definite shift:
\[
K_d(\delta_d)=\begin{pmatrix}H&A^\top\\A&-\delta_d I_m\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For a right-hand side \(b\in\mathbb R^{n+m}\), the regularized direction is any \(d_{\delta_d}\) satisfying \(K_d(\delta_d)d_{\delta_d}=b\). The shift is admissible when the matrix is nonsingular, has the inertia required by the primal–dual method, and the unregularized residual \(b-K_d(0)d_{\delta_d}\) meets the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual regularization inserts a negative diagonal shift in the multiplier block, seeking a nonsingular system with suitable inertia and an acceptably small original-system residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_d(\delta_d)d_{\delta_d}=b\), subject to nonsingularity, target inertia, and an unregularized-residual test.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Regularization Balance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint acceptance condition for primal and dual diagonal shifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
K=\begin{pmatrix}H&A^\top\\A&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad E(\delta_p,\delta_d)=\begin{pmatrix}\delta_p I_n&0\\0&-\delta_d I_m\end{pmatrix},
\]
a pair \((\delta_p,\delta_d)\in\mathbb R_+^2\) is balanced at tolerance \(\eta\in(0,1)\) if \(K+E(\delta_p,\delta_d)\) is nonsingular, has the target inertia, and
\[
\left\|K^{-1}E(\delta_p,\delta_d)\right\|\le\eta.
\]
When \(K\) is unavailable or singular, the last predicate is replaced operationally by \(\|b-Kd_{p,d}\|\le\eta\|b\|\), where \((K+E)d_{p,d}=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual shifts are balanced when they produce the desired inertia without perturbing the original Newton equation beyond a prescribed relative tolerance.
assumptions_latex: For the operator-norm form, \(K\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((\delta_p,\delta_d)\) is accepted only if stability, inertia, and perturbation requirements hold jointly.

children.title: Overregularization Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where stabilization excessively distorts the interior-point system.

knowledge_statements.title: Overregularization Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation threshold beyond which regularization accuracy is uncontrolled.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be nonsingular, let \(E\) denote the combined regularization, and define \(d=K^{-1}b\) and \(d_E=(K+E)^{-1}b\). If \(\theta=\|K^{-1}E\|<1\), then
\[
\frac{\|d_E-d\|}{\|d\|}\le \frac{\theta}{1-\theta}.
\]
Thus a permitted direction-error fraction \(\tau>0\) requires \(\theta\le\tau/(1+\tau)\). The boundary \(\theta\ge1\) is an overregularization boundary for this guarantee: invertibility of \(K+E\) and closeness of its direction to the unregularized direction no longer follow from the perturbation argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularization is quantitatively controlled only while its relative operator perturbation is below one; larger shifts may stabilize the factorization but destroy direction fidelity.
assumptions_latex: \(K+E\) is used to compute the perturbed direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\|K^{-1}E\|<1\), the displayed error bound holds; at \(\|K^{-1}E\|\ge1\), that guarantee fails.

children.title: Factorization-Guided Inertia Correction

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization-Guided Inertia Correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularization adjusted from symmetric-indefinite factorization inertia.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a symmetric primal–dual matrix \(K\), initial shifts \(\delta_p,\delta_d\ge0\), growth factor \(\gamma>1\), and target inertia \((n_+,n_-,0)\), form \(K(\delta_p,\delta_d)=K+\operatorname{diag}(\delta_p I,-\delta_d I)\). Compute a pivoted \(LDL^\top\) factorization and obtain the inertia from the signs of the eigenvalues of the diagonal pivot blocks. If the inertia is unsuitable or a pivot is numerically singular, increase the shift associated with the deficient sign by at least the factor \(\gamma\), refactor, and repeat. Return the first direction whose factorization has target inertia and whose original-system residual satisfies the acceptance tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pivoted symmetric factorization diagnoses the current inertia; primal or dual shifts are enlarged until the target signature and residual test are both satisfied.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma>1\), and a finite target inertia is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned factorization has inertia \((n_+,n_-,0)\), and its direction passes the original-system residual test.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inertia Correction Driven by a Symmetric-Indefinite Factorization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K(\delta,\gamma)=K(\delta,\gamma)^T\) be a regularized primal–dual matrix, and let its desired inertia be \((n_+,n_-,0)\). Suppose a pivoted factorization gives \(PK(\delta,\gamma)P^T=LBL^T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear interior-point systems. The target inertia is prescribed by the primal and constraint dimensions; the parameter search is factorization-guided rather than based on eigenvectors of the full matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A factorization-guided inertia correction is a rule that computes \(\operatorname{In}(K(\delta,\gamma))\) from the signed eigenvalue counts of the \(1\times1\) and \(2\times2\) blocks of \(B\), compares that count with \((n_+,n_-,0)\), and changes the regularization parameters until \[\operatorname{In}(K(\delta,\gamma))=(n_+,n_-,0).\] For the nonlinear primal–dual matrix with \(n\) primal variables, \(m\) inequalities, and \(l\) equalities, the standard target is \[(n_+,n_-,n_0)=(n+m,l+m,0).\] If zero eigenvalues are detected, a positive dual regularization may be introduced; if the positive/negative counts are unsuitable, the primal shift is increased and the matrix is refactored.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factorization-guided inertia correction reads the numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues from the pivot blocks of a symmetric-indefinite factorization. It adjusts primal and dual regularization and refactors until the matrix has the signature required by the interior-point model and has no zero eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[PK(\delta,\gamma)P^T=LBL^T,\qquad \operatorname{In}(K(\delta,\gamma))=\operatorname{In}(B)=(n_+,n_-,0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: By congruence invariance, counting the signs of \(B\)'s pivot-block eigenvalues gives the inertia of \(K(\delta,\gamma)\).
For the standard nonlinear primal–dual system, the acceptance test is \(\operatorname{In}(K)=(n+m,l+m,0)\).
special_cases_latex: If the unregularized factorization already has the target inertia, no correction is applied.
If the factorization reveals zero eigenvalues, setting \(\gamma>0\) addresses constraint-block singularity before the inertia test is repeated.
A geometric increase \(\delta\leftarrow10\delta\) is a standard trial rule after an unsuccessful factorization.
immediate_consequences_latex: An accepted corrected matrix is nonsingular because its zero-eigenvalue count is zero.
The inertia test simultaneously certifies the curvature signature required for a productive primal–dual direction.
boundary_notes: The correction rule does not identify the smallest possible perturbation unless an explicit optimization criterion is added.
Large primal shifts can make the step resemble a steepest-descent direction by suppressing Hessian information.

notation.meaning: Triple of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalue counts of \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient Shifts for the Target Saddle-Point Inertia
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient termination regime for primal-dual inertia correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K(\delta_p,\delta_d)=\begin{pmatrix}H+\delta_p I&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&-\delta_d I\end{pmatrix},
\qquad H=H^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},\quad A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}.
\]
If \(\delta_p> -\lambda_{\min}(H)\) and \(\delta_d>0\), then
\[
\operatorname{inertia}(K(\delta_p,\delta_d))=(n,m,0).
\]
Indeed, the primal block is positive definite and its Schur complement is \(-\delta_d I-A(H+\delta_pI)^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\prec0\). Consequently, a correction scheme that keeps a positive dual shift and increases the primal shift without bound must eventually enter the target-inertia regime in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently large primal shift together with any positive dual shift guarantees the standard nonsingular saddle-point inertia, regardless of constraint rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{inertia}(K(\delta_p,\delta_d))=(n,m,0)\).

notation.meaning: numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues
