children.top_down_role: Normalization choices and numerical safeguards affecting stopping decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Termination Scaling Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale floors and finite-data checks preventing misleading termination decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each raw residual \(r_j\geq0\) be compared with \(\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{rel}}S_j\). A safeguarded termination system requires \(1\leq S_j\leq S_{
max}\), computes \(S_j\) from fixed problem-data and iterate norms, and rejects termination whenever a residual, scale, objective, or multiplier used by the certificate is nonfinite. The same scaling convention must be used throughout a run. Consequently, multiplying data by a moderate positive unit-conversion factor changes the relative test predictably, while neither a vanishing denominator nor an overflowing scale can make an unresolved residual appear acceptable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use bounded scale floors, consistent conventions, and finite-value checks so tiny denominators or overflow cannot trigger false termination.
assumptions_latex:
\(S_{
max}\geq1\) is a finite implementation bound.
Absolute and relative tolerances are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
Termination is permitted only if every quantity is finite and every \(r_j\leq\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_j^{\mathrm{rel}}S_j\) with \(1\leq S_j\leq S_{
max}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the safeguard leaf, but the finite upper cap is an implementation convention and the claimed response to unit conversion depends on how each scale is constructed. No source is supplied. In addition, S_{\nmax} is malformed TeX and must be replaced by a defined symbol such as S_{\max} once the sourced convention is established.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unrestricted Iterate-Dependent Scaling Can Trivialize a Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: False acceptance when a residual's normalization is allowed to grow with that same residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}=0\) and \(0<\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}<1\). If the scale may be chosen as \(S=r/\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}\) for any \(r>0\), then \[r=\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}S\] and the relative stopping test passes for every residual magnitude. Thus a scale must be fixed by a declared normalization rule that does not make the tested inequality tautological.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unrestricted residual-dependent scale can make every residual pass, so normalization must be fixed independently enough to preserve the test's meaning.
assumptions_latex: The scale is permitted to equal \(r/\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The predicate \(r\leq\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}S\) holds for arbitrary \(r>0\) and therefore provides no accuracy discrimination.
knowledge_statements.title: Unrestricted Iterate-Dependent Scaling Can Trivialize a Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Quantity Requirement for Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility safeguard for numerical quantities used by a stopping certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numerical termination certificate based on residuals \(r_j\), scales \(S_j\), tolerances, objective values, or multipliers is admissible only when every quantity used to evaluate its predicates is finite. If any required quantity is NaN or infinite, the corresponding certificate is indeterminate and termination must not be declared from it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stopping certificate must reject nonfinite inputs; NaN or infinite residual data cannot certify termination.
assumptions_latex: Termination is decided from finite-dimensional numerical predicates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(\exists j:\ r_j\notin\mathbb R\text{ or }S_j\notin\mathbb R\bigr)\Rightarrow\text{the certificate does not pass}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Quantity Requirement for Termination

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covariance of a Scaled Residual Test under Unit Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation required to preserve a stopping decision under a common positive unit conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[r\leq\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}S,\qquad r,S\geq0.\] For \(\alpha>0\), set \(r'=\alpha r\), \(S'=\alpha S\), \((\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}})'=\alpha\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}\), and \((\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}})'=\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}\). Then \[r\leq\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r'\leq(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}})'+(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}})'S'.\] Keeping a nonzero absolute tolerance unchanged generally destroys this invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled residual decision is invariant under a common positive unit conversion when the residual, scale, and absolute tolerance co-scale while the relative tolerance stays fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\leq\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}S\iff \alpha r\leq\alpha\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}\alpha S\).

notation.meaning: scale expressed in the residual's units

knowledge_statements.title: Covariance of a Scaled Residual Test under Unit Changes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covariance of Scaled Residual Tests under Unit Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: How residual scales and absolute tolerances must transform under a common positive unit conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the test \[r\leq\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}S,\qquad r,S\geq0.\] For any \(\alpha>0\), define \(r'=\alpha r\), \(S'=\alpha S\), \((\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}})'=\alpha\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}\), and \((\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}})'=\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}\). Then \[r\leq\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r'\leq(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}})'+(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}})'S'.\] If the absolute tolerance is not transformed, this invariance generally fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled residual decision is invariant under a common positive unit conversion only when the residual, its scale, and the absolute tolerance co-scale while the relative tolerance remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r\leq\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}S\iff \alpha r\leq\alpha\varepsilon^{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon^{\mathrm{rel}}\alpha S.

notation.meaning: residual scale expressed in the same units as the residual

knowledge_statements.title: Covariance of Scaled Residual Tests under Unit Changes

children.title: Finite Active-Structure Identification
children.top_down_role: Interfaces between asymptotic interior convergence and finite solution identification.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite identification of the basic and nonbasic partition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a standard-form linear program, let \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\) be strictly positive primal-dual iterates converging to a strictly complementary solution \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite index-set identification for strictly complementary linear-programming limits; weak complementarity and nonlinear active manifolds are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the iterate-dependent partition \[\mathcal B_k=\{i:x_i^k\geq s_i^k\},qquad \mathcal N_k=\{1,ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B_k.\] The sequence has finite active-structure identification if there exists \(k_0<infty\) such that, for all \(k\geq k_0\), \[\mathcal B_k=mathcal B^*=\{i:x_i^*>0,s_i^*=0\},qquad \mathcal N_k=mathcal N^*=\{i:x_i^*=0,s_i^*>0\}.\] More generally, a threshold rule may replace the comparison \(x_i^k\geq s_i^k\), but finite identification requires eventual exact equality with the limiting partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite active-structure identification means that an index classifier based on the positive primal and dual-slack components becomes exactly equal to the strictly complementary limiting partition after some finite iteration and never changes thereafter. The canonical classifier places an index in the basic set when its primal component is at least its dual slack and in the nonbasic set otherwise.
assumptions_latex: Strict complementarity holds: for every index, exactly one of \(x_i^*\) and \(s_i^*\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite identification is the existence of \(k_0\) such that \((\mathcal B_k,mathcal N_k)=(\mathcal B^*,mathcal N^*)\) for every \(k\geq k_0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a convergent strictly complementary sequence, finite identification is equivalent to eventual correctness of every componentwise comparison \(x_i^k\geq s_i^k\).
special_cases_latex: The identified partition can be used as the zero pattern in a finite-termination projection.
A scaled comparison \(x_i^k/alpha_i\geq s_i^k/beta_i\) is a distinct classifier unless its positive scales are fixed.
immediate_consequences_latex: After identification, the complementarity pattern may be imposed as \(x_{mathcal N^*}=0\) and \(s_{mathcal B^*}=0\).
The definition concerns finite stabilization of the discrete partition, not finite arrival of the interior iterates at the boundary.
boundary_notes: If strict complementarity fails, the rule can remain ambiguous on indices with \(x_i^*=s_i^*=0\).
Identification does not alone guarantee that a projected point is primal-dual feasible.

notation.meaning: estimated basic or primal-positive index set
estimated nonbasic or dual-slack-positive index set

children.title: Finite-Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem classes and algorithmic settings supporting finite stopping behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Termination Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite stabilization of threshold-based active-set classification under strict separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x_k,z_k)\to(x^*,z^*)\) for constraints \(g_i(x)\geq0\), and suppose strict complementarity holds: for every \(i\), exactly one of \(g_i(x^*)\) and \(z_i^*\) is positive. Let \(e_k=\lVert(x_k,z_k)-(x^*,z^*)\rVert\), and choose thresholds \(\tau_k\downarrow0\) satisfying \(e_k/\tau_k\to0\). Define \(i\) as predicted active when \(g_i(x_k)\leq\tau_k\) and predicted inactive when \(z_{k,i}\leq\tau_k\). Then there exists a finite \(K\) such that, for every \(k\geq K\), both classifications equal the solution's active and inactive sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With strict complementarity and thresholds shrinking slower than iterate error, predicted active and inactive sets stabilize after finitely many iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(K<\infty\) such that the predicted active and inactive sets are exact for all \(k\geq K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a finite-identification theorem rather than a generic property. Moreover, convergence of x_k alone does not imply g_i(x_k)=o(τ_k); a local Lipschitz or equivalent error-control hypothesis for each g_i is needed. A direct source is required to establish the intended classifier and sufficient hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Interiority Precludes Exact Boundary Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between asymptotic barrier convergence and finite exact attainment of an active solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every iterate satisfies \(g_i(x_k)>0\) for every inequality \(i\). If every solution \(x^*\) satisfies \(g_j(x^*)=0\) for at least one index \(j\), then no finite strictly interior iterate can equal a solution. Exact finite termination therefore requires a boundary-producing operation; otherwise only tolerance-based finite stopping or asymptotic convergence is possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method that always remains strictly interior cannot finitely attain a boundary optimizer without a boundary-producing step.
assumptions_latex: Every generated iterate is strictly feasible for every inequality.
Every optimizer has at least one active inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k\notin X^*\text{ for every finite }k.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Interiority Precludes Exact Boundary Termination

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Stabilization under Lipschitz Error Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed active-classification stabilization theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_i(x)\ge0\) be locally Lipschitz near \(x^*\), let \((x_k,z_k)\to(x^*,z^*)\), suppose strict complementarity holds, and choose \(\tau_k\downarrow0\) with \(\|x_k-x^*\|+\|z_k-z^*\|=o(\tau_k)\). Then the corresponding slack-and-multiplier threshold classifier is eventually exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lipschitz control, strict complementarity, and error-threshold separation imply eventual exact active-set classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The threshold classification is exact after a finite index.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Stabilization under Lipschitz Error Separation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Tolerance Stopping from Residual Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic finite stopping regime distinguished from exact finite attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_k\ge0\) be a declared feasibility-and-optimality residual with \(R_k\to0\). For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(K<\infty\) such that \(R_k\le\varepsilon\) for all \(k\ge K\). Hence stopping at the first index satisfying \(R_k\le\varepsilon\) terminates finitely, although it need not return an exact solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual convergence guarantees finite termination at every positive tolerance, but not exact finite attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{k:R_k\le\varepsilon\}<\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Tolerance Stopping from Residual Convergence

children.title: Active-Constraint Identification
children.top_down_role: Recognition of constraints active at a limiting solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Constraint Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold classification of active inequalities from primal slacks and dual multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify constraints using small slacks and positive multipliers, while retaining ambiguous indices as undecided and requiring feasibility checks.
assumptions_latex:
\(\tau_{
 g}\) and \(\tau_z\) are positive and consistent with problem scaling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the active and inactive definitions overlap when s_i=τ_g and z_i=τ_z, contradicting the claimed disjoint output. The threshold symbols also contain malformed TeX. A source is needed to determine the intended tie-breaking, scaling, rejection, and verification policy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weakly Active Barrier Limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior sequence showing failure of a fixed positive multiplier threshold at a zero-multiplier active constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\ge0}x^2\). Its unique solution is \(x^*=0\) with multiplier \(z^*=0\). The logarithmic-barrier stationary point satisfies \[x(\mu)=\sqrt{\mu/2},\qquad z(\mu)=\mu/x(\mu)=\sqrt{2\mu}.\] Thus the constraint is active at the limit while both its slack and multiplier tend to zero. Any classifier requiring \(z(\mu)\ge\tau_z\) for a fixed \(\tau_z>0\) eventually fails to classify it as active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly active constraint can have both slack and multiplier vanish along the barrier path, defeating every fixed positive multiplier threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed positive multiplier thresholds cannot identify every active constraint without strict complementarity.

notation.meaning: Barrier primal point and complementarity multiplier.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Active Barrier Limit

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square-Root Complementarity Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eventual active-versus-inactive classification along an exactly complementary interior sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_i^k>0\), \(z_i^k>0\), and \(s_i^kz_i^k=\mu_k\downarrow0\) for finitely many inequalities. Suppose \((s^k,z^k)\to(s^*,z^*)\) and strict complementarity holds: for every \(i\), exactly one of \(s_i^*\) and \(z_i^*\) is positive. Define \[\widehat{\mathcal A}_k=\{i:s_i^k\le\sqrt{\mu_k},\ z_i^k\ge\sqrt{\mu_k}\},\qquad \widehat{\mathcal I}_k=\{i:s_i^k\ge\sqrt{\mu_k},\ z_i^k\le\sqrt{\mu_k}\}.\] Then, for all sufficiently large \(k\), these sets are disjoint and equal to the limiting active and inactive sets, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict complementarity, the square root of the complementarity parameter eventually separates active slacks from inactive multipliers exactly.
assumptions_latex: Strict complementarity holds at the limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat{\mathcal A}_k=\{i:s_i^*=0\}\text{ and }\widehat{\mathcal I}_k=\{i:s_i^*>0\}\text{ eventually}.
knowledge_statements.title: Square-Root Complementarity Identification

children.title: Optimal-Face Identification
children.top_down_role: Recovery of the optimal face approached by interior iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification of the minimal optimal face for a polyhedral feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a relative-interior optimal point, a suitably shrinking coordinate threshold identifies the minimal polyhedral optimal face after finitely many iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(K<\infty\) such that \(\widehat J_k=J_0\) and the identified coordinate face is \(F^*\) for every \(k\geq K\).

notation.meaning: minimal face containing the primal optimal set
coordinates fixed to zero on that face

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical claim is a finite-identification theorem, not a generic property, and it is specialized to standard-form polyhedra. No source is supplied for that exact specialization. The statement also contains malformed commands for nonnegativity and the infinity norm, which must be repaired after the sourced formulation is fixed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Boundary Limit Can Select a Proper Optimal Subface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of full optimal-face recovery when the limit is not in the relative interior of that face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x_1+x_2=1,\ x\geq0\}\] and let the objective be identically zero. Then the optimal set and its minimal containing face are \(F^*=P\). For integers \(k\geq4\), let \(x^k=(1/k,1-1/k)\) and \(\tau_k=2/k\). The sequence is strictly positive and converges to \(\bar x=(0,1)\notin\operatorname{relint}(F^*)\). Coordinate thresholding declares \(x_1\) zero and \(x_2\) nonzero for every \(k\geq4\), thereby selecting the proper vertex face \(\{(0,1)\}\) rather than \(F^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence to the boundary of an optimal face can make coordinate thresholding select a proper subface instead of the face containing all optima.

notation.meaning: minimal face containing the optimal set

knowledge_statements.title: A Boundary Limit Can Select a Proper Optimal Subface

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Limit Is Necessary for Global Optimal-Face Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convergent interior sequence may approach a proper face of a larger optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x_1+x_2=1,\ x\geq0\}\] and let the objective be identically zero. The entire segment \(P\) is the optimal set and therefore the minimal face containing the optimal set is \(F^*=P\). The strictly positive sequence \(x^k=(1/k,1-1/k)\) converges to \(\bar x=(0,1)\notin\operatorname{relint}(F^*)\). With \(\tau_k=2/k\), coordinate thresholding declares \(x_1\) fixed at zero for every \(k\), thereby selecting the proper vertex face \(\{(0,1)\}\) rather than \(F^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence to a boundary point of the optimal face can make coordinate thresholding identify a proper subface instead of the full minimal face containing all optima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in P:x_1=0\}=\{(0,1)\}\subsetneq F^*=P\), so the threshold estimate does not recover \(F^*\).

notation.meaning: minimal face containing the optimal set

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Limit Is Necessary for Global Optimal-Face Recovery

children.title: Identification Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degenerate or ambiguous regimes that obstruct finite structural identification.

knowledge_statements.title: Identification Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of uniform active-set identification when strict complementarity disappears.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the parametric problems \[\min_{x\geq0}(x-\delta)^2.\] For \(\delta>0\), the unique solution is \(x^*(\delta)=\delta>0\), so the bound is inactive and its multiplier is zero. For \(\delta<0\), the unique solution is \(x^*(\delta)=0\), so the bound is active with a positive multiplier. At \(\delta=0\), the bound is active but its multiplier is zero, violating strict complementarity. Thus arbitrarily small data perturbations near \(\delta=0\) change the active set, and no uniformly valid finite identification rule based solely on approximate slack and multiplier separation exists there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without strict complementarity, arbitrarily small perturbations can change activity, so slack-and-multiplier thresholds cannot identify the active set uniformly.
assumptions_latex: The constraint is the scalar bound \(x\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(\delta=0\), active-set identification lacks a uniform positive primal-dual separation margin.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits and the scalar example correctly shows loss of strict complementarity and of a uniform positive separation margin. However, the broader impossibility claim requires a specified observation-error model and class of identification rules; the example alone does not formalize that quantification. A source or a narrower sourced formulation is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Interior Iterates Need Not Identify Exact Activity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of exact-zero activity testing along a logarithmic-barrier path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{x:x\geq0\}\), whose unique solution is \(x^*=0\). For every \(\mu>0\), the barrier problem \[\min_{x>0}\;x-\mu\log x\] has minimizer \(x(\mu)=\mu>0\). Thus \(x(\mu)\to x^*\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\), but the estimator \(\widehat{\mathcal A}(x)=\{1:x=0\}\) remains empty at every positive barrier parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Barrier points can converge to an active bound while remaining strictly interior, so exact zero-slack testing need never identify that bound finitely.
assumptions_latex: Activity is estimated solely by exact equality to the bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat{\mathcal A}(x(\mu))=\varnothing\) for every \(\mu>0\), whereas \(\mathcal A(x^*)=\{1\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Interior Iterates Need Not Identify Exact Activity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-Set Instability at a Weakly Active Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of a uniform primal-dual separation margin when strict complementarity fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min_{x\geq0}(x-\delta)^2,\] the unique minimizer is \(x^*(\delta)=\max\{\delta,0\}\). If \(\delta>0\), the bound is inactive and its multiplier is zero. If \(\delta<0\), the bound is active with multiplier \(-2\delta>0\). At \(\delta=0\), the bound is active with zero multiplier. Hence arbitrarily small perturbations around \(\delta=0\) change activity, and no positive slack-or-multiplier separation margin holds uniformly in a neighborhood of that parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a weakly active bound, arbitrarily small problem perturbations can change activity, so no uniform positive primal-dual separation margin exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(\delta=0\), strict complementarity fails and the active set is not locally constant in \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Instability at a Weakly Active Bound

children.title: Basic-Solution Recovery Pipeline
children.top_down_role: Post-interior recovery of basic or active-set representations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Crossover from an optimal-face interior point to an optimal basis
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be the primal-dual solution set of a standard-form linear program with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) of full row rank. Let \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\in\Omega\) and suppose the strictly complementary partition \(\mathcal B\cup\mathcal N\) is known.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming basis recovery by primal and dual simplex-like phases; it does not cover nonlinear active-set recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A basic-solution recovery pipeline is a finite map \[\mathcal R_{mathrm{basis}}:(x^*,y^*,s^*,mathcal B,mathcal N,mathcal M_0)\mapsto(\bar x,bar y,bar s,mathcal M)\] such that \(\mathcal M\subseteq\{1,ldots,n\}\), \(|\mathcal M|=m\), \(A_{mathcal M}\) is nonsingular, \(\bar x_{mathcal M^c}=0\), \[A\bar x=b,qquad A^T\bar y+bar s=c,qquad \bar x,bar s\geq0,qquad \bar x^T\bar s=0.\] The primal phase changes the feasible optimal point and basis until no positive \(x_j\) remains outside the basis; the dual phase removes basis indices having positive dual slack. The resulting \(\bar x\) is the vertex solution associated with the optimal basis \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basic-solution recovery, also called crossover, maps an optimal point in the relative interior of an optimal face to an optimal vertex and basis. A primal phase pivots or drives positive nonbasic components to zero while maintaining primal feasibility and optimality. A dual phase removes basis indices with positive dual slack. The output basis has the row dimension, is nonsingular, and supports a primal-dual optimal basic solution.
assumptions_latex: The input triple is primal-dual optimal and its partition \(\mathcal B\cup\mathcal N\) is available.
The initial index set \(\mathcal M_0\) selects a nonsingular \(m\)-column submatrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pipeline returns an optimal basis \(\mathcal M\) and a corresponding primal-dual optimal vertex solution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The output is a crossover solution when it lies on the same optimal face as the input but has at most \(m\) potentially nonzero primal components associated with a nonsingular basis.
special_cases_latex: If the input already corresponds to an optimal basis, both phases may terminate without a pivot.
Degeneracy permits zero basic variables and may make the recovered optimal basis nonunique.
immediate_consequences_latex: The recovered basis can initialize a simplex solve for a nearby linear program.
Recovery changes the representation of the optimum without changing the optimal objective value.
boundary_notes: An approximately optimal interior iterate must first be projected or otherwise accepted; the cited basis-recovery procedure starts from an optimal solution.
Rank-deficient \(A\) requires prior row reduction or a generalized basis notion.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7, “Recovering an Optimal Basis,” including Megiddo’s two-phase method and Procedures OB-P and OB-D

children.title: Crossover Initialization
children.top_down_role: Interior solution information used to initialize a crossover procedure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Complementarity Status Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic justification for status guesses from a convergent interior primal-dual sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^k,s^k)\to(x^*,s^*)\), where \((x^*,s^*)\) is strictly complementary: for every \(j\), exactly one of \(x_j^*>0\) and \(s_j^*>0\) holds. If \(\tau_k>0\) and \(\tau_k\to0\), then, for all sufficiently large \(k\), \[x_j^*>0\Rightarrow x_j^k>\tau_k,\qquad s_j^*>0\Rightarrow s_j^k>\tau_k.\] This eventual status separation does not itself select a nonsingular basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a strictly complementary limit, shrinking thresholds eventually separate positive primal variables from positive dual slacks, but rank selection is still required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Threshold classification eventually identifies the strictly complementary primal-versus-dual status partition.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Complementarity Status Separation
Crossover Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization of linear-programming crossover from an interior primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the linear program \(\min\{c^{T}x:Ax=b,\ x
greaterthanorequalto0\}\), take an approximately feasible interior-point iterate \((x,y,z)\) with \(z=c-A^{T}y\). Choose tolerances and partition indices into likely basic candidates with relatively large \(x_j\), likely nonbasic candidates with relatively large \(z_j\), and ambiguous indices. Select a full-row-rank basis matrix \(A_B\) from the basic candidates using rank-revealing factorization, adding ambiguous columns if necessary. Compute \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\) and \(y=A_B^{-T}c_B\), then recompute nonbasic reduced costs. Output this basis state only if residual and bound checks pass; otherwise report initialization failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use an interior primal-dual iterate to select a full-rank candidate basis, reconstruct basic values and reduced costs, and verify feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The supplied iterate approximately satisfies primal and dual feasibility.
A rank-revealing factorization is available for basis selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a verified candidate basis \(B\) with reconstructed \(x_B\) and \(y\), or an explicit initialization-failure report.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits crossover initialization, but candidate partitioning, rank repair, numerical solves, and acceptance checks are implementation-dependent and unsupported. The LP display also contains a malformed nonnegativity command. A direct crossover reference must establish the selection and verification policy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic Score-Ordered Candidate Basis Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed rank-complete initialization from primal-dual interior scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), define \(w_j=x_j/(x_j+s_j)\), order indices by nonincreasing \(w_j\), and greedily retain rank-increasing columns until \(m\) columns have been selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-filter columns ordered by a primal-versus-dual score to obtain a candidate basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The greedy scan returns a nonsingular column basis in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Score-Ordered Candidate Basis Selection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Candidate Crossover State Acceptance Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank, primal, and dual checks applied after candidate-basis selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(|B|=m\), \(N=B^c\), and compute \(x_N=0\), \(A_Bx_B=b\), \(A_B^{\mathsf T}y=c_B\), and \(r_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y\). For declared tolerances \(\tau_{\rm rank},\tau_p,\tau_d\ge0\), accept only if \[\sigma_{\min}(A_B)\ge\tau_{\rm rank},\quad \|Ax-b\|_\infty\le\tau_p,\quad x_B\ge-\tau_p\mathbf1,\quad \|A_B^{\mathsf T}y-c_B\|_\infty\le\tau_d,\quad r_N\ge-\tau_d\mathbf1.\] With zero feasibility tolerances and \(\tau_{\rm rank}>0\), these conditions certify a primal-dual optimal basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a crossover candidate only after checking basis rank, reconstructed primal feasibility, basis dual equations, and nonbasic reduced costs.
assumptions_latex: The LP is in minimization standard form with nonnegative variables.
All tolerances are declared consistently with scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact acceptance certifies basis nonsingularity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementary slackness, and optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Candidate Crossover State Acceptance Test

children.title: Primal Basis Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of a primal basic representation from an interior solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic and Basic-Feasible Primal Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic target of primal basis recovery for a standard-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\). For \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\) and nonsingular \(A_B\), let \(N=B^c\) and define \[x_N=0,\qquad x_B=A_B^{-1}b.\] Then \(x\) is the basic solution associated with \(B\) and satisfies \(Ax=b\). It is a basic feasible solution of \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\) if and only if \(x_B\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular column basis defines a unique basic solution by setting nonbasic variables to zero; it is feasible exactly when all basic values are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The associated basic solution is primal feasible if and only if \(A_B^{-1}b\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Basic and Basic-Feasible Primal Representations
Primal Basis Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossover from a nearly optimal interior LP point to a primal basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard-form linear program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\), and let \(\bar x>0\) be an approximate solution. Select \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\), nonsingular \(A_B\), and preferably large components \(\bar x_i\) for \(i\in B\). Put \(N=B^c\), solve \(A_Bx_B=b\), and set \(x_N=0\). Accept the recovered point when \(x_B\ge-\tau_p\mathbf1\) and \(\|Ax-b\|\le\tau_p\); otherwise exchange an offending basic index with an index in \(N\) and repeat. The accepted vector is an approximate primal basic feasible solution, and it is exact when \(x_B\ge0\) and the linear solve is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an invertible basis suggested by the interior point, set nonbasic variables to zero, solve for basic variables, and exchange indices until primal feasibility is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x>0\) approximates a feasible LP solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_N=0\), \(A_Bx_B=b\), and acceptance gives \(x_B\ge-\tau_p\mathbf1\) with \(\|Ax-b\|\le\tau_p\).

notation.meaning: Submatrix formed from columns indexed by the basis.

source_refs.locator: 8.5 Stable and Large-scale Linear Programming p. 168

source_witnesses.locator: 8.5 Stable and Large-scale Linear Programming p. 168

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The basis-selection and exchange instructions are heuristic rather than a complete algorithm: “preferably large” does not define a selection rule, and exchanging an offending index does not ensure nonsingularity, progress, or a valid failure exit. The cited locator must be inspected to determine which crossover procedure it actually supports.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Phase-I Primal Basis Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic linear-programming feasibility phase proposed as crossover recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Solve \[\min_{x,a^+,a^-}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}(a^++a^-)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+a^+-a^-=b,\quad x,a^+,a^-\ge0\] by a lexicographic simplex method and remove zero artificial basic variables by rank-preserving pivots when the optimum is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use a generic lexicographic Phase-I problem to find a primal feasible basis or certify infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: A fixed anti-cycling rule is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The auxiliary problem returns a primal feasible basis when its optimum is zero, or certifies infeasibility when its optimum is positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Phase-I Primal Basis Recovery

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Largest-Component Selection Can Be Rank Deficient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of choosing basic columns solely from the largest interior primal components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad \bar x=(M,M,1)^{\mathsf T}>0,\qquad b=A\bar x=(2M,1)^{\mathsf T},\] where \(M>1\). The two largest components correspond to identical columns and do not form a basis. Nevertheless \(B=\{1,3\}\) is nonsingular and yields the feasible basic solution \((2M,0,1)^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest variables at an interior point can correspond to dependent columns even when a feasible nonsingular basis exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Magnitude ranking alone does not guarantee basis nonsingularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Largest-Component Selection Can Be Rank Deficient

children.title: Dual Basis Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of dual basis information and associated status structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Basis Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of LP multipliers and reduced costs from a candidate primal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), suppose \(B\) is a primal basis with nonsingular \(A_B\), and write \(N=B^c\). Solve \(A_B^{\mathsf T}y=c_B\), set \(s_B=0\), and compute \(s_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y\). Accept \((y,s)\) as the dual basis recovery when \(s_N\ge-\tau_d\mathbf1\) and \(\|A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\|\le\tau_d\). If a component of \(s_N\) violates the tolerance, use an offending nonbasic index as an entering candidate and update the basis. With exact arithmetic and \(s_N\ge0\), the recovered pair is dual feasible; together with a primal feasible basic vector it satisfies complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the transposed basis system for multipliers, derive nonbasic reduced costs, and update the basis until reduced-cost dual feasibility is achieved.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) defines a primal basic vector with \(x_N=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(s_B=0\), and exact acceptance with \(s_N\ge0\) yields dual feasibility and complementary slackness.

children.title: Degenerate Crossover
children.top_down_role: Crossover behavior in the presence of degeneracy or multiple valid bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Crossover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anti-cycling basis updates during crossover when zero basic variables or zero reduced costs permit degenerate pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a primal feasible basic vector for a linear program, let \(B\) be its nonsingular basis, and let \((y,s)\) be the associated dual recovery. Define \(D_p=\{i\in B:x_i\le\tau_p\}\) and \(D_d=\{j\notin B:|s_j|\le\tau_d\}\). If dual feasibility is violated, select an eligible entering index according to a fixed lexicographic pivot rule and apply the corresponding lexicographic minimum-ratio test to select the leaving index. Permit a zero step when the ratio test requires it, and pivot only when the resulting basis matrix is nonsingular. Stop when the primal and dual acceptance tests hold; report failure if no eligible pivot exists or numerical rank tests reject every eligible update. When all pivot comparisons are exact and the same lexicographic rule is applied throughout, the generated basis sequence does not cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: During degenerate crossover, use one fixed lexicographic entering and minimum-ratio rule, allow required zero steps, reject singular updates, and report failure if no eligible update remains. In exact arithmetic, the lexicographic rule prevents cycling.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has full row rank and \(B\) is a nonsingular basis.
\(x\) is primal feasible and \((y,s)\) is recovered consistently from \(B\).
The noncycling assertion applies to exact pivot comparisons and a consistently implemented lexicographic rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure either obtains a primal-dual acceptable basis or reports that no numerically admissible update was found; in exact arithmetic, consistent lexicographic pivoting precludes cycling.

notation.meaning: Indices of nearly zero basic variables.
Indices of nearly zero nonbasic reduced costs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal and Dual Basis Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-level degeneracy notions relevant to crossover pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a standard-form LP basis \(B\), with \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), \(N=B^c\), and \(s_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\), the basis is primal degenerate if \(x_i=0\) for some \(i\in B\), and dual degenerate if \(s_j=0\) for some \(j\in N\). Primal degeneracy permits zero-length primal pivots; dual degeneracy permits alternative zero-reduced-cost basis changes. Either can make the basis representation nonunique, even when the represented primal or dual solution is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero basic variables define primal degeneracy and zero nonbasic reduced costs define dual degeneracy; either can create zero-progress or nonunique basis changes.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) and \(N\) are the basic and nonbasic index sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zero basic variables and zero nonbasic reduced costs are the algebraic sources of primal and dual basis degeneracy, respectively.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal and Dual Basis Degeneracy

children.title: Crossover Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Numerical or structural conditions that prevent reliable basis recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Crossover Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural and numerical conditions under which an interior LP point cannot be reliably converted to an acceptable basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), crossover cannot certify a basic optimal solution from the tested candidates if every proposed \(m\)-column submatrix is singular or numerically rank deficient, or if no proposed nonsingular basis passes both the primal and dual acceptance tests. For a nonsingular candidate \(A_B\), the solution maps \(b\mapsto A_B^{-1}b\) and \(c_B\mapsto A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\) have Euclidean operator norm \(1/\sigma_{\min}(A_B)\). Consequently, worst-case perturbations in \(b\) or \(c_B\) can be amplified by that factor in the recovered \(x_B\) or \(y\). Degeneracy can make the acceptable basis nonunique and can produce zero-length pivots unless an anti-cycling rule is used. Failure of basis recovery does not, by itself, invalidate the approximate interior primal-dual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossover cannot certify a basis when all tested bases are singular or none passes the primal and dual tests. A small minimum singular value causes large worst-case sensitivity, while degeneracy can cause nonunique bases and zero-length pivots. Such crossover failure does not itself invalidate the interior solution.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has target basis size \(m\).
Candidate basic variables and multipliers are recovered by solving systems with \(A_B\) and \(A_B^{\mathsf T}\).
Numerical rank and primal-dual acceptance tolerances are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\sigma_{\min}(A_B)\) is small, the worst-case absolute sensitivity of basis recovery is large; if no acceptable nonsingular \(B\) is found, crossover cannot certify a basic solution.

notation.meaning: Smallest singular value of the candidate basis matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Polishing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded local primal-dual Newton refinement after an interior-point method has nearly identified the active constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le0\), where \(f\), \(h\), and \(g\) are twice continuously differentiable. From an approximate KKT triple \((x,\lambda,
u)\), select \(\mathcal A=\{i:g_i(x)\ge-	au_A\}\), set \(
u_i=0\) for \(i
otin\mathcal A\), and apply damped Newton or least-squares corrections to \(F_{\mathcal A}(x,\lambda,
u_{\mathcal A})=(

u^{\mathsf T}g\). Accept a trial correction only if it preserves required bounds, satisfies the multiplier sign safeguard \(
u_{\mathcal A}\ge0\), and decreases the selected residual norm or merit function; otherwise retain the previous iterate. Stop when primal feasibility, stationarity, complementarity, and multiplier sign residuals meet their tolerances. If \(\mathcal A\) equals the active set at a nearby KKT point, the corresponding KKT Jacobian is nonsingular, and full Newton steps are eventually accepted, sufficiently close iterates have the usual locally fast Newton convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Freeze a plausible active set and apply safeguarded Newton corrections to its KKT equations. Accept only corrections that improve the selected residual or merit measure and preserve multiplier signs; otherwise keep the previous point. Accepted corrections satisfy the stated residual or merit decrease and multiplier-sign safeguards.
The local fast-convergence assertion assumes correct active-set identification, a nonsingular active-set KKT Jacobian, and eventual full-step acceptance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polishing returns either an accepted point with a smaller selected residual or merit value, or the retained previous point; under the stated local assumptions, the Newton refinement is locally fast.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-active-set primal-dual solution polishing
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F(w)=0\) denote the KKT equations for a finite-dimensional optimization problem, let \(\widetilde w\) be an accepted approximate primal-dual solution, and let \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) be a fixed estimate of its active constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic postprocessing with a fixed active set and local KKT equations; global reoptimization is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solution-polishing map is a partial map \[\mathcal P_{widehat{\mathcal A}}:\widetilde w\mapsto w^+\] defined by solving the reduced KKT system in which constraints indexed by \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) are imposed as equalities, inactive inequality multipliers are set to zero, and primal variables fixed by the active structure are held at their bounds. The candidate \(w^+\) is accepted only if \[\|F(w^+)\|_{mathrm{sc}}leq\|F(\widetilde w)\|_{mathrm{sc}},\] all original-domain inequalities and multiplier sign conditions meet their polishing tolerances, and the objective does not violate the declared acceptance rule. Otherwise the map returns \(\widetilde w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solution polishing is a guarded postsolve map. It freezes an estimated active structure, solves the resulting reduced KKT equations to improve local accuracy, and accepts the polished point only when its scaled KKT residual is no worse and its feasibility, multiplier signs, and objective satisfy explicit tolerances. A failed polish leaves the original accepted point unchanged.
assumptions_latex: The estimated active set \(\widehat{\mathcal A}\) is fixed during one polishing attempt.
The reduced KKT system and all recovery substitutions are well defined.
Acceptance metrics are evaluated in the original model after any presolve recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned point is either an accepted reduced-KKT correction satisfying every polishing guard or the unchanged input \(\widetilde w\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a linear or quadratic model with a fixed active set, polishing is an equality-constrained primal-dual solve followed by sign and residual checks.
special_cases_latex: One-step Newton polishing solves the reduced KKT linearization once.
Iterative polishing repeats reduced solves while the active set remains fixed and acceptance metrics improve.
immediate_consequences_latex: The fallback rule makes polishing nondegrading with respect to the declared residual metric.
Polishing can improve feasibility and complementarity without rerunning the barrier-parameter sequence.
boundary_notes: A wrong active-set estimate may make the reduced system inconsistent or produce invalid multiplier signs.
No inspected source in the supplied locator set provided this complete guarded-map definition.

notation.meaning: estimated active set used for polishing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure-preserving interface from a model class to a barrier system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathfrak M\) be a class of optimization models, and let \(M\in\mathfrak M\) have primal variables, dual variables, cone or inequality domain, and model data \(d_M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-dimensional interface contract; detailed convergence theory remains attached to each model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A model-specific interior-point interface is a tuple \[\mathcal I_M=(E_M,Phi_M,J_M,rho_M)\] where \(E_M\) encodes the native model as a primal-dual residual map \(\Phi_M(w;mu)=0\) for \(\mu>0\), \(J_M(w;mu)=D_w\Phi_M(w;mu)\) is the Newton operator or an explicitly declared generalized derivative, and \(\rho_M\) maps solver variables and certificates back to native model objects. The interface is exact when \(\Phi_M(w;0)=0\), together with the stated domain conditions, is equivalent to the native KKT or complementarity system, and when every accepted solver output recovers through \(\rho_M\) without changing its represented primal-dual status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model-specific interior-point interface packages four objects: an encoding of the native model, a barrier residual map, its Newton operator, and a recovery map. Exactness requires the zero-barrier residual system to represent the native optimality or complementarity conditions and requires returned solver variables and certificates to recover correctly into the native model. The interface exposes common interior-point mechanics while leaving model-specific theory in its own model class.
assumptions_latex: The native model supplies a well-defined primal-dual or complementarity system.
For every \(\mu>0\) in the interface domain, \(\Phi_M\) and the declared Newton operator are evaluable.
The recovery map \(\rho_M\) is defined on every output status exposed by the interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact interface preserves the correspondence between native model solutions or certificates and the solver’s zero-barrier residual objects.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The interface may be viewed as a commutative representation in which native solutions encoded by \(E_M\) and then recovered by \(\rho_M\) retain their native feasibility and objective data.
special_cases_latex: Linear programming uses affine primal and dual residuals with componentwise complementarity.
Convex quadratic programming adds the linear term \(Gx\) to the dual residual while retaining linear constraints.
immediate_consequences_latex: Common stopping and linear-algebra components can operate on \(\Phi_M\) and \(J_M\).
Model-specific cones, complementarity products, and recovery rules remain explicit rather than being hidden by a generic label.
boundary_notes: This abstraction does not itself provide constraint qualifications, complexity bounds, or convergence guarantees.
No inspected source defined this four-component interface as a named canonical object.

notation.meaning: Newton operator for the residual map

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unified primal-dual barrier interface for linear and convex quadratic programs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). The model is \(\min \tfrac12x^TGx+c^Tx\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(x\geq0\). Linear programming is the case \(G=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex quadratic and linear programs in standard equality-plus-nonnegativity form; indefinite quadratic programs are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear-quadratic program interior-point interface family is the parameterized residual system \[\Phi_G(x,y,s;mu)=\begin{bmatrix}Ax-b\\Gx+c-A^Ty-s\\Xs\mathbf1-mu\mathbf1\end{bmatrix}=0,qquad x>0,s>0,mu>0,\] where \(X=operatorname{diag}(x)\). A Newton direction \((\Delta x,Delta y,Delta s)\) is defined by linearizing \(\Phi_G\). The interface is linear-programming specialized when \(G=0\) and convex-quadratic specialized when \(G\succeq0\). At \(\mu=0\), nonnegativity and \(Xs\mathbf1=0\) give the KKT system, which is sufficient for global optimality in the convex-quadratic regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface family represents both linear and convex quadratic programs with the same primal feasibility, dual stationarity, and perturbed complementarity residuals. The quadratic Hessian parameter is positive semidefinite; setting it to zero gives linear programming. Newton linearization of this residual system supplies the interior-point search direction. At zero barrier, the system becomes the convex KKT conditions.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual variables satisfy \(x>0\) and \(s>0\) while \(\mu>0\).
The equality and sign conventions are those displayed in \(\Phi_G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The same residual interface covers LP by \(G=0\) and convex QP by \(G\succeq0\), with the zero-barrier system equal to their primal-dual KKT conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The complementarity block may be written componentwise as \(x_is_i=mu\) for \(i=1,ldots,n\).
special_cases_latex: \(G=0\) yields the standard-form linear-programming primal-dual equations.
\(G\succ0\) makes the primal objective strictly convex, though the optimizer can still be constrained-degenerate.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Newton coefficient structure is constant in sparsity when \(A\) and \(G\) are fixed.
Predictor-corrector constructions for LP extend by retaining \(G\) in the stationarity linearization.
boundary_notes: For indefinite \(G\), KKT conditions are not sufficient for global optimality and this interface’s convex interpretation fails.
General bounds and inequalities require slacks or an alternative native formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-scaling and projective-scaling geometries for linear programming
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider a linear program over the positive orthant with a strictly positive feasible point \(x\). Let \(X=operatorname{diag}(x)\). For projective scaling, assume a normalized representation admitting a projective map that sends the current point to a designated center.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical primal LP interior geometry; modern primal-dual path-following is not included in the pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The classical scaling geometry pair consists of: (i) affine scaling, which applies the invertible diagonal change of variables \(x=Xe+Xu\), equivalently \(u=X^{-1}(x-Xe)\), so that the current positive point maps to the center \(u=0\) and the nonnegativity boundary is measured in coordinates scaled by \(X\); and (ii) projective scaling, which applies a fractional-linear map \[T(z)=frac{Pz+p}{q^Tz+alpha}\] on a domain where \(q^Tz+alpha>0\), chosen to map the current feasible point to a normalized center before taking a feasible descent step in transformed coordinates. The inverse map returns the step to the original polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical pair contains affine scaling and projective scaling. Affine scaling uses the diagonal matrix of the current positive point to normalize distances to the nonnegativity boundary. Projective scaling uses a fractional-linear transformation to send the current feasible point to a normalized center, computes a feasible descent step there, and maps it back. Both are primal geometric normalizations, but only the projective member changes coordinates by a fractional-linear map.
assumptions_latex: The current primal point is strictly positive and feasible.
The affine scaling matrix \(X\) is therefore nonsingular.
The denominator of the projective map is positive on every transformed point used by the method, and the map is invertible on that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair is distinguished by the coordinate action: diagonal affine normalization for affine scaling and fractional-linear normalization for projective scaling.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The affine-scaled local metric has norm \(\|X^{-1}d\|_2\), so equal scaled lengths represent coordinatewise relative displacements.
special_cases_latex: Dikin’s primal affine-scaling direction uses the current diagonal scaling \(X\).
Karmarkar’s method is the canonical projective-scaling member.

children.title: Affine-Scaling Methods
children.top_down_role: Classical interior methods based on affine-scaled search geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Scaling Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal affine-scaling iteration for a strictly feasible standard-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), start from \(x^0>0\) satisfying \(Ax^0=b\). At iteration \(k\), set \(D_k=\operatorname{Diag}(x^k)\), solve \((AD_k^2A^{\mathsf T})y^k=AD_k^2c\), and define \(d^k=-D_k^2(c-A^{\mathsf T}y^k)\). If \(d^k=0\), stop. If \(d^k\ge0\) and \(d^k\ne0\), then \(x^k+t d^k\) is feasible for every \(t\ge0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d^k<0\), so report an unbounded feasible descent ray. Otherwise define \(\theta_k=\min_{i:d_i^k<0}(-x_i^k/d_i^k)\), choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\), and set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_k\theta_kd^k\). Every such finite update satisfies \(Ax^{k+1}=b\), \(x^{k+1}>0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d^k\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the cost in the current diagonal scaling and take a fraction of the step to the boundary. If the nonzero direction has no negative component, report the resulting unbounded feasible descent ray.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
A strictly feasible point \(x^0>0\) satisfying \(Ax^0=b\) is available.
The projected normal equations are solved exactly for the stated invariance and descent conclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite fraction-to-boundary update preserves \(Ax=b\) and \(x>0\); a nonzero direction \(d^k\ge0\) certifies an unbounded feasible descent ray.

notation.meaning: Diagonal scaling formed from the current primal variables.

children.title: Projective-Scaling Methods
children.top_down_role: Classical interior methods based on projective transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Projective-Scaling Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Karmarkar-type projective scaling on a normalized homogeneous linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(Ax=0\), \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}x=1\), and \(x>0\). Given \(x^k>0\), set \(D_k=\operatorname{Diag}(x^k)\) and let \(p^k\) be the Euclidean projection of \(D_kc\) onto \(\ker(AD_k)\cap\ker(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T})\). If \(p^k=0\), stop. Otherwise choose \(0<\alpha_k<1\), form \(z^k=\mathbf1-\alpha_kp^k/\|p^k\|_2\), and map back by \(x^{k+1}=D_kz^k/(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}D_kz^k)\). Whenever \(z^k>0\), the new iterate is positive and normalized; feasibility follows from \(AD_kz^k=0\). The projective normalization distinguishes this update from affine scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the scaled cost in normalized coordinates, step inside the transformed simplex, and map back through a fractional projective transformation.
assumptions_latex: The LP has the normalized homogeneous form \(Ax=0\), \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}x=1\), and \(x>0\).
A strictly positive normalized iterate is available.
The step parameter is chosen so that \(z^k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapped iterate satisfies \(Ax^{k+1}=0\), \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}x^{k+1}=1\), and \(x^{k+1}>0\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal projective scaling at the current iterate.

children.title: Scaling-Geometry Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between affine-scaled and projective geometries.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Geometry Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of affine ellipsoidal scaling with projectively normalized simplex geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x>0\) and \(D=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\). Affine scaling represents nearby points as \(x^+=x+Du\), so positivity is controlled by \(\mathbf1+u>0\), and feasible transformed directions satisfy \(ADu=0\). Projective scaling instead represents a normalized point by \(x^+=D(\mathbf1+u)/(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}D(\mathbf1+u))\), with \(\mathbf1+u>0\); its tangent directions additionally remove the normalization component. The two maps agree to first order up to a radial correction: for small \(u\), \(x^+=x+Du-x\,\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Du+O(\|u\|_2^2)\). Thus affine scaling uses a local diagonal metric, whereas projective scaling identifies positive rays before restoring normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine scaling uses a local diagonal coordinate map; projective scaling additionally identifies positive rays and renormalizes, differing by a first-order radial correction.
assumptions_latex: The transformed displacement \(u\) is sufficiently small and satisfies \(\mathbf1+u>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projective and affine maps have the stated first-order relation, but only the projective map explicitly quotients and renormalizes positive rays.

children.title: Classical Scaling Limitations
children.top_down_role: Robustness and applicability boundaries of classical scaling approaches.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Scaling Limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-feasibility and conditioning boundaries of classical affine and projective scaling schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Classical diagonal scaling requires a strictly positive feasible iterate. If the feasible set lies in a proper face of the nonnegative orthant, no such initialization exists. For example, \(x_1=0\), \(x_1+x_2=1\), and \(x\ge0\) has the unique feasible point \((0,1)\), so \(D=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) is singular and neither an interior affine scaling nor the usual positive projective transformation is defined. Even with strict feasibility, components approaching zero make \(D\) increasingly anisotropic and can render scaled normal equations poorly conditioned. Classical primal scaling alone also supplies neither a primal-dual complementarity neighborhood nor an infeasibility certificate without additional embeddings or dual constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical scaling fails without a strictly positive feasible point and can become ill-conditioned near a face; primal scaling alone does not certify infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Classical scaling uses \(D=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) at a feasible point.
No homogeneous self-dual embedding or separate infeasibility mechanism is added.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every feasible point has a zero component, strict-interior scaling cannot initialize; near such faces, diagonal scaling may be severely ill-conditioned.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Programming Primal–Dual Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasible-start primal-dual Newton path following for standard-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min c^{\mathsf T}x\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(x\ge0\), with dual equations \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), initialize \(x^0>0\) and \(s^0>0\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(\sigma_k\in[0,1]\), set \(\mu_k=(x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k/n\), and solve the Newton system for \((\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta s)\) obtained from \(A(x+\Delta x)=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}(y+\Delta y)+(s+\Delta s)=c\), and \((X+\Delta X)(s+\Delta s)\approx\sigma_k\mu_k\mathbf1\). Choose primal and dual fraction-to-boundary step lengths preserving positivity, update the iterates, and stop when primal residual, dual residual, and \(x^{\mathsf T}s\) meet prescribed tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton linearize primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and perturbed complementarity, then use positivity-preserving steps until residuals and the duality gap are small.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
The initial primal and dual slack vectors satisfy \(x^0>0\) and \(s^0>0\).
Newton systems are solved to the required accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination certifies small primal residual, dual residual, and complementarity gap \(x^{\mathsf T}s\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual path-following method for standard-form linear programming
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min c^Tx\) subject to \(Ax=b\), \(x\geq0\), and its dual \(\max b^Ty\) subject to \(A^Ty+s=c\), \(s\geq0\). Let \(X=operatorname{diag}(x)\) and \(e\) be the all-ones vector.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic primal-dual path-following for linear programming, allowing feasible or infeasible residual equations but requiring positive primal and dual slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear-programming primal-dual interior method generates iterates \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\) with \(x^k>0\) and \(s^k>0\) by choosing \(\mu_k>0\), a centering parameter \(\sigma_k\in[0,1]\), and a Newton direction satisfying \[\begin{bmatrix}0&A^T&I\\A&0&0\\S^k&0&X^k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta y^k\\\Delta x^k\\\Delta s^k\end{bmatrix}=-begin{bmatrix}A^Ty^k+s^k-c\\Ax^k-b\\X^kS^ke-sigma_k\mu_ke\end{bmatrix}.\] It then selects primal and dual step lengths preserving \(x^{k+1}>0\) and \(s^{k+1}>0\), updates the variables, and drives feasibility residuals and \(\mu_k=(x^k)^Ts^k/n\) toward zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-programming primal-dual interior method applies Newton’s method to primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and perturbed complementarity simultaneously. Every iterate keeps the primal variables and dual slacks strictly positive. Centering controls the target complementarity, step lengths preserve positivity, and the method seeks to reduce both infeasibility residuals and average complementarity to zero.

For feasible iterates, the duality gap equals \((x^k)^Ts^k=n\mu_k\).

\(\sigma_k=1\) targets a centering direction at the current complementarity level.
Infeasible-start methods retain the same positivity and complementarity blocks while including nonzero primal and dual residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratic-Program Interior Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual interior iteration for a convex quadratic program with equality and bound constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(x\ge0\), where \(Q\succeq0\). Initialize \(x^0>0\) and \(s^0>0\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(\mu_k>0\) and apply Newton's method to \(Qx+c-A^{\mathsf T}y-s=0\), \(Ax=b\), and \(Xs=\mu_k\mathbf1\). Use primal and dual fraction-to-boundary step lengths, reduce \(\mu_k\), and stop when stationarity, feasibility, and complementarity residuals meet their tolerances. Because \(Q\succeq0\), any feasible limit satisfying these KKT conditions is a global minimizer; it is unique when the objective is strictly convex on \(\ker(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply positivity-preserving Newton steps to the convex QP KKT equations and reduce complementarity; any feasible KKT limit is globally optimal.
assumptions_latex: The equality constraints are consistent and the QP has a finite solution.
Interior primal and dual slack iterates are maintained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible KKT limit is globally optimal, and it is unique if \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd>0\) for every nonzero \(d\in\ker(A)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex quadratic-program primal–dual interior interface
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive semidefinite, \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Consider \(\min\{\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), with multiplier \(y\in\mathbb R^m\), dual slack \(s\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex quadratic programs in equality-plus-nonnegativity form; general linear inequalities can be converted to this form with slacks and split variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex quadratic-program primal–dual interior method is a method whose admissible states satisfy \(x>0\) and \(s>0\), and whose central target for each \(\mu>0\) is the perturbed KKT system \[Ax=b,\qquad A^Ty+s-Qx=c,\qquad Xs=\mu\mathbf1.\] An inexact interior state may have nonzero primal, dual, and complementarity residuals, but it remains in \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R_{++}^n\) and computes Newton-type corrections for those three equations while driving \(\mu=x^Ts/n\) and the residuals toward zero. Positive semidefiniteness of \(Q\) is part of the definition of this convex interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quadratic program with a positive-semidefinite Hessian, a primal–dual interior method maintains positive primal variables and positive dual slacks. Its central path consists of triples satisfying primal feasibility, dual stationarity, and componentwise perturbed complementarity, with every product of a primal component and its dual slack equal to the positive parameter mu. Iterations approximately solve these equations and reduce mu and any feasibility residuals. The positive-semidefinite Hessian distinguishes this interface from an indefinite quadratic-program interior method and makes the KKT target a convex-program optimality system rather than merely a stationarity system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C=\bigcup_{\mu>0}\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^Ty+s-Qx=c,\ Xs=\mu\mathbf1,\ x>0,\ s>0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Eliminating \(s=\mu X^{-1}\mathbf1\) gives the equality-constrained logarithmic-barrier stationarity system \[Ax=b,\qquad Qx+c-A^Ty-\mu X^{-1}\mathbf1=0,\qquad x>0.\]
For a primal–dual feasible state, the duality gap is \(x^Ts=n\mu\) on the central path.
special_cases_latex: When \(Q=0\), the interface reduces to the standard-form linear-program primal–dual central path.
Bound constraints and general linear inequalities are represented by introducing nonnegative slack variables before applying the definition.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every central-path point is strictly primal and dual feasible.
Any accumulation point for which the feasibility residuals and \(\mu\) vanish satisfies the unperturbed KKT complementarity equation \(Xs=0\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not cover an indefinite Hessian \(Q\), for which KKT points need not be global minimizers.
Existence of a central-path point for every \(\mu>0\) requires additional feasibility and regularity conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Quadratic-Program Interior Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized barrier method for nonconvex quadratic programs, targeting first- or second-order stationarity rather than global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(x\ge0\), with symmetric but indefinite \(Q\). For \(\mu_k>0\), form the barrier objective \(\phi_{bc_k}(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x-bc_k\sum_i\log x_i\). From \(x^k>0\), compute a feasible regularized Newton or trust-region step for \(\phi_{bc_k}\), choosing regularization so the reduced model has acceptable curvature, and use a fraction-to-boundary line search. Reduce \(\mu_k\) only after the barrier stationarity residual is small. Accumulation points may satisfy KKT conditions under standard constraint qualifications, but indefiniteness prevents KKT conditions from certifying global optimality; second-order acceptance additionally requires nonnegative Lagrangian curvature on the critical cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularize or restrict barrier Newton steps to handle negative curvature; convergence targets KKT or second-order stationary points, not certified global optima.
assumptions_latex: The iterates remain strictly positive and satisfy or approach \(Ax=b\).
A line-search or trust-region globalization accepts only adequate model progress.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method targets KKT points; global optimality is not implied, and second-order stationarity requires nonnegative reduced curvature on the critical cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier and primal–dual interface for a proper cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(K\subset E\) be a proper cone with dual \(K^*\), and let \(A:E\to\mathbb R^m\). The primal–dual conic pair is \(\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex cone programs over proper symmetric or nonsymmetric cones possessing an explicitly evaluable interior barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conic interior-point interface consists of the conic pair, strict states \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) and \(s\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), and a barrier coupling. If \(F:\operatorname{int}K\to\mathbb R\) is a logarithmically homogeneous barrier, its primal central relation is \[Ax=b,\qquad A^*y+s=c,\qquad s=-\mu\nabla F(x),\qquad \mu>0.\] An interior method computes approximate Newton corrections to primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and this coupling while preserving membership in the two interiors. For a symmetric cone, the coupling can be expressed by a Jordan-algebra complementarity equation; for a nonsymmetric cone, the gradient or primal–dual barrier relation is the primary interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic interior-point interface describes how a cone program, its dual cone program, and a barrier are presented to an interior solver. The state contains a primal point in the interior of the cone, a dual slack in the interior of the dual cone, and an equality multiplier. Central points satisfy both affine feasibility systems and couple the primal point to the dual slack through the gradient of a logarithmically homogeneous barrier. Symmetric cones admit additional scaling and Jordan-product representations, whereas nonsymmetric cones generally retain the barrier-gradient representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_F=\bigcup_{\mu>0}\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^*y+s=c,\ x\in\operatorname{int}K,\ s\in\operatorname{int}K^*,\ s=-\mu\nabla F(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The primal central point minimizes \(\langle c,x\rangle+\mu F(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\), when that barrier problem has a minimizer.
For a logarithmically homogeneous barrier of parameter \(\nu\), the central relation gives \(\langle x,s\rangle=\nu\mu\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(F(x)=-\sum_i\log x_i\), the coupling becomes \(x_is_i=\mu\) for every component.
Positive-semidefinite and Lorentz cones give semidefinite and second-order-cone interfaces.
immediate_consequences_latex: The affine primal–dual gap equals \(\langle x,s\rangle\) at feasible states.
The interface is undefined in ambient coordinates when the affine feasible set does not meet \(\operatorname{int}K\).
boundary_notes: A cone without a known tractable barrier can be written as a cone program but does not automatically provide a computational interior-point interface.
The inspected generalized-inequality source supports conic primal–dual form and strict feasibility, but not the full barrier-gradient interface stated here.

notation.meaning: Dual cone consisting of s with nonnegative inner product against every x in K.
Logarithmically homogeneous barrier on the cone interior.

children.title: Second-Order Cone Interior Methods
