knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Cone Interior Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual path following for linear optimization over products of Lorentz cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given strictly feasible iterates \(x,s\in\operatorname{int}K\), where \(K\) is a product of Lorentz cones, choose \(\mu=\sigma\langle x,s\rangle/r\) with \(0<\sigma<1\). Compute a Newton direction for \[Ax=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\qquad x\circ s=\mu e,\] using the Lorentz-cone Jordan product \(\circ\), unit \(e\), and total rank \(r\). Select the largest fraction-to-boundary step retaining \(x+\alpha\Delta x\in\operatorname{int}K\) and \(s+\alpha\Delta s\in\operatorname{int}K\), update the iterates, and stop when primal residual, dual residual, and \(\langle x,s\rangle\) meet their tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton steps enforce primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and Jordan complementarity while fraction-to-boundary steps keep second-order-cone variables strictly interior.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite product of Lorentz cones.
A strictly feasible primal–dual starting point is available.
The Newton systems are solved to the prescribed accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) and \(s\) remain strictly interior, while the residuals and complementarity gap are driven toward zero.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and second-order-cone scope fit the terminal container, and the displayed mathematics is syntactically delimited. However, no source is cited for the Jordan-algebra central-path system, scaling convention, step rule, or the claim that residuals and complementarity are driven to zero.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–dual interior method on a product of Lorentz cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(n_i\geq2\), let \(\mathcal L_{n_i}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n_i-1}:t\geq\|u\|_2\}\), and let \(K=\prod_{i=1}^q\mathcal L_{n_i}\). Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional second-order cone programs over a product of self-dual Lorentz cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A second-order-cone interior method is a conic primal–dual method whose states satisfy \(x_i=(t_i,u_i)\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal L_{n_i}\) and \(s_i\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal L_{n_i}\), meaning \(t_i>\|u_i\|_2\) in every block. With the Lorentz Jordan product \[(t,u)\circ(\tau,v)=(t\tau+u^Tv,\ tv+\tau u),\] its central target is \[Ax=b,\qquad A^Ty+s=c,\qquad x\circ s=\mu e,\qquad \mu>0,\] where the product is blockwise and \(e=((1,0),\ldots,(1,0))\). Newton-type corrections are restricted by a step length that keeps every updated primal and dual block in the strict Lorentz-cone interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order-cone interior method applies a primal–dual central-path construction to a product of Lorentz cones. Each primal and dual block has a scalar component strictly larger than the Euclidean norm of its vector component. Primal and dual affine equations are coupled through blockwise Jordan complementarity. Interior steps linearize these equations and choose a fraction-to-the-boundary step so that all blocks remain strictly inside their cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C=\bigcup_{\mu>0}\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^Ty+s=c,\ x,s\in\operatorname{int}K,\ x\circ s=\mu e\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(z=(t,u)\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal L_n\), the standard logarithmic barrier is \(-\log(t^2-\|u\|_2^2)\); its gradient coupling gives the same cone-interior geometry.
The block complementarity measure is commonly normalized as \(\mu=x^Ts/q\), where \(q\) is the number of Lorentz blocks.
special_cases_latex: A one-dimensional Lorentz block is the nonnegative ray and recovers scalar complementarity.
Norm constraints \(\|Bz+d\|_2\leq a^Tz+\beta\) are affine inverse images of Lorentz-cone membership.
immediate_consequences_latex: Primal–dual feasibility gives duality gap \(c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts\).
Strict cone membership permits a positive step in every finite search direction.
boundary_notes: Rotated second-order cones are covered after a linear isomorphism to a Lorentz cone.
The definition does not cover arbitrary nonsymmetric cones.

notation.meaning: Jordan identity of the product cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Interior Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual path following for linear semidefinite optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For strictly positive-definite \(X,S\in\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\), choose \(\mu=\sigma\operatorname{tr}(XS)/n\) with \(0<\sigma<1\). Compute a symmetrized Newton direction for \[\mathcal A(X)=b,\qquad \mathcal A^*(y)+S=C,\qquad H(XS)=\mu I,\] where \(H\) is a fixed admissible symmetrization. Choose a fraction-to-boundary step preserving \(X+\alpha\Delta X\succ0\) and \(S+\alpha\Delta S\succ0\), update the variables, and terminate when primal and dual residuals and the normalized gap \(\operatorname{tr}(XS)/n\) satisfy their tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite interior method Newton-linearizes feasibility and symmetrized matrix complementarity, with step lengths chosen to preserve positive definiteness.
assumptions_latex: Strictly feasible primal and dual matrices are available.
The chosen symmetrization yields a nonsingular Newton system locally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates remain positive definite and target primal–dual feasibility with \(\operatorname{tr}(XS)\to0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits semidefinite interior methods, but no source supports the formula or conclusion. In particular, a fixed 'admissible symmetrization' H is not defined precisely enough to determine whether H(XS)=mu I and its Newton linearization represent AHO, HKM, NT, or another valid direction.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–dual interior method on the positive-semidefinite cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb S^n\) carry the trace inner product \(U\bullet V=\operatorname{tr}(UV)\). Let \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\), with adjoint \(\mathcal A^*\). The primal SDP is \(\min\{C\bullet X:\mathcal A(X)=b,\ X\succeq0\}\), and the dual is \(\max\{b^Ty:\mathcal A^*(y)+Z=C,\ Z\succeq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real semidefinite programs with symmetric matrix variables and positive-definite primal–dual interior iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A semidefinite interior method is a primal–dual method whose admissible iterates satisfy \(X\succ0\) and \(Z\succ0\) and which computes Newton-type corrections for \[\mathcal A(X)=b,\qquad \mathcal A^*(y)+Z=C,\qquad \mathcal H_P(XZ)=\mu I,\] where \(P\) is nonsingular and \(\mathcal H_P(M)=\tfrac12(PMP^{-1}+(PMP^{-1})^T)\). On the exact central path the equivalent unsymmetrized relation is \(XZ=\mu I\). A step length is selected so that the updated primal and dual slack matrices remain positive definite while feasibility residuals and \(\mu=(X\bullet Z)/n\) decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite interior method maintains positive-definite primal and dual slack matrices for a semidefinite program. It follows a matrix-valued perturbed KKT system consisting of primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and matrix complementarity. Because the product of two symmetric matrices need not be symmetric, implementations commonly apply a parameterized symmetrization before linearizing complementarity. Exact central points satisfy the simpler product equation XZ equals mu times the identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C=\bigcup_{\mu>0}\{(X,y,Z):\mathcal A(X)=b,\ \mathcal A^*(y)+Z=C,\ X\succ0,\ Z\succ0,\ XZ=\mu I\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The primal barrier subproblem uses \(-\mu\log\det X\) on \(X\succ0\).
At a feasible state the duality gap is \(C\bullet X-b^Ty=X\bullet Z=n\mu\) on the central path.
special_cases_latex: Diagonal \(X\) and \(Z\) reduce matrix complementarity to componentwise nonnegative-orthant complementarity.
The choice \(P=I\) yields the unscaled arithmetic symmetrization used by the AHO direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive definiteness makes \(\log\det X\), matrix inverses, and sufficiently short interior steps well defined.
A finite limit with \(\mu\to0\) and vanishing affine residuals satisfies SDP KKT complementarity.
boundary_notes: If the feasible affine space meets the semidefinite cone only on a proper face, an ambient positive-definite primal point does not exist.
Different symmetrizations define different search directions away from the central path.

notation.meaning: Trace inner product on symmetric matrices.

children.title: Symmetric-Cone Primal–Dual Scaling
children.top_down_role: Nesterov–Todd, HKM, and AHO scaling families.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric-Cone Primal–Dual Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling representation in a Euclidean Jordan algebra, including common SDP symmetrizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a symmetric cone in a Euclidean Jordan algebra and let \(x,s\in\operatorname{int}K\). The Nesterov–Todd scaling point is the unique \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\) satisfying \[P(w)s=x,\] where \(P(w)\) is the quadratic representation. Thus the primal and dual variables are mapped to a common scaled variable by mutually inverse automorphisms derived from \(P(w)\). For the positive-semidefinite cone, AHO, primal-HKM, dual-HKM, and Nesterov–Todd directions correspond to different admissible symmetrizations or scalings of the linearized matrix equation \(XS=\mu I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric-cone scaling maps primal and dual interior points into common coordinates; NT, HKM, and AHO use distinct complementarity symmetrizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\) with \(P(w)s=x\), furnishing balanced primal–dual coordinates.

notation.meaning: quadratic representation at the scaling point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind matches the scaling-family container, and the NT scaling equation is plausible under a standard quadratic-representation convention. An authoritative source with a precise locator is required to verify uniqueness, the direction of P(w), the claimed mutually inverse scaled coordinates, and the classification of AHO, HKM, and NT directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–dual scaling on a symmetric cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a Euclidean Jordan algebra with symmetric cone \(K\), identity \(e\), Jordan product \(\circ\), and quadratic representation \(P(w)\) for \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\). Let \(x,s\in\operatorname{int}K\) be primal and dual interior variables.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric cones, including nonnegative orthants, Lorentz cones, and positive-semidefinite cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric-cone primal–dual scaling is an invertible cone automorphism \(W:E\to E\), selected from an interior pair \((x,s)\), that maps primal and dual variables into a common scaled geometry and is used to symmetrize the linearization of \(x\circ s=\mu e\). In Nesterov–Todd scaling, the scaling point \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\) is characterized by \[P(w)s=x,\] and the common scaled variable may be written \[v=P(w)^{-1/2}x=P(w)^{1/2}s.\] In the semidefinite realization, AHO takes the identity symmetrization, while primal and dual HKM directions use one-sided square-root scalings based respectively on the current primal or dual matrix. These choices agree on the exact central path but generally generate different Newton directions away from it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric-cone primal–dual scaling transforms an interior primal–dual pair into common coordinates in which complementarity can be linearized symmetrically. Nesterov–Todd scaling chooses the unique interior scaling point whose quadratic representation sends the dual slack to the primal point. AHO and the primal or dual HKM directions are alternative semidefinite symmetrizations. The scaling choice is part of the method because it changes the off-path Newton equation even though all standard choices represent the same central complementarity relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[w\in\operatorname{int}K,\quad P(w)s=x,\quad v=P(w)^{-1/2}x=P(w)^{1/2}s\] defines the Nesterov–Todd common scaling, while AHO and HKM are alternative symmetrizations of the same primal–dual complementarity equation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For the positive-semidefinite cone, the Nesterov–Todd scaling matrix can be characterized by \(WSW=X\) with \(W\succ0\).
On the exact central path \(x\circ s=\mu e\), the scaled point satisfies \(v\circ v=\mu e\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), the scaling is componentwise and \(w_i=\sqrt{x_i/s_i}\).
For Lorentz cones, the same construction uses the Lorentz Jordan algebra.
immediate_consequences_latex: The scaling preserves cone interiors because it is a cone automorphism.
Different admissible scalings can share the same central path while producing different linear systems away from it.
boundary_notes: Self-scaled symmetric-cone geometry is unavailable for a general nonsymmetric cone.
The inspected local sources mention self-scaled methods and SDP symmetrizations but do not fully state the Nesterov–Todd, HKM, and AHO family in the unified form used here.

notation.meaning: Quadratic representation of the Euclidean Jordan algebra.
Cone automorphism or its matrix realization.

review_flags: A dedicated symmetric-cone source is needed for the unified Nesterov–Todd, HKM, and AHO definition.
The available source only partially supports SDP symmetrization choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsymmetric-Cone Interior Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier path following without self-scaled symmetric-cone geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the conic program \(\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), let \(F\) be a logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\). Given \(\mu>0\), compute an approximate solution of \[Ax=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\qquad s=-\mu\nabla F(x).\] Newton-linearize these equations using \(\nabla^2F(x)\), choose a damped step that retains \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) and the required dual interiority, reduce \(\mu\), and repeat. Stop when feasibility residuals and the barrier-based complementarity measure satisfy their tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonsymmetric cone, a self-concordant barrier supplies local primal–dual geometry even though no self-scaled cone automorphism is available.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a regular closed convex cone.
\(F\) is a computable logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\).
The central Newton systems are solvable along the iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method follows \(s=-\mu\nabla F(x)\) toward feasibility and optimality as \(\mu\downarrow0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the nonsymmetric-cone container, but the dual cone and the meaning of 'required dual interiority' are not introduced. A source is also needed to support this primal–dual barrier system and the stated approach to feasibility and optimality for nonsymmetric cones.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier-based interior method without self-scaled cone symmetry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subset E\) be a proper cone that is not assumed homogeneous or self-dual, let \(K^*\) be its dual, and let \(F:\operatorname{int}K\to\mathbb R\) be a logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier. Consider the standard primal–dual conic affine equations \(Ax=b\) and \(A^*y+s=c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cone programs whose cone has a tractable barrier but lacks the symmetric self-scaled geometry used by Nesterov–Todd methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonsymmetric-cone interior method is a barrier or primal–dual method with \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) and \(s\in\operatorname{int}K^*\) whose central coupling is expressed through barrier derivatives rather than a self-scaled Jordan product. Its primal central relation is \[Ax=b,\qquad A^*y+s=c,\qquad s=-\mu\nabla F(x),\qquad \mu>0.\] A primal–dual implementation may additionally use the local metric \(H_x=\nabla^2F(x)\) and a compatible dual barrier to form corrections, but it does not assume an automorphism that exchanges every interior primal–dual pair or a scaling point satisfying a symmetric-cone equation such as \(P(w)s=x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsymmetric-cone interior method works with a proper cone and its dual by using an explicitly supplied barrier, its gradient, and usually its Hessian. Centrality couples the dual slack to the negative barrier gradient at the primal point. Unlike a symmetric-cone method, the definition does not assume self-duality, transitive cone automorphisms, a Euclidean Jordan product, or Nesterov–Todd scaling. The barrier oracle therefore forms part of the problem interface rather than being recoverable solely from a symmetric cone representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_F=\bigcup_{\mu>0}\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^*y+s=c,\ x\in\operatorname{int}K,\ s\in\operatorname{int}K^*,\ s=-\mu\nabla F(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The primal component is a stationary point of \(\langle c,x\rangle+\mu F(x)\) on \(Ax=b\).
For a logarithmically homogeneous barrier with parameter \(\nu\), centrality implies \(\langle x,s\rangle=\nu\mu\).
special_cases_latex: Exponential, power, and other non-self-dual cones are representative targets when equipped with suitable barriers.
A symmetric cone also admits this gradient formulation, but it is not classified as nonsymmetric when self-scaled geometry is used.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Hessian \(H_x\) supplies a local norm and a primal-to-dual linear map.
Absence of self-scaled symmetry prevents direct transplantation of symmetric-cone scaling identities.
boundary_notes: Existence of a self-concordant barrier is not by itself a statement that the barrier and its derivatives are computationally accessible.
No inspected source in the supplied corpus supported this exact nonsymmetric-cone interface.
review_flags: A modern authoritative source on nonsymmetric-cone primal–dual barriers is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior interface for monotone equilibrium systems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be monotone on a neighborhood of \(G\). When \(G=\{z:g_i(z)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(G_g(z)\) denote the Jacobian of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional monotone complementarity and variational-inequality models having a smooth inequality representation suitable for primal–dual perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An equilibrium-problem interior interface represents the target either as the variational inequality \[z^*\in G,\qquad (z-z^*)^T\Phi(z^*)\geq0\quad\forall z\in G,\] or, under an appropriate constraint qualification for a smooth convex-inequality representation of \(G\), as \[\Phi(z)+G_g(z)^T\lambda=0,\quad g(z)+w=0,\quad \lambda\geq0,\quad w\geq0,\quad \lambda^Tw=0.\] Its interior path replaces complementarity by \(\Lambda w=\mu\mathbf1\) with \(\lambda,w>0\), and an interior method applies Newton-type corrections to the stationarity, constraint, and perturbed-complementarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equilibrium-problem interior interface covers a monotone variational inequality and its smooth complementarity representation. The solution must lie in a closed convex set and make the mapping form a nonnegative inner product with every feasible displacement. If the set is described by convex inequalities and a suitable qualification holds, multipliers and positive slacks convert this condition into a mixed nonlinear complementarity system. Interior path following keeps multipliers and slacks positive and replaces zero complementarity by a positive componentwise product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Phi(z)+G_g(z)^T\lambda=0,\quad g(z)+w=0,\quad \Lambda w=\mu\mathbf1,\quad \lambda>0,\quad w>0,\quad \mu>0\] is the canonical perturbed equilibrium interface when the inequality representation is valid.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(G=\mathbb R_+^n\), the variational inequality becomes a nonlinear complementarity problem after a consistent sign convention.
The normal-cone form is \(0\in\Phi(z^*)+N_G(z^*)\).
special_cases_latex: An affine \(\Phi(z)=Mz+q\) over the nonnegative orthant yields a linear complementarity problem.
A smooth monotone \(\Phi\) over the nonnegative orthant yields a monotone nonlinear complementarity problem.
immediate_consequences_latex: The family contains linear complementarity, nonlinear complementarity, and constrained monotone variational inequalities as distinct interfaces.
Constraint qualification is necessary for the displayed multiplier system to characterize the variational inequality.
boundary_notes: Nonmonotone equilibrium problems are outside this scope.
Nonsmooth set descriptions require generalized derivatives or alternative proximal interfaces.

notation.meaning: Normal cone of G at z.
Nonnegative slack for g(z) less than or equal to zero.

children.title: Linear Complementarity Interior Methods

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Complementarity Interior Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-path Newton method for a monotone linear complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=Mx+q\), initialize \(x>0\) and \(z>0\). At each iteration choose \(\mu=\sigma x^{\mathsf T}z/n\) with \(0<\sigma<1\), and solve \[\Delta z=M\Delta x,\qquad Z\Delta x+X\Delta z=\mu\mathbf1-Xz.\] Choose a fraction-to-boundary step \(\alpha>0\) such that \(x+\alpha\Delta x>0\) and \(z+\alpha\Delta z>0\), then update both vectors. Stop when \(\|z-Mx-q\|\) and \(x^{\mathsf T}z\) meet their tolerances; return the resulting approximate complementarity pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LCP central path replaces componentwise complementarity by positive products equal to a decreasing parameter and follows it using damped Newton steps.
assumptions_latex: A strictly positive initial pair satisfying or approximating \(z=Mx+q\) is available.
The reduced Newton system is solved accurately enough.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates preserve \(x>0\) and \(z>0\) while targeting \(z=Mx+q\), \(x\ge0\), \(z\ge0\), and \(x^{\mathsf T}z=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits linear-complementarity interior methods, but the displayed equation Delta z=M Delta x preserves any existing residual z-Mx-q rather than reducing it. This conflicts with the allowed approximately feasible initial pair and the residual-based stopping test. A cited formulation is needed to decide between requiring exact affine feasibility and adding the affine residual correction to the Newton system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior path following for a monotone linear complementarity problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be positive semidefinite in the monotonicity sense \(u^TMu\geq0\) for all \(u\), and let \(q\in\mathbb R^n\). Define \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\) and \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional monotone linear complementarity problems; infeasible-start variants may relax the affine equation during iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The monotone linear complementarity problem is to find \((x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \[s=Mx+q,\qquad x\geq0,\qquad s\geq0,\qquad x^Ts=0.\] A linear-complementarity interior method maintains \(x>0\) and \(s>0\) and targets the central path \[s=Mx+q,\qquad Xs=\mu\mathbf1,\qquad \mu>0.\] Its basic primal–dual correction linearizes the affine residual and perturbed complementarity; a feasible-start method preserves \(s=Mx+q\), whereas an infeasible-start method drives \(Mx+q-s\) to zero together with \(\mu=x^Ts/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone linear complementarity problem asks for nonnegative vectors linked by an affine mapping whose componentwise products vanish. An interior method replaces zero products with a common positive value, keeps both vectors strictly positive, and follows this perturbed system toward complementarity. Feasible-start methods remain on the affine equation throughout; infeasible-start methods also reduce its residual. Positive semidefiniteness of the matrix is the monotonicity condition for this canonical interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C=\bigcup_{\mu>0}\{(x,s):s=Mx+q,\ Xs=\mu\mathbf1,\ x>0,\ s>0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(x,s\geq0\), the scalar equation \(x^Ts=0\) is equivalent to \(x_is_i=0\) for every \(i\).
The central-path equations can be written \(F_\mu(x,s)=(Mx+q-s,\ Xs-\mu\mathbf1)=0\).
special_cases_latex: KKT systems of convex quadratic programs can be represented as mixed monotone LCPs.
When \(M=0\), feasibility is determined directly by the sign pattern of \(q\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every central-path point lies in the strict positive orthant.
A finite central-path limit as \(\mu\downarrow0\) solves the LCP if the affine relation is retained.
boundary_notes: For a nonmonotone matrix, global convergence and polynomial results for monotone LCP methods do not automatically apply.
A solution may exist without strict complementarity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 8, “The Monotone LCP,” equations (8.1)–(8.3), followed by the feasible sets and central-path definition, pp. 153–156

children.title: Nonlinear Complementarity Interior Methods

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Complementarity Interior Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior Newton continuation for nonlinear complementarity equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a continuously differentiable mapping \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), initialize \(x>0\) with \(F(x)>0\). Given \(\mu>0\), compute \(\Delta x\) from \[\bigl(\operatorname{Diag}(F(x))+\operatorname{Diag}(x)F'(x)\bigr)\Delta x=\mu\mathbf1-\operatorname{Diag}(x)F(x).\] Choose a damped fraction-to-boundary step preserving \(x>0\) and \(F(x)>0\), update \(x\), reduce \(\mu\), and repeat. Terminate when the residuals of \(x\ge0\), \(F(x)\ge0\), and \(\operatorname{Diag}(x)F(x)=0\) meet their tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear complementarity interior method follows positive perturbed complementarity equations using Jacobian-based Newton steps and interior-preserving damping.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the iterates.
A point satisfying \(x>0\) and \(F(x)>0\) is available.
The displayed Newton matrix is nonsingular along the computed path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(\mu\downarrow0\), accumulation points satisfying vanishing residuals solve \(x\ge0\), \(F(x)\ge0\), and \(x_iF_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and Newton derivative of Diag(x)F(x) fit the nonlinear-complementarity container. No source is provided for path existence, interior-preserving continuation, or sufficient convergence hypotheses; continuous differentiability and nonsingularity alone do not establish the broader algorithmic behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior method for a smooth monotone nonlinear complementarity mapping
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(\mathbb R_+^n\), and suppose \((f(x_1)-f(x_2))^T(x_1-x_2)\geq0\) for relevant \(x_1,x_2\in U\). Set \(s=f(x)\), \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), and \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth monotone nonlinear complementarity problems over the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonlinear complementarity problem is to find \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \[x\geq0,\qquad f(x)\geq0,\qquad x^Tf(x)=0.\] Equivalently, with \(s=f(x)\), it requires \(x,s\geq0\) and \(x^Ts=0\). A nonlinear-complementarity interior method maintains \(x>0\) and \(s>0\) and targets \[s=f(x),\qquad Xs=\mu\mathbf1,\qquad \mu>0.\] A Newton-type correction linearizes both equations, using \(\nabla f(x)\Delta x-\Delta s\) for the nonlinear feasibility equation and \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s\) for complementarity. Infeasible-start variants allow \(s-f(x)\neq0\) but reduce that residual with \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth monotone nonlinear complementarity problem seeks a nonnegative point whose mapped value is nonnegative and complementary to it. An interior method introduces the mapped value as a positive dual vector and replaces zero componentwise products by a positive centrality parameter. Each step linearizes the nonlinear mapping and complementarity while choosing a length that retains positivity. Unlike the linear case, an ordinary line segment need not preserve the nonlinear equation, so infeasible-interior residual control is normally part of the interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_f=\bigcup_{\mu>0}\{(x,s):s=f(x),\ Xs=\mu\mathbf1,\ x>0,\ s>0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The unperturbed problem is \(0\leq x\perp f(x)\geq0\).
The perturbed residual mapping is \(F_\mu(x,s)=(f(x)-s,\ Xs-\mu\mathbf1)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=Mx+q\) with \(M\succeq0\), the definition reduces to a monotone LCP.
A gradient mapping \(f=\nabla\varphi\) with convex \(\varphi\) gives the bound-constrained first-order optimality system for minimizing \(\varphi\).
immediate_consequences_latex: At any finite limit with feasibility residual and \(\mu\) vanishing, \(x\) solves the nonlinear complementarity conditions.
Monotonicity distinguishes this interface from general nonlinear equations with complementarity constraints.
boundary_notes: Nonsmooth mappings require generalized-Newton or smoothing variants not defined here.
Local monotonicity alone does not establish existence of a global central path.

children.title: Monotone Variational-Inequality Path Following
children.top_down_role: Path-following methods for monotone variational inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Variational-Inequality Path Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier continuation for a monotone variational inequality on a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex with nonempty interior, let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\) be monotone, and let \(\phi\) be a self-concordant barrier for \(K\). For decreasing \(\mu>0\), approximately solve the regularized equation \[F(x)+\mu\nabla\phi(x)=0,\qquad x\in\operatorname{int}K,\] by damped Newton steps when \(F\) is differentiable. Retain interiority, reduce \(\mu\) only after the regularized residual is sufficiently small, and return an iterate whose variational-inequality gap \(\sup_{y\in K}\langle F(x),x-y\rangle\) meets the requested tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Barrier regularization replaces the normal-cone inclusion by an interior equation and traces its solutions as the regularization parameter decreases.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is monotone and continuously differentiable along the central path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any convergent path with \(\mu\downarrow0\) and vanishing regularized residual approaches a solution of \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for all \(y\in K\).

notation.meaning: self-concordant barrier for the feasible set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits monotone variational-inequality path following, but the proposed supremum gap need not be finite on an unbounded K. Moreover, mu tending to zero and a vanishing regularized residual do not by themselves ensure that mu times the barrier gradient vanishes. A precise path-following theorem and its hypotheses are required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path following for a smooth monotone variational inequality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(\Phi\) be continuous and monotone on a neighborhood of \(G\). Suppose additionally that \(G=\{z:g_i(z)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) for differentiable convex functions when the multiplier path is used.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional monotone variational inequalities with a smooth convex-inequality representation satisfying a suitable constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The monotone variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(G,\Phi)\) is to find \(z^*\in G\) such that \[(z-z^*)^T\Phi(z^*)\geq0\quad\text{for every }z\in G.\] For a qualified inequality representation of \(G\), a path-following interior formulation consists of \[\Phi(z)+G_g(z)^T\lambda=0,\qquad g(z)+w=0,\qquad \Lambda w=\mu\mathbf1,\qquad \lambda>0,\quad w>0,\quad \mu>0.\] A path-following method computes approximate Newton corrections to these equations, retains positive multipliers and slacks, and decreases \(\mu=\lambda^Tw/m\) together with the stationarity and constraint residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone variational inequality asks for a feasible point at which the mapping has nonnegative inner product with every feasible displacement. When the feasible set has a smooth convex inequality description, normal-cone multipliers and slacks convert the variational inequality into a mixed complementarity system. Path following replaces multiplier-slack complementarity by a positive product, follows these perturbed systems, and reduces both centrality and residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C=\bigcup_{\mu>0}\{(z,\lambda,w):\Phi(z)+G_g(z)^T\lambda=0,\ g(z)+w=0,\ \Lambda w=\mu\mathbf1,\ \lambda>0,\ w>0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The variational inequality is equivalently \(0\in\Phi(z^*)+N_G(z^*)\).
Under constraint qualification, the limit system is stationarity, primal feasibility, multiplier nonnegativity, and complementary slackness.
special_cases_latex: For \(G=\mathbb R_+^n\), the problem becomes nonlinear complementarity after adopting the corresponding normal-cone sign convention.
For affine \(\Phi\) and polyhedral \(G\), the path equations reduce to a mixed linear complementarity interface.
immediate_consequences_latex: Monotonicity makes the solution set convex when the standard existence conditions hold.
A zero-residual limit with \(\mu\to0\) satisfies the multiplier form of the variational inequality.
boundary_notes: The multiplier representation is not intrinsic: it depends on the chosen constraint description and a constraint qualification.
This definition excludes nonsmooth feasible-set representations and nonmonotone variational inequalities.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the vector of constraint functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Predicate taxonomy for interior-point applicability boundaries
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal P=(K,A,b,c,F,\mathfrak O)\) denote a represented optimization problem, where \(K\) is its constraint cone or barrier domain, \(F\) is the selected barrier, and \(\mathfrak O\) is the collection of numerical oracles used to evaluate derivatives and solve linearized systems.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal classification device for finite-dimensional barrier and primal–dual interior methods, not a convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The interior-point applicability boundary of \(\mathcal P\) is classified by failure of one or more predicates: \[\begin{aligned}G(\mathcal P)&:\ \{x:Ax=b\}\cap\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing,\\ A_n(\mathcal P)&:\ F\text{ is defined and has the required differentiability and curvature on }\operatorname{int}K,\\ R(\mathcal P)&:\ \text{the relevant KKT or central-path linearizations are solvable with controlled regularity},\\ L(\mathcal P)&:\ \text{a globalization rule can retain the interior while reducing its merit or residual measure},\\ C(\mathcal P)&:\ \mathfrak O\text{ can evaluate and solve the required systems within the stated resource model}.\end{aligned}\] The taxonomy assigns a boundary label from \(\{G,A_n,R,L,C\}\) to each failed predicate; multiple labels may apply simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The applicability boundary taxonomy treats an interior-point model as usable only when five distinct predicates hold: the represented feasible set has an ambient strict interior point; the barrier has the required analytic properties; the central or KKT linearization has adequate regularity; globalization can retain the interior while producing progress; and the required evaluations and linear solves are computationally available. A problem can cross several boundaries at once, so these are labels rather than mutually exclusive cases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial_{\mathrm{IP}}\mathcal P=\{j\in\{G,A_n,R,L,C\}:j(\mathcal P)\text{ is false}\}.\]
special_cases_latex: Failure of \(G\) includes a nonempty feasible set contained in a proper face of the ambient cone.
Failure of \(R\) includes singular or arbitrarily ill-conditioned central-path Newton systems near the target.
immediate_consequences_latex: The empty label set means only that this interface-level checklist is passed; it is not itself a convergence guarantee.
Facial reduction can change the representation and thereby turn \(G\) from false to true without changing the underlying feasible set.
boundary_notes: The labels are representation-dependent, especially the geometric and computational predicates.
No inspected authoritative source stated this five-predicate taxonomy as a canonical definition.

notation.meaning: Geometric, analytic, regularity, globalization, and computational applicability predicates.

review_flags: The taxonomy appears blueprint-specific and lacks a matching authoritative source.
The five predicates require validation as the intended canonical partition.
knowledge_statements.title: Predicate taxonomy for interior-point applicability boundaries

children.title: Interior-Certification Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where conventional barriers or stable status certificates are unavailable.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary where ambient interior paths or stable status certificates fail
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a proper cone \(K\subset E\), consider the conic feasibility system \(\mathcal F=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\), its affine space \(L=\{x:Ax=b\}\), and dual separation certificates expressed through \(K^*\) and \(A^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic representations; the boundary concerns ambient strict feasibility and stable feasible-versus-infeasible certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The interior-certification failure boundary is the class of represented conic systems for which at least one of the following holds: \[(i)\quad \mathcal F\neq\varnothing\ \text{but}\ L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing;\] \[(ii)\quad \mathcal F=\varnothing\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0;\] or \[(iii)\quad \text{every available feasible or infeasible certificate lies on the boundary of its certificate cone and is destroyed by arbitrarily small data perturbations}.\] Case (i) prevents an ambient primal barrier path, case (ii) is weak infeasibility and prevents strict separation, and case (iii) records failure of robust status recovery even when an exact limiting certificate can be written.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior-certification failure occurs when the chosen conic representation cannot simultaneously support an ambient interior trajectory and a stable status certificate. This includes feasible systems confined to a proper face, infeasible affine spaces whose distance from the cone is zero, and boundary certificates that disappear under arbitrarily small perturbations. The definition concerns the representation: a reformulation or facial reduction may remove the failure without changing the underlying mathematical feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak B_{\mathrm{cert}}=\{(K,A,b):[(\mathcal F\neq\varnothing\wedge L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing)\vee(\mathcal F=\varnothing\wedge\operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0)\vee\text{unstable boundary certification}]\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Condition (i) says that Slater strict feasibility fails in the ambient cone despite feasibility.
Condition (ii) says that infeasibility is not strongly separated by a positive distance.
special_cases_latex: A feasible SDP whose feasible matrices are all singular satisfies condition (i).
A weakly infeasible SDP satisfies condition (ii).
immediate_consequences_latex: The standard logarithmic barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\) cannot start from an exactly feasible point in case (i).
A positive-margin separating certificate cannot exist in case (ii).
boundary_notes: Failure of strict feasibility does not imply infeasibility.
The stability clause requires a specified perturbation norm and certificate normalization for quantitative use.

notation.meaning: Infimum distance between the affine space and cone in the chosen norm.

review_flags: No inspected source supported this combined strict-feasibility, weak-infeasibility, and certificate-stability boundary as one canonical definition.
A conic pathology or facial-reduction source is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary where ambient interior paths or stable status certificates fail

children.title: Ambient-Representation Interior Failures
children.top_down_role: Barrier failure caused by unsuitable ambient representations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of ambient strict interior despite relative interior feasibility
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subset E\) be a closed convex cone with nonempty interior, let \(L=\{x\in E:Ax=b\}\), and suppose \(L\cap K\neq\varnothing\). Let \(F_{\min}\) be the smallest face of \(K\) containing \(L\cap K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic systems whose feasible set is nonempty but lies in a lower-dimensional face of the represented cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ambient-representation interior failure occurs when \[L\cap K\neq\varnothing,\qquad L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing,\qquad L\cap\operatorname{relint}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing.\] Thus the system is feasible and has a strict point relative to its minimal face, but no feasible point belongs to the interior of the ambient cone. A barrier defined only on \(\operatorname{int}K\) therefore has no feasible ambient-domain point, whereas a barrier on \(\operatorname{relint}F_{\min}\), after identifying the span of that face, can possess a valid relative-interior domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambient-representation interior failure is a mismatch between the cone used to encode a feasible problem and the lower-dimensional face that actually contains every feasible point. The feasible set is nonempty, but it never enters the ambient cone interior. It does enter the relative interior of its minimal face. Consequently, the ordinary ambient barrier cannot be evaluated at a feasible point, even though the same problem can have a strict interior after reduction to the correct face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{ambient failure}\iff \varnothing\neq L\cap K\subseteq F_{\min},\quad L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing,\quad L\cap\operatorname{relint}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Ambient Slater feasibility fails, while relative Slater feasibility holds on the minimal face.
For \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), every feasible matrix is singular in ambient coordinates but some feasible matrix is positive definite on the common support subspace.
special_cases_latex: Redundant zero coordinates in a nonnegative-orthant representation create this failure.
An SDP constrained to matrices with a common nullspace creates this failure.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any feasible sequence lies arbitrarily close to the ambient boundary because it lies on that boundary exactly.
Facial reduction or an equivalent lower-dimensional parametrization can restore a nonempty strict interior.
boundary_notes: A merely empty feasible set is not an ambient-representation interior failure under this definition.
Relative interior depends on the affine hull or face span, whereas ambient interior is taken in E.

notation.meaning: Smallest face of K containing the feasible set.
Interior relative to the affine hull of the set.

source_refs.locator: §2.1.3, definition of affine dimension and relative interior, pp. 23–24; §5.2.3 and §5.9, Slater strict feasibility and generalized cone inequalities, pp. 226–227 and 268–272

review_flags: The source directly supports relative interior and ambient Slater distinctions; the minimal-face packaging should be checked against a facial-reduction reference.

children.title: Lower-Dimensional Feasible Sets
children.top_down_role: Feasible regions whose intrinsic dimension is smaller than the ambient model space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Relative Interior Is Nonempty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic interior existence for a nonempty convex set despite loss of ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has nonempty relative interior: \[\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing.\] Hence, if \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)<n\), the equality \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing\) is an ambient-dimensional obstruction, not absence of intrinsically interior feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite-dimensional convex set always has relative-interior points, even when its ambient interior is empty.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: interior of \(C\) relative to its affine hull

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Relative Interior Is Nonempty
Lower-Dimensional Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of ambient strict feasibility for sets confined to a proper affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. If \(\operatorname{aff}C\) is a proper affine subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\), then \[\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing.\] Consequently, any barrier formulation whose domain requires an ambient strictly feasible point in \(C\) has no admissible initialization, even when \(\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\). The obstruction is dimensional rather than infeasibility: feasible points may exist, but no ambient open ball centered at such a point lies inside \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible set contained in a proper affine subspace has no ambient interior, so ambient strict-feasibility initialization fails despite possible relative-interior points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing\), although \(\operatorname{ri}C\) may be nonempty.

notation.meaning: relative interior of C in its affine hull

children.title: Empty Ambient Interiors
children.top_down_role: Models lacking an interior relative to their stated ambient space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empty Ambient Interior Prevents Ambient-Strict Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization boundary for methods whose declared invariant requires membership in the ambient interior of the represented feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and suppose a method requires every iterate, including its initial point, to belong to \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C\). If
\[
\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing,
\]
then no point satisfies that ambient-strict-interiority invariant, so the method cannot be initialized in this representation. This conclusion applies only to methods whose barrier domain or iterate invariant is explicitly the ambient interior of \(C\); it does not preclude a relative-interior, reduced-space, or alternative barrier representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a method explicitly requires an ambient-interior starting point and the represented feasible set has empty ambient interior, that method cannot be initialized in the representation.
assumptions_latex: The method explicitly requires initialization in \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing\) implies that no admissible initial point exists for the stated ambient-interior invariant.

notation.meaning: interior of the represented feasible set in the ambient Euclidean topology

review_flags: The conclusion is representation- and method-qualified and makes no claim about alternative barriers or relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.title: Empty Ambient Interior Prevents Ambient-Strict Initialization
Empty Ambient Interiors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient-interior emptiness as an initialization boundary for barrier methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible region \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), an ambient-interior barrier method requiring strict feasibility is applicable only if \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C\ne\varnothing\). If \[C\ne\varnothing\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing,\] then no feasible point admits a positive-radius Euclidean ball contained in \(C\). Hence no iterate can satisfy an ambient strict-interiority invariant, and an ambient log-barrier domain for the represented feasible set is empty. A reduced-space or relative-interior formulation is required before such a method can be initialized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a nonempty feasible set has empty ambient interior, no ambient strictly feasible starting point exists; reduction to its affine hull is necessary.
assumptions_latex: The method requires iterates in \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing\), the stated ambient-interior method cannot be initialized on \(C\).

notation.meaning: interior of C in the ambient Euclidean topology

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and ambient-interior obstruction fit the container. A source is required, and the statement about an 'ambient log-barrier domain for the represented feasible set' depends on the precise barrier representation; the initialization impossibility is valid only for methods explicitly requiring membership in the ambient interior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient Interior and Affine Dimension of Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed convex-geometric equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing\) if and only if \(\dim\operatorname{aff}(C)<n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex set has empty ambient interior exactly when its affine hull is lower-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing\iff\dim\operatorname{aff}(C)<n\).
review_flags: The affine-dimension characterization is primarily owned by the Lower-Dimensional Feasible Sets sibling; cross-index it here.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Interior and Affine Dimension of Convex Sets

The proposed affine-dimension theorem is deferred to Lower-Dimensional Feasible Sets. Representation-induced loss and relative-interior remedies remain excluded sibling scopes.

children.title: Representation-Induced Interior Loss
children.top_down_role: Interior loss caused by redundant, lifted, or otherwise unsuitable formulations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Everywhere-Active Represented Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-level condition eliminating the strict domain of the associated logarithmic barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C=\{x:g_i(x)\ge0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\ne\varnothing. If g_j(x)=0 for every x\in C for some j, then \[\{x:g_i(x)>0\ \forall i\}=\varnothing.\] Hence -\sum_i\log g_i(x) has empty domain on the represented system, even when \operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality active everywhere on the feasible set makes the represented strict interior, and therefore the naive log-barrier domain, empty.
assumptions_latex: Some represented inequality vanishes throughout C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:g_i(x)>0\ \forall i\}=\varnothing.

notation.meaning: feasible set represented by the inequalities

knowledge_statements.title: Everywhere-Active Represented Inequality
Representation-Induced Interior Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A redundant inequality representation can destroy strict feasibility without changing the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R\). Represent the hyperplane \(C=\{x:a^{\mathsf T}x=b\}\) by \[a^{\mathsf T}x-b\le0,\qquad b-a^{\mathsf T}x\le0.\] The feasible set is nonempty and satisfies \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\), but strict satisfaction of both displayed inequalities would require simultaneously \(a^{\mathsf T}x<b\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}x>b\), which is impossible. Thus a log barrier formed from both slacks has empty domain, even though eliminating the equality or parameterizing the affine hull yields a valid reduced representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding one equality as two opposite inequalities leaves the feasible set unchanged but makes simultaneous strict inequality, and hence the naive log barrier, impossible.
assumptions_latex: The equality is represented by the two displayed inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The represented system has no strictly feasible point although \(C\ne\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\).

notation.meaning: relative interior in the affine hull

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind exactly fits representation-induced interior loss, and the equality-as-two-inequalities example is mathematically coherent. It has no citation or inspectable locator supporting the representation pathology and barrier-domain interpretation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Everywhere-Active Redundant Inequality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General representation-level condition that destroys the strict domain of a logarithmic barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x:g_i(x)\ge 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\ne\varnothing\). If some represented inequality satisfies \(g_j(x)=0\) for every \(x\in C\), then \[\{x:g_i(x)>0\ \forall i\}=\varnothing.\] Consequently the logarithmic barrier \(-\sum_i\log g_i(x)\) has no feasible domain, even if \(\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak and ill-posed conic feasibility certification
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subset E\) be a closed convex cone and \(L=\{x:Ax=b\}\) an affine space. Feasibility is \(L\cap K\neq\varnothing\). A strict separating certificate for infeasibility is a continuous linear functional having a positive normalized separation margin between \(L\) and \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic feasibility systems, with pathology measured in a fixed norm and data representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasibility-certification pathology is present when the exact status of \(L\cap K\) lacks a stable strict witness. The canonical cases are \[\text{weak infeasibility}:\quad L\cap K=\varnothing\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0,\] and \[\text{ill-posed feasibility}:\quad L\cap K\neq\varnothing\ \text{but}\ L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing.\] More generally, a status instance is pathological when it lies on the boundary, in the chosen data norm, between feasible and infeasible instances, so arbitrarily small perturbations can change status or destroy every normalized certificate margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasibility-certification pathology occurs when feasibility or infeasibility has no robust positive-margin witness. Weak infeasibility means that the affine constraints and cone do not intersect, although their distance is zero. Ill-posed feasibility means that they intersect only on the cone boundary. Both regimes sit at a status boundary: small perturbations can change the answer, and residual-based stopping rules can confuse near-feasible sequences with genuine certificates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{feas}}=\{(K,L):(L\cap K=\varnothing\wedge\operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0)\vee(L\cap K\neq\varnothing\wedge L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Weak infeasibility is infeasibility without strong separation in the selected normed representation.
Ill-posed feasibility is failure of ambient Slater feasibility at a feasible instance.
special_cases_latex: Weakly infeasible semidefinite systems are the standard nonpolyhedral example.
For closed polyhedral cones and affine spaces, disjointness yields positive distance under standard finite-dimensional conditions, so the weakly infeasible case is excluded.
immediate_consequences_latex: A sequence of points can have distance to both \(L\) and \(K\) tending to zero without converging to a feasible point in the weakly infeasible case.
No strictly feasible primal point exists in the ill-posed feasible case.
boundary_notes: The numerical size of a certificate margin depends on scaling, normalization, and the selected norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-by-Two Semidefinite Weak Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small semidefinite affine system that is infeasible at zero distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \mathbb S^2 let K=\mathbb S_+^2 and \[L=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&t\end{bmatrix}:t\in\mathbb R\right\}.\] No member of L is positive semidefinite. For t>0, however, \[X_t=\begin{bmatrix}1/t&1\\1&t\end{bmatrix}\succeq0,\qquad Y_t=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&t\end{bmatrix}\in L,\qquad \|X_t-Y_t\|_F=1/t.\] Hence K\cap L=\varnothing and \operatorname{dist}(K,L)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-by-two semidefinite affine system has no feasible matrix although positive-semidefinite matrices approach its affine line arbitrarily closely.
assumptions_latex: Distance is measured in the Frobenius norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb S_+^2\cap L=\varnothing,\qquad\operatorname{dist}(\mathbb S_+^2,L)=0.

notation.meaning: cone of real two-by-two positive-semidefinite matrices

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Margin Separation Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate boundary distinguishing weak from strong infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If nonempty closed convex sets K and L are disjoint with \operatorname{dist}(K,L)=0, there are no a\ne0 and \alpha<\beta such that \[\langle a,u\rangle\le\alpha<\beta\le\langle a,v\rangle\quad\forall u\in K,\ v\in L.\] Thus a positive-margin separation certificate can establish strong, but not weak, infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly infeasible sets admit no positive-margin separating functional.
assumptions_latex: K and L are nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ and }L\text{ admit no positive-margin affine separation}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Feasibility and Escape to Infinity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence characterization and boundedness consequence of weak infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^n be closed and L\subseteq\mathbb R^n be a closed affine space with K\cap L=\varnothing. Then \operatorname{dist}(K,L)=0 if and only if there are u_k\in K and v_k\in L with \|u_k-v_k\|\to0. Every such pair of sequences is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak infeasibility is equivalent to arbitrarily accurate approximate feasibility, and its approximating pairs must escape every bounded set.
assumptions_latex: L is a closed affine space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(K,L)=0\iff\exists u_k\in K,v_k\in L:\|u_k-v_k\|\to0,\quad \sup_k(\|u_k\|+\|v_k\|)=\infty.

notation.meaning: approaching points in K and L

Weak Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean weak infeasibility for an affine conic feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone and let \(L=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}\) be a nonempty affine space. The conic system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\) is weakly infeasible when \[K\cap L=\varnothing\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{dist}(K,L)=0,\] where \(\operatorname{dist}(K,L)=\inf\{\|u-v\|:u\in K,\ v\in L\}\). Thus no feasible point exists, yet pairs from \(K\) and \(L\) can approach each other arbitrarily closely; consequently, no positive distance separates the two sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system is weakly infeasible when its cone and affine constraint set are disjoint but have zero distance.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak infeasibility is exactly \(K\cap L=\varnothing\) together with \(\operatorname{dist}(K,L)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Separation Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate boundary distinguishing weak from strong infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If closed convex sets \(K\) and \(L\) are weakly infeasible, then no affine functional can separate them with a positive margin: there do not exist \(a\), \(\alpha<\beta\) such that \[\langle a,u\rangle\le\alpha<\beta\le\langle a,v\rangle\qquad\forall u\in K,\ v\in L.\] Such a strict margin would imply \(\operatorname{dist}(K,L)>0\). Thus ordinary positive-margin separation certificates characterize strong, not weak, infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly infeasible sets admit no positive-margin separating hyperplane, so standard strong-infeasibility certificates cannot exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) and \(L\) have no positive-margin affine separation.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Separation Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing-Width Feasible Interval Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary family of feasible instances whose distance to infeasibility tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \varepsilon\ge0 consider x\ge0 and x\le\varepsilon. The feasible set is [0,\varepsilon]. Measuring perturbations only in the scalar upper-bound datum, the infeasible data are values q<0, so \[\operatorname{dist}(\varepsilon,(-\infty,0))=\varepsilon.\] Hence feasible instances with \varepsilon\downarrow0 have vanishing distance to infeasibility while their feasible sets collapse to \{0\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible interval of width epsilon is epsilon away from inconsistent bounds, so narrow feasible intervals form a near-infeasible family.
assumptions_latex: Only the scalar upper-bound datum is perturbed, with absolute-value distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_{\mathrm{inf}}(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\to0\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\downarrow0.
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Width Feasible Interval Family
Near-Infeasible Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation-based proximity of a feasibility instance to infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(d)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:G(x,d)\in K\}\), where \(d\) denotes problem data and \(K\) is closed. With a prescribed data norm, define the infeasibility radius by \[\rho_{\mathrm{inf}}(d)=\inf\{\|\Delta d\|:F(d+\Delta d)=\varnothing\}.\] A feasible instance \(d\) is \(\varepsilon\)-near-infeasible when \(F(d)\ne\varnothing\) and \(\rho_{\mathrm{inf}}(d)\le \varepsilon\max\{1,\|d\|\}\). Thus a perturbation at the stated relative scale can change the feasibility status, even though the unperturbed instance remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible problem is near-infeasible when a data perturbation no larger than the chosen relative tolerance can make its feasible set empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_{\mathrm{inf}}(d)\le \varepsilon\max\{1,\|d\|\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance to the Feasibility-Status Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric conditioning associated with the topological set of ill-posed feasibility data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D be a normed data space, let \mathcal D_F and \mathcal D_I be its feasible and infeasible data, and set \Sigma=\overline{\mathcal D_F}\cap\overline{\mathcal D_I}. Define \[\rho_\Sigma(d)=\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma).\] Thus \rho_\Sigma(d)=0 for d\in\Sigma; when \Sigma is closed, \rho_\Sigma(d)>0 exactly for data outside \Sigma.

The feasibility model fixes subsets \mathcal D_F and \mathcal D_I.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance to the Feasibility-Status Boundary
Ill-Posed Feasibility Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological boundary between feasible and infeasible problem data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the parameterized feasibility system \(F(d)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:G(x,d)\in K\}\), let \(\mathcal D_F=\{d:F(d)\ne\varnothing\}\) and \(\mathcal D_I=\{d:F(d)=\varnothing\}\). An instance \(d\) is feasibility-ill-posed when \[d\in\overline{\mathcal D_F}\cap\overline{\mathcal D_I}.\] Equivalently, every neighborhood of \(d\) contains both feasible and infeasible data. Consequently, no positive perturbation radius around \(d\) preserves a single feasibility status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance is ill-posed when arbitrarily small data perturbations can produce either feasible or infeasible systems.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) belongs to a normed data space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\in\overline{\mathcal D_F}\cap\overline{\mathcal D_I}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance-to-Ill-Posedness Condition Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative conditioning attached to the feasibility-status boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a normed data space, let \(\mathcal D_F\) and \(\mathcal D_I\) denote the feasible and infeasible data, and set \(\Sigma=\overline{\mathcal D_F}\cap\overline{\mathcal D_I}\). Define \[\rho(d)=\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma),\qquad \mathcal C(d)=\begin{cases}\|d\|/\rho(d),&\rho(d)>0,\\+\infty,&\rho(d)=0.\end{cases}\] Then finite relative condition requires a positive distance from the ill-posed set, while every ill-posed instance has \(\mathcal C(d)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal normalized distance to the feasibility-status boundary is a condition measure; it diverges at ill-posed data.
assumptions_latex: Feasible and infeasible subsets are defined for the chosen feasibility model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\in\Sigma\Longrightarrow\rho(d)=0\Longrightarrow\mathcal C(d)=+\infty\).

children.title: Unstable Status Certification
children.top_down_role: Difficulties in recovering reliable feasibility or infeasibility status.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Status-Margin Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric sufficient condition for uniform feasibility-status robustness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D_F,D_I partition the admissible data by feasibility status. For d of either status, let D_{\mathrm{opp}} be the opposite-status set and \rho_{\mathrm{opp}}(d)=\operatorname{dist}(d,D_{\mathrm{opp}}). If 0\le\delta<\rho_{\mathrm{opp}}(d), then every admissible d' satisfying \|d'-d\|\le\delta has the same status as d. Thus a verified lower bound \underline\rho>\delta certifies status uniformly over the uncertainty ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified distance to the opposite status larger than the uncertainty radius certifies robust status.
assumptions_latex: Admissible data have a binary feasibility status.
The uncertainty and distance use the same norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|d'-d\|\le\delta\Longrightarrow d'\text{ has the same status as }d.

notation.meaning: distance to admissible data of opposite status

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Status-Margin Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncertainty Beyond the Status Margin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct metric boundary at which an uncertainty ball necessarily includes opposite-status data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With the same notation, if \delta>\rho_{\mathrm{opp}}(d), then the closed uncertainty ball \{d':\|d'-d\|\le\delta\} contains opposite-status data. If \delta=\rho_{\mathrm{opp}}(d), the same conclusion holds when the distance to D_{\mathrm{opp}} is attained; without attainment, equality alone does not imply that the closed ball contains an opposite-status instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncertainty strictly exceeding the status margin necessarily includes opposite-status data; equality requires attainment of the distance.
assumptions_latex: Admissible data have a binary feasibility status.
The uncertainty and distance use the same norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta>\rho_{\mathrm{opp}}(d)\Longrightarrow\exists d'\in D_{\mathrm{opp}}:\|d'-d\|\le\delta.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncertainty Beyond the Status Margin
Unstable Status Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification fails when perturbation uncertainty reaches the distance to the opposite status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\) be problem data and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{opp}}(d)\) be its distance to data having the opposite feasibility status. Suppose a computation represents or evaluates \(d\) only within uncertainty \(\delta>0\). If \(\rho_{\mathrm{opp}}(d)\le\delta\), then the uncertainty ball contains an instance of the opposite status. Hence no certificate based solely on the uncertain data and valid uniformly over that ball can unambiguously certify the nominal feasibility status; additional exact information, stronger margins, or higher precision is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility status is unstable when numerical uncertainty is at least the distance to an instance with the opposite status.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) lies in a normed data space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_{\mathrm{opp}}(d)\le\delta\Longrightarrow\) uniform status certification on \(\{d':\|d'-d\|\le\delta\}\) is impossible.

children.title: Facial-Reduction Interface
children.top_down_role: Boundary between barrier preprocessing and minimal-face methods.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facial-Reduction Chain Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite bound for an exact sequence of proper face reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If K=K_0\supsetneq K_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq K_d=K_{\min} is a finite-dimensional chain of faces, then every proper inclusion lowers dimension and \[d\le \dim K-\dim K_{\min}.\] Accordingly, any exact facial-reduction process making one proper face reduction per step terminates within this bound once it reaches K_{\min}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper facial-reduction sequence has at most the dimension drop from the original cone to the minimal face many steps.
assumptions_latex: Every step is a proper inclusion of faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\le\dim K-\dim K_{\min}.
knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Chain Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal-Face Strict-Feasibility Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric endpoint of facial reduction for a nonempty finite-dimensional conic feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space and F=K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing. There is a unique minimal face K_{\min}\unlhd K containing F, and \[F\cap\operatorname{ri}K_{\min}\ne\varnothing.\] Replacing K by K_{\min} therefore preserves F and supplies strict feasibility relative to the reduced cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty conic feasible set has a unique minimal containing face and intersects that face's relative interior.
assumptions_latex: K is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\subseteq K_{\min},\quad F\cap\operatorname{ri}K_{\min}\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: minimal face of K containing F

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Face Strict-Feasibility Interface
Facial-Reduction Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic preprocessing that replaces the ambient cone by a smaller face containing all feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), initialize \(K_0=K\). At iteration \(j\), seek \(y_j\) satisfying \(A^*y_j\in K_j^*\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\langle b,y_j\rangle=0\). If found, set \[K_{j+1}=K_j\cap(A^*y_j)^\perp\] and repeat; every feasible \(x\) remains in \(K_{j+1}\). Stop when the reduced system has a point in \(\operatorname{ri}K_j\), or when an infeasibility certificate is obtained. The resulting cone is a face containing the feasible set and supplies the proper domain for a relative-interior barrier method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial reduction repeatedly exposes smaller cone faces until the feasible set has relative interior or infeasibility is certified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\subseteq K_j\), with termination sought at strict feasibility relative to \(K_j\).

notation.meaning: dual cone of the current face

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal-face preprocessing interface for conic interior methods
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subset E\) be a closed convex cone, let \(L=\{x:Ax=b\}\), and assume \(L\cap K\neq\varnothing\) but possibly \(L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\). A face \(F\unlhd K\) is exposed by \(z\in K^*\) when \(F=K\cap z^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional feasible conic systems lacking ambient strict feasibility; the output is a reduced cone representation suitable for a barrier on its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A facial-reduction interface is a finite sequence of faces \[K=F_0\supsetneq F_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq F_r=F_{\min},\qquad F_{i+1}=F_i\cap z_i^\perp,\] where each exposing vector \(z_i\in F_i^*\setminus F_i^\perp\) satisfies \(\langle z_i,x\rangle=0\) for every \(x\in L\cap F_i\). The terminal face is required to contain the same feasible set, \(L\cap F_{\min}=L\cap K\), and to satisfy relative strict feasibility \[L\cap\operatorname{relint}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing.\] The interface passes the reduced face, its span, the transformed affine equations, and exposing certificates to the subsequent interior-point method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial reduction is the preprocessing interface that replaces an ambient cone by the smallest face containing every feasible point. Each reduction step finds a dual exposing vector that vanishes on the feasible set and intersects the current cone with its orthogonal hyperplane. The process terminates when the same feasible set has a point in the relative interior of the remaining face. An interior solver can then work in that face's span, where a relative barrier domain exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[L\cap K=L\cap F_{\min},\qquad L\cap\operatorname{relint}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing,\qquad F_{\min}=F_r\unlhd\cdots\unlhd F_0=K.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F_{\min}\) is the intersection of all faces of \(K\) that contain \(L\cap K\).
The number \(r\) of strict exposing steps is the singularity degree of the chosen reduction sequence when minimal.
special_cases_latex: For an SDP, exposing vectors identify common null directions and reduce the matrix variable to a smaller positive-semidefinite block.
For the nonnegative orthant, facial reduction deletes coordinates forced to zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: The reduced problem has the same feasible points after embedding back into the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite face-chain bound for exact facial reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an exact facial-reduction sequence produces proper inclusions \(K=K_0\supsetneq K_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq K_d=K_{\min}\), with every \(K_j\) a face of \(K\). Then \(d\) is at most the maximum length of a strict face chain from \(K\) to \(K_{\min}\); in particular, \[d\le \dim K-\dim K_{\min}.\] The least attainable number of proper exposing reductions is the singularity degree of the feasibility system relative to the chosen reduction model.
