knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resource-Relative Computational Applicability Boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathfrak I\) be a family of optimization instances, \(R(I,x)\) a prescribed residual or quality measure, and \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{IP}}\) an interior-point implementation. Fix tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), memory budget \(M_{\max}\), and time or work budget \(T_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational, implementation-relative definition. Applicability is not an intrinsic property of a mathematical problem without specifying accuracy, hardware, resource budgets, and a solver implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The interior-point implementation is computationally applicable to instance \(I\in\mathfrak I\) at \((\varepsilon,M_{\max},T_{\max})\) if it returns \(x\) satisfying \(R(I,x)\le\varepsilon\) while \[M_{\mathrm{peak}}(I)\le M_{\max},\qquad T(I)\le T_{\max}.\] The computational applicability boundary is the set of instances or parameter values at which at least one inequality becomes active or fails. A comparative boundary additionally requires an alternative method \(\mathcal B\) that satisfies all three requirements where \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{IP}}\) does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Computational applicability is defined relative to a target residual, memory limit, work or time limit, and concrete solver. The boundary consists of instances where the interior-point solver reaches or exceeds one of those limits; a comparative boundary also requires another method to meet the same requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\mathfrak I_{\mathrm{IP}}=\partial\{I:R(I,x_{\mathrm{IP}})\le\varepsilon,\ M_{\mathrm{peak}}(I)\le M_{\max},\ T(I)\le T_{\max}\}.\)
special_cases_latex: Memory-limited, warm-start-limited, and low-accuracy comparative regimes are distinct projections of this resource-relative boundary.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing hardware, implementation, tolerance, or the comparison method can move the boundary.
boundary_notes: No inspected source provides this exact unified mathematical definition.
Asymptotic complexity alone does not determine finite-instance applicability.

notation.meaning: Peak memory and elapsed time or work measures for the specified implementation.

review_flags: Needs a source that explicitly formalizes computational applicability as a joint accuracy, memory, and work budget.
The available textbooks discuss computational costs but not this exact canonical boundary object.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Relative Computational Applicability Boundary

children.title: Factorization-Memory Boundary
children.top_down_role: Large-scale regimes dominated by sparse fill and memory demand.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse-Factor Storage Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memory demand determined by the filled factor rather than input sparsity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sparse symmetric factorization \(P^TKP=LDL^T\), let \(c_j=\operatorname{nnz}(L_{:,j})\). Stored numerical factor data require \(\Theta(\sum_j c_j+n)\) scalars, with additional storage linear in indices and symbolic metadata and implementation-dependent temporary workspace. Consequently, factor memory can be large even when \(\operatorname{nnz}(K)\) is small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse direct-solve memory is governed by filled factor nonzeros, metadata, and workspace, not by input nonzeros alone.
assumptions_latex: a specified sparse symmetric ordering and factorization scheme are used
\(c_j\) counts stored entries in factor column \(j\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stored factor data use \(\Theta(\sum_jc_j+n)\) scalars, before implementation-dependent workspace.
review_flags: constant factors depend on factor format, pivoting, supernodes, index width, and workspace policy
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Factor Storage Measure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symbolic Estimate Is Not a Universal Memory Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on predicting peak factorization memory from a no-pivot symbolic analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symbolic factor count for a fixed permutation determines structural storage for the corresponding no-pivot factorization. It need not bound peak memory for a stabilized indefinite factorization: delayed pivots, dynamic permutations, supernodal padding, and temporary workspace may increase storage. A safe in-memory test must therefore incorporate the numerical factorization policy and a workspace allowance, not only symbolic \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symbolic no-pivot fill estimate is not by itself a guaranteed peak-memory bound for a dynamically pivoted indefinite factorization.
assumptions_latex: the numerical factorization may change pivots or storage after symbolic analysis
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{nnz}(L_{\mathrm{symbolic}})\) alone need not upper-bound peak numerical-factorization memory.
knowledge_statements.title: Symbolic Estimate Is Not a Universal Memory Certificate
Factorization-Memory Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse primal-dual factorization exceeds available memory because symbolic elimination produces excessive fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K_k\) be the sparse primal-dual Newton matrix at iteration \(k\), and let \(F_k\) denote the stored factors produced by a specified ordering and sparse direct factorization. If one stored scalar and its index require at least \(b>0\) bytes and the available factorization memory is \(M>0\), then direct factorization is outside the memory boundary whenever
\[
b\,\operatorname{nnz}(F_k)>M.
\]
This boundary depends on elimination fill rather than only on \(\operatorname{nnz}(K_k)\). Crossing it prevents the prescribed in-memory direct Newton solve, even when the original optimization data and unfactored matrix fit in memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The memory boundary is crossed when fill in the sparse Newton factors requires more storage than available, preventing the prescribed in-memory direct solve.
assumptions_latex: \(K_k\) is solved by a specified sparse direct factorization and ordering.
\(M\) is the memory available for stored factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(b\operatorname{nnz}(F_k)>M\), the prescribed in-memory factorization cannot be stored.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse-Factorization Memory Boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K(I)\) be a sparse symmetric KKT matrix for instance \(I\). A direct solver computes a permuted factorization \(P^TK(I)P=LBL^T\), where \(L\) is unit lower triangular and \(B\) is block diagonal. Let \(b_L,b_B>0\) denote storage per retained nonzero, including implementation overhead when desired.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct sparse factorization of primal-dual systems. Iterative methods and matrix-free methods have different memory models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the factor-storage requirement by \[M_{\mathrm{fact}}(I,P)=b_L\operatorname{nnz}(L)+b_B\operatorname{nnz}(B)+M_{\mathrm{aux}}(I,P).\] Given available memory \(M_{\max}\), instance \(I\) lies beyond the factorization-memory boundary if \[\min_{P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{stable}}}M_{\mathrm{fact}}(I,P)>M_{\max},\] where \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{stable}}\) is the permitted class of numerically stable symmetric permutations and pivots. The equality case defines the boundary surface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The factorization-memory boundary is crossed when every permitted stable ordering and pivoting strategy produces sparse factors and auxiliary data whose total storage exceeds available memory. Fill-in is measured through nonzeros created in the factors, not merely nonzeros in the original KKT matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{stable}}}M_{\mathrm{fact}}(I,P)>M_{\max}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With a fixed ordering policy \(P(I)\), the operational boundary is \(M_{\mathrm{fact}}(I,P(I))=M_{\max}\).
special_cases_latex: Condensation can reduce matrix dimension while increasing fill through \(A_I^TDA_I\).
For simple bound constraints, this term is diagonal and the fill contribution can be much smaller.
immediate_consequences_latex: The original matrix fitting in memory does not ensure that its factors fit.
Ordering, pivoting, and formulation choice can move the boundary substantially.
boundary_notes: The minimization over stable permutations is conceptual; finding a globally fill-minimizing ordering is itself difficult.
Peak workspace, symbolic-factorization data, and parallel replication must be included in \(M_{\mathrm{aux}}\) for a hardware-realistic boundary.

notation.meaning: Number of explicitly stored nonzero entries in the triangular factor.
Allowed stable ordering and pivoting choices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memory and arithmetic measures determined by the filled factor rather than the input matrix alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sparse symmetric factorization \(P^TKP=LDL^T\), let \(c_j=\operatorname{nnz}(L_{:,j})\). Stored numerical factor data require \(\Theta(\sum_j c_j+n)\) scalars, with additional storage linear in indices and symbolic metadata. children.title: Warm-Start Boundary
children.top_down_role: Sequential regimes where strict-interior maintenance limits solution reuse.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Interior Reuse and Centrality Are Distinct Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation-aware distinction between domain admissibility and quality of a primal-dual warm start.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a primal-dual logarithmic-barrier formulation, reused slacks and inequality multipliers are in the strict domain when \(s^{\mathrm{old}}>0\) and \(z^{\mathrm{old}}>0\). A feasible-start formulation additionally requires the new slack equations and equalities to hold, whereas an infeasible-start formulation may admit their residuals. In either case, strict positivity alone does not imply closeness to the new central path; that additionally requires small declared feasibility, stationarity, and centered-complementarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive reused slacks and multipliers establish strict-domain admissibility, not centrality. Feasible-start methods additionally require the new constraint equations, while infeasible-start methods may begin with residuals.
assumptions_latex: the selected primal-dual formulation requires positive slacks and multipliers
feasible-start and infeasible-start conventions are distinguished
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict positivity certifies domain membership but does not certify feasibility or proximity to the new central path.
review_flags: the precise residual equations and sign convention depend on the selected formulation
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Interior Reuse and Centrality Are Distinct Tests

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interiorization–Complementarity Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative complementarity loss when a boundary solution is shifted into a strict interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a reused complementary pair \((s_i,z_i)=(0,z_i^*)\) with \(z_i^*>0\). Any interiorization imposing \(\widehat s_i\geq\delta_s>0\) and \(\widehat z_i\geq\delta_z>0\) satisfies \[\widehat s_i\widehat z_i\geq\delta_s\delta_z.\] If the positive multiplier is retained with \(\widehat z_i\geq z_i^*/2\), then \(\widehat s_i\widehat z_i\geq\delta_s z_i^*/2\). A fixed positive interior margin therefore cannot preserve arbitrarily small complementarity residual on that active constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moving an active warm start a fixed distance into the strict interior necessarily introduces a positive complementarity residual.
assumptions_latex: the interiorized pair has positive lower margins
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat s_i\widehat z_i\geq\delta_s\delta_z\), and it is at least \(\delta_s z_i^*/2\) when the multiplier is approximately retained.
knowledge_statements.title: Interiorization–Complementarity Tradeoff
Warm-Start Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A reused solution lies on the barrier-domain boundary and therefore cannot directly initialize a strict-interior iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For inequalities \(g_i(x)\geq0\), a logarithmic-barrier method requires \(g_i(x)>0\) for every \(i\). Let \(x^{\mathrm{old}}\) solve a preceding problem in a sequence. Direct warm starting is inadmissible for the new problem whenever
\[
\min_i g_i^{\mathrm{new}}(x^{\mathrm{old}})\leq0.
\]
In a primal-dual formulation, the analogous boundary is reached if any reused slack or multiplier is nonpositive. Such a point cannot be substituted directly into logarithms or reciprocal complementarity expressions; an interiorization procedure must perturb or replace it, potentially discarding the closeness that made the warm start useful.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct warm starting fails when the reused solution has a nonpositive new slack or multiplier, placing it outside the strict barrier domain and requiring interiorization.
assumptions_latex: \(x^{\mathrm{old}}\) is reused for a modified inequality-constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\min_i g_i^{\mathrm{new}}(x^{\mathrm{old}})\leq0\), the reused point is not a valid strict-interior initialization.

notation.meaning: i-th inequality function of the new problem
solution or iterate reused from the preceding problem

review_flags: no supplied locator specifically addresses warm starts for barrier methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Strict positivity is standard for logarithmic-barrier variables, but the record has no source for the claimed warm-start applicability boundary or for the extension from primal slacks to reused primal-dual multipliers. Those details depend on the particular interior-point formulation and interiorization procedure.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Warm-Start Benefit Boundary for Sequential Instances
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(I_j\) be a sequence of related optimization instances. Let \(w_{j-1}^*\) be the computed primal-dual solution of \(I_{j-1}\), \(C_j^{\mathrm{cold}}\) the work from a standard cold initialization, and \(C_j^{\mathrm{warm}}\) the work after mapping \(w_{j-1}^*\) into a strictly interior, admissible initialization for \(I_j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition for sequential optimization. It depends on the initialization map, neighborhood requirements, work metric, and problem perturbation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a required gain \(g_0>1\), define the warm-start gain \[G_j:=\frac{C_j^{\mathrm{cold}}}{C_j^{\mathrm{warm}}}.\] The sequence lies beyond the warm-start applicability boundary when \[\limsup_{j\to\infty}G_j<g_0.\] It lies on the boundary when \(\limsup_jG_j=g_0\). The warm cost includes restoration of strict positivity and any centering or regularization needed before the inherited point is accepted as an interior-point initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The warm-start boundary is reached when reusing the previous solution no longer supplies the prescribed work reduction over a cold start, after accounting for the cost of restoring strict interiority, centrality, and admissibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}C_j^{\mathrm{cold}}/C_j^{\mathrm{warm}}\le g_0\) at or beyond the selected boundary.
special_cases_latex: If the previous solution lies on an active boundary, it cannot be used unchanged as a strictly positive slack-multiplier state.
An active-set method can have a larger warm-start gain when the previous active set remains predictive.
immediate_consequences_latex: Warm-start applicability cannot be inferred from closeness of primal solutions alone; dual and complementarity neighborhoods also matter.
boundary_notes: No inspected source gives this gain-threshold definition.
The threshold \(g_0\) is application-dependent, so the boundary is not intrinsic.

notation.meaning: Cold-start work divided by warm-start work on sequential instance j.

review_flags: The available source states that interior-point methods are less able to exploit warm starts but does not support this exact quantitative definition.
Needs a dedicated warm-start source with a formal neighborhood and complexity model.
knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Benefit Boundary for Sequential Instances

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reusable Strict-Interior Warm Start
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient admissibility condition for directly reusing primal-dual variables in a logarithmic-barrier formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a new slack-form problem, a reused primal-dual pair \((x^{\mathrm{old}},s^{\mathrm{old}},z^{\mathrm{old}})\) is directly admissible for logarithmic and reciprocal complementarity expressions when \[c^{\mathrm{new}}(x^{\mathrm{old}})+s^{\mathrm{old}}=0,\qquad s^{\mathrm{old}}>0,\qquad z^{\mathrm{old}}>0,\] with any unchanged equality-domain requirements also satisfied. This is an admissibility test only; closeness to the new central path additionally requires small new stationarity, feasibility, and centered-complementarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-dual warm start can be inserted directly only if it satisfies the new slack equations and retains strictly positive slacks and multipliers. Positivity alone does not make it a good central-path start.
assumptions_latex: the new formulation uses positive slacks and multipliers
the stated sign convention is used for the slack equation
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict positivity plus the new slack equation gives domain admissibility, but not centrality.
review_flags: the exact slack-equation sign must match the selected formulation
knowledge_statements.title: Reusable Strict-Interior Warm Start

children.title: Low-Accuracy Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where cheaper low-accuracy methods are more appropriate.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Accuracy Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The requested tolerance is too loose for an interior-point method's setup and linear-solve costs to be competitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a termination residual \(R\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and computational environment. Let \(W_{\mathrm{IP}}(\varepsilon)\) and \(W_{\mathrm{alt}}(\varepsilon)\) be the expected work required by an interior-point method and an admissible alternative to return \(z\) with \(R(z)\leq\varepsilon\). The low-accuracy boundary is the regime in which
\[
W_{\mathrm{alt}}(\varepsilon)<W_{\mathrm{IP}}(\varepsilon),
\]
with both methods satisfying the same residual convention. Here the interior-point method's barrier updates, factorizations, or accurate Newton solves cost more than the accuracy request justifies; the boundary is therefore relative to a specified problem family, work metric, and alternative algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The low-accuracy boundary is the tolerance regime where another admissible method reaches the same residual target with less expected work than the interior-point method.
assumptions_latex: Both methods use the same termination residual \(R(z)\leq\varepsilon\).
Expected work is measured in one fixed computational environment and cost metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(W_{\mathrm{alt}}(\varepsilon)<W_{\mathrm{IP}}(\varepsilon)\), the interior-point method is outside its low-accuracy competitiveness region.

notation.meaning: expected interior-point work to tolerance epsilon
expected work of the comparison method

review_flags: no supplied locator establishes a method-comparison low-accuracy boundary
work metric and comparison method must be fixed by application context

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison inequality is internally consistent and correctly makes the boundary relative to a problem family, cost metric, and alternative method. Nevertheless, it is essentially a stipulated competitiveness criterion, and no evidence supports the substantive claim that low requested accuracy creates such a boundary for interior-point methods.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparative Low-Accuracy Applicability Boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(I\) be an optimization instance, \(R(I,x)\ge0\) a solution-quality residual, and \(C_{\mathrm{IP}}(I,\varepsilon)\) the least measured work used by a specified interior-point implementation to return \(x\) with \(R(I,x)\le\varepsilon\). Let \(C_{\mathcal B}(I,\varepsilon)\) be the corresponding work for an alternative method family \(\mathcal B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparative and implementation-dependent. “Low accuracy” is defined by a target residual, not by iteration count or barrier parameter alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a required comparative advantage factor \(q_0\ge1\), the low-accuracy boundary between the interior-point method and \(\mathcal B\) is the set of tolerances satisfying \[C_{\mathrm{IP}}(I,\varepsilon)=q_0C_{\mathcal B}(I,\varepsilon).\] The low-accuracy regime favoring \(\mathcal B\) is \[\{\varepsilon>0:C_{\mathrm{IP}}(I,\varepsilon)>q_0C_{\mathcal B}(I,\varepsilon)\}.\] Both costs are defined as \(+\infty\) when the method fails to reach the requested residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The low-accuracy boundary is the target tolerance at which the measured cost of an interior-point solver equals a prescribed multiple of the cost of an alternative method. Looser tolerances belong to the alternative-favored regime only when the stated cost inequality actually holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{IP}}(I,\varepsilon)=q_0C_{\mathcal B}(I,\varepsilon)\) on the selected comparative boundary.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(q_0=1\), the boundary is the cost-crossover set between the two specified methods.
special_cases_latex: Work may be wall time, energy, matrix-vector products, factorizations, or another fixed metric, but the same metric must be used for both methods.
immediate_consequences_latex: There is no method-independent numerical value of “low accuracy.”
A change in residual normalization or stopping rule can move the crossover.
boundary_notes: No inspected source supplies this exact cost-crossover definition.
The claim that another family is cheaper at low accuracy is empirical unless supported by a complexity theorem or benchmark model for the specified families.

notation.meaning: Measured work required by the specified interior-point implementation to achieve tolerance epsilon.

review_flags: Needs a source that formalizes or quantitatively establishes a low-accuracy crossover between interior-point and alternative solver families.
